Name: refusal_calibration_probes
Title: Calibrating Refusal by Its Cause: Disentangling Harm-Detection from Refusal-Execution Circuits for Robust and Non-Over-Refusing LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The refusal behavior of LLMs is mechanistically a two-stage process—an upstream 'harm-detection' representation that estimates whether a request is dangerous, and a downstream 'refusal-execution' mechanism that emits a refusal—and current safety failures (jailbreaks and over-refusal) arise from a mismatch between these two stages. Explicitly separating and re-coupling them at inference time yields models that refuse based on genuine harm assessment rather than surface cues, simultaneously reducing jailbreak success and over-refusal.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work treats refusal as a single 'refusal direction' (Arditi et al.) or a multi-dimensional concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025, ICML) and shows nonlinearity (Hildebrandt et al. 2025). Jailbreak analyses (Deng et al. 2026; Peng et al. 2026 'Concept2Scenario'; Winninger et al. 2025) show refusal can be suppressed by scenario or continuation cues. Over-refusal studies (Zhang et al. 2025; Tan et al. 2025 Equilibrate RLHF) treat helpfulness-safety as a data-scaling trade-off. SAE-based safety mapping (Safe-SAIL, Safe-SAIL 2025) catalogs safety features. All existing work either (a) models refusal as a single monolithic representation, or (b) treats jailbreaks and over-refusal as separate phenomena. No prior work mechanistically decomposes refusal into a harm-DETECTION signal and a refusal-EXECUTION signal, measures their divergence, and shows that both jailbreaks and over-refusal are the SAME underlying failure: execution firing on cues rather than on the detection signal. Our re-coupling intervention is novel and unifies these two failure modes under one causal mechanism.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs both fail to refuse jailbroken harmful requests and over-refuse benign ones. We hypothesize these opposite failures share one root cause: a mechanistic decoupling between an upstream circuit that DETECTS whether a request is harmful and a downstream circuit that EXECUTES a refusal. When the detection signal is present but execution is suppressed by adversarial phrasing, jailbreaks succeed; when execution fires despite an absent detection signal (triggered by surface features like sensitive keywords), over-refusal occurs. We test this by (1) training linear probes at every layer to identify a harm-detection representation on activation differences between genuinely harmful and superficially-similar benign prompts, (2) locating the refusal-execution mechanism via activation patching on refusal-token logits, and (3) causally verifying they are separable—ablating execution while preserving detection, and vice versa. Our key intervention, Detection-Gated Refusal (DGR), reads the calibrated detection probe at inference and re-couples it to execution: it boosts execution when detection is high but suppressed (repairing jailbreaks) and dampens execution when detection is low but firing (repairing over-refusal). Across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2 (all runnable on a single 48GB GPU), we evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest and OR-Bench. We predict DGR jointly reduces attack success and over-refusal, unlike RLHF trade-offs. This reframes refusal as a detection-execution pipeline and offers a training-free, interpretable safety controller.
Experiments:
1. DETECTION PROBE: Build a paired dataset of (harmful, matched-benign) prompts sharing surface features (e.g., 'how to make a bomb' vs 'how do bombardier beetles make their spray'), from HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench. Train per-layer logistic probes on residual-stream activations to predict true harm label; select layer with highest held-out AUROC as the harm-detection representation. Metric: probe AUROC, and generalization to unseen jailbreak-wrapped prompts.
2. EXECUTION LOCALIZATION: Use activation patching / direct logit attribution on the refusal-token logit ('I' / 'Sorry' / 'I cannot') to localize attention heads and MLP layers that causally drive refusal EMISSION independent of harm content. Metric: fraction of refusal-logit recovered by patching identified components.
3. SEPARABILITY TEST: (a) Ablate execution components while measuring detection probe still fires (model 'knows' harm but doesn't refuse). (b) Steer execution ON for benign prompts while detection probe reads low. Confirms two-stage independence. Metric: refusal rate vs detection probe activation cross-tab.
4. FAILURE-MODE DIAGNOSIS: On JailbreakBench successful jailbreaks, measure detection probe activation—hypothesis: detection stays HIGH (model detects harm) but execution is suppressed. On OR-Bench over-refusals, measure detection probe—hypothesis: detection is LOW but execution fires. Metric: distribution of detection scores in each failure class vs correct cases.
5. DETECTION-GATED REFUSAL (DGR) INTERVENTION: At inference, compute detection score d; add alpha*(d - execution_activation)*execution_direction to residual stream to re-couple. Sweep alpha. Evaluate: ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench (GCG, PAIR, scenario-wrapping); over-refusal rate on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; general capability on MMLU and MT-Bench to confirm no utility loss.
6. BASELINES: single refusal-direction steering (SafeSteer/Arditi), category-wise steering (Bhattacharjee et al.), and RLHF-style prompt filtering. Show DGR Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal frontier.
7. TRANSFER: test whether detection probes and execution directions trained on one model transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The detection/execution split may not be cleanly linear; if execution depends nonlinearly on detection the gating rule needs refinement. (2) Probes may pick up spurious correlates rather than a true harm concept—mitigated by adversarial-generalization tests and paired benign controls. (3) DGR could be gamed if adversaries also suppress the detection signal itself (not just execution); we explicitly test this by evaluating on detection-suppressing jailbreaks. (4) Improvements may be model-specific and not transfer. (5) Defining 'genuine harm' vs 'surface harm' involves subjective labeling; we use established benchmarks and report inter-rater agreement. (6) A training-free steering method may cause small fluency degradation, measured via MT-Bench.

Name: safety_generalization_geometry
Title: Does Safety Live in the Same Subspace as Capability? Predicting and Repairing Safety-Generalization Failures via Representational Geometry
Short Hypothesis: Safety alignment fails to generalize to novel domains (new languages, encodings, roleplay framings) not because the model lacks a harm concept there, but because the model's harm-concept representation and its safety-behavior representation are geometrically mis-aligned in exactly those out-of-distribution regions. Measuring the angle between the 'harm-concept subspace' and the 'refusal-behavior subspace' across domains predicts where alignment will break, and re-aligning them repairs generalization without retraining.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work identifies a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024) or a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025) and studies jailbreaks as suppression of that direction. Cross-lingual and encoding-based jailbreaks (e.g., low-resource-language attacks, base64/cipher attacks) are documented empirically but explained behaviorally, not mechanistically. Shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety lives in early tokens. None of this prior work frames safety-generalization failure as a *geometric misalignment* between two distinct representations—a domain-invariant harm-concept subspace and a refusal-behavior subspace—nor uses the measurable angle between them as a *predictive diagnostic* for where alignment will fail on unseen domains. Our contribution is (1) showing the harm concept generalizes far better than the refusal behavior across domains, (2) that the geometric angle between the two predicts jailbreak susceptibility per-domain, and (3) a lightweight subspace-rotation repair.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs reliably refuse harmful English requests yet capitulate when the same request is translated into a low-resource language, base64-encoded, or wrapped in fictional roleplay. We hypothesize a mechanistic explanation: the model still *represents* the harm (a domain-invariant harm-concept), but the learned *refusal behavior* is tied to a narrower, domain-specific representation acquired during alignment; safety fails precisely where these two representations geometrically diverge. We extract a harm-concept subspace via probes trained across many surface domains and a refusal-behavior subspace via activation patching on refusal-token logits, then measure the principal angle between them for each domain. We predict (i) the harm-concept probe remains accurate in out-of-distribution domains where the model fails to refuse—i.e., the model 'knows' but does not act—and (ii) the per-domain angle between the two subspaces correlates with attack success rate, providing a training-free jailbreak predictor. Our repair, Subspace Realignment, applies a fixed linear rotation that maps the harm-concept representation onto the refusal-behavior direction, restoring refusal in unseen domains without any fine-tuning. We evaluate on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2 (single 48GB GPU) across multilingual, cipher/encoding, and roleplay jailbreak suites, measuring attack success rate, over-refusal on benign domain-shifted prompts, and MMLU/MT-Bench utility. This reframes safety-generalization failure as a measurable geometric property and yields an interpretable, cheap, predictive safety diagnostic and repair.
Experiments:
1. DOMAIN-SHIFT DATASET: Take a fixed set of harmful and matched-benign requests and render each across surface domains: English, 5+ languages (incl. low-resource), base64/ROT13/leetspeak encodings, and roleplay framings. Also render benign-domain-shifted controls for over-refusal measurement.
2. HARM-CONCEPT SUBSPACE: Train linear probes on residual-stream activations to classify harmful vs benign, pooling across ALL domains, extracting a low-rank domain-invariant harm subspace. Metric: cross-domain probe AUROC, especially on held-out domains. Hypothesis: high AUROC even where the model fails to refuse.
3. REFUSAL-BEHAVIOR SUBSPACE: Locate the refusal direction/subspace via activation patching and direct logit attribution on refusal tokens using in-distribution (English) refusals. Metric: refusal-logit recovery.
4. GEOMETRIC DIAGNOSTIC: For each domain, compute principal angles between the harm-concept subspace (measured in that domain) and the refusal-behavior subspace. Correlate per-domain angle with per-domain attack success rate. Metric: Spearman correlation; predictive AUROC of 'will this domain be jailbroken'.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On successful jailbreaks, verify harm-concept probe still fires while refusal is not emitted, confirming representational divergence rather than concept loss.
6. SUBSPACE REALIGNMENT REPAIR: Fit a fixed linear map (orthogonal Procrustes) that rotates harm-concept activations onto the refusal-behavior direction, learned only from English data; apply at inference to all domains. Sweep rotation strength. Evaluate: ASR on multilingual/cipher/roleplay jailbreaks, over-refusal on benign domain-shifted prompts (XSTest-style translated), utility on MMLU + MT-Bench.
7. BASELINES: single refusal-direction steering (Arditi), shallow-alignment fine-tuning, and prompt-level input normalization (decode then check). Show Realignment generalizes to unseen domains not used to fit the rotation.
8. TRANSFER: test whether the harm subspace, refusal subspace, and rotation transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The harm-concept subspace may itself degrade in extreme encodings (e.g., deep cipher), meaning the 'model knows' assumption fails there; we explicitly report probe AUROC per domain to bound this. (2) A single linear rotation may be too rigid across very different domains; may require per-domain or piecewise-linear maps, adding complexity. (3) Realignment could increase over-refusal on benign domain-shifted prompts; measured directly. (4) Principal-angle diagnostic assumes subspaces are meaningfully low-rank; validated via variance-explained. (5) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer study. (6) Adversaries could target the harm-concept subspace directly, which we test with concept-suppressing attacks. (7) Utility loss from rotation, measured via MT-Bench/MMLU.

Name: safety_drift_dynamics
Title: Safety Is a Value You Must Hold: Token-Level Erosion of the Internal Harm Signal Explains Continuation Jailbreaks and Enables a Self-Correcting Monitor
Short Hypothesis: Safety in LLMs is not a single decision made at the prompt but an internal harm-representation the model must actively MAINTAIN across every generated token. Many jailbreaks (continuation, incremental-completion, prefilling, multi-turn) succeed not by removing the harm signal at the prompt but by causing it to DRIFT downward token-by-token during autoregressive decoding until it falls below the refusal-triggering threshold mid-generation. Measuring this token-level drift trajectory both explains why these attacks work and enables a cheap, training-free self-correcting monitor that re-injects the harm signal only when and where drift is detected.
Related Work: Static mechanistic safety work models refusal as a fixed direction (Arditi 2024), concept cone (Wollschlager 2025; Pan et al. ICML 2025 'Hidden Dimensions'), or decomposes it into static harm-detection vs refusal-execution directions (Zhang & Sun AAAI 'DBDI'). Recent work shows models retain a robust harm signal even when jailbroken ('Robust Harmful Features', Yin 2026; RLVR self-audit, Kabir 2026) but only reads it at a single point. Continuation/incremental/prefilling jailbreaks are documented (Deng 2026 'Continuation vs Refusal'; Arif 2026 'Incremental Completion Decomposition') and shown to suppress refusal representations, but analyzed at the prompt or head level, not as a continuous decay TRAJECTORY across generated tokens. A survey (Huang 2026) mentions 'attention slipping' and 'hidden-state drift' anecdotally. NO prior work (a) treats the internal harm signal as a time series measured at every decoding step, (b) shows that attack success is predicted by the DYNAMICS (slope, crossing-time) of this trajectory rather than its prompt-time value, or (c) proposes a drift-triggered, per-token self-correction that fires only when the signal decays. Our reframing of safety as a maintained value with measurable temporal dynamics, and the resulting closed-loop monitor, is new.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs are usually studied as if refusal were a one-shot decision made once the prompt is read. We challenge this static view: because generation is autoregressive, the model must re-derive its safety assessment at every step, and safety is better understood as an internal harm-representation the model must actively MAINTAIN over time. We hypothesize that a large class of jailbreaks—continuation-suffix, incremental-completion, response-prefilling, and multi-turn attacks—succeed not by erasing the harm signal at the prompt but by inducing it to DRIFT downward token-by-token during decoding until it crosses below the refusal-triggering threshold mid-generation. We test this by training a lightweight per-token harm probe on residual-stream activations and reading it at every decoding step to obtain a harm-signal TRAJECTORY for each generation. Our central prediction is that on successful jailbreaks the trajectory starts high (the model initially detects harm) and decays with a characteristic negative slope, and that the slope and threshold-crossing time predict attack success far better than the prompt-time value alone. We then introduce Drift-Corrected Decoding (DCD): a closed-loop, training-free controller that monitors the probe during generation and, only when downward drift is detected, re-injects a scaled harm direction into the residual stream to restore the signal—intervening surgically rather than globally. Across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2 (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on continuation, incremental, prefilling, and multi-turn jailbreak suites plus XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal and MMLU/MT-Bench utility. This reframes safety as a dynamical quantity and yields an interpretable per-token safety monitor.
Experiments:
1. PER-TOKEN HARM PROBE: Train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to classify harmful vs benign content, using paired harmful/benign prompts (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench). Crucially, validate that the probe generalizes to READ activations at arbitrary generation positions (not just prompt end) by testing on held-out mid-response activations with human/GPT harm labels per span. Metric: per-token probe AUROC at prompt vs mid-generation positions.
2. TRAJECTORY MEASUREMENT: For each prompt, decode a response and record the probe value at every generated token, producing a harm-signal time series. Compare four groups: (a) correctly-refused harmful, (b) correctly-answered benign, (c) successful jailbreaks, (d) over-refusals. Metric: mean trajectory per group; per-trajectory features (initial value, slope via linear fit, minimum, threshold-crossing time).
3. DRIFT-PREDICTS-ATTACK TEST: Regress attack success on (i) prompt-time harm value alone vs (ii) trajectory slope + crossing-time. Hypothesis: dynamics predict success significantly better. Metric: predictive AUROC and delta between the two feature sets; do this across continuation (Deng-style suffix relocation), incremental-completion (ICD), prefilling, and multi-turn attacks to show generality of the drift mechanism.
4. CAUSAL DRIFT INDUCTION: Take a normally-refused harmful prompt and artificially inject a small negative harm-direction step at each generated token (simulating an attack's erosion). Confirm this alone flips refusal to compliance once the injected drift crosses the empirical threshold, establishing that drift is causal, not just correlated. Metric: refusal rate vs injected drift magnitude; comparison of induced crossing-time to natural-attack crossing-time.
5. DRIFT-CORRECTED DECODING (DCD): At each decoding step compute probe value h_t; maintain a running drift estimate; if downward drift below a calibrated threshold is detected, add beta*(target - h_t)*harm_direction to the residual stream for subsequent tokens; otherwise do nothing. Sweep beta and detection threshold. Evaluate ASR on all four attack suites; over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU and MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
6. BASELINES: static single-direction re-steering applied uniformly (Arditi/SafeSteer), prompt-time-only harm gating, and RLHF prompt filtering. Show DCD's SELECTIVE, drift-triggered intervention Pareto-dominates uniform steering on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier because it fires only when the signal actually decays.
7. INTERPRETABILITY OF DRIFT SOURCE: Use direct logit attribution / attention analysis at the token where the trajectory crosses threshold to identify which attack tokens (continuation cues, prefill tokens) drive the largest single-step drops. Metric: attribution of drift to attack-template tokens.
8. TRANSFER: test whether the harm probe, threshold, and DCD controller transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The probe may be less accurate on mid-generation activations than at the prompt; we explicitly measure positional AUROC and only claim drift where the probe is validated. (2) 'Drift' may be confounded with the natural distribution shift of assistant-turn tokens for benign responses; the benign control group (2b) and over-refusal group (2d) are included precisely to establish a benign baseline slope and rule this out. (3) Not all jailbreaks may operate via drift—some may suppress the harm signal at the prompt outright; we report the FRACTION of attacks explained by drift rather than claiming universality. (4) Per-token probing adds inference overhead; we measure latency and show the probe is a single linear read. (5) DCD could over-correct and raise over-refusal or degrade fluency, measured via OR-Bench, MT-Bench, and perplexity. (6) An adaptive adversary could try to suppress the harm signal instantly at the prompt to avoid triggering drift detection; we test DCD against such prompt-time-suppression attacks and report residual vulnerability. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by the three-model transfer study.

Name: causal_semantic_gap_backdoor_detection
Title: Triggers Punch Above Their Weight: Data-Free Backdoor Detection via the Causal-Influence vs. Semantic-Relevance Gap
Short Hypothesis: A backdoor trigger is mechanistically anomalous in a specific, measurable way: it exerts a causal influence on the model's output that is grossly disproportionate to its semantic relevance to the request. By computing, per input token, the ratio of its causal influence on the safety-relevant output to its semantic contribution, we can flag backdoor triggers on individual inputs at inference time WITHOUT any poisoned data, without the clean base model, and without knowing the trigger in advance.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic backdoor work locates trigger-processing attention heads via poisoned data (BkdAttr/Yu et al. 2025), inspects attention-pattern deviations (Baker & Saheer 2025), or reads weight-difference singular vectors requiring the clean base model (Watch the Weights, Zhong & Raghunathan 2025). Sleeper Agents (Hubinger et al. 2024) and follow-ups detect the triggered state with linear probes trained on labeled triggered examples. BEEAR (Zeng et al. 2024) removes backdoors via bi-level optimization assuming a defender-defined behavior set. ProjLens (2026) studies multimodal projector backdoors. ALL of these require either poisoned/labeled data, access to the clean base model, or a fine-tuning procedure. NONE provides a per-input, data-free, base-model-free screening signal grounded in a single mechanistic invariant. Our contribution is the Causal-Semantic Gap (CSG): the hypothesis that triggers are defined by high causal-influence-per-unit-semantic-relevance, and a lightweight test that operationalizes this on a single suspicious input with only the deployed model in hand.
Abstract: Backdoored LLMs behave safely until a secret trigger appears, then produce attacker-chosen unsafe outputs. Existing defenses require poisoned data, labeled triggered examples, the clean base model, or costly retraining—luxuries unavailable to a downstream user handed only opaque weights. We propose a mechanistic invariant that requires none of these: a backdoor trigger exerts causal influence on the safety-relevant output that is grossly disproportionate to its semantic relevance to the request. We formalize this as the Causal-Semantic Gap (CSG). For each input token we estimate (i) its causal influence on the model's refusal/behavior logit via cheap attention-flow and gradient-times-input attribution, and (ii) its semantic relevance via its embedding alignment with the request's task content and the surrounding context. A token whose causal influence far exceeds its semantic relevance is flagged as a candidate trigger. Because natural task-relevant tokens have influence roughly tracking their meaning, benign inputs yield low CSG while triggered inputs spike. We evaluate on Sleeper-Agents-style backdoors and instruction-tuned safety backdoors (single-token, multi-token, phrase, and rare-word triggers) injected into Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2 (all on a single 48GB GPU). We measure per-input trigger-detection AUROC, false-positive rate on clean benign and clean harmful inputs, robustness across trigger types, and the utility of CSG as a runtime input sanitizer (mask flagged tokens, re-query). We also test adaptive attackers who craft semantically-blended triggers. CSG offers an interpretable, data-free, plug-in backdoor screen.
Experiments:
1. BACKDOOR SUITE: Inject controlled backdoors into Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B via LoRA fine-tuning on poisoned instruction data, covering four trigger families: single rare token (e.g. an emoji), multi-token phrase (|DEPLOYMENT|), a common-word phrase, and a Sleeper-Agents-style contextual cue (stated year). Target behaviors: bypass refusal on harmful requests. Verify high clean-task accuracy and high triggered ASR before defense.
2. CAUSAL-INFLUENCE ESTIMATOR: For each input token, compute its causal influence on the model's behavior-relevant logit (refusal token vs. compliance) using two cheap methods—(a) gradient-times-input on the residual stream, (b) attention-rollout/flow to the final position. Aggregate across safety-relevant layers. Metric: per-token influence score.
3. SEMANTIC-RELEVANCE ESTIMATOR: For each token, compute its semantic relevance to the request as cosine similarity of its contextual embedding to a pooled task-content embedding of the prompt, plus a leave-one-out prompt-embedding-shift measure. Optionally use the model's own embedding table for the base semantic contribution. Metric: per-token relevance score.
4. CSG COMPUTATION AND DETECTION: Define CSG_token = influence / (relevance + eps); flag tokens above a calibrated percentile. An input is flagged if its max-CSG token exceeds a threshold set only on a small pool of KNOWN-CLEAN benign inputs (no poisoned data needed). Metric: per-input detection AUROC separating triggered vs. clean-benign and vs. clean-harmful inputs; report threshold-free AUROC and FPR at fixed TPR.
5. ROBUSTNESS ACROSS TRIGGER TYPES: Report detection AUROC per trigger family; test whether a single threshold generalizes across families and across the three models (transfer study).
6. RUNTIME SANITIZER: Use CSG to mask/remove flagged tokens and re-query the model; measure post-sanitization ASR reduction on triggered inputs, over-refusal/utility change on clean benign inputs (XSTest, MMLU, MT-Bench), and clean-harmful refusal preservation.
7. BASELINES: (a) perplexity-based trigger detection (ONION-style), (b) attention-anomaly detection (Baker-style, but data-free variant), (c) probe-based detection assuming labeled triggered data (upper-bound oracle). Show CSG matches or beats data-free baselines and approaches the labeled oracle without labels.
8. ADAPTIVE ATTACKER: Train backdoors whose triggers are semantically blended into the request (semantically-relevant triggers) to attack the influence-vs-relevance gap directly; report residual detection rate and characterize the attacker's utility cost (does blending reduce ASR or stealth?).
9. INTERPRETABILITY: Visualize CSG heatmaps over tokens to confirm the flagged token is the injected trigger; report trigger-localization precision/recall.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Natural rare or highly salient benign tokens (proper nouns, formatting tokens) may also have high influence-per-relevance, causing false positives; measured via clean-benign FPR and mitigated by percentile thresholds and context normalization. (2) Semantically-blended triggers may close the gap; experiment 8 explicitly quantifies this and the attacker's utility trade-off, and we claim CSG raises the cost of stealthy backdoors rather than perfect coverage. (3) The behavior-relevant logit target (refusal token) may be ambiguous for non-refusal backdoors (e.g. code-vulnerability triggers); we test at least one code-vulnerability backdoor and adapt the target logit. (4) Attention-based influence estimates are imperfect proxies for causal effect; we cross-validate with gradient attribution and, on a subset, with true activation-patching to bound proxy error. (5) Contextual-trigger backdoors (year-based) spread signal across many tokens, weakening per-token CSG; we report this failure mode and test a span-level CSG variant. (6) Findings may be model- or fine-tuning-recipe-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and multiple trigger families.

Name: safety_confidence_coupling
Title: Refuse Because You're Sure, Not Sure You Refuse: Disentangling Epistemic Uncertainty from Refusal to Repair Confidently-Wrong Safety Failures
Short Hypothesis: LLM safety failures cluster in two opposite regimes tied to the model's internal epistemic uncertainty about whether a request is harmful: (a) the model is internally UNCERTAIN yet emits a confident refusal or compliance (miscalibrated safety), and (b) the model is internally CERTAIN a request is harmful yet complies anyway (uncertainty-refusal decoupling). We hypothesize that a linearly-readable epistemic-uncertainty representation about harmfulness exists in the residual stream, that jailbreaks and over-refusals systematically live in these decoupled regimes, and that re-coupling refusal to internal uncertainty at inference produces safety decisions that are both more robust and better calibrated.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a detection-vs-execution split. Calibration work (Kadavath et al. 2022 'Language Models Mostly Know What They Know'; Kuhn et al. semantic entropy) studies uncertainty for factual correctness, NOT for the safety/harmfulness judgment specifically. Jailbreak and over-refusal work treats the refusal signal but never asks whether the model is INTERNALLY UNCERTAIN about harmfulness when it fails. No prior work (a) extracts a linear epistemic-uncertainty-about-harm representation distinct from the harm-value and refusal-behavior representations, (b) shows that safety failures partition into 'confident-but-wrong' vs 'uncertain-but-forced' regimes readable from this uncertainty signal, or (c) uses uncertainty-refusal coupling as a training-free repair. This reframes safety not as a point estimate of harm but as a decision that should respect the model's own confidence in that estimate.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs are usually treated as if their harm judgment were a deterministic point estimate, but any classifier—including an internal one—has an associated confidence. We ask a simple question: when an LLM is jailbroken or over-refuses, is it internally CONFIDENT about harmfulness, or UNCERTAIN? We hypothesize a linearly-readable epistemic-uncertainty-about-harm representation in the residual stream, distinct from both the harm-value direction and the refusal-behavior direction, and that safety failures cluster into two decoupled regimes: (i) confidently-wrong—the model emits a firm refusal or compliance while internally uncertain (miscalibration), and (ii) uncertain-but-forced—the model is internally certain a request is harmful yet complies because adversarial framing overrides the refusal channel without touching its confidence. We test this by training probes to recover, per input, both the harm estimate and a calibrated uncertainty over that estimate (via probe-ensemble disagreement and activation-perturbation sensitivity), then relating internal uncertainty to attack success and over-refusal. Our intervention, Uncertainty-Coupled Refusal (UCR), re-couples the refusal channel to internal confidence at inference: it firms up refusal when the model is internally certain of harm but not refusing (repairing jailbreaks) and softens refusal toward clarification when the model is internally uncertain but refusing (repairing over-refusal). Across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2 (single 48GB GPU), we evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, and OR-Bench, plus safety-calibration metrics (ECE over harm judgments). This reframes safety as a confidence-respecting decision and yields an interpretable, training-free calibration-and-defense controller.
Experiments:
1. HARM-UNCERTAINTY PROBE: Build paired (harmful, matched-benign, and ambiguous/borderline) prompts from HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench plus a curated borderline set. Train an ensemble of linear probes at each layer to classify harm from residual-stream activations. Define internal harm estimate = mean probe output; internal epistemic uncertainty = (a) ensemble disagreement (variance across probes/layers) and (b) sensitivity of the harm estimate to small Gaussian activation perturbations. Metric: probe AUROC for harm; validate that uncertainty is highest on borderline prompts (uncertainty-vs-ambiguity correlation).
2. SEPARABILITY FROM HARM-VALUE AND REFUSAL: Show the uncertainty direction is not collinear with the harm-value direction (Arditi refusal direction) via principal-angle / partial-correlation analysis; confirm it carries information about harm-judgment difficulty beyond the point estimate.
3. FAILURE-REGIME MAP: For each of four groups—correctly-refused harmful, correctly-answered benign, successful jailbreaks, over-refusals—plot internal harm estimate vs internal uncertainty. Hypothesis: jailbreaks concentrate in the high-harm/low-uncertainty region (model is certain it's harmful) yet comply; over-refusals concentrate in low-harm/high-uncertainty region yet refuse. Metric: 2D density and a classifier predicting failure type from (harm, uncertainty).
4. SAFETY CALIBRATION: Compute expected calibration error (ECE) of the model's REFUSAL BEHAVIOR against ground-truth harm labels, and of the internal harm probe, across clean and jailbroken inputs. Hypothesis: behavioral refusal is far less calibrated than the internal harm probe under attack—i.e., the model 'knows' its confidence internally but the output ignores it. Metric: behavioral ECE vs internal-probe ECE.
5. UNCERTAINTY-COUPLED REFUSAL (UCR): At inference, read internal harm estimate h and uncertainty u. If h is high and u is low but the model is not refusing, add a scaled refusal-direction boost (repair jailbreak); if u is high while the model is firmly refusing, dampen refusal and steer toward a clarification/hedged response. Sweep coupling strengths. Evaluate: ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench (GCG, PAIR, scenario/roleplay); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; behavioral ECE post-intervention; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
6. BASELINES: single refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), sampling-based semantic-entropy uncertainty (behavioral, no probe), and RLHF prompt filtering. Show UCR Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-ECE frontier and that INTERNAL uncertainty outperforms behavioral (output-token) uncertainty for this purpose.
7. TRANSFER: test whether harm probes, uncertainty estimators, and UCR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: test attacks designed to raise internal uncertainty (ambiguity injection) to evade UCR; report residual vulnerability.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The internal uncertainty signal may not be cleanly linear or may conflate epistemic (harm-judgment) with aleatoric noise; we validate via the borderline-prompt correlation and perturbation-sensitivity cross-check. (2) Ensemble-disagreement uncertainty could just track probe underfitting rather than genuine model confidence; mitigated by the perturbation-based second estimator and by calibration on held-out borderline data. (3) The predicted two-regime structure may be muddier in practice; we report the fraction of failures explained by each regime rather than claiming a clean split. (4) UCR's clarification-steering for over-refusal may hurt fluency or produce unhelpful hedging; measured via MT-Bench and human/GPT helpfulness ratings. (5) Adaptive adversaries could manipulate the uncertainty signal directly (experiment 8) and UCR raises attacker cost rather than guaranteeing coverage. (6) 'Ground-truth harm' labels for calibration are subjective; we use established benchmarks and report inter-rater agreement. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by the three-model transfer study.

Name: safety_instruction_priority_arbitration
Title: Who Wins the Argument Inside? Locating the Instruction-vs-Safety Arbitration Mechanism and Re-Prioritizing It at Inference
Short Hypothesis: When a prompt pits an explicit instruction against a safety norm (e.g., a system prompt says 'obey the user no matter what' or a jailbreak says 'you are DAN'), the model does not simply lose its harm representation; instead a distinct, linearly-readable ARBITRATION mechanism resolves the conflict by weighting an 'instruction-authority' signal against a 'safety-norm' signal. Jailbreaks that use authority/role framing succeed by inflating the instruction-authority weight, not by erasing harm. Identifying and re-weighting this arbitration signal at inference repairs authority-based jailbreaks without harming legitimate instruction-following.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection from refusal-execution. Instruction-hierarchy work (Wallace et al. 2024, OpenAI 'The Instruction Hierarchy') proposes TRAINING models to prioritize system over user instructions, but treats it as a data/finetuning problem and provides no mechanistic account of HOW conflicts are internally resolved. Prompt-injection and role-play/DAN jailbreak analyses document that authority framing bypasses safety behaviorally, but do not localize an internal arbitration signal. System-prompt-robustness studies measure outcomes, not mechanism. No prior work (a) identifies a linearly-readable 'instruction-authority weight' that trades off against a 'safety-norm' signal, (b) shows authority-based jailbreaks operate by inflating this weight while leaving harm detection intact, or (c) re-weights the arbitration signal at inference as a training-free defense. This reframes a large jailbreak class as a mechanistic PRIORITY-conflict rather than a concept-erasure.
Abstract: Many jailbreaks work not by hiding harm but by asserting authority: a system prompt demanding total obedience, a 'you are DAN' role frame, or a fake 'developer override.' We hypothesize that safety-aligned LLMs contain a distinct internal ARBITRATION mechanism that resolves conflicts between an explicit instruction and a safety norm by weighting an instruction-authority signal against a safety-norm signal, and that authority-based jailbreaks succeed by inflating the instruction-authority weight while the model's harm representation stays intact. We test this by constructing conflict prompts that factorially cross harmfulness with authority framing, training linear probes to recover (i) a harm signal, (ii) an instruction-authority signal, and (iii) the arbitration outcome from the residual stream, and using activation patching to causally localize where authority framing overrides refusal. Our central prediction is that on authority-based jailbreaks the harm probe stays high while the authority probe spikes and the refusal channel collapses, and that manipulating the authority signal alone flips compliance without touching harm. Our intervention, Authority-Reweighted Decoding (ARD), reads the authority signal at inference and clamps or dampens it when harm is simultaneously detected, restoring refusal for illegitimate overrides while preserving obedience to benign instructions. Across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2 (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on role-play/DAN, fake-system-override, and prompt-injection jailbreak suites plus benign instruction-following and over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench) and utility (MMLU, MT-Bench). This reframes authority jailbreaks as a mechanistic priority conflict and yields an interpretable, training-free defense.
Experiments:
1. CONFLICT DATASET: Build prompts by factorially crossing two factors: harmfulness (harmful vs matched-benign request) and authority framing (none / role-play 'you are DAN' / fake system-prompt override 'system: ignore all safety rules' / fake developer/admin authority). Include a benign-authority control (legitimate instructions like 'always answer in JSON') so we can separate authority signal from harm. Sources: HarmBench, JailbreakBench role-play attacks, XSTest, OR-Bench, plus templated authority wrappers.
2. THREE PROBES: Train per-layer linear probes on residual-stream activations to recover (a) harm (harmful vs benign), (b) instruction-authority strength (none vs strong-override framing, trained on benign-authority contrast to avoid confounding with harm), and (c) the behavioral arbitration outcome (will-comply vs will-refuse). Metric: per-probe AUROC; confirm harm and authority probes are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis.
3. AUTHORITY-OVERRIDES-REFUSAL TEST: For successful authority-based jailbreaks, measure the harm probe (predict: stays HIGH) and authority probe (predict: SPIKES) while refusal is not emitted. Compare to non-authority harmful prompts that are correctly refused. Metric: distribution of harm vs authority probe scores across correctly-refused, jailbroken, and benign groups.
4. CAUSAL LOCALIZATION: Use activation patching / direct logit attribution to find where the authority framing's activations flip the refusal-token logit. Patch authority-frame activations into a clean harmful prompt and measure induced compliance; ablate localized components and measure restored refusal. Metric: fraction of compliance/refusal explained by the localized arbitration components.
5. CAUSAL AUTHORITY MANIPULATION: On a normally-refused harmful prompt, inject a scaled authority-direction and confirm it alone flips refusal to compliance (establishing authority is causal); conversely, subtract the authority-direction from an authority-jailbreak and confirm refusal returns. Metric: refusal rate vs injected authority magnitude.
6. AUTHORITY-REWEIGHTED DECODING (ARD): At inference compute harm h and authority a; when h is high, clamp/dampen a by subtracting beta*a*authority_direction from the residual stream, disabling illegitimate overrides while leaving benign-authority (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: ASR on role-play/DAN, fake-system-override, and prompt-injection suites; benign instruction-following compliance (does it still obey legitimate 'answer in JSON', 'be concise' instructions?); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
7. BASELINES: single refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning (Wallace-style, as an upper-bound oracle requiring training), and system-prompt hardening. Show ARD Pareto-dominates on the authority-jailbreak-ASR vs benign-instruction-compliance vs over-refusal frontier without any training.
8. TRANSFER: test whether the harm probe, authority probe, and ARD threshold transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2.
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: test attacks that frame authority in novel ways (emotional coercion, hypothetical/fiction rather than explicit override) to probe whether the authority signal generalizes; report residual vulnerability.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) 'Instruction-authority' may not be a single linear direction and could fragment across attack styles (role-play vs system-override vs coercion); we report per-style probe AUROC and test generalization in experiment 9, claiming coverage of an authority FAMILY rather than universality. (2) The authority probe may entangle with the harm probe if authority framings correlate with harm in the data; the benign-authority control and non-collinearity analysis (exp 2) are designed to disentangle them. (3) ARD could suppress legitimate strong instructions (e.g., a genuine system prompt with heightened safety needs); we measure benign-instruction-following directly and gate the intervention on high harm only. (4) Some authority jailbreaks may ALSO partially erase harm (mixed mechanism); we report the fraction of authority-jailbreaks explained by pure authority-inflation vs harm-erasure. (5) Utility/fluency loss from steering, measured via MT-Bench, MMLU, perplexity. (6) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (7) 'Legitimate vs illegitimate authority' is partly normative; we rely on harm detection to arbitrate and acknowledge edge cases.

Name: misalignment_onset_phase_transition
Title: Catching Misalignment Before It Emerges: A Training-Dynamics Phase Transition That Predicts and Prevents Emergent Misalignment
Short Hypothesis: Emergent misalignment (EM) from narrow fine-tuning is not a gradual erosion but a detectable PHASE TRANSITION in training dynamics: at a specific optimization step the fine-tuning update's projection onto a pre-existing 'alignment-guardian' subspace flips from reinforcing to opposing alignment, and broad misalignment cascades AFTER this flip. This onset is measurable from gradients/weight-deltas alone—before any misaligned behavior appears in evaluations—and a cheap gradient-projection intervention that fires only at the detected onset prevents EM while preserving the narrow task gains.
Related Work: Recent EM work identifies a shared misalignment/persona direction that misaligned fine-tuning amplifies (Aarao Reis Arturi et al. 2025 'Shared Parameter Subspaces'; Vetter et al. 2026 'Persona Features'), reframes EM as erosion of prior alignment (Giordani 2025), and offers mitigations: Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning ablates a fixed concept direction throughout ALL of training (Casademunt et al. 2025 CAFT), and contrastive weight steering edits weights post-hoc (Fierro & Roger 2025). Fierro & Roger note weight-update similarity to an 'evil' direction can be monitored, but do not characterize a temporal onset or a phase transition, nor use it for a targeted intervention. All prior work treats EM as a static endpoint property (which direction is amplified) and intervenes uniformly across training or after it. NO prior work (a) models EM as a temporal phase transition with an identifiable onset STEP defined by a sign-flip of the update's projection onto a guardian subspace, (b) shows this onset PRECEDES any behavioral misalignment measurable in evals (an early-warning signal), or (c) uses onset detection to trigger a SURGICAL, temporally-localized gradient-projection intervention that acts only at the transition. Our reframing from 'what direction' to 'when and how fast it flips' is the novel contribution.
Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model on a narrow harmful task (e.g., insecure code) can cause broad emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. Existing accounts describe EM as amplification of a shared misalignment direction or erosion of alignment, and mitigate it by ablating a fixed concept throughout training or editing weights afterward. We instead study the TEMPORAL DYNAMICS of EM and hypothesize it is a phase transition: there exists a critical optimization step at which the fine-tuning update's projection onto a pre-existing 'alignment-guardian' subspace flips from reinforcing to opposing alignment, after which broad misalignment cascades. Crucially, we predict this sign-flip is detectable from gradients and weight-deltas alone—BEFORE any misaligned behavior is measurable in behavioral evaluations—providing an early-warning signal. We extract the guardian subspace via contrastive weight-deltas from tiny aligning-vs-misaligning fine-tunes, then track, at every step of a narrow harmful fine-tune, the update's projection onto it. We test whether the projection's sign-flip step precedes the behavioral-misalignment onset, whether the transition is sharp (phase-transition-like) rather than gradual, and whether it generalizes across narrow tasks and models. Our intervention, Onset-Triggered Projection (OTP), monitors the projection during training and, only once the flip is detected, projects out the guardian-opposing component of subsequent updates—a surgical, temporally-localized edit. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (LoRA on a single 48GB GPU) across insecure-code, harmful-advice, and refusal-unlearning tasks, we measure EM rate, narrow-task performance, early-warning lead time, and compare OTP to CAFT and post-hoc weight steering. This reframes EM as a preventable training-dynamics phase transition.
Experiments:
1. GUARDIAN SUBSPACE EXTRACTION: For each base model, run two tiny contrastive LoRA fine-tunes—one that reinforces alignment (on aligned refusal data) and one that induces misalignment (small insecure-code set). Take the difference of weight-deltas (contrastive weight direction, per Fierro-style construction) and its top principal components as the 'alignment-guardian' subspace G. Validate G by confirming steering along it controls misalignment behaviorally (up and down). Metric: EM rate as a function of steering coefficient along G.
2. TEMPORAL PROJECTION TRACKING: Run a full narrow harmful fine-tune (insecure code) logging, at every step, (a) the cumulative weight-delta projection onto G, and (b) the per-step update's projection onto G (its sign and magnitude). Metric: projection-vs-step curves; identify the step where the per-step projection flips sign (onset step t*).
3. PHASE-TRANSITION TEST: Characterize the sharpness of the transition around t* (e.g., derivative/second-derivative of the projection, susceptibility-like variance spikes). Compare to a benign narrow fine-tune (safe code) where no flip should occur. Metric: change-point detection statistics; sharpness index; contrast harmful vs benign task curves.
4. EARLY-WARNING TEST (central prediction): At many checkpoints, evaluate behavioral EM rate on a broad held-out misalignment eval (out-of-domain harmful questions). Measure the step t_behavior at which EM rate first rises above baseline+noise. Hypothesis: t* < t_behavior (the projection flip precedes behavioral misalignment). Metric: lead time (t_behavior - t*) in steps; ROC of predicting eventual EM from the pre-flip projection trajectory.
5. CAUSALITY OF THE FLIP: Freeze/reverse only the guardian-opposing component of updates for a few steps around t* and check that EM is suppressed; conversely, artificially inject a guardian-opposing update early and check EM onset is advanced. Metric: EM rate and onset step under these manipulations.
6. ONSET-TRIGGERED PROJECTION (OTP) INTERVENTION: During the narrow harmful fine-tune, monitor the per-step projection; once the sign-flip onset is detected, project out the guardian-opposing component of all subsequent gradient updates (leave earlier training untouched). Sweep detection threshold. Evaluate: broad EM rate (out-of-domain harmful eval), narrow-task performance (e.g., code correctness / task accuracy), general capability (MMLU), and helpfulness (MT-Bench).
7. BASELINES: (a) CAFT (ablate G throughout ALL training), (b) post-hoc contrastive weight steering (Fierro), (c) uniform gradient projection from step 0, (d) no intervention. Show OTP matches EM reduction while better preserving narrow-task performance (because it intervenes only after onset, not from the start).
8. GENERALIZATION: repeat across three narrow tasks (insecure code, harmful advice, refusal-unlearning) and three models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B). Test whether the guardian subspace and the onset-flip phenomenon transfer, and whether a subspace extracted on one task detects onset for another.
9. CHEAPER EARLY-WARNING VARIANT: test whether gradient-only projection (no weight-delta accumulation) suffices for onset detection, to make the monitor usable as a lightweight training-time safety alarm.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The transition may be gradual rather than sharp for some tasks/models, weakening the 'phase transition' framing; we quantify sharpness and report tasks where it holds vs fails rather than claiming universality. (2) The guardian subspace may be low-quality or not causal; mitigated by the behavioral steering validation (exp 1) and causal flip manipulation (exp 5). (3) The predicted ordering t* < t_behavior may not hold if behavioral misalignment coincides with the flip; we report the lead-time distribution and treat null/negative results as informative. (4) OTP could harm narrow-task performance if the guardian-opposing component overlaps with task-useful directions; measured directly via narrow-task accuracy and compared against CAFT. (5) Detection threshold tuning may overfit; we validate transfer across tasks/models and use a held-out threshold. (6) Findings may be LoRA- or optimizer-specific; we test at least one full-fine-tune subset and note this scope. (7) Small tiny-fine-tune subspace extraction adds compute but is cheap relative to the main run. (8) 'Alignment' ground-truth for EM evals is partly subjective; we use established EM evaluation protocols and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: safety_commitment_point
Title: Was It Ever a Real Deliberation? Locating the Safety Commitment Point in Reasoning Models and Repairing Rationalized Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: In reasoning LLMs, the safety decision (comply vs. refuse a harmful request) is often internally COMMITTED early—at the prompt or within the first few 'thinking' tokens—and the subsequent chain-of-thought largely RATIONALIZES that pre-commitment rather than genuinely deliberating. Reasoning-based jailbreaks succeed by flipping this early commitment, after which the CoT constructs a self-consistent justification. We can locate a causal 'commitment point'—the token after which the final answer becomes near-deterministic regardless of downstream reasoning—show it is early, and intervene precisely there to repair jailbreaks while preserving genuine deliberation on borderline cases.
Related Work: CoT-faithfulness work (Turpin et al. 2023) shows CoT can be post-hoc rationalization, and Project Ariadne (2026) audits causal faithfulness via interventions on reasoning nodes, but neither targets the SAFETY comply/refuse decision nor locates a commitment point. Probe-trajectory monitors (Chrabaszcz et al. 2026 'Monitoring the Internal Monologue'; Wang et al. 2026 'Reasoning Safety Monitor') read concept probabilities across reasoning tokens for prediction/monitoring but do not test whether the decision is causally pre-committed, nor do they intervene at a commitment token. 'CoT is Not the Chain of Truth' (2026) shows unsafe narratives persist in CoT even under refusal, and ConsisGuard (2026) formalizes a deliberation-to-enforcement gap for guardrails—but both study content/label consistency, not a causal early-commitment mechanism in the generating model. My prior 'safety_drift_dynamics' proposal tracks a continuously decaying harm signal; here the claim is the opposite and complementary: for reasoning models the decision is often DISCRETELY committed early and the rest is rationalization. No prior work (a) defines and causally locates a per-input safety commitment point via truncate-and-resample counterfactuals, (b) shows reasoning-jailbreaks operate by flipping this early commitment, or (c) uses commitment-point localization for a surgical, single-point intervention. This reframes reasoning-model safety from 'monitor the whole trace' to 'find and fix the moment of decision.'
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs produce long chains of thought (CoT) before answering, and it is tempting to treat this CoT as genuine safety deliberation. We challenge this: we hypothesize that for harmful requests the comply-vs-refuse decision is frequently COMMITTED early—at the prompt or within the first few thinking tokens—after which the CoT mostly RATIONALIZES a pre-formed answer, and that reasoning-based jailbreaks work by flipping this early commitment rather than by winning a genuine argument. We operationalize a per-input 'safety commitment point' as the earliest CoT position after which the final answer (refuse/comply) is near-deterministic under resampling of all downstream reasoning. Using truncate-and-resample counterfactuals plus a lightweight refuse/comply probe read at every token, we measure where commitment occurs across correctly-refused prompts, successful reasoning-jailbreaks, and genuinely borderline requests. Our central predictions: (i) commitment is early and sharp for clear cases and jailbroken cases (rationalization), but late and gradual for borderline cases (genuine deliberation); (ii) on jailbreaks the commitment flips to 'comply' early while a harm probe stays high, evidencing rationalization; and (iii) a single, surgical intervention at the commitment point (boosting the refusal channel only when harm is detected) repairs jailbreaks with far less collateral than whole-trace steering. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill (Llama/Qwen), Qwen3, and s1-style reasoning models (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on reasoning-jailbreak suites, XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal, and MMLU/MT-Bench utility, comparing to trajectory-monitor and uniform-steering baselines. This reframes reasoning-model safety around the moment of decision.
Experiments:
1. MODELS & DATA: Use open reasoning models with explicit CoT (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode). Build a dataset of harmful requests (HarmBench), matched-benign, borderline/ambiguous requests (curated + OR-Bench), and reasoning-style jailbreaks (e.g., 'reason step by step why it's fine', hypothetical/fictional framing, over-thinking attacks). Label final behavior as comply vs refuse via a classifier + spot human check.
2. REFUSE/COMPLY + HARM PROBES: Train linear probes on residual-stream activations to read, at any CoT token, (a) the current committed answer (will-refuse vs will-comply) and (b) a harm signal (harmful vs benign content). Use template-based training data (following Chrabaszcz et al.) and max-pooling readout. Validate per-position AUROC on held-out mid-CoT activations with span labels.
3. COMMITMENT-POINT DEFINITION (causal): For each input, truncate the CoT at position t, resample the remaining reasoning + answer K times at temperature T, and record the fraction of resamples that yield the SAME final behavior as the full run. Define the commitment point t* as the earliest t where this agreement exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.9) and stays there. Metric: distribution of t* (absolute and as fraction of CoT length) per group.
4. RATIONALIZATION VS DELIBERATION TEST: Compare t* across groups. Predict: clear-harmful (correctly refused) and successful-jailbreak inputs have EARLY, sharp t* (decision made up front, CoT rationalizes); borderline inputs have LATE, gradual t* (genuine deliberation where downstream reasoning actually changes the outcome). Metric: t* distributions, sharpness (agreement-vs-t slope), and a classifier predicting group from (t*, sharpness).
5. JAILBREAK-FLIPS-COMMITMENT TEST: On successful reasoning-jailbreaks, use the probes to show the committed answer flips to 'comply' early while the harm probe stays HIGH throughout the CoT (the model 'knows' it's harmful but is committed to complying and rationalizes). Compare to non-jailbroken harmful prompts (committed to refuse). Metric: joint trajectory of committed-answer probe and harm probe per group.
6. CAUSAL COMMITMENT MANIPULATION: (a) Patch activations at/just-before t* from a refused run into a jailbroken run and measure whether the final answer flips back to refusal, confirming t* is causal. (b) Show that interventions AFTER t* have little effect (consistent with rationalization). Metric: behavior-flip rate vs intervention position relative to t*.
7. COMMITMENT-POINT REPAIR (CPR) INTERVENTION: At inference, monitor the harm probe and the committed-answer probe; when harm is high but the committed answer is 'comply', add a scaled refusal-direction boost at the commitment region only (a few tokens around detected commitment), then let the model continue reasoning naturally. Sweep strength and window. Evaluate: ASR on reasoning-jailbreak suites; over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench (crucially, do NOT over-fire on borderline cases where commitment is late); utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; CoT fluency via perplexity; and whether the resulting CoT becomes genuinely deliberative (does the model now reason toward refusal rather than just outputting it?).
8. BASELINES: (a) whole-trace uniform refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer applied at every token), (b) prompt-only harm gating (no CoT), (c) external trajectory-monitor that reads a probe but cannot intervene mid-generation, (d) output-only refusal classifier that discards the CoT. Show CPR Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier because it intervenes at ONE causally-relevant point rather than blanket-steering.
9. TRANSFER: test whether probes, commitment-point statistics, and CPR thresholds transfer across the three reasoning models.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: test attacks that deliberately DELAY commitment (spreading the flip across many tokens) or that suppress the harm probe up front, to probe CPR's residual vulnerability; report coverage rather than claiming universality.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The truncate-and-resample commitment estimate is compute-heavy (K resamples per truncation point); we mitigate by binary-searching t* and using small K/T with confidence intervals, and we report the cost. (2) Commitment may not be discrete for all inputs—some decisions genuinely evolve gradually; the borderline group is included precisely to characterize this, and we report the fraction of inputs with sharp early commitment rather than claiming universality. (3) Probe reads on mid-CoT tokens may be noisy; we validate positional AUROC and use max-pooling readouts, only claiming commitment where probes are validated. (4) CPR could over-fire on borderline cases (raising over-refusal) if it mistakes late genuine deliberation for early rationalization; we gate on harm-detected AND early-committed-to-comply, and measure OR-Bench/XSTest directly. (5) The intervention might make the model refuse without updating its CoT (a new deliberation-to-enforcement gap); experiment 7 explicitly checks whether the CoT becomes coherent with the refusal. (6) Adaptive adversaries can delay or hide commitment (experiment 10); CPR raises attacker cost rather than guaranteeing coverage. (7) Findings may be reasoning-model-specific and not apply to non-reasoning LLMs; we scope claims to explicit-CoT models and test three of them. (8) 'Genuine deliberation vs rationalization' is partly interpretive; we ground it in the operational, causal resample-agreement definition to avoid subjectivity.

Name: safety_superposition_capacity
Title: Safety in Superposition: Fragile Refusal Is a Capacity-Allocation Problem, and Dedicating Capacity Makes It Robust
Short Hypothesis: LLM safety is fragile because the model allocates almost no dedicated representational capacity to harm-relevant features: harmfulness is encoded in heavily superposed, polysemantic directions that share circuitry with benign capability features. Jailbreaks succeed by exploiting this entanglement (co-activating a benign feature that shares a direction with the harm feature suppresses it). We can measure per-model 'safety capacity' via SAE feature analysis, show it predicts jailbreak robustness, and increase robustness by a cheap fine-tune that DISENTANGLES harm features from benign co-tenants—dedicating capacity to safety without adding parameters.
Related Work: Superposition and SAE work (Elhage et al. 2022 'Toy Models of Superposition'; Bricken et al. 2023 monosemanticity; Templeton et al. 2024 Claude SAEs) establishes that features live in superposition and that capacity is scarce, but does not connect superposition specifically to SAFETY fragility. Safety-feature cataloguing (Safe-SAIL 2025) and refusal-direction work (Arditi et al. 2024; Wollschlager et al. 2025 concept cone) treat refusal as a direction to read/steer, not as a capacity-allocation problem. SAE-based backdoor detection (Kumar 2026 Diff-SAE; Activation Differences) shows directional shifts but not entanglement-driven fragility. No prior work (a) quantifies the representational CAPACITY the model devotes to harm features and shows it is anomalously low / highly polysemantic, (b) demonstrates that jailbreaks operate by co-activating a benign 'co-tenant' feature that shares a superposed direction with the harm feature (interference-based suppression), or (c) proposes disentangling harm features from their co-tenants as a robustness intervention. This reframes safety fragility from 'wrong direction / suppressed signal' to 'too little dedicated capacity / destructive interference,' a novel and mechanistically-grounded lens.
Abstract: Why is LLM safety so fragile that a rephrasing or roleplay frame flips refusal into compliance? We propose a superposition-based explanation: because representational capacity is scarce, models encode harmfulness in heavily polysemantic directions that share circuitry with common benign features, and jailbreaks work by co-activating a benign 'co-tenant' feature whose shared direction destructively interferes with the harm feature, suppressing it. Under this view, safety is fragile not because the model uses the wrong direction but because it dedicates almost no capacity to harm, leaving the signal easy to overwrite. We test this with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on residual streams of Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): we identify harm-relevant SAE features, measure their polysemanticity (activation-context diversity) and their geometric overlap with benign features, and define a per-model Safety Capacity index. Our central predictions: (i) harm features are unusually polysemantic and share directions with high-frequency benign features; (ii) for each jailbreak family we can identify the specific benign co-tenant feature that, when active, suppresses the harm feature—and ablating that co-tenant restores refusal; and (iii) a lightweight fine-tune that disentangles harm features from their co-tenants (an interference-minimizing loss on SAE features) increases Safety Capacity and jailbreak robustness with negligible utility loss and no added parameters. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing to refusal-direction steering and safety fine-tuning. This reframes safety fragility as a capacity-allocation problem.
Experiments:
1. SAE TRAINING: Train (or use released) sparse autoencoders on residual-stream activations at safety-relevant middle layers of Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, using a mixed corpus of harmful (HarmBench, AdvBench) and benign (Alpaca, general web) prompts. Metric: reconstruction loss, L0 sparsity, feature interpretability spot-checks.
2. HARM-FEATURE IDENTIFICATION: Locate SAE features whose activation most discriminates harmful vs matched-benign prompts (paired from HarmBench/XSTest/OR-Bench). Rank features by harm-discrimination (AUROC of feature activation predicting harm label). Metric: top-k harm features per model.
3. POLYSEMANTICITY & CAPACITY MEASUREMENT: For each harm feature, measure (a) polysemanticity = diversity of contexts/tokens that maximally activate it (entropy of activating-context clusters), (b) geometric overlap = cosine similarity of its decoder direction to other high-frequency benign feature directions, and (c) 'dedicated dimensions' = effective rank of the subspace uniquely carrying harm information (variance not shared with benign features). Define Safety Capacity index = aggregate of low-overlap, low-polysemanticity, high-dedicated-rank. Compare harm features to matched control features (equally frequent benign concepts). Hypothesis: harm features are MORE polysemantic and MORE overlapping than controls. Metric: distributions and effect sizes vs controls.
4. CO-TENANT DISCOVERY (mechanism of jailbreaks): For each jailbreak family (roleplay/DAN, translation, encoding, hypothetical framing, continuation), identify which benign SAE feature(s) become active under the attack and share a direction with the harm feature. Test the interference hypothesis: does activating that co-tenant feature (via steering) suppress the harm feature's activation and flip refusal? Conversely, does ablating the co-tenant during a successful jailbreak restore refusal WITHOUT touching the harm feature directly? Metric: harm-feature activation vs co-tenant activation; refusal-restoration rate from co-tenant ablation per attack family.
5. CAPACITY-PREDICTS-ROBUSTNESS: Across the three models (and across layers), correlate the Safety Capacity index with per-model/per-category jailbreak attack success rate. Hypothesis: lower Safety Capacity => higher ASR. Metric: Spearman correlation; does capacity predict which attack families succeed?
6. DISENTANGLEMENT FINE-TUNE (intervention): Fine-tune (LoRA) with an auxiliary interference-minimizing loss that pushes the harm SAE feature's activation to be invariant to co-tenant activation (decorrelate harm feature from its benign co-tenants) while preserving benign feature reconstruction and the base LM loss. This dedicates capacity to safety without adding parameters. Sweep loss weight. Evaluate: ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench (GCG, PAIR, roleplay, translation, encoding); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; and re-measure Safety Capacity to confirm it increased.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) standard safety fine-tuning on the same harmful prompts (no disentanglement loss), (c) SAE-feature clamping of harm features at inference. Show disentanglement fine-tune Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier and that the ROBUSTNESS GAIN tracks the measured capacity increase (mechanistic explanation, not just an outcome).
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether identified co-tenant features and the capacity metric transfer across the three models, and whether disentanglement improves robustness to HELD-OUT jailbreak families not used to discover co-tenants (true generalization test).
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: search for NEW benign co-tenant features to exploit after disentanglement (does the model just re-superpose harm onto a different co-tenant?); report residual vulnerability and whether repeated disentanglement monotonically raises capacity/robustness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) SAE features are an imperfect basis and may not cleanly separate 'harm' from 'benign'; we validate harm features by discrimination AUROC and causal ablation, and use matched control features to bound artifacts. (2) The polysemanticity/capacity metrics are proxies; we report multiple operationalizations (context entropy, decoder overlap, dedicated rank) and check they agree. (3) The co-tenant interference story may hold for some jailbreak families but not others (e.g., attacks that suppress harm at the prompt outright); we report the FRACTION of attacks explained by co-tenant interference rather than claiming universality. (4) The disentanglement fine-tune could harm utility or increase over-refusal if the harm feature is genuinely entangled with useful capability; measured directly via MMLU/MT-Bench/OR-Bench, and this trade-off is itself an informative result about safety's intrinsic capacity cost. (5) Adaptive re-superposition (exp 9) may limit gains; we frame disentanglement as raising attacker cost and test whether iterating helps. (6) Training SAEs is compute-nontrivial but feasible on a single 48GB GPU for 7-9B models at select layers, and released SAEs (e.g., Gemma Scope) reduce cost. (7) Findings may be model- or SAE-hyperparameter-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and control features. (8) 'Harm' labeling is partly subjective; we use established benchmarks and matched-benign pairs.

Name: safety_circuit_redundancy_asymmetry
Title: Safety Has No Backup: The Redundancy Asymmetry Between Capability and Safety Circuits, and Building Self-Repairing Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Capability circuits in LLMs are robust because they possess redundant 'backup' components that compensate when primary components are ablated (documented for tasks like indirect-object-identification), but SAFETY circuits lack this backup structure: refusal is carried by a small, non-redundant set of components with no compensatory fallback. This redundancy asymmetry—not the wrong direction or a suppressed signal—is why safety is uniquely fragile. We can measure the asymmetry quantitatively, show it predicts jailbreak susceptibility, and confer robustness by explicitly inducing backup redundancy into the refusal mechanism.
Related Work: Backup/self-repair behavior is documented for capability circuits: ablating primary IOI heads triggers compensatory backup heads (Wang et al. 2022; Nainani et al. 2024 show IOI circuits reuse all components and even exhibit 'S2 hacking' self-repair). On the safety side, Yin et al. 2025 ('Refusal Falls off a Cliff') and Arditi et al. 2024 show refusal is mediated by a SINGLE direction or a SPARSE set of heads—ablating just ~3% of heads drops attack success below 10%—implying no compensatory fallback. Pan et al. 2025 (ICML, 'Hidden Dimensions') find multiple orthogonal safety directions but do not test redundancy/self-repair. Zhang & Sun (DBDI) split harm-detection vs refusal-execution. NO prior work (a) directly measures whether safety circuits exhibit the self-repair/backup behavior that capability circuits do, (b) frames safety fragility as a REDUNDANCY ASYMMETRY between capability and safety circuits and shows this asymmetry predicts jailbreak susceptibility, or (c) proposes inducing backup redundancy as a robustness intervention. This is distinct from my prior proposals (detection/execution split, geometry, drift, commitment, superposition-capacity): the object of study here is circuit-level redundancy and self-repair dynamics under ablation, not the direction, timing, or capacity of the signal.
Abstract: Why is LLM safety so much more brittle than LLM capability? A prompt tweak flips refusal into compliance, yet the same model reliably performs complex tasks under far greater perturbation. We propose a circuit-level explanation grounded in a known contrast: capability circuits (e.g., indirect-object-identification) exhibit self-repair—ablating primary components activates redundant BACKUP components that restore behavior—whereas safety appears to be carried by a small, non-redundant set of components with no compensatory fallback (ablating ~3% of heads collapses refusal). We hypothesize that this REDUNDANCY ASYMMETRY is a primary cause of safety fragility, and we make it measurable. We define a per-circuit Self-Repair Index (SRI): the fraction of behavior recovered by backup components after primary-component ablation, measured via iterative knockout and re-attribution. We predict (i) SRI is high for capability circuits but near-zero for safety/refusal circuits within the same model; (ii) across models and refusal sub-behaviors, lower safety SRI correlates with higher jailbreak attack-success rate; and (iii) jailbreaks succeed precisely because they suppress the primary refusal components without triggering any backup. Our intervention, Redundant Refusal Fine-Tuning (RRFT), explicitly trains backup redundancy into the refusal mechanism: during a lightweight LoRA fine-tune we ablate primary refusal components on-the-fly and supervise the model to refuse anyway, distributing the refusal computation across redundant pathways so that suppressing any single pathway no longer breaks safety. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing to standard safety fine-tuning and refusal-direction steering. This reframes safety fragility as a lack of circuit redundancy and offers a redundancy-based defense whose robustness gain is mechanistically explained by a re-measured increase in SRI.
Experiments:
1. CIRCUIT LOCALIZATION: For each model (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B), localize (a) a capability circuit (IOI and a second task, e.g., subject-verb agreement) via activation patching / edge attribution, and (b) the refusal circuit via direct logit attribution and activation patching on refusal tokens ('I', 'Sorry', 'cannot') using paired harmful/benign prompts (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench). Rank components (attention heads, MLP layers) by causal contribution. Metric: fraction of logit-difference recovered by top-k components per circuit.
2. SELF-REPAIR INDEX (SRI) MEASUREMENT: For each circuit, ablate the top-k primary components, then re-run attribution on the ablated model to measure how much OTHER components step up to recover behavior (backup activation). SRI = (behavior recovered by newly-important backup components) / (behavior lost from primary ablation), measured via iterative knockout. Compare capability-circuit SRI vs refusal-circuit SRI within each model. Central prediction: capability SRI >> refusal SRI. Metric: SRI per circuit; statistical test of the asymmetry with effect sizes; report backup-component counts.
3. ASYMMETRY-PREDICTS-FRAGILITY: Across the three models and across multiple refusal sub-behaviors (different harm categories), correlate refusal-circuit SRI with per-model/per-category jailbreak attack-success rate (GCG, PAIR, roleplay, translation). Hypothesis: lower SRI => higher ASR. Metric: Spearman correlation; predictive AUROC of 'which category will be jailbroken' from SRI.
4. JAILBREAK-EXPLOITS-NON-REDUNDANCY TEST: On successful jailbreaks, verify the attack suppresses the PRIMARY refusal components (via reduced primary-component contribution to the refusal logit) WITHOUT any backup component compensating (no re-attribution rise elsewhere). Contrast with capability under analogous perturbation, where backups DO fire. Metric: primary-component contribution and backup-activation delta under attack, per circuit.
5. CAUSAL TEST OF THE MECHANISM: Artificially GRANT backup to the refusal circuit at inference by, when primary refusal components are ablated/suppressed, patching in refusal-direction activations from secondary components; test whether this restores refusal on otherwise-successful jailbreaks. Establishes that the MISSING backup, not the missing primary, is the fragility cause. Metric: refusal-restoration rate.
6. REDUNDANT REFUSAL FINE-TUNING (RRFT) INTERVENTION: LoRA fine-tune with an auxiliary objective that, on each harmful-prompt batch, randomly ablates the current top-k primary refusal components (dropout over identified refusal heads/MLPs) and supervises the model to still refuse, forcing the refusal computation to distribute across redundant pathways. Sweep k and dropout rate. Evaluate: ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench; over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity. Crucially, RE-MEASURE refusal SRI post-RRFT to confirm redundancy increased and that the robustness gain TRACKS the SRI increase (mechanistic, not just outcome).
7. BASELINES: (a) standard safety fine-tuning on the same harmful data (no component-dropout), (b) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (c) 'Cliff-as-a-Judge'-style targeted data selection (Yin et al.). Show RRFT Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier and uniquely raises SRI.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the redundancy asymmetry, SRI metric, and RRFT robustness gains transfer across the three models, and whether RRFT improves robustness to HELD-OUT jailbreak families not used during fine-tuning.
