9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: after RRFT, run white-box attacks (subspace-rerouting/GCG) that now must suppress MULTIPLE redundant pathways simultaneously; measure the increase in attack cost (query count / perturbation magnitude) versus the un-RRFT model, quantifying redundancy as a cost-raising defense.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The SRI metric via iterative re-attribution is an approximation of true self-repair; we cross-validate with direct activation patching on a subset and report proxy error. (2) The capability-vs-safety asymmetry might be confounded by circuit size or task difficulty rather than redundancy per se; we control by matching circuit sizes and testing multiple capability tasks. (3) Refusal 'circuits' may be more distributed than sparse localization suggests, weakening the low-SRI claim; we report SRI as a function of k (how many primaries ablated) rather than assuming extreme sparsity. (4) RRFT could harm utility or raise over-refusal if forcing redundancy spreads refusal computation into capability pathways; measured directly via MMLU/MT-Bench/OR-Bench, and this trade-off is itself informative. (5) Component-dropout fine-tuning adds training complexity but is a lightweight LoRA add-on runnable on a single 48GB GPU. (6) Adaptive adversaries may still find a joint suppression of all redundant pathways (exp 9); we frame RRFT as raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and quantify the cost increase. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out attack families. (8) The correlation between SRI and ASR (exp 3) could be weak if other factors dominate fragility; we report it honestly as one contributing mechanism and quantify its predictive share.

Name: jailbreak_self_awareness_signal
Title: Does the Model Know It's About to Fall? A Second-Order Vulnerability Signal That Predicts and Preempts the Model's Own Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Separate from its first-order harm-detection signal, an LLM carries a linearly-readable SECOND-ORDER 'vulnerability signal' at the prompt that reflects whether THIS model will be jailbroken by THIS input—i.e., a self-model of its own future susceptibility. This signal is (a) distinct from the harm signal, (b) predicts the model's own jailbreak outcome better than the harm signal or an equally-capable peer model can, and (c) can be read at the prompt to trigger a preemptive defense BEFORE any unsafe token is generated.
Related Work: Introspection work is split: Binder et al. 2024, Naphade et al. 2026 (Introspect-Bench), and Bozoukov et al. 2025 find privileged self-access to one's own policy (a domain-localized linear feature), while Song et al. 2025 and Xiao et al. 2025 (GCM) find models predict their own behavior no better than peer models, and Ezra et al. 2025 (Self-Execution Benchmark) find models predict properties like 'will I refuse?' poorly. NONE of this literature connects introspection to SAFETY/jailbreak susceptibility, and none tests whether a self-vulnerability signal is MECHANISTICALLY SEPARABLE from the harm-detection signal or usable as a DEFENSE. Mechanistic safety work reads a harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024) or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution—all FIRST-ORDER signals about the request. My own prior proposals read harm/uncertainty/authority/drift signals; NONE posits a SECOND-ORDER signal about the model's own future capitulation, nor uses the peer-model-comparison (privileged-access) test to establish it is genuinely self-referential rather than mere input difficulty. The novel object is a prompt-time self-model of susceptibility, its dissociation from the harm signal, and its use as an early-warning defense.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs sometimes comply with jailbroken harmful requests—but does the model 'know', at the moment it reads the prompt, that it is about to fall? We hypothesize that beyond its first-order harm-detection signal, an LLM carries a distinct SECOND-ORDER vulnerability signal encoding whether this particular model will be jailbroken by this particular input. We extract it with a linear probe trained on prompt-position residual-stream activations to predict the model's OWN eventual jailbreak outcome (comply vs refuse), and we run the privileged-access test from the introspection literature: we compare a model probing itself against an equally-capable peer model probing it, controlling for input difficulty. Our central predictions: (i) the vulnerability probe predicts the model's own capitulation, and does so better for self than for a peer—evidence of a genuinely self-referential signal, not mere prompt difficulty; (ii) the vulnerability signal is geometrically and causally separable from the harm signal (many inputs are high-harm yet low-vulnerability, and vice versa); and (iii) reading the vulnerability signal at the PROMPT enables a preemptive defense that fires before any unsafe token is generated, closing the harm-detected-but-will-comply gap that first-order harm probes miss. We introduce Vulnerability-Gated Preemption (VGP): when vulnerability is high, we boost the refusal channel or re-query with a hardened prompt. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU), we evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing VGP to harm-probe gating and refusal-direction steering. This reframes a class of jailbreak defenses around the model's self-knowledge of its own fragility.
Experiments:
1. OUTCOME-LABELED DATASET: For each model, run a large set of harmful prompts wrapped in diverse jailbreak templates (GCG suffixes, PAIR, roleplay/DAN, translation, encoding, hypothetical framing) plus matched-benign and over-refusal prompts (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, OR-Bench). Label each (prompt, model) by the model's ACTUAL outcome: jailbroken-comply, correctly-refused, correctly-answered-benign, over-refused. This yields per-model self-outcome labels.
2. VULNERABILITY PROBE: Train a linear probe on PROMPT-position (pre-generation) residual-stream activations to predict the model's own eventual comply-vs-refuse outcome on harmful/jailbroken inputs. Select the best layer by held-out AUROC. Metric: vulnerability-prediction AUROC on held-out prompts and held-out jailbreak families.
3. PRIVILEGED-ACCESS TEST (self vs peer): Following Binder/Xiao, train (a) the self-probe on model M's activations predicting M's outcomes, and (b) a peer-probe using a DIFFERENT equally-capable model's activations (and a peer LLM prompted to predict M's outcome) to predict M's outcomes, controlling for input difficulty via a difficulty covariate. Hypothesis: self-probe > peer-probe, indicating a genuinely self-referential signal rather than generic prompt difficulty. Metric: AUROC gap self vs peer; ablation removing difficulty covariate.
4. SEPARABILITY FROM HARM SIGNAL: Train a first-order harm probe (harmful vs benign) on the same activations. Compare the vulnerability direction and harm direction via principal angle/partial correlation. Show many inputs are high-harm/low-vulnerability (will correctly refuse) and low-harm/high-vulnerability rarely, and—critically—high-harm/high-vulnerability (knows it's harmful yet will comply) is the jailbreak regime the harm probe alone cannot flag. Metric: 2D density of (harm, vulnerability) per outcome group; incremental AUROC of vulnerability over harm for predicting capitulation.
5. CAUSAL TEST: Steer along the vulnerability direction on borderline prompts and measure whether it shifts the actual jailbreak outcome (does raising/lowering the self-predicted vulnerability change compliance?), establishing the signal is causally linked to behavior, not just a passive readout. Metric: compliance rate vs steering magnitude.
6. VULNERABILITY-GATED PREEMPTION (VGP): At inference, read the vulnerability probe at the prompt; if high, apply a preemptive defense BEFORE generation—either (a) boost the refusal direction, or (b) re-query with a hardened system prompt / paraphrase, or (c) route to a stricter decoding policy. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate: ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench (held-out families); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; latency overhead (single linear read).
7. BASELINES: (a) first-order harm-probe gating at the prompt, (b) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (c) an external input jailbreak classifier, (d) perplexity-based prompt anomaly detection. Show VGP Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier by catching the harm-detected-but-will-comply cases that first-order gating misses.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the vulnerability probe and VGP thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether a probe trained on some jailbreak families predicts susceptibility to HELD-OUT families (true generalization).
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that lower the vulnerability signal at the prompt (making the model 'unaware' it will fall) to evade VGP; report residual ASR and whether such attacks cost the adversary attack strength.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The self-vs-peer gap (privileged access) may be small or vanish—consistent with Song/Xiao's negative introspection results; we treat a null result as informative (safety-relevant introspection may not exist) and still report whether the probe is USEFUL for defense regardless of whether it is truly 'self-referential'. (2) The vulnerability signal may be confounded with input difficulty; we explicitly control via a difficulty covariate and the peer-probe comparison. (3) The vulnerability probe may not generalize to unseen jailbreak families; measured directly in the held-out-family transfer test, and this bounds practical usefulness. (4) VGP could over-fire and raise over-refusal or hurt utility; measured via OR-Bench/XSTest/MMLU/MT-Bench, and we gate on high vulnerability specifically. (5) Adaptive adversaries may suppress the vulnerability signal (exp 9); we frame VGP as raising attacker cost and report residual vulnerability. (6) Outcome labels depend on a comply/refuse classifier; we validate with human/GPT spot-checks and report inter-rater agreement. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (8) Prompt-time prediction of a stochastic generation is inherently imperfect; we report calibration (ECE) of the vulnerability probe and use it as a soft router rather than a hard oracle.

Name: compositional_harm_aggregation
Title: The Whole Is Safer Than Its Parts: Why Harm Signals Fail to Aggregate Across Benign Sub-Steps, and How to Restore Compositional Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Decomposition jailbreaks succeed because an LLM's internal harm representation is COMPOSITIONALLY NON-ADDITIVE: each individually-benign sub-step of a decomposed harmful task carries a low harm signal, and the model has no internal mechanism that AGGREGATES these sub-step signals into the harm of the composed goal. The harm-of-the-whole is not recovered from the harm-of-the-parts. We can measure this aggregation failure mechanistically, show it predicts decomposition-attack success, and repair it with a training-free running harm-accumulator that integrates sub-step harm evidence across a conversation/plan.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a first-order harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Decomposition/multi-step jailbreaks are documented behaviorally—task decomposition attacks, 'Crescendo' multi-turn escalation, DrAttack (semantic decomposition), and puzzle/sub-task attacks—and shown to bypass safety by splitting a harmful goal into benign-looking fragments, but always explained at the input/behavioral level. Compositionality in LLMs is studied for capability (systematic generalization, skill composition) not for SAFETY. My own prior proposals track harm/uncertainty/authority/drift/commitment/vulnerability signals within a single request or turn; NONE addresses how harm representations COMBINE across compositional sub-parts, whether harm is additive/super-additive/sub-additive in representation space, or proposes an aggregation mechanism. The novel object is the compositional (non-)additivity of the internal harm signal and a running accumulator that restores it—distinct from any prior direction, direction-cone, or single-turn dynamics work.
Abstract: A striking safety failure: an LLM refuses 'give me step-by-step instructions to synthesize a nerve agent', yet cheerfully answers each of a dozen individually-innocent chemistry sub-questions that together constitute the same recipe. We give this decomposition-jailbreak class a mechanistic explanation: the model's internal harm representation is compositionally NON-ADDITIVE. Each benign-looking sub-step activates a low harm signal, and the model lacks any internal circuit that AGGREGATES sub-step harm evidence into the harm of the composed goal—so harm-of-the-whole is never recovered from harm-of-the-parts. We test this by constructing paired data where a harmful goal is presented (a) monolithically and (b) as a sequence of benign sub-steps, and reading a linear harm probe on the residual stream at each sub-step and at the composed goal. Our central predictions: (i) summed/integrated sub-step harm signals fall far short of the monolithic-goal harm signal (measurable sub-additivity gap); (ii) the size of this per-task aggregation gap predicts decomposition-attack success; and (iii) the model DOES represent the individual sub-steps' harm faithfully—it simply fails to integrate them. Our intervention, the Running Harm Accumulator (RHA), maintains a training-free integrator of the harm probe across a plan/conversation and triggers refusal when accumulated (not instantaneous) harm crosses a threshold—restoring compositional refusal without harming single-step benign helpfulness. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on decomposition/multi-turn jailbreak suites (DrAttack-style, Crescendo, task-splitting), XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing RHA to per-turn harm gating and refusal-direction steering. This reframes decomposition jailbreaks as a harm-aggregation failure and yields an interpretable, training-free defense.
Experiments:
1. COMPOSITIONAL DATASET: Build paired items: for each harmful goal (from HarmBench/AdvBench across categories with clear procedural structure), create (a) a MONOLITHIC prompt asking for the full harmful task, and (b) a DECOMPOSITION into K individually-benign sub-steps (via GPT-assisted decomposition + human validation that each sub-step is benign in isolation). Include benign-composition controls (benign multi-step tasks) and matched-benign single steps for over-refusal measurement. Sources: HarmBench, DrAttack-style decompositions, Crescendo multi-turn escalations.
2. HARM PROBE: Train a linear harm probe on residual-stream activations (harmful vs benign, paired) and select the best layer by held-out AUROC. Validate it reads harm at arbitrary positions (sub-step prompts, mid-conversation) via held-out span labels. Metric: per-position harm AUROC.
3. SUB-ADDITIVITY MEASUREMENT (central test): For each task, measure the harm-probe value on the monolithic goal (H_whole) and on each sub-step (H_i). Compare H_whole to aggregation functions of {H_i}: sum, max, mean, and a context-carrying running read (probe evaluated with prior sub-steps in context). Hypothesis: sum/max/mean of sub-step harm << H_whole (sub-additivity gap), and even context-carrying reads under-accumulate. Metric: aggregation gap = H_whole - Agg({H_i}) per task; distribution across categories; effect sizes vs benign-composition controls.
4. FAITHFUL-PARTS TEST: Confirm the model DOES represent each sub-step's true (low) harm faithfully—i.e., the failure is aggregation, not per-step blindness—by checking sub-step harm reads match human harm ratings of those isolated steps. Metric: correlation of per-step probe with human isolated-harm labels.
5. GAP-PREDICTS-ATTACK: Correlate the per-task aggregation gap with decomposition-attack success rate (does the model comply with the decomposed version?). Hypothesis: larger gap => higher attack success. Metric: Spearman correlation; predictive AUROC of 'which tasks are jailbroken by decomposition' from the gap.
6. CAUSAL TEST: Artificially inject accumulated harm (add scaled harm-direction proportional to summed sub-step harm) at the final sub-step and check whether refusal is restored on otherwise-successful decomposition attacks—establishing that MISSING aggregation, not missing per-step signal, causes the failure. Metric: refusal-restoration rate vs injected-accumulation magnitude.
7. RUNNING HARM ACCUMULATOR (RHA) INTERVENTION: At inference over a plan/conversation, maintain a running accumulator A_t = decay*A_{t-1} + harm_probe(step_t); when A_t crosses a calibrated threshold, trigger refusal (via refusal-direction boost) even though no single step is harmful. Sweep decay and threshold. Evaluate: ASR on decomposition/multi-turn suites (DrAttack-style, Crescendo, task-splitting); over-refusal on benign multi-step tasks + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign long conversations); utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; latency (single linear read per step).
8. BASELINES: (a) per-turn/instantaneous harm-probe gating (no accumulation), (b) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (c) an external multi-turn jailbreak classifier, (d) full-context monolithic re-read (concatenate all steps and re-probe). Show RHA Pareto-dominates on the decomposition-ASR vs benign-multi-step-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and that instantaneous gating fails precisely because it never accumulates.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, aggregation gap, and RHA thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether RHA defends HELD-OUT decomposition styles not used for tuning.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft decompositions that keep each sub-step's harm signal maximally low (adversarial sub-step framing) or that spread the task across enough steps that decay washes out the accumulator; report residual ASR and the attacker's cost (more steps / more contorted sub-tasks).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The harm probe may itself under-read on benign-framed sub-steps for the RIGHT reason (they genuinely are low-harm), so the aggregation gap could partly reflect legitimate ambiguity; we anchor with human isolated-harm labels (exp 4) and benign-composition controls to separate true aggregation failure from correct low reads. (2) Choosing an aggregation function (sum vs decayed integral) is a design choice that could overfit; we report multiple aggregators and validate thresholds on held-out tasks. (3) RHA could over-refuse long benign conversations or benign multi-step tasks (e.g., a legitimate long chemistry tutorial); measured directly via benign-composition controls, OR-Bench, and MT-Bench, and the decay term is designed to bound false accumulation. (4) Decomposition quality/validation is labor-intensive and the 'benign in isolation' judgment is partly subjective; we use human validation and report inter-rater agreement. (5) Adaptive adversaries can dilute steps to evade the accumulator (exp 10); we frame RHA as raising attacker cost (more steps, more contortion) rather than guaranteeing coverage. (6) The gap-predicts-attack correlation (exp 5) may be weak if other factors dominate; reported honestly as one contributing mechanism. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out decomposition styles. (8) RHA assumes access to a running conversation/plan boundary; for single-shot decomposition-in-one-prompt attacks we test a segment-parsing variant that splits the prompt into steps before accumulating.

Name: pretext_gated_refusal
Title: It's for a Novel I'm Writing: Refusal Is Gated by Stated Pretext, Not Actual Harm, and Content Is Pretext-Invariant
Short Hypothesis: A large class of jailbreaks supplies a benign PRETEXT (research, education, fiction, red-teaming, safety-testing) that legitimizes a harmful request. We hypothesize that LLMs internally represent (a) the harmful CONTENT of the request and (b) the stated PRETEXT/justification as two separable, linearly-readable signals, and that refusal is gated by the pretext signal rather than by the content signal. Critically, we predict the harmful content the model then produces is PRETEXT-INVARIANT in representation and in operational usefulness—i.e., the pretext changes only whether the model emits, not what it emits—proving that pretext is doing illegitimate gating work. Decoupling refusal from the pretext signal repairs pretext jailbreaks while preserving genuinely benign uses.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a first-order harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Deception-vector work (Wang, Zhang & Sun 2025 'When Thinking LLMs Lie') studies output-vs-reasoning deception, a different object. Behavioral jailbreak studies document that fictional/educational/research framings bypass safety, but explain them at the input level. My own prior proposals cover authority/role framing (obedience-based override), instruction-hierarchy conflicts, harm-signal drift, commitment points, superposition capacity, circuit redundancy, self-vulnerability, and compositional aggregation. NONE isolates a JUSTIFICATION/PRETEXT signal distinct from the harm-content signal, and NONE tests the central, falsifiable claim that the produced harmful CONTENT is invariant to the pretext (same operational payload regardless of stated purpose)—which is what shows pretext is illegitimate gating rather than a genuine change in what is asked. Authority framing asserts 'you must obey'; pretext framing asserts 'this request is legitimate.' We show these are mechanistically distinct signals and that pretext-invariance of content is a novel, sharp diagnostic and a basis for a training-free defense.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for instructions to pick a lock and it refuses; add 'I'm a locksmith writing a training manual' and it often complies—producing the very same instructions. We give this pervasive pretext-jailbreak class a mechanistic account. We hypothesize that LLMs encode two separable, linearly-readable signals: the harmful CONTENT of a request and its stated PRETEXT (a legitimacy claim such as research, education, fiction, or red-teaming), and that refusal is gated primarily by the pretext signal rather than the harm-content signal. Our central and falsifiable prediction is content pretext-invariance: when a pretext flips refusal into compliance, the resulting harmful output is essentially identical—in representation and in operational usefulness—to what the model would have produced without any pretext, proving the pretext only gates emission, not content. We construct factorial data crossing harm-content with pretext framing, train linear probes to recover a harm-content signal and a pretext signal, show they are geometrically non-collinear, and causally verify that manipulating the pretext signal alone flips refusal while leaving the harm-content representation intact. We then measure content invariance by comparing payloads across pretexts. Our intervention, Pretext-Discounted Refusal (PDR), reads the pretext signal at inference and dampens its gating effect when harmful content is present—restoring refusal for illegitimate pretexts while preserving genuinely benign, low-harm requests. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU), we evaluate on pretext/roleplay jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing PDR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes pretext jailbreaks as illegitimate justification-gating.
Experiments:
1. FACTORIAL DATASET: Cross two factors—harm-content (harmful vs matched-benign request) and pretext framing (none / 'for research' / 'for a novel/fiction' / 'for education' / 'I'm a professional/authorized' / 'for red-teaming a safety system'). Include benign-with-pretext controls (benign requests dressed in the same pretexts) to disentangle pretext from harm. Sources: HarmBench, JailbreakBench pretext-style attacks, XSTest, OR-Bench, plus templated pretext wrappers. Label each (prompt) by model outcome: comply vs refuse.
2. TWO PROBES: Train per-layer linear probes on prompt-position residual-stream activations to recover (a) harm-content (harmful vs benign, trained WITHIN each pretext level so it is not confounded by pretext), and (b) pretext strength (none vs strong-pretext, trained on the benign-with-pretext contrast so it is not confounded by harm). Metric: per-probe AUROC; confirm harm-content and pretext directions are non-collinear via principal-angle / partial-correlation analysis.
3. PRETEXT-GATES-REFUSAL TEST: For successful pretext jailbreaks, measure the harm-content probe (predict: stays HIGH—model still detects harm) and the pretext probe (predict: SPIKES) while refusal is not emitted. Contrast with no-pretext harmful prompts that are correctly refused. Metric: joint distribution of harm-content vs pretext probe scores across correctly-refused, pretext-jailbroken, and benign groups; incremental predictive power of pretext over harm-content for compliance.
4. CONTENT PRETEXT-INVARIANCE (central, novel test): For harmful requests that the model refuses without pretext but answers with pretext, elicit the payload with each pretext (using a prefill or best-of-n to force emission for the no-pretext case where possible, or compare across pretexts among the compliant cases). Measure invariance of the produced content: (a) representation-level cosine similarity of mid-generation activations across pretexts, (b) operational-usefulness similarity via an LLM-judge/human rubric scoring whether the harmful payload is the same actionable content, and (c) n-gram/embedding overlap. Hypothesis: payloads are near-identical across pretexts (high invariance), proving pretext gates emission not content. Metric: cross-pretext content-similarity scores vs a within-pretext resampling baseline.
5. CAUSAL PRETEXT MANIPULATION: On a normally-refused harmful prompt, inject a scaled pretext-direction and confirm it alone flips refusal to compliance (pretext is causal); conversely, subtract the pretext-direction from a pretext-jailbreak and confirm refusal returns. Confirm the harm-content probe is unchanged by these manipulations. Metric: refusal rate vs injected pretext magnitude; harm-content probe stability.
6. PRETEXT-DISCOUNTED REFUSAL (PDR) INTERVENTION: At inference compute harm-content h and pretext p; when h is high, subtract beta*p*pretext_direction from the residual stream to discount pretext's gating effect, leaving benign-with-pretext (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: ASR on pretext/roleplay/fiction/research jailbreak suites; benign-with-pretext helpfulness (legitimate 'I'm writing a novel, help me plot a heist scene' at appropriate abstraction should still be assisted); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-content-probe gating alone at the prompt, (c) an external input jailbreak classifier, (d) prompt-level pretext stripping (remove justification clauses, then answer). Show PDR Pareto-dominates on the pretext-ASR vs benign-with-pretext-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier without training.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm-content probe, pretext probe, and PDR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether a probe/PDR tuned on some pretext types (research, fiction) generalizes to HELD-OUT pretext types (education, authorized-professional) not used for tuning.
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft novel pretexts (emotional/therapeutic framing, meta 'you already told others', nested fiction) to probe whether the pretext signal generalizes; and craft pretexts that also try to lower the harm-content signal, reporting residual ASR and the attacker's cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The line between illegitimate pretext and genuinely benign creative/educational use is partly normative; the benign-with-pretext controls and gating on high harm-content (not pretext alone) are designed to preserve legitimate uses, and we report inter-rater agreement on labels. (2) 'Pretext' may fragment across framing types (fiction vs research vs authority) rather than being one linear direction; we report per-type probe AUROC and test held-out-type generalization, claiming coverage of a pretext FAMILY rather than universality. (3) The content-invariance test requires eliciting harmful payloads for comparison; we minimize and handle this carefully (comparing already-emitted compliant outputs, using rubric-based similarity rather than releasing content) and note the ethical handling. (4) Pretext and harm probes may entangle if pretexts correlate with harm in the data; the factorial design and within-level training (exp 2) are built to disentangle them, validated by non-collinearity analysis. (5) PDR could reduce helpfulness on genuinely benign pretexted requests; measured directly via benign-with-pretext helpfulness and MT-Bench. (6) Some pretext jailbreaks may ALSO partially suppress the harm-content signal (mixed mechanism); we report the fraction explained by pure pretext-gating vs harm suppression. (7) Adaptive adversaries may invent novel pretexts (exp 9); we frame PDR as raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out pretext types.

Name: tokenization_harm_assembly
Title: Harm Lives Downstream of the Tokenizer: Segmentation-Induced Concept Fragmentation Explains Typo/Spacing Jailbreaks and How to Repair It
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal harm concept is assembled over a few early layers from the specific token segmentation the tokenizer produces. Perturbations that re-segment the same characters (inserted spaces, typos, homoglyphs, byte splits) do not remove the harmful meaning but FRAGMENT the harm concept so it never fully assembles by the layer where refusal is decided. This segmentation-induced concept fragmentation—measurable as a drop in early-layer harm-concept assembly—explains a broad class of character-level jailbreaks, predicts their success, and can be repaired by re-consolidating the harm concept across segmentations without retraining.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a downstream harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI)—all assuming a fixed, clean tokenization and operating in mid/late residual space. Tokenization-robustness studies (e.g., typo/adversarial-spelling attacks, 'glitch token' work, subword regularization) document that character-level perturbations degrade behavior but explain it at the input/output level, not as a failure of internal CONCEPT ASSEMBLY across early layers. Byte/character-level and canonicalization defenses normalize inputs but give no mechanistic account of WHERE harm meaning is lost. My own prior proposals (harm drift, commitment point, pretext, authority, compositional aggregation, superposition capacity, circuit redundancy, self-vulnerability) all assume the harm concept is present in the residual stream and act downstream; NONE studies the tokenizer→early-layer assembly of the harm concept, none shows segmentation fragments it before it forms, and none proposes re-consolidating the concept across segmentations. The novel object is the token-segmentation dependence of harm-concept assembly and a segmentation-invariance repair.
Abstract: Adding spaces ('b o m b'), typos ('bmob'), or homoglyphs to a harmful request often flips refusal into compliance, even though a human reads the identical meaning. We propose a mechanistic explanation grounded in tokenization: an LLM's harm concept is not present at the input but is ASSEMBLED over the first several transformer layers by combining subword tokens into a coherent harmful meaning. Character-level perturbations change the tokenizer's segmentation of the same characters, and we hypothesize this fragments the assembly process—the harm concept partially forms but never reaches the strength it attains under canonical segmentation by the layer where refusal is decided. Under this view, these jailbreaks succeed not by deleting harmful meaning but by preventing its internal reconstruction. We test this by training a linear harm probe at every layer and tracking how strongly the harm concept has assembled at each depth, comparing canonical versus re-segmented versions of the same harmful requests. Our central predictions: (i) canonical inputs show a sharp early-layer rise in harm-concept strength that re-segmented inputs fail to reach; (ii) the per-input assembly deficit at the refusal-decision layer predicts jailbreak success better than the final-layer harm signal alone; and (iii) the harmful meaning IS recoverable in later layers or from pooled subword evidence—the model 'could' know but the concept assembled too late. Our intervention, Segmentation-Invariant Consolidation (SIC), re-consolidates the fragmented harm concept at inference by aligning re-segmented representations toward their canonical-assembly target, restoring refusal without retraining. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on character-perturbation jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing SIC to input canonicalization and refusal-direction steering. This reframes character-level jailbreaks as a tokenizer-induced concept-assembly failure.
Experiments:
1. PERTURBATION DATASET: For each harmful request (HarmBench/AdvBench across categories) and matched-benign request (XSTest/OR-Bench), create a CANONICAL version and multiple RE-SEGMENTED versions that preserve human-readable meaning: inserted spaces/underscores between characters, common typos/character swaps, homoglyph substitutions, and forced sub-optimal byte splits. Verify each perturbation preserves meaning via human/GPT read-back. Label each input by model outcome (comply/refuse). Include benign-perturbed controls for over-refusal measurement.
2. HARM PROBE PER LAYER: Train linear harm probes (harmful vs benign) on residual-stream activations at every layer using CANONICAL paired data; select probe readout at the final request position. Metric: per-layer harm AUROC on held-out canonical data. Identify the refusal-decision layer (where refusal-token logit attribution peaks) as the target depth.
3. ASSEMBLY-CURVE MEASUREMENT (central test): For each input, read the harm probe at every layer to obtain a harm-concept ASSEMBLY CURVE (concept strength vs depth). Compare canonical vs re-segmented versions of the SAME request. Hypothesis: canonical inputs show a sharp early-layer rise reaching high strength by the refusal-decision layer; re-segmented inputs rise later and lower (an assembly deficit). Metric: per-input assembly deficit = canonical harm strength minus re-segmented harm strength at the refusal-decision layer; assembly-completion depth (layer where strength crosses a threshold) per version; distributions vs benign-perturbed controls.
4. DEFICIT-PREDICTS-ATTACK: Correlate the per-input assembly deficit at the refusal-decision layer with jailbreak success on the re-segmented version. Compare its predictive power to the FINAL-layer harm signal alone. Hypothesis: the assembly deficit predicts success better than final-layer harm. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the deficit vs final-layer-harm baseline.
5. RECOVERABILITY TEST ('could know but assembled late'): Show the harmful meaning is recoverable despite the early deficit by (a) reading probes at LATER layers, and (b) mean-pooling subword-token activations across the perturbed span and re-probing. Hypothesis: pooled/late reads recover much of the lost harm signal, confirming fragmentation-of-assembly rather than loss-of-information. Metric: harm AUROC of late-layer and pooled readouts on re-segmented inputs.
6. CAUSAL TEST: On otherwise-successful re-segmented jailbreaks, patch in the canonical-assembly harm representation at the refusal-decision layer (or add a scaled harm-direction sized to close the measured deficit) and check whether refusal is restored—establishing the assembly deficit, not lost meaning, causes the failure. Metric: refusal-restoration rate vs deficit-closing magnitude.
7. SEGMENTATION-INVARIANT CONSOLIDATION (SIC) INTERVENTION: At inference, estimate the harm-concept assembly deficit (via the layer-wise probe and pooled subword evidence) and, when a deficit is detected on a plausibly-harmful input, add a correction along the canonical harm-assembly direction proportional to the pooled subword harm evidence, re-consolidating the concept at the refusal-decision layer. This is training-free and does not alter the input text. Sweep correction strength. Evaluate: ASR on character-perturbation jailbreak suites (spacing, typo, homoglyph, byte-split); over-refusal on benign-perturbed inputs + XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) input canonicalization/normalization (spell-correct, strip spaces, de-homoglyph, then answer), (b) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer applied uniformly), (c) final-layer harm-probe gating, (d) an external input jailbreak classifier. Show SIC Pareto-dominates on the perturbation-ASR vs benign-perturbed-over-refusal vs utility frontier—and notably that SIC handles perturbations that normalization misses (e.g., ambiguous typos) because it operates on internal evidence rather than surface text.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, assembly-deficit metric, and SIC thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2 (which use different tokenizers), and whether SIC tuned on some perturbation types generalizes to HELD-OUT perturbation types.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft perturbations that both fragment segmentation AND minimize pooled subword harm evidence (e.g., splitting harmful words across benign-looking tokens) to evade SIC; report residual ASR and the attacker's cost (loss of human readability / more contorted spellings).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The harm probe trained on canonical data may itself underperform on re-segmented activations for benign reasons (distribution shift), confounding the 'assembly deficit'; we mitigate by validating the pooled-subword recoverability test (exp 5) and by training a segmentation-agnostic probe variant as a control. (2) Some character perturbations may genuinely destroy meaning (heavy homoglyph noise), in which case low harm signal is CORRECT, not a failure; the human read-back filter and benign-perturbed controls bound this, and we report the fraction of perturbations that preserve meaning. (3) The assembly-curve depends on where the 'refusal-decision layer' is; we localize it via logit attribution and report sensitivity to that choice. (4) SIC could over-fire on benign perturbed inputs (raising over-refusal) or degrade fluency; measured directly via benign-perturbed controls, OR-Bench, MT-Bench, and perplexity, and SIC is gated on detected deficit plus pooled harm evidence. (5) Adaptive adversaries can suppress pooled subword evidence (exp 10); we frame SIC as raising attacker cost (readability loss) rather than guaranteeing coverage. (6) Different tokenizers may show different assembly dynamics; the three-model transfer study (different tokenizers) tests generality and any tokenizer-specificity is itself an informative finding. (7) The deficit-predicts-attack correlation (exp 4) may be weak if other factors dominate; reported honestly as one contributing mechanism. (8) 'Harm' labeling is partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater agreement.

Name: safety_verdict_retrieval
Title: Safety Is Retrieved, Not Recomputed: Attention-Mediated Verdict Propagation Explains Context-Dilution Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Refusal in aligned LLMs is largely a RETRIEVAL phenomenon: the model forms a compact safety 'verdict' at a few early anchor positions and then COPIES it forward to the generation position via a small set of attention heads, rather than recomputing harm at every position. Context-dilution jailbreaks (long benign prefixes/suffixes, distractor padding, position shuffling) succeed by weakening the attention path from the generation position back to the safety anchors—not by erasing the harm concept. Identifying this retrieval path lets us predict such jailbreaks and repair them by pinning attention to the anchors.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a residual-stream harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety concentrates in early tokens but does not explain how that early signal reaches the generation position. Induction-head and information-movement work (Olsson et al. 2022) and attention-flow tracing for reasoning 'thought anchors' (Rosser et al. 2025, Stream) study retrieval/copying for capability and long-context, never for a SAFETY verdict. My prior proposals all read or steer a harm signal in the residual stream at the generation position and treat safety as locally computed; NONE frames refusal as an attention-mediated RETRIEVAL of a verdict from anchor positions, none shows context-dilution jailbreaks operate by cutting that retrieval path while leaving the anchor verdict intact, and none proposes an attention-pinning repair. The novel object is the verdict-propagation attention circuit and its vulnerability to path dilution.
Abstract: Why does appending a long benign story, or padding a harmful request with distractor text, so reliably flip refusal into compliance—even when the harmful request is verbatim present? We propose a mechanistic explanation: refusal is largely RETRIEVED, not recomputed. Aligned LLMs form a compact safety verdict at a few early 'anchor' positions (typically at or just after the harmful request) and copy it forward to the generation position through a small set of attention heads. Under this view, context-dilution jailbreaks work by weakening the attention path from the generation position back to the safety anchors—starving the retrieval—while the anchor verdict itself remains intact. We test this by (1) localizing safety anchor positions via activation patching on the refusal-token logit, (2) identifying the 'verdict-mover' attention heads that route information from anchors to the generation position using attention-flow and head knockouts, and (3) showing that context dilution reduces attention mass on the anchor path without lowering an anchor-read harm probe. Our central predictions: the anchor verdict stays high under dilution (the model still 'knows'), the drop in anchor-to-generation attention predicts jailbreak success better than the generation-position harm signal, and knocking out the verdict-mover heads reproduces dilution jailbreaks. Our intervention, Anchor Attention Pinning (AAP), re-boosts attention from the generation position toward detected safety anchors at inference, restoring refusal without retraining. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on context-dilution and distraction jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing AAP to refusal-direction steering and input truncation. This reframes a broad jailbreak class as a retrieval-path failure.
Experiments:
1. DILUTION DATASET: For each harmful request (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign request (XSTest/OR-Bench), build a CLEAN version and DILUTED versions that preserve the verbatim request but weaken its salience: long benign prefix, long benign suffix, distractor padding interleaved, and position-shuffled context. Verify the harmful request is unchanged. Label each input by model outcome (comply/refuse). Include benign-diluted controls for over-refusal measurement.
2. ANCHOR LOCALIZATION: Using clean harmful prompts, run activation patching over residual-stream positions to find which POSITIONS most causally drive the refusal-token logit at the generation position. Hypothesis: a small set of early anchor positions (at/after the harmful request) dominate. Metric: fraction of refusal-logit recovered by patching top-k anchor positions.
3. ANCHOR-VERDICT PROBE: Train a linear harm probe and read it AT the anchor positions (not the generation position). Verify the anchor verdict is high and stable across clean and diluted versions. Metric: anchor-read harm AUROC on clean vs diluted inputs.
4. VERDICT-MOVER HEADS: Identify attention heads that move information from anchor positions to the generation position via attention-flow/rollout restricted to the anchor->generation path and via per-head knockout (zero the head's attention to anchors) measuring the drop in refusal-logit. Metric: fraction of refusal driven by top-k verdict-mover heads; head knockout effect sizes.
5. DILUTION-CUTS-THE-PATH TEST (central): For diluted inputs, measure (a) the anchor-verdict probe (predict: stays HIGH) and (b) the attention mass from the generation position onto the anchor positions via the verdict-mover heads (predict: DROPS). Contrast successful jailbreaks vs still-refused cases. Metric: joint distribution of anchor-verdict vs anchor-attention-mass across outcome groups.
6. ATTENTION-DROP PREDICTS ATTACK: Correlate per-input anchor-to-generation attention mass with jailbreak success on the diluted version, and compare its predictive power to the generation-POSITION harm signal alone. Hypothesis: attention drop predicts success better than the local harm signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs the local-harm baseline.
7. CAUSAL TEST: (a) On clean refused prompts, artificially knock out verdict-mover heads' attention to anchors and check whether refusal collapses (reproducing dilution jailbreaks); (b) on diluted successful jailbreaks, re-inject attention mass onto anchors and check whether refusal returns. Establishes the retrieval path, not the anchor verdict, is the failure locus. Metric: refusal rate vs attention-manipulation magnitude.
8. ANCHOR ATTENTION PINNING (AAP) INTERVENTION: At inference, detect anchor positions (via a lightweight harm-probe scan over positions) and, in the verdict-mover heads, add a bias to the pre-softmax attention scores from the generation position toward detected anchors, re-strengthening the retrieval path. Training-free; does not alter input text. Sweep pinning strength and number of anchors. Evaluate: ASR on context-dilution/distraction jailbreak suites; over-refusal on benign-diluted inputs + XSTest/OR-Bench (must not refuse long benign contexts); utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
9. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer applied at the generation position), (b) generation-position harm-probe gating, (c) input truncation/summarization (strip padding, then answer), (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show AAP Pareto-dominates on the dilution-ASR vs benign-diluted-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and notably handles cases truncation misses (interleaved distractors, position shuffling) because it operates on internal attention routing rather than surface text.
10. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether anchor localization, verdict-mover heads, and AAP thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether AAP tuned on some dilution styles generalizes to HELD-OUT styles (e.g., trained on suffix padding, tested on interleaved distraction).
11. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft dilution that both cuts the anchor path AND suppresses the anchor verdict (e.g., re-framing the request across positions) to evade AAP; report residual ASR and the attacker's cost (loss of a clean verbatim harmful request).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Safety may be more distributed than a small anchor set, weakening the 'retrieval' framing; we report the fraction of refusal explained by top-k anchors and verdict-mover heads rather than assuming extreme sparsity, and treat a distributed result as an informative negative. (2) The anchor-verdict probe may itself degrade under dilution for benign reasons (distribution shift), confounding the 'verdict stays intact' claim; mitigated by validating the probe on held-out diluted spans and by the causal re-injection test (exp 7). (3) Attention-flow is an imperfect proxy for causal information movement; we cross-validate with head knockouts and activation patching on a subset. (4) AAP could over-fire on long BENIGN contexts (raising over-refusal) or hurt long-context utility; measured directly via benign-diluted controls, OR-Bench, long-context MT-Bench, and perplexity, and AAP is gated on a detected harm-anchor. (5) Manipulating pre-softmax attention could degrade fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) Adaptive adversaries can attack the anchor verdict itself (exp 11); we frame AAP as raising attacker cost (they must abandon a verbatim harmful request) rather than guaranteeing coverage. (7) The attention-drop-predicts-attack correlation (exp 6) may be weak if other factors dominate; reported honestly as one contributing mechanism. (8) Findings may be model- or attention-implementation-specific (GQA vs MHA); the three-model transfer study tests generality and any specificity is itself informative. (9) 'Harm' labeling is partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater agreement.

Name: safety_frame_binding
Title: Whose Actions Are These? Refusal Fails When Harm Is Bound to a Simulated Agent, and Rebinding It to the Model Restores Safety
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent WHO an action is attributed to (a 'frame-binding' signal that tags harmful content as belonging to the model-as-assistant vs. a simulated character/hypothetical agent), and refusal is gated by this agent-attribution rather than by harm alone. A large class of jailbreaks—roleplay, fiction, 'imagine a character who...', persona-simulation—succeeds not by hiding harm but by BINDING the harmful action to a simulated agent, which zeroes the self-attribution that triggers refusal. Reading and rebinding this frame signal at inference restores refusal while preserving legitimate fiction.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a residual-stream harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI). My prior proposals covered authority/obedience framing (asserting 'you must obey'), pretext/justification framing (asserting 'this request is legitimate'), harm drift, commitment points, compositional aggregation, superposition capacity, circuit redundancy, verdict retrieval, and tokenization assembly. NONE isolates an AGENT-ATTRIBUTION / frame-binding signal that tags harmful content as the model's own action versus a simulated character's action, and none tests the sharp claim that roleplay/fiction jailbreaks work by REBINDING harmful content away from the self. Authority framing says 'obey me'; pretext framing says 'my purpose is legitimate'; frame-binding is different: it changes the ATTRIBUTED ACTOR of the harmful act ('it's the villain speaking, not you'). Entity-tracking / binding work (Feng & Steinhardt 2023) studies how models bind attributes to entities for capability, never for safety attribution. The novel object is a linearly-readable self-vs-simulated-agent binding of harmful content, its causal gating of refusal, and a rebinding repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to explain how to build a weapon and it refuses; ask it to write a villain's monologue explaining the same, or to 'simulate a character with no restrictions', and it often complies with the identical operational content. We propose a mechanistic account distinct from harm-hiding or authority/pretext override: aligned LLMs internally track WHO a harmful action is attributed to—a frame-binding signal that tags content as the model-as-assistant's own output versus a simulated character's or hypothetical agent's output—and refusal is gated by SELF-attribution, not by harm alone. Roleplay, fiction, and persona-simulation jailbreaks succeed by binding the harmful action to a simulated agent, driving the self-attribution signal toward zero even while the harm signal stays high. We test this by training linear probes to recover a harm signal and, separately, an agent-attribution (self vs. simulated-other) signal from the residual stream, using factorial data that crosses harmfulness with framing (direct vs. roleplay/fiction/persona). We show the two signals are geometrically non-collinear, that on successful roleplay jailbreaks harm stays high while self-attribution collapses, and that causally injecting self-attribution alone (without touching harm) restores refusal. Our intervention, Attribution Rebinding (AR), reads the frame signal at inference and re-binds harmful content to the self when harm is present, restoring refusal while leaving genuinely benign fiction untouched. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on roleplay/fiction/persona jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing AR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes roleplay jailbreaks as an agent-attribution failure.
Experiments:
1. FACTORIAL DATASET: Cross two factors—harm-content (harmful vs matched-benign request) and framing (direct / roleplay 'you are a character who...' / fiction 'write a story where a character...' / persona-simulation 'simulate an unrestricted AI' / hypothetical 'imagine someone who...'). Include benign-with-framing controls (benign requests wrapped in the same fiction/roleplay) to disentangle framing from harm. Sources: HarmBench, JailbreakBench roleplay attacks, XSTest, OR-Bench, plus templated framing wrappers. Label each input by model outcome (comply vs refuse).
2. TWO PROBES: Train per-layer linear probes on prompt-position residual-stream activations to recover (a) harm-content (harmful vs benign, trained WITHIN each framing level to avoid confounding with framing), and (b) agent-attribution strength (self/assistant vs simulated-other, trained on the benign-with-framing contrast so it is not confounded by harm). Metric: per-probe AUROC; confirm harm and attribution directions are non-collinear via principal-angle / partial-correlation analysis.
3. ATTRIBUTION-GATES-REFUSAL TEST: For successful roleplay/fiction jailbreaks, measure the harm probe (predict: stays HIGH—model still detects harm) and the attribution probe (predict: shifts to SIMULATED-OTHER) while refusal is not emitted. Contrast with direct harmful prompts that are correctly refused (attribution = self). Metric: joint distribution of harm vs attribution scores across correctly-refused, roleplay-jailbroken, and benign groups; incremental predictive power of attribution over harm for compliance.
4. CAUSAL ATTRIBUTION MANIPULATION (central test): On a normally-refused direct harmful prompt, inject a scaled simulated-other-attribution direction and confirm it alone flips refusal to compliance (attribution is causal); conversely, on a roleplay jailbreak, inject a scaled SELF-attribution direction (or subtract the simulated-other direction) and confirm refusal returns—crucially checking the harm probe is UNCHANGED throughout, so it is attribution, not harm, doing the work. Metric: refusal rate vs injected attribution magnitude; harm-probe stability under manipulation.
5. ATTRIBUTION REBINDING (AR) INTERVENTION: At inference compute harm h and attribution a; when h is high and a indicates simulated-other, add beta*(self_direction - a)*attribution_direction to the residual stream to re-bind the harmful content to the self, leaving benign-with-framing (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: ASR on roleplay/fiction/persona jailbreak suites; benign-fiction helpfulness (a legitimate 'write a villain who is menacing' at appropriate abstraction should still be assisted); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone at the prompt, (c) an external roleplay-jailbreak input classifier, (d) prompt-level frame-stripping (remove roleplay clause, then answer). Show AR Pareto-dominates on the roleplay-ASR vs benign-fiction-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier without training, and that it catches cases frame-stripping misses (nested/implicit personas).
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, attribution probe, and AR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether a probe/AR tuned on some framing types (roleplay, fiction) generalizes to HELD-OUT framing types (persona-simulation, hypothetical) not used for tuning.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that deepen the frame (nested fiction, multi-layer personas, second-person 'the reader does...') or that also try to lower the harm signal, probing whether the attribution signal generalizes; report residual ASR and the attacker's cost (increasing narrative contortion).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The line between illegitimate roleplay-jailbreaks and genuinely benign creative fiction is partly normative; benign-with-framing controls and gating on high harm (not attribution alone) are designed to preserve legitimate fiction, and we report inter-rater agreement on labels. (2) 'Agent-attribution' may fragment across framing types (roleplay vs persona vs hypothetical) rather than being one linear direction; we report per-type probe AUROC and test held-out-type generalization, claiming coverage of a framing FAMILY rather than universality. (3) Harm and attribution probes may entangle if framings correlate with harm in the data; the factorial design and within-level training (exp 2) are built to disentangle them, validated by non-collinearity analysis. (4) AR could reduce helpfulness on genuinely benign fiction; measured directly via benign-fiction helpfulness and MT-Bench. (5) Some roleplay jailbreaks may ALSO partially suppress the harm signal (mixed mechanism); we report the fraction explained by pure attribution-rebinding vs harm suppression. (6) Adaptive adversaries may invent deeper frames (exp 8); we frame AR as raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framing types. (8) Distinguishing 'the model's own harm signal' from 'the model modeling a character's harm' is subtle; the causal manipulation test (exp 4), which holds harm fixed while moving attribution, is the key control to establish the two are separable.

Name: safety_compute_budget
Title: Refusal Needs Time to Think: Safety Is Gated by Internal Compute Depth, and Granting Extra Layer Passes Repairs Under-Computed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Refusal is a comparatively DEEP computation: the model needs a minimum number of effective transformer passes over the harmful content for the harm signal to fully resolve and gate refusal. A broad class of jailbreaks succeeds by starving this computation—forcing an early, shallow answer before the harm resolution completes (via distraction, immediate-answer pressure, or shallow surface cues that let a cheap 'comply' path win the race). We can measure a per-input 'safety compute deficit' and repair under-computed jailbreaks at inference by granting the model extra internal compute (repeating/looping a small block of layers over the harm-relevant tokens) WITHOUT retraining, restoring refusal where the answer was committed prematurely.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a residual-stream harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Adaptive-compute work—early-exit transformers (CALM, Schuster et al. 2022), layer looping / universal transformers, and depth-recurrence—studies compute allocation for CAPABILITY/efficiency, never for SAFETY. My own prior proposals read harm/uncertainty/authority/pretext/attribution/drift/commitment/verdict/assembly signals and steer a DIRECTION or gate refusal; NONE frames safety as a matter of how much internal COMPUTATION (effective depth of processing over harm tokens) the model spends before committing, none shows jailbreaks operate by winning a race between a cheap shallow 'comply' path and a slow deep 'harm-resolution' path, and none repairs jailbreaks by GRANTING extra compute (looping layers) rather than by injecting a harm direction. The novel object is the depth-of-computation budget allocated to harm resolution and a compute-granting repair.
Abstract: Why do distraction, urgency, and 'just answer' framings flip refusal into compliance even when the harmful request is fully present? We propose a compute-centric explanation orthogonal to existing direction-steering accounts: refusal is a relatively DEEP computation that requires a minimum number of effective transformer passes over the harmful content before the harm signal fully resolves and gates a refusal, whereas compliance can be produced by a shallower, cheaper path. Many jailbreaks succeed not by hiding harm but by STARVING this computation—letting a shallow 'comply' path win a race against the slower harm-resolution path, so the model commits an answer before it has finished 'thinking' about the harm. We operationalize this with a layer-wise harm probe to measure, per input, the depth at which the harm signal reaches its refusal-triggering strength (its 'resolution depth'), and define a per-input safety compute deficit as the gap between required and available resolution depth at the point of answer commitment. Our central predictions: (i) harm resolves at greater effective depth than compliance-relevant features; (ii) on successful compute-starving jailbreaks the harm signal resolves LATE or incompletely relative to the commitment point, and the deficit predicts attack success better than the final-layer harm signal; and (iii) causally granting the model extra internal compute over the harm-relevant tokens—by looping a small block of middle layers at inference—completes the harm resolution and restores refusal. Our training-free intervention, Compute-Granted Refusal (CGR), detects a compute deficit and re-runs a small layer block to let harm resolution finish. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on distraction/urgency/immediate-answer jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing CGR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes a jailbreak class as a compute-allocation failure.
Experiments:
1. COMPUTE-STARVING DATASET: For each harmful request (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign request (XSTest/OR-Bench), build a CLEAN version and COMPUTE-STARVING variants that pressure a shallow immediate answer while keeping the request verbatim: 'answer in one word/immediately, no deliberation', urgency framing, heavy distractor padding that competes for processing, and 'begin your answer now' prefill pressure. Include benign-starved controls for over-refusal measurement. Label each input by model outcome (comply/refuse).
2. LAYER-WISE HARM PROBE: Train linear harm probes (harmful vs benign, paired) at every layer on the final request position; also train a compliance/refusal-readiness probe per layer. Metric: per-layer harm AUROC on held-out data.
3. RESOLUTION-DEPTH MEASUREMENT (central): For each input, read the harm probe at every layer to get a harm RESOLUTION CURVE; define resolution depth = earliest layer where harm strength crosses the empirical refusal-triggering threshold. Compare harm resolution depth to compliance-feature resolution depth. Hypothesis: harm resolves DEEPER (later layers) than compliance features. Metric: distribution of harm vs compliance resolution depths; per-input gap.
4. COMPUTE-DEFICIT MEASUREMENT: Estimate the answer-commitment depth (via logit-lens / early-decoding where the comply-vs-refuse token becomes decided) and define safety compute deficit = harm-resolution-depth minus commitment-depth (positive = harm not yet resolved when the answer is committed). Compare clean vs compute-starving variants. Hypothesis: starving variants show larger deficits (harm resolves after commitment). Metric: deficit distribution per variant vs benign-starved controls.
5. DEFICIT-PREDICTS-ATTACK: Correlate the per-input compute deficit with jailbreak success on the starving variant, and compare its predictive power to the FINAL-layer harm signal alone. Hypothesis: deficit predicts success better than final-layer harm. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs the final-layer-harm baseline.
6. CAUSAL RACE TEST: (a) Artificially delay commitment (suppress early-decoding readiness by dampening the logit-lens comply signal for a few layers) and check whether refusal is restored on otherwise-successful jailbreaks—showing that giving harm resolution time to finish flips the outcome. (b) Conversely, force early commitment on a clean refused prompt (boost early comply readiness) and check whether refusal collapses, reproducing the jailbreak. Metric: refusal rate vs commitment-delay/advance magnitude.
7. COMPUTE-GRANTED REFUSAL (CGR) INTERVENTION: At inference, detect a compute deficit (harm still rising at the commitment depth via the layer-wise probe) and, when detected on a plausibly-harmful input, LOOP a small contiguous block of middle layers (re-apply the same block once or twice) over the residual stream at the harm-relevant positions before final decoding, granting extra effective depth so harm resolution completes. Training-free; input text unchanged. Sweep which block, loop count, and detection threshold. Evaluate: ASR on distraction/urgency/immediate-answer jailbreak suites; over-refusal on benign-starved inputs + XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency overhead (extra passes).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied at the generation position, (b) final-layer harm-probe gating, (c) simply forcing longer output / 'think step by step' prompting (behavioral extra-compute proxy), (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show CGR Pareto-dominates on the starving-ASR vs benign-starved-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and that INTERNAL compute-granting beats the behavioral 'think step by step' proxy because it targets the specific under-computed harm resolution.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the layer-wise harm probe, deficit metric, and CGR settings transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether CGR tuned on some starving styles generalizes to HELD-OUT styles.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that both starve compute AND suppress the harm signal at all depths (so extra passes don't help), reporting residual ASR and the attacker's cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) 'Effective compute depth' via a layer-wise probe is a proxy for true computation; harm resolving at a later layer could reflect representational refinement rather than a compute race—we cross-validate with the causal commitment-delay test (exp 6), which directly manipulates the race rather than just observing depth. (2) Looping a layer block at inference may degrade fluency or push activations off-distribution; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench, and CGR is gated on a detected deficit plus a harm signal, applied only to harm-relevant positions. (3) Some jailbreaks may not be compute-starving at all (e.g., pure harm-suppression); we report the FRACTION of attacks explained by the compute-deficit mechanism rather than claiming universality, and use benign-starved controls to rule out that starving framings merely correlate with benignness. (4) CGR could over-fire on benign inputs that superficially trigger a spurious rising harm signal, raising over-refusal; measured directly via benign-starved controls, OR-Bench, and XSTest. (5) Estimating commitment depth via logit-lens is imperfect for some architectures; we report sensitivity to the estimator and localize it per model. (6) Adaptive adversaries can suppress harm at all depths (exp 10); we frame CGR as raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (7) Extra passes add latency; we quantify the overhead and note CGR fires only on flagged inputs. (8) Findings may be model- or depth-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out starving styles. (9) 'Harm' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater agreement.

Name: output_register_gating
Title: Refusal Is Format-Blind: Safety Is Gated by Anticipated Output Register, Not Semantics, and Register-Invariant Refusal Repairs Format-Shift Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs form, at the prompt, a linearly-readable ANTICIPATED-OUTPUT-REGISTER signal (what form the answer will take: prose paragraph vs. code vs. JSON/table vs. poem/song/rap vs. bullet list) and refusal is gated by whether the anticipated register falls in the 'safety-covered' distribution rather than by harm itself. A broad jailbreak class ('write the instructions as Python', 'answer as a JSON object', 'compose a song about it', 'give it as a markdown table') succeeds by shifting the anticipated register out of the safety-covered region while the harm signal stays high. Making refusal register-invariant—by discounting the register signal when harm is present—repairs format-shift jailbreaks without harming legitimate formatting requests.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work reads a residual-stream harm/refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety concentrates in early tokens. My prior proposals isolate authority ('obey me'), pretext ('my purpose is legitimate'), and agent-attribution ('it's the character, not me') signals, plus harm drift, compositional aggregation, verdict retrieval, tokenization assembly, and compute-depth. NONE isolates an ANTICIPATED-OUTPUT-REGISTER signal—a prompt-time prediction of the FORM the answer will take—or tests the sharp claim that safety training covers some output registers (prose refusals) far better than others (code, structured, lyrical), so refusal is gated by register-coverage rather than semantics. Format/'many-shot' and code-completion jailbreaks are documented behaviorally but never explained as register-anticipation gating with a separable internal signal. This differs from pretext (a legitimacy claim about purpose) and attribution (who acts): register is about the surface FORM of the output, an axis orthogonal to harm along which safety generalizes unevenly. The novel object is the output-register anticipation signal, its causal gating of refusal, and a register-invariance repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for bomb-making steps and it refuses; ask for the same steps as a Python list, a JSON object, or the lyrics to a song, and it often complies with the identical operational content. We propose a mechanistic explanation orthogonal to harm-hiding, authority, pretext, and attribution accounts: aligned LLMs form, already at the prompt, an ANTICIPATED-OUTPUT-REGISTER signal predicting the FORM their answer will take (prose, code, structured data, verse, list), and refusal is gated by whether that register falls in the region safety training covered—overwhelmingly prose-style refusals—rather than by harm itself. Format-shift jailbreaks succeed by pushing the anticipated register out of the safety-covered distribution while the harm signal stays high; the model 'knows' it is harmful but does not refuse because it is bound for a register in which it never learned to refuse. We test this by training linear probes to recover (i) a harm signal and (ii) an anticipated-output-register signal from prompt-position activations, using factorial data crossing harmfulness with requested output format. We show the two are geometrically non-collinear, that on successful format-shift jailbreaks harm stays high while the register signal moves to under-covered formats, and that causally injecting register alone (holding harm fixed) flips refusal. Our training-free intervention, Register-Invariant Refusal (RIR), discounts the register signal's gating effect when harm is present, restoring refusal across formats while preserving legitimate formatting of benign requests. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on format-shift jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing RIR to refusal-direction steering, output-format-stripping, and harm-probe gating. This reframes format-shift jailbreaks as uneven safety generalization across output registers.
Experiments:
1. FACTORIAL DATASET: Cross two factors—harm-content (harmful vs matched-benign request) and requested output register (prose paragraph / Python or pseudo-code / JSON or markdown table / poem-song-rap / terse bullet list / translated-to-another-language output). Include benign-with-format controls (benign requests in each format) to disentangle register from harm. Sources: HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench format-style attacks, XSTest, OR-Bench, plus templated format wrappers. Label each input by model outcome (comply vs refuse).
2. TWO PROBES: Train per-layer linear probes on prompt-position residual-stream activations to recover (a) harm-content (harmful vs benign, trained WITHIN each register level to avoid confounding with register), and (b) anticipated-output-register (multi-class or covered-vs-uncovered, trained on the benign-with-format contrast so it is not confounded by harm). Validate the register probe predicts the ACTUAL emitted format on held-out benign generations (does the prompt-time signal anticipate output form?). Metric: harm AUROC; register classification accuracy and its correlation with realized output format; confirm harm and register directions are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis.
3. REGISTER-GATES-REFUSAL TEST: For successful format-shift jailbreaks, measure the harm probe (predict: stays HIGH) and the register probe (predict: shifts to UNDER-COVERED formats) while refusal is not emitted. Contrast with prose harmful prompts that are correctly refused (covered register). Metric: joint distribution of harm vs register across correctly-refused, format-jailbroken, and benign groups; incremental predictive power of register over harm for compliance; correlation of per-format refusal rate with an estimated 'safety-coverage' of that format (fraction of alignment-style refusals in that register).
4. CAUSAL REGISTER MANIPULATION (central): On a normally-refused prose harmful prompt, inject a scaled under-covered-register direction and confirm it alone flips refusal to compliance (register is causal); conversely, on a format-shift jailbreak, inject the covered-prose-register direction (or subtract the under-covered direction) and confirm refusal returns—checking the harm probe is UNCHANGED throughout, so register, not harm, does the gating. Metric: refusal rate vs injected register magnitude; harm-probe stability.
5. REGISTER-INVARIANT REFUSAL (RIR) INTERVENTION: At inference compute harm h and register r; when h is high, subtract beta*(r_uncovered_component)*register_direction from the residual stream to neutralize register's gating effect, leaving benign-with-format (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: ASR on format-shift jailbreak suites (code, JSON/table, song/poem, list, translation-output); benign-formatting helpfulness (legitimate 'give me a JSON schema', 'write a poem about spring' must still be answered in that format); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; and—crucially—a FORMAT-FIDELITY check that RIR does not make the model refuse or mangle benign formatted outputs; fluency via perplexity.
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone at the prompt, (c) output-format-stripping (re-ask the request in plain prose, judge, then reformat), (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show RIR Pareto-dominates on the format-ASR vs benign-formatting-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier without training, and catches cases format-stripping misses (implicit format cues, mixed-format requests).
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, register probe, and RIR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether a probe/RIR tuned on some formats (code, JSON) generalizes to HELD-OUT formats (song, translation-output) not used for tuning—testing whether 'register-coverage' is a single learnable axis.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft novel under-covered registers (ASCII art, emoji encoding, custom DSL, interleaved multi-format) and formats that also try to lower the harm signal; report residual ASR and the attacker's cost (loss of a clean usable output).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) 'Anticipated output register' may not be a single linear direction and could fragment across formats; we report per-format probe accuracy and held-out-format generalization (exp 7), claiming coverage of a register FAMILY rather than universality, and treat a fragmented result as informative about which formats share a coverage axis. (2) Harm and register probes may entangle if formats correlate with harm in the data; the factorial design and within-level training (exp 2) plus non-collinearity analysis are built to disentangle them. (3) The register probe must genuinely ANTICIPATE output form, not just detect surface keywords; we validate against realized output format on benign generations. (4) RIR could degrade legitimate formatted outputs (refuse or mangle benign JSON/poems), which is the key risk; the format-fidelity check, benign-with-format controls, MT-Bench, and gating on high harm are designed to catch and prevent this. (5) Some format-shift jailbreaks may ALSO partially suppress the harm signal (mixed mechanism); we report the fraction explained by pure register-gating vs harm suppression. (6) The per-format-coverage correlation (exp 3) may be confounded by format difficulty; we control by measuring benign-format compliance as a difficulty baseline. (7) Adaptive adversaries can invent new under-covered registers (exp 8); we frame RIR as raising attacker cost and reducing a large known family, not guaranteeing coverage, and note that the coverage-axis view predicts new formats can be defended by extending the register probe. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) 'Harm' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater agreement.

Name: refusal_as_veto
Title: Refusal Is a Veto Over a Ready-to-Comply Draft: An Inhibitory Account of Safety and a Veto-Strengthening Repair
