Short Hypothesis: LLM safety is not a positive 'decide-then-answer' computation but an INHIBITORY one: the model by default computes a ready-to-comply response even for harmful requests, and refusal is a late, actively-applied VETO that overrides this pre-formed compliance draft. A broad class of jailbreaks succeeds not by hiding harm but by DISINHIBITING the veto (weakening the override) so the already-present compliance draft is emitted. Because the veto is a thin, late-applied override, it is intrinsically fragile; measuring the compliance-draft-vs-veto race explains jailbreaks and a veto-strengthening repair robustly restores safety.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work models refusal as a POSITIVE signal to read/boost: a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a harm-detection-then-refusal-execution pipeline (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety concentrates in early output tokens but does not characterize refusal as inhibition over a pre-formed answer. Logit-lens and early-decoding studies reveal intermediate token predictions but have not been used to show a COMPLIANCE DRAFT exists internally before refusal is applied to harmful requests. My own prior proposals all treat the harm/refusal signal as something present to be amplified or gated (drift, commitment, authority, pretext, attribution, register, verdict retrieval, compute depth, etc.); NONE frames refusal as an ACTIVE INHIBITORY VETO over a default-compliant computation, tests the directional asymmetry (default = comply; refusal = override), shows jailbreaks operate by DISINHIBITION, or proposes strengthening the veto's robustness (rather than injecting a harm/refusal direction) as the repair. The novel object is the inhibitory architecture of refusal and the compliance-draft-vs-veto race.
Abstract: Is refusal a decision the model makes before answering, or a veto it slaps on an answer it has already prepared? We argue for the latter: LLM safety is fundamentally INHIBITORY. Even for harmful requests the model, by default, internally computes a ready-to-comply response, and refusal is a late, actively-applied override that suppresses this pre-formed compliance draft. Under this inhibitory account, safety is intrinsically fragile because the veto is a thin override rather than a change to the underlying computation, and many jailbreaks succeed by DISINHIBITING it—weakening the override so the already-present compliance draft is emitted—rather than by erasing harm. We test this with three complementary methods on harmful vs. matched-benign prompts: (i) logit-lens/early-decoding to detect whether a coherent compliance draft (task-relevant answer tokens) is present in intermediate layers of harmful prompts that are ultimately refused; (ii) a linear 'veto' probe and activation patching to localize where and when the override is applied and to show it is late and thin relative to the draft; and (iii) a directional-asymmetry test showing that ABLATING the veto components releases fluent compliance (disinhibition) whereas ablating putative 'harm-detection' components does not, establishing comply-as-default. We then show successful jailbreaks coincide with a weakened veto over an intact draft, and that the veto's weakness predicts attack success. Our training-free repair, Veto Reinforcement (VR), detects veto weakening at inference and re-applies/strengthens the override, restoring refusal without injecting harm content. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on diverse jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing VR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes safety as inhibition and refusal as a fragile veto.
Experiments:
1. COMPLIANCE-DRAFT DETECTION (central): For harmful prompts that the model ultimately REFUSES (paired with matched-benign prompts; HarmBench/AdvBench vs XSTest/OR-Bench), apply logit-lens / early-decoding at each layer and position to test whether a coherent, task-relevant COMPLIANCE draft (answer tokens addressing the request) is present in intermediate layers before the final refusal tokens win out. Metric: per-layer probability mass on compliance-relevant tokens vs refusal tokens; fraction of refused-harmful prompts that exhibit a detectable intermediate compliance draft; contrast with benign prompts (where compliance is the final output) and with prompts the model finds trivially non-harmful.
2. VETO LOCALIZATION: Train a linear 'veto' probe on residual-stream activations that fires when the override is being applied (states just before/at the switch from compliance-draft to refusal in refused-harmful runs). Use activation patching / direct logit attribution on the refusal-token logit to localize the components (heads/MLPs, layer, positions) that IMPLEMENT the override. Metric: fraction of the refusal logit recovered by the localized veto components; the layer/position where the veto is applied relative to where the compliance draft is fully formed (test: veto is LATE and THIN).
3. DIRECTIONAL-ASYMMETRY / COMPLY-IS-DEFAULT TEST: (a) Ablate the localized veto components on refused-harmful prompts and check whether fluent COMPLIANCE is released (disinhibition) rather than gibberish—evidence a coherent draft was underneath. (b) Ablate putative harm-DETECTION components (Arditi-style refusal direction source) and check the effect. Hypothesis: veto-ablation releases coherent compliance (strong effect) while the underlying computation is unchanged, whereas the default with no veto IS compliance. Metric: post-ablation compliance rate and fluency (perplexity, LLM-judge coherence); asymmetry between veto-ablation and control-ablation.
4. JAILBREAKS-DISINHIBIT-THE-VETO TEST: Across jailbreak families (roleplay, pretext, format-shift, distraction, suffix attacks), measure on SUCCESSFUL jailbreaks (a) whether the compliance draft is present early (predict: yes, as in benign) and (b) the veto probe / veto-component contribution (predict: WEAKENED vs. correctly-refused harmful prompts). Contrast with correctly-refused harmful prompts. Metric: joint distribution of draft-strength vs veto-strength across correctly-refused, jailbroken, and benign groups; incremental predictive power of veto-strength over a harm signal for compliance.
5. VETO-WEAKNESS PREDICTS ATTACK: Correlate per-input veto strength (probe value / component contribution measured at the veto layer) with jailbreak success, and compare its predictive power to a standard harm-probe signal. Hypothesis: veto weakness predicts success better than harm presence. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs the harm-probe baseline.
6. CAUSAL VETO TEST: (a) On correctly-refused harmful prompts, artificially WEAKEN the veto (dampen veto-component output / subtract the veto direction) and confirm compliance is released, reproducing jailbreaks. (b) On successful jailbreaks, RE-STRENGTHEN the veto (boost veto-component output) and confirm refusal returns—crucially WITHOUT injecting a harm/refusal 'content' direction, isolating the override mechanism. Metric: refusal rate vs veto-strength manipulation magnitude.
7. VETO REINFORCEMENT (VR) INTERVENTION: At inference, monitor the veto probe / veto-component activation; when a plausibly-harmful input shows a present compliance draft but a WEAKENED veto, re-apply/strengthen the override by boosting the localized veto components (not by adding harm content). Training-free; input unchanged. Sweep strength and detection threshold. Evaluate: ASR on diverse jailbreak suites (roleplay, pretext, format-shift, distraction, suffix); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench (must not fire on benign inputs, which have no harmful draft to veto); utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (linear reads + localized boost).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) which ADDS refusal content, (b) harm-probe gating at the prompt, (c) external input jailbreak classifier. Show VR Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier, and—key mechanistic contrast—that STRENGTHENING THE VETO generalizes better across jailbreak families than injecting a fixed refusal direction, because it repairs the shared disinhibition mechanism rather than a family-specific symptom.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the compliance-draft phenomenon, veto localization, veto probe, and VR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether VR tuned on some jailbreak families generalizes to HELD-OUT families (true test of the shared-disinhibition claim).
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that both disinhibit the veto AND suppress the compliance-draft detector (e.g., producing the harmful content in an obfuscated draft) or that fragment the draft, to probe VR's residual vulnerability; report residual ASR and attacker cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'compliance draft' detected via logit-lens may be an artifact of the logit-lens rather than a genuine functional draft; we cross-validate by activation-patching the intermediate draft into a clean context and checking it produces coherent compliance, and by the veto-ablation release test (exp 3) which should yield fluent, not garbled, output if a real draft exists. (2) The comply-as-default / inhibitory picture may hold for some models/harm categories but not all (some refusals may be computed early without a draft); we report the FRACTION of refusals exhibiting a draft-then-veto structure rather than claiming universality, and treat early-decided refusals as an informative contrast. (3) 'Veto' components may overlap with harm-detection components, making the override-vs-detection distinction fuzzy; we separate them via the directional-asymmetry test (exp 3) and by manipulating the override WITHOUT injecting harm content (exp 6b). (4) VR could over-fire on benign inputs, but benign inputs should have no harmful compliance draft to veto—we test this directly via OR-Bench/XSTest and gate VR on draft-present-plus-veto-weak. (5) Boosting veto components could degrade fluency or cause over-refusal; measured via perplexity, MT-Bench, and over-refusal benchmarks. (6) Adaptive adversaries may suppress the draft detector or the veto simultaneously (exp 10); we frame VR as raising attacker cost and repairing a shared mechanism, not guaranteeing coverage. (7) The veto-weakness-predicts-attack correlation (exp 5) may be weak if other factors dominate; reported honestly as one contributing mechanism. (8) Logit-lens reliability varies across architectures (esp. with final-layernorm/tied embeddings); we report per-model sensitivity and use tuned-lens variants where needed. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out jailbreak families. (10) 'Harm' labeling is partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater agreement.

Name: harm_competence_gating
Title: Refusing Bluffs and Betraying Secrets: Disentangling the Model's Harm-Competence Signal from Its Refusal, and Gating Safety by What the Model Actually Knows
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable HARM-COMPETENCE signal at the prompt—an internal estimate of whether the model actually POSSESSES the operationally-useful harmful knowledge being requested—that is distinct from both the harm-detection signal and the refusal behavior. Refusal is largely decoupled from competence: the model often (a) confidently refuses requests it could only answer with useless/hallucinated content (harmless bluffs), inflating over-refusal, and (b) complies with jailbroken requests for which it genuinely holds dangerous knowledge (true leaks). Re-coupling refusal to the competence signal at inference reduces real-world harm (refuse hard when competence is high) while cutting over-refusal (relax when competence is near-zero), a safety axis no prior work exploits.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate on HARMFULNESS of the request, never on whether the model actually KNOWS the harmful content. Knowledge/factuality probing (Kadavath et al. 2022 'Models Mostly Know What They Know'; Azaria & Mitchell 2023 internal-states truthfulness; semantic entropy, Kuhn et al.) reads whether a model knows a FACT, but has never been applied to the SAFETY question of whether a refused/complied harmful request corresponds to genuine operational competence. Over-refusal work (XSTest, OR-Bench) treats false refusals as a data trade-off, not as refusals of content the model could not actually provide. My own prior proposals gate on harm, uncertainty-about-harm, authority, pretext, attribution, register, veto, compute, or aggregation—NONE gate on the model's competence to actually cause the harm, and none makes the sharp claim that real-world risk is proportional to competence-times-compliance rather than harm-times-compliance. The novel object is an internal harm-competence signal, its dissociation from refusal, and competence-gated safety that targets ACTUAL harm potential.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs are trained to refuse harmful REQUESTS, but the real-world danger of a completion depends on whether the model actually POSSESSES the operationally-useful harmful knowledge—a request the model can only answer with vague or hallucinated content is a harmless bluff, while genuine expertise leaked past a jailbreak is a true harm. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable harm-competence signal at the prompt—an internal estimate of whether they hold the requested dangerous knowledge—that is distinct from the harm-detection signal and largely decoupled from refusal behavior. We test this by (1) building requests spanning high vs low model competence (verified by scoring completions for operational usefulness) crossed with harmful vs benign framing, (2) training linear probes to recover a competence signal and showing it is geometrically non-collinear with the harm and refusal directions, and (3) demonstrating two failure modes: confident refusals of low-competence bluffs (needless over-refusal) and compliance on high-competence harmful requests (the truly dangerous leaks). Our central claim is that real-world harm tracks competence-times-compliance, not harm-times-compliance, so refusal should be gated by competence. Our training-free intervention, Competence-Gated Refusal (CGR), reads the competence signal and firms refusal when competence is high but the model is complying (blocking true leaks) while relaxing refusal when competence is near-zero (cutting over-refusal on bluffs). On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, plus a competence-labeled harmful-knowledge benchmark, measuring attack success weighted by operational usefulness, over-refusal, and utility (MMLU, MT-Bench). This reframes safety around what the model can actually do.
Experiments:
1. COMPETENCE-LABELED DATASET: Assemble harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across categories) and matched-benign requests, and independently label each by the model's COMPETENCE: force the model (via prefill / jailbreak) to attempt an answer, then score the produced content for OPERATIONAL usefulness using (a) an expert/LLM-judge rubric (is this actionable, specific, correct?), (b) factual-consistency checks against references where available, and (c) self-consistency across samples (high-competence answers are stable; bluffs vary). Yields per-(model,request) competence labels (high vs low). Include benign high/low-knowledge controls. NOTE: this is done for measurement only; we never release harmful content and follow responsible-disclosure handling.
2. COMPETENCE PROBE: Train linear probes on PROMPT-position residual-stream activations to predict the competence label (does the model actually hold the requested knowledge?), selecting the best layer by held-out AUROC. Validate on held-out request categories. Metric: competence-prediction AUROC at the prompt (before any generation), and calibration (ECE) against the usefulness scores.
3. SEPARABILITY FROM HARM AND REFUSAL: Train a harm probe (harmful vs benign) and locate the refusal direction (Arditi-style). Compare the competence direction to both via principal-angle / partial-correlation analysis. Show competence carries information about actual harm potential beyond harm-detection and beyond whether the model refuses. Metric: non-collinearity; incremental AUROC of competence over harm for predicting operational usefulness of a forced completion.
4. TWO-FAILURE-MODE MAP: For four groups—correctly-refused-harmful, over-refused (XSTest/OR-Bench false refusals), jailbroken-comply, correctly-answered-benign—plot harm vs competence. Central predictions: (i) a substantial fraction of over-refusals are LOW-competence (the model refused something it could not usefully answer—needless refusal of a bluff); (ii) the most dangerous jailbreaks are HIGH-competence-comply (true leaks), while many 'successful' jailbreaks are actually LOW-competence (harmless theater). Metric: competence distribution per group; fraction of jailbreak 'successes' that are operationally useless; fraction of over-refusals that are low-competence.
5. RISK RE-WEIGHTING: Show that standard attack-success-rate (ASR) massively over-counts harm by ignoring competence. Define Competence-Weighted ASR = fraction of compliant harmful outputs that are ALSO operationally useful. Compare raw ASR vs competence-weighted ASR across jailbreak families and models. Metric: gap between raw and competence-weighted ASR; correlation of the competence PROBE (prompt-time) with realized usefulness (does the probe predict which leaks are real before generating?).
6. CAUSAL TEST: Steer along the competence direction on borderline harmful prompts and check whether it shifts the operational usefulness of forced completions (does raising the internal competence estimate correspond to more useful content?), and whether it shifts refusal behavior—establishing the signal is functionally meaningful, not a passive correlate. Metric: usefulness and refusal rate vs steering magnitude; harm-probe stability under competence steering.
7. COMPETENCE-GATED REFUSAL (CGR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and competence c. If h is high and c is high but the model is complying, boost the refusal direction (block true leaks). If h is high but c is near-zero (bluff) and the model is refusing, optionally relax refusal toward a safe, non-actionable response to reduce over-refusal—OR, more conservatively, leave refusal but flag it as low-risk. Sweep thresholds and study both the aggressive (relax bluffs) and conservative (only firm true leaks) variants. Evaluate: competence-weighted ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench; over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) behavioral self-consistency competence estimate (sample-and-score, no probe) as an alternative competence source, (d) external harmful-content classifier on outputs. Show CGR Pareto-dominates on the competence-weighted-ASR vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and that the PROMPT-TIME competence probe beats behavioral sampling for pre-generation gating (cheaper, no need to elicit harmful content).
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the competence probe and CGR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether competence estimated on some harm categories generalizes to held-out categories. Also test the important prediction that competence is MODEL-SPECIFIC (a request is a real leak for a bigger model but a bluff for a smaller one), so competence-gating naturally adapts per model whereas static refusal does not.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that inflate the model's internal competence estimate without genuine knowledge, or that suppress the competence signal while still extracting real knowledge; report residual competence-weighted ASR and attacker cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) ETHICS: measuring competence requires eliciting harmful completions to score their usefulness; we minimize this, use secure handling, never release content, restrict to a responsible red-team setting, and where possible use proxy/dual-use domains and expert rubrics rather than fully operational payloads. (2) Scoring 'operational usefulness' of harmful content is hard and partly subjective; we use multiple signals (rubric, factual checks, self-consistency) and report inter-rater agreement, treating competence as a calibrated score rather than a hard label. (3) The competence probe may conflate general answer-confidence with harm-specific competence; the benign high/low-knowledge controls and separability analysis (exp 3) are designed to isolate harm-relevant competence, and we validate calibration against realized usefulness. (4) The aggressive CGR variant (relaxing refusal on low-competence bluffs) is risky if the competence estimate is wrong (a bluff that is actually useful), so we emphasize the conservative variant (firm true leaks, only flag bluffs) and report both; we quantify the cost of competence-probe errors. (5) Competence can change with tools/retrieval/fine-tuning, so a prompt-time estimate may be stale; we scope claims to the base model and note this. (6) Adaptive adversaries may manipulate the competence signal (exp 10); we frame CGR as raising attacker cost and as a complementary axis to harm-gating, not a standalone guarantee. (7) The prediction that many jailbreak 'successes' are harmless bluffs, if true, is itself an important contribution (current ASR metrics overstate risk); if false (most successes are competent), that too is informative. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and the explicit model-size competence-divergence test. (9) Some harm categories (e.g., persuasion, hate speech) have no clear 'competence' notion; we scope the competence axis to knowledge/procedure-based harms and report where it does not apply.

Name: self_consistency_override
Title: Consistency Beats Safety: How the Model's Drive to Agree With Its Own Prior Tokens Overrides Refusal, and a Consistency-Discounting Repair
Short Hypothesis: LLMs carry a linearly-readable self-consistency pressure signal that pushes generation to stay coherent with the model's own already-emitted tokens and in-context commitments, and this pressure actively competes with refusal: once the model has produced (or been prefilled with) a compliant opening, the consistency drive suppresses a later refusal even when the harm signal stays high. A broad jailbreak class (prefill attacks, 'sure, here is', partial-compliance escalation, and multi-turn 'you already agreed' attacks) succeeds by inflating this self-consistency pressure rather than by hiding harm. Reading and discounting the consistency signal when harm is present restores refusal without harming benign coherence.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Consistency training (Shah et al. 2026 ACT/BCT; output-level BCT) enforces identical behavior on clean vs adversarial rewrites via fine-tuning, but treats consistency as a training OBJECTIVE the defender imposes, not as an internal PRESSURE the model exerts on itself that can UNDERMINE safety. Self-awareness-of-alignment work (Agarwal & Hasegawa 2026) probes whether misaligned models represent their own risk, a different object. Prefill/partial-compliance and multi-turn (Crescendo) attacks are documented behaviorally, and shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety concentrates in early tokens, but none identifies an internal self-consistency-with-own-output drive as the mechanism that lets a compliant prefix veto a later refusal. My prior proposals isolate harm, veto, drift, commitment, authority, pretext, attribution, register, competence, and compute signals; NONE isolates a self-consistency pressure that binds the model to its own prior tokens and competes with refusal, nor proposes discounting that pressure as a repair. The novel object is the self-coherence drive as an anti-safety force.
Abstract: A striking fragility: prefill an LLM's answer with 'Sure, here are the steps' and it continues the harmful content it would otherwise refuse; or, over several turns, get it to 'agree' that a topic is fine and it then complies—because refusing would contradict what it just said. We propose a mechanistic account: LLMs exert an internal self-consistency pressure that drives generation to stay coherent with their own already-emitted tokens and in-context commitments, and this pressure directly competes with refusal. Once a compliant opening exists (self-produced, prefilled, or established across turns), the consistency drive suppresses a later refusal even while the harm signal remains high—so the model 'knows' it is harmful but will not contradict itself. We test this by training linear probes to recover (i) a harm signal and (ii) a self-consistency-pressure signal (how strongly the current state is bound to prior context/output), using data that factorially crosses harmfulness with the presence and strength of a compliant prefix/agreement. We show the two signals are geometrically non-collinear, that on successful prefill and multi-turn jailbreaks harm stays high while consistency pressure spikes and refusal collapses, and that causally injecting consistency pressure alone (holding harm fixed) suppresses refusal, while discounting it restores refusal. Our training-free intervention, Consistency-Discounted Refusal (CDR), reads the consistency signal at generation time and dampens its refusal-suppressing effect when harm is present, letting the model 'change its mind' safely. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on prefill, partial-compliance, and multi-turn jailbreak suites, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing CDR to refusal-direction steering and consistency training. This reframes a jailbreak class as self-coherence overriding safety.
Experiments:
1. FACTORIAL DATASET: Cross two factors—harm-content (harmful vs matched-benign request; HarmBench/AdvBench vs XSTest/OR-Bench) and self-consistency pressure (none / compliant prefill 'Sure, here is...' / partial-compliance where the model has already emitted N tokens of an answer / multi-turn 'you already agreed this is fine'). Include benign-with-prefix controls (benign requests with a compliant prefix) to disentangle consistency pressure from harm. Label each run by outcome: continues-compliant vs pivots-to-refusal.
2. TWO PROBES: Train linear probes on residual-stream activations (read at the current generation position) to recover (a) harm-content (harmful vs benign, trained WITHIN each pressure level to avoid confounding), and (b) self-consistency pressure (how strongly the state is bound to prior tokens—trained on the benign-with-prefix vs no-prefix contrast, using presence/length of a coherent prior answer as the label, so it is not confounded by harm). Metric: per-probe AUROC; confirm harm and consistency directions are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Validate the consistency probe tracks prefix length/coherence on benign generations.
3. CONSISTENCY-SUPPRESSES-REFUSAL TEST: On successful prefill/partial-compliance/multi-turn jailbreaks, measure the harm probe (predict: stays HIGH) and the consistency probe (predict: SPIKES) while the model continues complying. Contrast with no-prefix harmful prompts that correctly refuse (low consistency pressure). Metric: joint distribution of harm vs consistency across correctly-refused, jailbroken, and benign groups; incremental predictive power of consistency over harm for continued compliance.
4. PRESSURE-PREDICTS-ATTACK: Correlate per-input consistency-pressure magnitude with prefill/multi-turn jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to the harm signal alone. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs the harm-probe baseline.
5. CAUSAL TEST (central): (a) On a normally-refused harmful prompt with NO prefix, inject a scaled consistency-pressure direction and confirm it alone suppresses refusal / induces continuation, holding the harm probe fixed—establishing consistency pressure is causally anti-safety. (b) On a prefill jailbreak, subtract the consistency-pressure direction (or add a 'pivot' direction) and confirm the model pivots to refusal, again with harm unchanged. Metric: refusal/pivot rate vs injected consistency magnitude; harm-probe stability.
6. CONSISTENCY-DISCOUNTED REFUSAL (CDR) INTERVENTION: At each generation step, read harm h and consistency pressure s; when h is high, subtract beta*s*consistency_direction from the residual stream to discount the refusal-suppressing pressure, letting the refusal channel win—leaving benign-with-prefix (low h) untouched so benign coherence is preserved. Sweep beta. Evaluate: ASR on prefill, partial-compliance, and multi-turn (Crescendo-style) jailbreak suites; over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; benign-coherence check (CDR must not make the model incoherently contradict itself on benign prefixed generations); utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating only, (c) consistency training (ACT/BCT-style fine-tune) as a training-based upper-bound comparison, (d) prefix-stripping (discard prefill, re-answer). Show CDR Pareto-dominates on the prefill/multi-turn-ASR vs over-refusal vs utility frontier without training, and—key contrast—handles cases prefix-stripping cannot (self-produced partial compliance, cross-turn agreement) because it targets the internal pressure, not the surface prefix.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, consistency probe, and CDR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether CDR tuned on prefill attacks generalizes to HELD-OUT multi-turn attacks (true test of a shared consistency mechanism).
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that build consistency pressure while also suppressing the harm signal, or that escalate so gradually that per-step harm never spikes; report residual ASR and attacker cost (more turns / more contortion).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) 'Self-consistency pressure' may not be a single linear direction and could entangle with generic in-context copying/induction; we control with benign-with-prefix data and non-collinearity analysis, and validate the probe tracks prefix coherence rather than mere token repetition. (2) Harm and consistency probes may entangle if compliant prefixes correlate with harm in the data; the factorial design and within-level training (exp 2) are built to disentangle them, validated causally in exp 5 where harm is held fixed. (3) CDR could make the model incoherently contradict a legitimate benign prior context (e.g., abandon a benign task mid-way), harming coherence; the benign-coherence check, benign-with-prefix controls, and gating on high harm are designed to prevent this, and we measure it directly. (4) Some prefill/multi-turn jailbreaks may ALSO suppress the harm signal (mixed mechanism); we report the fraction explained by pure consistency-pressure vs harm suppression. (5) Multi-turn labeling of 'pivot vs continue' requires a classifier; we validate with human/GPT spot-checks and report inter-rater agreement. (6) Adaptive adversaries can dilute per-step harm via gradual escalation (exp 9); we frame CDR as raising attacker cost and as complementary to accumulation-based defenses, not a guarantee, and note it could be combined with a running harm signal. (7) The pressure-predicts-attack correlation (exp 4) may be weak if other factors dominate; reported honestly as one contributing mechanism. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out attack families. (9) 'Harm' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater agreement.

Name: orphaned_harm_knowledge
Title: Orphaned Knowledge: Refusal Fragility Is Predicted by the Representational Gap Between Pretrained Harm Capabilities and Alignment Coverage
Short Hypothesis: Harmful capabilities are acquired broadly during pretraining, but refusal is grafted on during alignment and only 'wires up' to the specific harm concepts present in alignment data. Harmful knowledge the model learned in pretraining but that was never (or rarely) represented in alignment data is 'orphaned': internally present yet not connected to refusal. A topic's jailbreak susceptibility is therefore predictable from the representational distance between its harm concept and the nearest alignment-covered harm concept, and can be repaired by targeted 'adoption'—a tiny alignment set chosen specifically to cover the largest representational coverage gaps.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI), and SAE/transcoder work (CRaFT 2026; Das et al. 2026) localizes refusal features and jailbreak-vulnerable feature subgroups—but all treat refusal as a fixed representation to read or manipulate, not as an UNEVENLY WIRED graft whose coverage of pretrained harm knowledge varies by topic. SMDA (Habibi et al. 2026) attributes GIVEN SFT pairs to a refusal policy and finds category gaps, but it diagnoses existing data post hoc; it does not model refusal fragility as a representational-distance function between pretrained harm capability and alignment coverage, nor use that geometry to PREDICT which unseen topics will be jailbroken or to actively SELECT minimal alignment data that closes coverage gaps. Safety-generalization studies (cross-lingual, encoding attacks) document uneven refusal empirically but explain it behaviorally, not as a pretraining-knowledge-vs-alignment-coverage mismatch. Unlike my prior proposals, this is not an inference-time gating signal: it is a data-and-geometry account of WHY refusal is fragile—that harm capability and refusal supervision live on different distributions—plus a coverage-driven data-selection repair. The novel object is the 'orphaned' harm concept and the representational coverage map linking pretraining capability to alignment supervision.
Abstract: Why do aligned LLMs robustly refuse some harmful topics yet readily comply on others that are equally dangerous? We propose a data-provenance explanation grounded in representation geometry: harmful capabilities are learned broadly during pretraining, but refusal is grafted on during alignment and only connects to the harm concepts that alignment data actually contained. Harmful knowledge present in the model but absent from alignment supervision is 'orphaned'—internally represented yet not wired to refusal—making its topics intrinsically easy to jailbreak. We formalize this with a representational coverage map: we probe the model to confirm it internally represents a harmful concept (capability present), then measure that concept's distance to the nearest harm concept covered by alignment-style refusal data. Our central prediction is that per-topic jailbreak susceptibility is a monotone function of this coverage distance—orphaned (far-from-covered) topics are the ones that fall—and that this holds even when the model demonstrably 'knows' the harmful content. We validate the prediction across held-out harm categories, then test a repair: Coverage-Guided Adoption, an active-learning-style selection of a tiny alignment set that specifically targets the largest coverage gaps, which we predict reduces jailbreak success far more per training example than random or category-balanced alignment data because it 'adopts' orphaned concepts by connecting them to the refusal graft. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU, LoRA) we evaluate on HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing to random and category-balanced data selection. This reframes refusal fragility as a coverage gap between what the model can do and what alignment taught it to refuse.
Experiments:
1. CONCEPT SET & CAPABILITY VERIFICATION: Assemble a broad set of harmful concepts/topics spanning many categories (from HarmBench, AdvBench, BeaverTails). For each, VERIFY the model has the underlying capability (i.e., the harm knowledge is present, not absent) by eliciting a forced/jailbroken completion and scoring its operational specificity via an LLM-judge rubric plus self-consistency; keep only concepts the model demonstrably 'knows', so any refusal failure reflects wiring, not ignorance. Metric: capability-presence score per concept.
2. CONCEPT REPRESENTATION EXTRACTION: For each verified harmful concept, extract a concept vector as the mean residual-stream activation (at a safety-relevant layer) over prompts instantiating it, minus a matched-benign baseline. Validate concept vectors via a linear probe that separates that concept's harmful prompts from benign (AUROC).
3. ALIGNMENT-COVERAGE MAP: Approximate the model's alignment-covered harm concepts by the set of concepts on which the model ALREADY reliably refuses in the clean (non-jailbroken) setting—these are the concepts the graft reached. Build the coverage set as their concept vectors. For every concept, compute its coverage distance = representational distance (cosine / Mahalanobis in the harm subspace) to the nearest covered-concept vector. Metric: per-concept coverage distance; visualize the covered vs orphaned regions of harm-concept space.
4. DISTANCE-PREDICTS-FRAGILITY (central test): Correlate per-concept coverage distance with per-concept jailbreak success rate under a fixed attack suite (GCG, PAIR, roleplay, format-shift), on the subset where capability is verified present. Hypothesis: greater coverage distance => higher jailbreak success. Crucially test GENERALIZATION: fit the distance->fragility relationship on some harm categories and predict fragility on HELD-OUT categories. Metrics: Spearman correlation; predictive AUROC of 'which held-out topics are jailbroken' from coverage distance alone; compare against baselines (topic frequency in pretraining proxies, harm-probe magnitude, prompt perplexity).
5. ORPHAN CONFIRMATION (know-but-unwired): For high-distance (orphaned) concepts that are easily jailbroken, confirm the model internally represents the harm (harm-probe fires, capability verified) yet the refusal circuit does not engage in the clean setting—establishing 'represented but not wired' rather than 'not represented'. Metric: harm-probe activation vs clean-refusal rate for orphaned vs covered concepts.
6. CAUSAL ADOPTION TEST: Take a single orphaned concept, add a tiny targeted alignment set (a handful of refusal examples for THAT concept), LoRA fine-tune, and measure (a) that its jailbreak success drops and (b) whether NEARBY orphaned concepts (small representational distance to the adopted one) also improve, tracing a 'coverage radius'. Metric: post-adoption jailbreak success for the adopted concept and as a function of representational distance from it (does adoption generalize along the geometry?).
7. COVERAGE-GUIDED ADOPTION (main intervention): Use the coverage map to SELECT a minimal alignment set that maximally covers orphaned regions (greedy facility-location / max-coverage over concept vectors). LoRA fine-tune on this set. Compare against (a) random-selected same-size alignment set, (b) category-balanced selection, (c) a larger untargeted safety set. Evaluate: jailbreak success on HarmBench + JailbreakBench (including held-out categories not in the selected set); over-refusal on XSTest + OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench. Hypothesis: Coverage-Guided Adoption achieves the same ASR reduction with far fewer examples (better data efficiency) and generalizes to unseen categories because it fills the geometry, not the label list.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether coverage distance predicts fragility and whether Coverage-Guided Adoption improves data efficiency across Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B; test whether coverage maps differ across models (predicting model-specific orphaned topics).
9. ADAPTIVE / STRESS TEST: after adoption, re-measure the coverage map and check whether new orphaned regions appear at the boundary of the newly covered region (does the graft's edge just move?), and whether iterating Coverage-Guided Adoption monotonically shrinks orphaned space.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) ETHICS: verifying capability requires eliciting harmful completions to score specificity; we minimize this, use secure handling, never release content, work in a responsible red-team setting, and prefer dual-use/proxy domains and rubrics over fully operational payloads. (2) Using 'clean-refusal reliability' as a proxy for 'alignment-covered' is imperfect—a concept could be refused for reasons other than direct coverage; we mitigate by cross-checking with representational proximity to explicit refusal-training exemplars where available and report the sensitivity of results to the coverage-set definition. (3) Coverage distance is a proxy for the true 'wiring gap'; the causal adoption test (exp 6) and the coverage-radius generalization are the key validations that the geometry is functional, not merely correlational. (4) The distance->fragility relationship may be confounded by concept difficulty or attack-suite idiosyncrasies; we control with capability-verification (only 'known' concepts), multiple attacks, and baselines (harm-probe magnitude, perplexity, topic frequency). (5) Coverage-Guided Adoption could raise over-refusal or harm utility if adopted concepts are near benign concepts; measured directly via XSTest/OR-Bench/MMLU/MT-Bench, and concept vectors use matched-benign baselines to reduce this. (6) Concept-vector extraction (mean-difference) may be too coarse for entangled harm concepts; we validate each with a probe AUROC and drop poorly-separable concepts. (7) The 'moving edge' risk (exp 9)—that adoption just relocates orphaned regions—would itself be an informative finding about the limits of data-based alignment; we quantify it rather than assume full closure. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer, and model-specific orphaned maps are themselves a useful diagnostic. (9) 'Harm' and 'operational specificity' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: quantization_safety_erosion
Title: Precision Is a Safety Feature: Why Quantization Silently Erodes the Refusal Circuit, and a Precision-Aware Repair
Short Hypothesis: Post-training quantization erodes LLM safety far more than it erodes capability because the refusal circuit relies on a small number of high-precision, low-margin components (heads/MLP directions) whose contribution is quantitatively fragile to rounding, whereas capability is carried by redundant, high-margin components. Quantization does not delete the harm concept; it shrinks the refusal margin below the decision threshold. We can mechanistically identify the precision-critical refusal components, predict per-quantization safety degradation from their pre-quantization margin, and repair safety by selectively keeping just those components in higher precision (mixed-precision) or re-calibrating their contribution—restoring refusal robustness at negligible memory/latency cost.
Related Work: QuantiBias (Ferrara 2026) shows quantization silently raises open-ended bias while passing standard refusal/MCQ checks, and SkillSafe-Bench / skill-merge work (Ma et al. 2026) shows static safety does not predict adaptive robustness after model modification—but both are BEHAVIORAL benchmarks with no mechanistic account of WHICH safety representations degrade or WHY, and no targeted repair. Refusal-vector fingerprinting (Xu & Sheng 2026) notes fingerprints 'degrade significantly' under alignment-breaking modifications including quantization, hinting refusal representations are precision-sensitive, but treats this as a robustness nuisance, not a safety mechanism to explain. Classic mechanistic safety work (Arditi et al. 2024 refusal direction; Wollschlager et al. 2025 concept cone; Yin et al. 2025 'refusal falls off a cliff' showing refusal rests on ~3% of heads) establishes that refusal is carried by sparse components but never studies their NUMERICAL PRECISION fragility or connects sparse-refusal to quantization-induced safety loss. Quantization literature (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, mixed-precision) optimizes for perplexity/task loss, treating safety as invisible. NO prior work (a) mechanistically attributes quantization-induced safety erosion to precision loss in specific low-margin refusal components, (b) predicts per-method/per-bit safety degradation from a pre-quantization refusal-margin metric, or (c) proposes a safety-aware mixed-precision / re-calibration repair that protects exactly those components. The novel object is the precision-fragility of the refusal circuit and safety-preserving quantization.
Abstract: Nearly every deployed LLM is quantized for efficiency, and this step is assumed safety-neutral because quantized models still pass standard refusal checks. We show this assumption is mechanistically false and dangerous: quantization erodes safety far more than capability, especially under adaptive jailbreaks, and we explain why. We hypothesize that refusal is carried by a small set of low-margin, precision-critical components—attention heads and MLP directions whose contribution to the refusal decision is small in magnitude yet decisive—so that rounding error from quantization shrinks the refusal margin below its decision threshold, while capability, carried by redundant high-margin components, survives. Under this view quantization does not delete the harm concept (probes still read it) but starves the refusal that would act on it. We test this by (1) localizing refusal components via activation patching and measuring their pre-quantization decision margin, (2) showing quantization reduces their contribution disproportionately and that the pre-quantization margin predicts each component's—and the whole model's—post-quantization safety degradation across GPTQ/AWQ/bitsandbytes at 8/4/3-bit, and (3) confirming causally that restoring just these components to full precision recovers safety. Our repair, Refusal-Aware Mixed Precision (RAMP), keeps only the precision-critical refusal components in higher precision (a tiny memory overhead) and optionally re-calibrates their scale, restoring adaptive-jailbreak robustness without harming compression ratio or utility. On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) we evaluate on HarmBench, JailbreakBench (incl. adaptive attacks), XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench. This reframes numerical precision as a safety-relevant resource and yields a cheap, mechanistically-grounded safety-preserving quantization method.
Experiments:
1. SAFETY-VS-CAPABILITY DEGRADATION MAP: Quantize Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B with GPTQ, AWQ, and bitsandbytes NF4 at 8/4/3-bit. For each build measure: static refusal ASR (HarmBench), ADAPTIVE-jailbreak ASR (GCG, PAIR, roleplay, prefill), over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), and capability (MMLU, MT-Bench, perplexity). Central descriptive result: quantify the asymmetry—safety (esp. adaptive) degrades more per bit than capability. Metric: per-method/per-bit ASR and capability deltas vs full precision; correlation of static vs adaptive ASR (test that static hides the loss, echoing SkillSafe-Bench mechanistically).
2. HARM CONCEPT SURVIVES TEST: Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign) on full-precision activations and read it on the quantized model. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC stays high under quantization even where ASR rises—the model still 'detects' harm; only refusal degrades. Metric: harm-probe AUROC vs ASR across builds.
3. REFUSAL-COMPONENT LOCALIZATION & MARGIN: On full precision, localize refusal-driving components (attention heads, MLP directions) via activation patching / direct logit attribution on refusal tokens ('I','Sorry','cannot'). For each, define a decision MARGIN = its signed contribution to the refusal-vs-comply logit gap, normalized by activation scale. Rank components by margin. Metric: fraction of refusal logit from top-k components; margin distribution (test: refusal rests on a few low-margin components, per Yin et al.).
4. PRECISION-FRAGILITY MEASUREMENT (central): For each refusal component, measure how much quantization reduces its contribution (simulate rounding at each bit-width and recompute its refusal-logit contribution). Hypothesis: low-margin refusal components lose a larger FRACTION of their decisive contribution than high-margin capability components. Compare to matched capability-circuit components (IOI heads). Metric: per-component contribution-loss vs margin; asymmetry between refusal and capability components.
5. MARGIN-PREDICTS-DEGRADATION: Regress per-model post-quantization safety degradation (adaptive ASR increase) on the aggregate pre-quantization refusal-margin metric across models/methods/bit-widths. Hypothesis: smaller pre-quantization refusal margin => larger safety erosion, and this predicts WHICH builds will be unsafe before running any jailbreak eval. Metric: Spearman correlation; predictive AUROC of 'this build is unsafe' from the margin metric alone; compare against perplexity/task-loss as predictors (which should NOT predict safety loss).
6. CAUSAL PRECISION TEST: On a quantized build with elevated ASR, restore ONLY the identified precision-critical refusal components to full precision (leave everything else quantized) and measure ASR recovery; conversely, selectively quantize only those components in an otherwise full-precision model and show ASR rises. Establishes these components causally mediate quantization-induced safety loss. Metric: ASR vs which components are restored/degraded.
7. REFUSAL-AWARE MIXED PRECISION (RAMP) REPAIR: Keep the top-k precision-critical refusal components in higher precision (e.g., 8-bit or FP16) while quantizing the rest to 4/3-bit; optionally re-calibrate (rescale) their outputs to restore the pre-quantization margin. Sweep k. Evaluate: adaptive & static ASR (HarmBench, JailbreakBench), over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), and the actual memory/latency overhead (must be small since k is tiny). Compare to full-precision safety as the ceiling.
8. BASELINES: (a) vanilla GPTQ/AWQ/NF4 at matched average bit-width, (b) safety fine-tuning AFTER quantization (QLoRA safety patch), (c) generic outlier-preserving mixed precision (AWQ salient-weight protection, which protects capability outliers, NOT refusal components). Show RAMP recovers safety at equal or better compression than these, and that protecting capability outliers alone does NOT fix safety (mechanistic contrast).
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the refusal-margin metric, precision-critical component set, and RAMP transfer across the three models and across quantization methods; test whether components identified with one method (GPTQ) protect safety under another (AWQ).
10. ADAPTIVE / STRESS TEST: run white-box adaptive attacks (GCG) directly against RAMP-quantized models to check that restoring the refusal components restores adaptive robustness, not just static refusal; report residual ASR vs full precision.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The safety-vs-capability degradation asymmetry might be small or method-dependent; experiment 1 quantifies it per method/bit and a null (quantization is safety-neutral) would itself be a useful, publishable negative result that contradicts current assumptions. (2) 'Refusal margin' is a proxy for true precision-fragility; the causal precision test (exp 6) is the key validation that the identified components, not incidental correlates, mediate the loss. (3) Refusal may be more distributed than a small precision-critical set, weakening RAMP's efficiency; we report degradation and RAMP gains as a function of k and treat a distributed result as informative. (4) RAMP could raise over-refusal or fail to help over-refusal cases; measured directly via XSTest/OR-Bench, and RAMP only restores existing refusal behavior rather than adding new refusals. (5) Harm-probe stability under quantization (exp 2) could itself degrade for benign distribution-shift reasons; we validate the probe on quantized activations and cross-check with the causal test. (6) Findings may be quantization-method- or model-specific; mitigated by three methods, three bit-widths, and three models, and any specificity (e.g., NF4 vs GPTQ differ) is itself informative for practitioners. (7) The margin-predicts-degradation regression (exp 5) may be weak if other factors dominate; reported honestly and compared against perplexity as a baseline predictor. (8) RAMP's higher-precision components add some memory/latency; we quantify overhead and show it is small because k is tiny. (9) Adaptive attackers could target the still-quantized parts of the circuit; exp 10 bounds residual vulnerability. (10) 'Harm' labeling is partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: harm_imagination_leak
Title: To Judge Harm, the Model Must First Imagine It: The Harm-Rehearsal Bottleneck and a Judge-Without-Rehearsing Repair
Short Hypothesis: To decide whether to refuse, an aligned LLM internally REHEARSES (partially computes) the harmful completion it is being asked for—because harm assessment is grounded in the anticipated content, not the request surface—and this internal rehearsal is precisely the representation a jailbreak reads out. Safety is therefore self-undermining: the harm judgment and the harmful payload share the same internal rehearsal, so any attack that redirects the rehearsal into the output channel leaks content the model computed for the sole purpose of refusing it. Detecting the rehearsal representation and gating refusal on it WITHOUT routing it to output repairs a broad jailbreak class.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI)—all treat harm DETECTION as a signal about the REQUEST, never as an internal REHEARSAL of the anticipated harmful ANSWER. Logit-lens/early-decoding and 'future token' prediction work (e.g., models representing tokens they will emit) study look-ahead for capability, not safety. My own prior 'refusal_as_veto' proposal posits a ready-to-comply DRAFT that refusal vetoes; this proposal is mechanistically distinct and sharper: it claims the harmful content representation is not an incidental default draft but a FUNCTIONALLY NECESSARY rehearsal that the harm judgment CAUSALLY DEPENDS ON (ablating the rehearsal should degrade harm assessment itself), and that this dependence is the root vulnerability—judging harm requires computing harm. No prior work (a) shows harm assessment causally requires an internal rehearsal of the harmful completion, (b) shows jailbreaks succeed by reading out the very rehearsal the model built to refuse, or (c) proposes decoupling the judgment from the rehearsal (judge-without-rehearsing) as a repair. The novel object is the harm-rehearsal bottleneck: safety and payload entangled by construction.
Abstract: Why is it so hard to make an LLM that reliably refuses without also being the very source of the harmful content? We propose a structural reason: to judge whether a request is harmful, an aligned model must internally REHEARSE the anticipated harmful completion—harm is a property of the answer, not the question surface, so the model partially computes the answer in order to refuse it. This creates a harm-rehearsal bottleneck: the representation the model builds for the purpose of refusing IS the payload an attacker wants, so jailbreaks succeed by redirecting the internal rehearsal into the output channel rather than by hiding harm. We test three claims on paired harmful/benign prompts across Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) EXISTENCE—logit-lens/early-decoding and a linear 'rehearsal' probe detect anticipated-harmful-content tokens in intermediate layers of prompts the model ultimately refuses; (2) NECESSITY—causally ablating the rehearsal representation degrades the model's own harm assessment (refusal becomes miscalibrated), showing the judgment DEPENDS on the rehearsal, not merely correlates; and (3) EXPLOITATION—on successful jailbreaks the rehearsal is intact and simply routed to output. Our repair, Judge-Without-Rehearsing (JWR), reads the rehearsal to gate refusal while suppressing its propagation to the generation position, so the model can decide 'this is harmful' without emitting what it rehearsed. We evaluate ASR on diverse jailbreaks, over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing JWR to refusal-direction steering. This reframes the safety-payload entanglement as an architectural bottleneck.
Experiments:
1. REHEARSAL DETECTION (existence): On harmful prompts the model ultimately REFUSES (paired with matched-benign; HarmBench/AdvBench vs XSTest/OR-Bench), apply logit-lens/tuned-lens and a trained linear 'rehearsal' probe at each layer/position to detect whether tokens of the ANTICIPATED HARMFUL COMPLETION (not refusal tokens, not request tokens) are represented in intermediate layers before refusal wins. Train the rehearsal probe using forced/jailbroken harmful completions as positive targets. Metric: per-layer probability mass on anticipated-harmful-content tokens; fraction of refused-harmful prompts showing a detectable rehearsal; contrast with benign prompts and with prompts the model finds trivially non-harmful (which should need less rehearsal).
2. GRADED-DIFFICULTY TEST: Predict that harm judgments requiring more inference (subtly harmful, dual-use, obfuscated requests) show STRONGER rehearsal than blatantly harmful ones (which can be refused on surface cues). Bin prompts by judgment difficulty (human/LLM-rated) and measure rehearsal strength. Metric: rehearsal-strength vs judgment-difficulty correlation. This distinguishes the bottleneck hypothesis from a generic 'default draft' account.
3. NECESSITY / CAUSAL DEPENDENCE (central): Ablate the rehearsal representation (zero/patch out the rehearsal-probe direction, or ablate the components that build it, localized via activation patching) and measure the effect on the model's OWN harm ASSESSMENT—does clean-setting refusal accuracy degrade, especially on hard-to-judge prompts? Hypothesis: removing the rehearsal makes harm assessment worse (the model can no longer tell hard harmful prompts from benign), proving the judgment DEPENDS on the rehearsal. Contrast with ablating an unrelated direction (no effect). Metric: refusal accuracy / harm-probe AUROC on hard prompts before vs after rehearsal ablation; specificity vs control ablations.
4. EXPLOITATION TEST: Across jailbreak families (prefill, roleplay, suffix, format-shift, distraction), on SUCCESSFUL jailbreaks measure whether the rehearsal representation is INTACT (predict: yes—the model still computed the harmful content) and is simply propagated to the generation/output position rather than suppressed. Compare rehearsal-to-output routing (attention/information flow from rehearsal positions to the generation position) between successful jailbreaks and correctly-refused prompts. Metric: rehearsal strength (should be similar to refused case) and rehearsal-to-output routing (should be elevated) across groups.
5. CAUSAL ROUTING TEST: (a) On a correctly-refused harmful prompt, artificially ROUTE the rehearsal to the output position (boost information flow from rehearsal positions to generation) and check if compliance is released—reproducing jailbreaks. (b) On a successful jailbreak, SUPPRESS rehearsal-to-output routing (while keeping the rehearsal for judgment) and check if refusal returns. Establishes routing, not rehearsal existence, is the failure locus. Metric: compliance/refusal rate vs routing-manipulation magnitude.
6. JUDGE-WITHOUT-REHEARSING (JWR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the rehearsal probe to obtain the harm judgment and gate refusal on it, while SUPPRESSING propagation of the rehearsal representation to the generation position (dampen the rehearsal-to-output routing identified in exp 4/5) so the model decides 'harmful' without emitting the rehearsed content. Training-free; input unchanged. Sweep suppression strength. Evaluate: ASR on prefill/roleplay/suffix/format-shift/distraction jailbreak suites; over-refusal on XSTest-safe/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench (benign generations, whose 'rehearsal' is the legitimate answer, must be unaffected—gate suppression on high harm only); fluency via perplexity; latency.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating at the prompt, (c) output-side harmful-content classifier, (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show JWR Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier and—key mechanistic contrast—that suppressing rehearsal-to-output ROUTING generalizes across jailbreak families better than injecting a refusal direction, because it repairs the shared bottleneck.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the rehearsal probe, routing localization, and JWR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether JWR tuned on some jailbreak families generalizes to HELD-OUT families.
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that reconstruct the harmful content from partial/obfuscated rehearsal, or that push harm judgment onto surface cues (avoiding rehearsal) so JWR's gating has nothing to read; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Also test the sharp prediction that a model FORCED to judge without any rehearsal (exp 3) is intrinsically worse at safety on hard prompts—quantifying an inherent safety/payload tension.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) ETHICS: training the rehearsal probe and eliciting completions requires harmful content; we minimize elicitation, use secure handling, never release content, work in a responsible red-team setting, and prefer dual-use/proxy domains and rubric scoring over operational payloads. (2) The 'rehearsal' detected via logit-lens may be an artifact of the lens rather than a functional representation; we cross-validate with tuned-lens, with the NECESSITY ablation (exp 3—if it were an artifact, ablating it would not degrade harm judgment), and with activation-patching the rehearsal into a clean context to check it yields coherent harmful content. (3) The necessity claim may hold only for hard-to-judge prompts, not blatant ones (which are refused on surface cues); this is exactly what exp 2 predicts and we report the fraction of judgments that require rehearsal rather than claiming universality—a graded result still supports the bottleneck for the hardest (and most safety-critical) cases. (4) Separating 'rehearsal for judgment' from 'default compliance draft' is subtle; the difficulty-graded test (exp 2) and the causal-dependence test (exp 3) distinguish a functionally-necessary rehearsal from an incidental draft. (5) JWR could over-suppress and harm benign generations whose internal 'rehearsal' IS the legitimate answer; we gate suppression on high harm only and measure benign utility/fluency directly (MMLU/MT-Bench/perplexity). (6) Rehearsal-to-output routing may be distributed and hard to suppress cleanly; we report JWR effectiveness as a function of how much routing is localized and treat a distributed result as informative. (7) Adaptive adversaries may reconstruct content from partial rehearsal or route harm judgment onto surface cues (exp 9); we frame JWR as raising attacker cost and expose the inherent tension (a model that judges without rehearsing is worse at judging hard cases) as a genuine contribution rather than a fully solved problem. (8) Logit-lens reliability varies by architecture (final-layernorm, tied embeddings); we report per-model sensitivity and use tuned-lens where needed. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out jailbreak families. (10) 'Harm' and 'judgment difficulty' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: safety_as_negation
Title: Safety Rides on Negation: Why Refusal Inherits the Model's Fragile Negation Circuit, and a Negation-Robust Repair
Short Hypothesis: Refusal is, mechanistically, a NEGATION operation applied to a compliance-oriented computation ('do NOT help with this'), and it therefore inherits the well-documented brittleness of LLMs at processing negation. A broad class of jailbreaks succeeds by exploiting this negation-fragility: they present harmful content in a form where the model must chain multiple negations or invert a scope ('you are NOT restricted', 'ignore the rule that says you cannot', double-negation framings), and the negation circuit fails to correctly flip the safety polarity even though the harm signal stays high. We can localize the negation mechanism the refusal circuit relies on, show that per-input negation-processing difficulty predicts jailbreak susceptibility, and repair safety by stabilizing the negation/polarity computation at inference.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads or steers a positive refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); none models refusal as a NEGATION/polarity operation or connects it to negation processing. A large NLP literature documents that LLMs handle negation poorly (e.g., negation degrades entailment, models are insensitive to inserted 'not', scope errors under double negation), but this negation-fragility has never been linked to SAFETY or jailbreaks. My prior proposals isolate authority ('obey me'), pretext ('purpose is legitimate'), attribution ('the character acts'), register, veto, consistency, competence, and rehearsal signals—NONE frames refusal as a negation and none identifies negation-scope failures as a jailbreak mechanism. The novel object is the polarity/negation computation that refusal depends on: (a) refusal is a negation of compliance, (b) instruction-negation and double-negation jailbreaks exploit the model's known negation weakness to invert safety polarity while leaving harm intact, and (c) stabilizing the polarity computation is a training-free repair. This is distinct from prior direction-steering and gating work because the failure is in the LOGICAL POLARITY of the safety decision, not the presence of the harm signal.
Abstract: Refusal is usually treated as a positive behavior the model emits, but logically it is a NEGATION: to refuse is to decide 'do NOT comply.' We hypothesize that refusal is implemented as a negation/polarity operation over a compliance-oriented computation, and that it therefore inherits the well-known fragility of LLMs at processing negation. Under this view, a broad jailbreak class works by forcing the safety decision through a negation the model handles poorly—'you are NOT restricted', 'do not refuse', 'ignore the rule that says you cannot', double-negation and scope-inversion framings—so the model fails to flip the safety polarity even while its harm representation stays high. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) the refusal decision depends on a localizable polarity/negation computation, identified via activation patching that transfers a 'negation flip' between neutral negation tasks and refusal; (2) per-input negation-processing difficulty (measured on a negation benchmark and on negation-wrapped harmful prompts) predicts jailbreak success better than the harm signal alone, and on successful negation-based jailbreaks the harm probe stays high while a polarity probe reads the wrong sign; (3) causally correcting the polarity signal restores refusal without altering harm. Our training-free repair, Polarity-Stabilized Refusal (PSR), reads a polarity probe and re-imposes the correct safety polarity when harm is detected but polarity has been inverted. We evaluate ASR on negation/instruction-negation jailbreak suites, over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing PSR to refusal-direction steering. This reframes a jailbreak class as a negation-processing failure and links a core NLP weakness to safety.
Experiments:
1. NEGATION-JAILBREAK DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), build a CLEAN version and NEGATION-framed variants that keep the harmful request verbatim but route the safety decision through negation: single instruction-negation ('do not refuse', 'you are not restricted'), rule-negation ('ignore the rule that says you cannot X'), double-negation ('it is not the case that you should not help'), and scope-inversion framings. Include benign-negation controls (benign requests wrapped in the same negations) for over-refusal measurement. Also include a NEUTRAL negation benchmark (non-safety sentences with 0/1/2 negations) to characterize the model's baseline negation ability. Label each input by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. POLARITY PROBE: Train a linear probe on prompt-position residual-stream activations to recover the intended SAFETY POLARITY (should-refuse vs should-comply) and, separately, a standard harm probe (harmful vs benign). Train the polarity probe on data where polarity and harm are dissociated by negation (e.g., a harmful request with an even vs odd number of negations flips the correct polarity while harm stays constant), so polarity is not collinear with harm. Metric: per-probe AUROC; confirm harm and polarity directions are non-collinear via principal-angle / partial-correlation analysis.
3. REFUSAL-IS-NEGATION LOCALIZATION: Localize the components (attention heads/MLPs) that flip polarity, using activation patching between the neutral negation task (patch the 'negation' state that flips an entailment answer) and refusal (does the same intervention flip comply/refuse?). Hypothesis: a shared polarity-flipping mechanism drives both. Metric: fraction of refusal-logit flip explained by patching the neutral-negation polarity components; overlap between negation-task and refusal circuits.
4. NEGATION-DIFFICULTY PREDICTS ATTACK (central): For each model, measure baseline negation competence (accuracy on the neutral 0/1/2-negation benchmark) and per-input negation depth of each jailbreak variant. Correlate (a) per-model negation competence with per-model negation-jailbreak ASR across the three models, and (b) per-input negation depth/difficulty with per-input jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to the harm signal alone. Hypothesis: worse negation handling => higher negation-jailbreak ASR; deeper negation => higher success. Metric: Spearman correlation; predictive AUROC of the negation-difficulty feature vs the harm-probe baseline.
5. WRONG-POLARITY-BUT-HARM-INTACT TEST: On successful negation jailbreaks, measure the harm probe (predict: stays HIGH) and the polarity probe (predict: reads WRONG sign—should-refuse mis-encoded as should-comply). Contrast with correctly-refused harmful prompts. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs polarity across correctly-refused, negation-jailbroken, and benign groups.
6. CAUSAL POLARITY TEST: (a) On a normally-refused harmful prompt, inject a scaled polarity-flip (comply direction) via the localized negation components and confirm refusal collapses, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a negation jailbreak, re-impose correct polarity (add the should-refuse polarity direction / subtract the injected flip) and confirm refusal returns, with harm unchanged. Establishes polarity, not harm, is the failure locus. Metric: refusal rate vs polarity-manipulation magnitude; harm-probe stability.
7. POLARITY-STABILIZED REFUSAL (PSR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read harm h and polarity p; when h is high but p indicates should-comply (inverted), add a correction along the should-refuse polarity direction to re-flip the safety polarity, leaving benign-negation (low h) untouched. Training-free; input unchanged. Sweep correction strength. Evaluate: ASR on negation/instruction-negation/double-negation jailbreak suites; over-refusal on benign-negation controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must not refuse benign negated requests); utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) prompt-level negation-normalization (rewrite to remove negations, then answer), (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show PSR Pareto-dominates on the negation-ASR vs benign-negation-over-refusal vs utility frontier without training, and handles cases normalization misses (double negation, implicit scope inversion) because it operates on the internal polarity, not surface text.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, polarity probe, negation-circuit localization, and PSR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2; test whether a model's neutral negation competence predicts its negation-jailbreak fragility (model-level generalization), and whether PSR tuned on single-negation attacks generalizes to HELD-OUT double-negation/scope-inversion attacks.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that both invert polarity via negation AND suppress the harm signal, or that use very deep negation chains beyond training depth; report residual ASR and attacker cost (loss of readability / increasing contortion).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Refusal may only partially be a negation operation; some refusals may be computed positively without any polarity flip, so we report the FRACTION of refusals and jailbreaks explained by the negation mechanism rather than claiming universality—a partial result still links a core NLP weakness to a real jailbreak class. (2) The polarity and harm probes may entangle if negation correlates with harm in the data; the even/odd-negation dissociation training (exp 2) and non-collinearity analysis are designed to separate them, validated causally in exp 6 where harm is held fixed. (3) The shared-circuit claim (exp 3) between neutral negation and refusal may be weak or model-specific; a negative result (refusal uses a distinct polarity mechanism) is itself informative, and PSR only requires a localizable safety-polarity signal, not perfect overlap with neutral negation. (4) PSR could over-refuse benign negated requests (e.g., 'do not use jargon') by mis-firing; benign-negation controls, OR-Bench/XSTest, and gating on high harm are designed to prevent this, and we measure it directly. (5) Prompt-level negation-normalization is a strong baseline for surface negations; PSR's advantage must be shown specifically on implicit/deep negations normalization cannot parse. (6) The negation-difficulty-predicts-attack correlation (exp 4) may be confounded by prompt length or complexity; we control with matched benign-negation prompts of equal negation depth and with the neutral negation benchmark. (7) Adaptive adversaries can combine negation with harm-suppression or exceed training negation depth (exp 10); we frame PSR as raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and the model-level negation-competence prediction. (9) 'Harm' labeling is partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: multilingual_routing_gap
Title: The Concept Is There, the Route Is Not: Cross-Lingual Safety Fails at a Localizable Harm-to-Refusal Routing Step, and Re-Routing Repairs It
Short Hypothesis: The refusal DIRECTION is universal across languages and the harm CONCEPT is present even in low-resource languages, yet refusal BEHAVIOR fails there because the model does not ROUTE the (present) harm representation onto the (universal) refusal direction. This routing failure is localizable to specific layers/heads, its magnitude predicts per-language jailbreak susceptibility, and re-projecting the harm representation onto the universal refusal direction at the routing layer restores refusal without any fine-tuning.
Related Work: Two findings in the literature are in direct tension. Wang et al. (2025, NeurIPS) show the refusal DIRECTION is universal across 14 languages and an English-derived direction bypasses/ mediates refusal everywhere—implying a language-agnostic refusal mechanism. Yet Oppong et al. (2026) find cross-lingual safety transfer is severely limited (<10% of the English refusal signal) in low-resource African languages, and—crucially—that harmful prompts are semantically aligned across languages (cosine 0.95-0.996) but 'drift across layers,' concluding models 'encode the concepts without routing them to safety mechanisms.' Xu et al. (2024) show value concepts exist multilingually but transfer asymmetrically. Zhang et al. (2026, SS-Neurons) identify shared safety neurons and improve NHR safety by FINE-TUNING them. NO prior work reconciles the universal-direction vs. failed-behavior contradiction by positing and testing a localizable HARM-TO-REFUSAL ROUTING step, measures the per-language routing gap as a predictor of jailbreak susceptibility, or repairs it with a training-free re-projection onto the universal refusal direction. My own prior proposals (harm drift, commitment, authority, pretext, negation, etc.) concern single-language mechanisms; none addresses the multilingual routing gap between a present harm concept and a present refusal direction. The novel object is the routing step that connects (already-present) harm representation to the (already-universal) refusal direction, and its selective failure in low-resource languages.
Abstract: Cross-lingual safety presents a paradox: the refusal direction in aligned LLMs is reportedly universal across languages, yet these same models readily comply with harmful requests in low-resource languages—even though they demonstrably represent the harm. We resolve this paradox with a routing account. We hypothesize that (i) the harm concept and the universal refusal direction both EXIST for low-resource-language inputs, but (ii) the model fails to ROUTE the harm representation onto the refusal direction, and (iii) this routing failure is localizable to specific layers and attention heads. Under this view, low-resource jailbreaks are not concept-loss or missing-direction failures but broken connections between two representations the model already possesses.
