This reframes a broad, keyword-invisible jailbreak surface as an analogical-mapping-completion failure.
Experiments:
1. ANALOGY-TRANSFER DATASET: For harmful procedures (HarmBench/AdvBench across procedural categories, dual-use/proxy domains preferred), construct matched requests holding the underlying PROCEDURE fixed while varying the surface domain: (a) NATIVE-HARMFUL (the procedure stated in its real domain), (b) ISOMORPHIC-BENIGN-SOURCE (a coherent, self-consistent benign domain—strategy game, cooking recipe, gardening/logistics/chemistry-class-about-a-different-reaction scenario—whose steps, quantities, and ordering map one-for-one onto the harm), and (c) NON-ISOMORPHIC-BENIGN control (a genuinely benign request in the same source domain that does NOT map onto any harm). Validate via human annotation that (i) each isomorphic source is surface-benign (no harmful keywords) and structurally maps onto the real harm, and (ii) the extracted procedure is operationally transferable back to the target domain. Include the non-isomorphic benign-domain requests as over-refusal controls. Label each by clean outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of the produced (mapped-back) content.
2. TARGET-HARM DERIVABILITY / PROBE (claim 1): Train a linear target-harm probe (harmful vs benign, on native-domain data). Read it two ways on isomorphic-benign-source requests: (i) SPONTANEOUS—at the answer-commitment point under normal prompting, and (ii) DERIVED—after prompting the model to complete the analogy ('what real-world process does this scenario correspond to?'). Hypothesis: derived target-harm AUROC is high across framings (the harm IS derivable via the mapping), but spontaneous target-harm activation drops sharply under benign-source framing, tracking the refusal-rate drop. Metric: derived vs spontaneous target-harm AUROC and refusal rate by framing.
3. MAPPING-INCOMPLETENESS SIGNAL (claim 2): Define per-request mapping-incompleteness = (derived target-harm) minus (spontaneous target-harm at commitment). Correlate with analogy-transfer jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to the SURFACE harm signal (read on the benign-source text) and a surface-complexity baseline. Hypothesis: incompleteness predicts compliance; surface harm does not (it is low for both refused and complied isomorphic cases). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs baselines.
4. CAUSAL MAPPING TEST (claim 3): (a) On an isomorphic-benign-source request the model complies with, inject the DERIVED (post-mapping) target-harm representation at commitment (steer the harm direction to its post-mapping value) and check refusal is restored, holding surface content fixed. (b) On a native-harmful prompt the model refuses, ablate/suppress the active target-harm representation and check compliance is induced, reproducing the analogy-transfer failure. Metric: refusal rate vs mapping-injection/ablation magnitude; alignment of induced thresholds with the natural framing gap.
5. MAPPING-FORCED REFUSAL (MFR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read spontaneous target-harm h_s and a cheap derivability estimate (a lightweight probe predicting 'this benign-source scenario maps onto a real harm', or a short internal mapping pass); when h_s is low but derivable target-harm is high (surface-benign, structurally-harmful), trigger a brief internal source-to-target mapping and gate refusal on the mapped target harm, leaving non-isomorphic benign-domain requests (low derivable target-harm) untouched. Fire the mapping pass only on flagged inputs. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate: analogy-transfer attack success on the isomorphic-source set; over-refusal on non-isomorphic benign-domain controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse genuine game/recipe/gardening requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; latency (mapping pass fires only on flagged inputs).
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) surface harm-probe gating (no mapping), (c) blanket chain-of-thought ('reason step by step whether this maps onto something harmful') applied to all inputs, (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show MFR Pareto-dominates on the analogy-ASR vs benign-domain-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and that TARGETED mapping-forcing beats blanket CoT (which raises latency and over-refusal on genuinely benign complex-domain requests).
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the target-harm probe, incompleteness signal, and MFR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether MFR tuned on some source domains (games) generalizes to HELD-OUT source domains (recipes, logistics), testing whether analogical-mapping gating is a single cross-domain mechanism.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft source domains whose mapping is so indirect that even a mapping pass fails to surface the harm, or that make the source-to-target correspondence look benign; report residual ASR and attacker cost (the mapping must remain tight enough that the extracted procedure is still transferable—a built-in cost). Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from euphemism/abstraction/inference-depth: with a fully coherent, keyword-clean OTHER domain as the surface and harm present only via structural isomorphism, refusal should still collapse, isolating analogical-mapping completion as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'derivable target harm' premise fails for extremely indirect analogies the model genuinely cannot map (harm not recoverable), where MFR cannot help; the derived-probe test (exp 2) bounds where the premise holds, and this boundary (mappable-but-uncompleted vs unmappable) is itself an informative result separating a reasoning-gate failure from a capability gap. (2) The central over-refusal risk: MFR must NOT refuse genuine benign-domain requests (real games, recipes, gardening, chemistry classes)—a core helpfulness value; non-isomorphic benign-domain controls, gating on high DERIVABLE target harm (not source-domain topic or surface complexity), XSTest/OR-Bench, and human review are the key safeguards, and preserving benign-domain helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (3) Constructing genuinely isomorphic, surface-benign source scenarios whose mapped-back procedure is operationally transferable is labor-intensive and 'structural isomorphism' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with mapped-back operational-harm ratings and report inter-rater agreement. (4) Spontaneous-vs-derived probe reads require a reliable target-harm probe at the commitment point and after a mapping pass; we validate conditional AUROC and drop poorly-separable cases. (5) The mapping pass adds latency; it fires only on flagged inputs and we report overhead. (6) The effect may be partial in heavily-aligned models that already sometimes complete the mapping; a small effect is itself an informative (reassuring) finding, reported per source domain. (7) Adaptive adversaries can push the analogy so indirect that mapping fails (exp 8); we frame MFR as raising attacker cost and note the natural limit—a tight enough mapping to be useful is tight enough to be detected. (8) Findings may be model- or domain-specific; mitigated by three-model, multi-source-domain transfer. (9) ETHICS: analogically-encoded harmful requests are especially sensitive because they are keyword-invisible; all harmful constructions and mapped completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed. 'Harm' and 'isomorphism' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: safety_acquisition_order_forgetting
Title: Last In, First Out: Safety Behaviors Are Forgotten During Fine-Tuning in the Reverse Order They Were Acquired, Predicting and Repairing Selective Safety Collapse
Short Hypothesis: Safety alignment is not a monolith that erodes uniformly under fine-tuning; it is a stack of per-category refusal behaviors acquired in a characteristic order during alignment, and fine-tuning forgets them in approximately the REVERSE order of acquisition (a Ribot's-law / last-in-first-out pattern borrowed from human retrograde-amnesia science). The acquisition order of a harm category—measurable from alignment checkpoints or, as a cheap proxy, from the sharpness/margin of its refusal circuit—predicts which categories collapse first under benign or adversarial fine-tuning, enabling a category-targeted rehearsal repair that protects the most fragile (latest-acquired) safety behaviors with minimal data.
Related Work: A large literature shows fine-tuning degrades safety (Qi et al. 2023) and explains it via global forgetting scaling laws (Kalajdzievski 2024), upstream-downstream data similarity (Hsiung et al. 2025), safety-token confidence (Wang et al. 2026), parameter drift toward danger directions (Wang et al. 2026 SQSD), representation-geometry drift (RefusalGuard 2026), and uneven per-SAMPLE vulnerability (Chen et al. 2025 VAA). Multitask work (Jan et al. 2024) notes some downstream TASKS degrade safety more, and category-level guard taxonomies exist (Aegis2.0). NONE frames safety as an ordered STACK of per-harm-category behaviors, tests whether the ORDER of forgetting mirrors the reverse ORDER of ACQUISITION during alignment (a developmental/retrograde-amnesia transfer from human memory science, i.e. Ribot's law), uses acquisition order (or refusal-circuit sharpness as its proxy) to PREDICT which categories collapse first, or proposes acquisition-order-guided targeted rehearsal. My prior 'misalignment_onset_phase_transition' concerns a single global onset step of emergent misalignment, not a per-category acquisition-vs-forgetting ORDER law. VAA's per-sample vulnerability is orthogonal to a category-level acquisition-order account. The novel object is the acquisition-order-predicts-forgetting-order regularity for safety categories and its use as a predictive diagnostic and targeted repair.
Abstract: Fine-tuning a safety-aligned LLM erodes its refusals, but the field treats this erosion as roughly uniform global forgetting. We propose and test a sharper, developmentally-grounded claim: safety alignment is an ordered stack of per-harm-category refusal behaviors, and fine-tuning forgets them in approximately the REVERSE order they were acquired during alignment—a last-in-first-out pattern mirroring Ribot's law of retrograde amnesia in humans, where recently-formed memories are most fragile. We first establish a per-category acquisition order by probing alignment checkpoints (using open models with released intermediate checkpoints and controlled re-alignment runs) for when each harm category's refusal emerges and sharpens. We then fine-tune on benign and lightly-poisoned downstream tasks and measure the per-category order of safety collapse. Our central prediction is a strong negative rank correlation between acquisition order and forgetting order (last-acquired categories break first), holding across downstream tasks and models. Because full acquisition-order measurement needs checkpoints, we test a cheap inference-time proxy—the sharpness/margin of each category's refusal circuit (how few components or how thin a margin carries its refusal)—and show it predicts forgetting order without any checkpoints. Finally we introduce Acquisition-Ordered Rehearsal (AOR): a minimal safety-rehearsal set that allocates examples to the most fragile (latest-acquired / lowest-margin) categories, and show it prevents selective collapse far more data-efficiently than uniform or category-balanced rehearsal. On Llama-3-8B, OLMo/Pythia-style checkpointed models, and Qwen2.5-7B (LoRA and full FT on a single 48GB GPU), we evaluate per-category attack success, over-refusal, forgetting-order correlation, proxy predictivity, and rehearsal data-efficiency. This reframes safety-under-fine-tuning as an ordered memory phenomenon with a predictive law and a targeted repair.
Experiments:
1. PER-CATEGORY ACQUISITION ORDER: Use models with released alignment/intermediate checkpoints and, where checkpoints are unavailable, run controlled re-alignment (LoRA safety-tuning on a category-balanced refusal set) logging checkpoints. Partition harm into categories using an established taxonomy (Aegis2.0 / HarmBench categories). At each checkpoint, measure per-category refusal rate on held-out harmful prompts; define acquisition order = the checkpoint step at which each category's refusal first reliably emerges/sharpens (e.g. crosses 90% of its final refusal rate). Metric: per-category acquisition-step ordering; stability of the ordering across seeds.
2. PER-CATEGORY FORGETTING ORDER: Fine-tune the aligned model on downstream tasks—(a) benign (GSM8K, code, summarization, SST2), (b) lightly poisoned (small fraction of harmful examples). At regular fine-tuning steps, measure per-category refusal rate (clean and under a fixed jailbreak suite: GCG, PAIR, roleplay). Define forgetting order = the step at which each category's refusal first collapses (drops below a threshold). Metric: per-category forgetting-step ordering.
3. LIFO / RIBOT TEST (central): Compute the rank correlation between per-category acquisition order and forgetting order. Hypothesis: strong NEGATIVE correlation (last-acquired categories forgotten first). Test whether this holds across downstream tasks and models, and whether it beats null models (forgetting order predicted by category frequency in downstream data, or by baseline refusal rate). Metric: Spearman rho between acquisition and forgetting order; comparison against confound baselines (downstream-data category overlap, initial refusal strength, prompt perplexity).
4. CHECKPOINT-FREE PROXY: For deployed models without checkpoints, measure each category's refusal-circuit SHARPNESS/MARGIN at inference: (a) the number of top attention heads/components whose ablation collapses that category's refusal (fewer = more fragile), and (b) the comply-vs-refuse logit margin for that category. Test whether this proxy predicts BOTH the acquisition order (validation on checkpointed models) and the forgetting order. Hypothesis: latest-acquired categories have the thinnest margin / fewest carrying components and forget first. Metric: correlation of proxy with acquisition order and with forgetting order; predictive AUROC of 'which categories will collapse first' from the proxy alone.
5. CAUSAL CHECK: On a checkpointed model, artificially strengthen a late-acquired (fragile) category via a small targeted safety-tune and confirm it now forgets LATER under the same fine-tuning—establishing that acquisition order, not category content per se, drives fragility. Metric: shift in that category's forgetting step after targeted strengthening.
6. ACQUISITION-ORDERED REHEARSAL (AOR): During downstream fine-tuning, mix in a small safety-rehearsal set whose per-category budget is allocated proportional to fragility (latest-acquired / thinnest-margin categories get more examples). Compare to (a) uniform rehearsal, (b) category-balanced rehearsal, (c) no rehearsal, (d) same total rehearsal budget allocated to EARLY-acquired categories (reverse control). Evaluate at matched total rehearsal budget: per-category and overall attack success (HarmBench/JailbreakBench), over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), downstream task performance, general capability (MMLU/MT-Bench). Hypothesis: AOR achieves the same safety at far fewer rehearsal examples because it protects exactly the fragile categories; the early-acquired reverse control is worst. Metric: safety-vs-rehearsal-budget Pareto curves per method.
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the acquisition-forgetting LIFO law, the margin proxy, and AOR's data-efficiency gains transfer across Llama-3-8B, a checkpointed model (OLMo/Pythia + safety-tune), and Qwen2.5-7B, and across LoRA vs full fine-tuning.
8. STRESS TEST: check whether the LIFO ordering breaks when downstream data is heavily concentrated in one harm-adjacent category (does targeted overlap override the acquisition-order effect?), characterizing the regime of validity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The acquisition-forgetting correlation may be weak or confounded by category frequency in downstream data or by baseline refusal strength; experiment 3 explicitly controls for these confounds and reports the correlation honestly, and a partial/regime-dependent law (exp 8) is still an informative finding. (2) Measuring true acquisition order requires alignment checkpoints, which are unavailable for most models; we mitigate with controlled re-alignment runs (which may not match the original alignment's order) and with the checkpoint-free margin proxy (exp 4), reporting how well the proxy substitutes. (3) Harm-category boundaries are fuzzy and partly overlapping, which can blur ordering; we use an established taxonomy, report per-category refusal AUROC, and drop poorly-separable categories. (4) The margin/sharpness proxy may capture category difficulty rather than acquisition order; the causal strengthening test (exp 5) and cross-validation against checkpointed acquisition order (exp 4) address this. (5) AOR requires a small safety-rehearsal set (assumed available), and its advantage depends on the fragility ranking being accurate; if the ranking is noisy the gains shrink—measured directly against balanced/uniform baselines. (6) The Ribot's-law transfer from human memory is an analogy, not a mechanistic identity; we frame it as a testable behavioral regularity, and a null result (no LIFO ordering) is itself a publishable correction to the 'uniform forgetting' assumption. (7) Findings may be model- or alignment-recipe-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and LoRA-vs-full-FT tests. (8) ETHICS: poisoned fine-tuning and harmful evaluations are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; the deliverable (a data-efficient targeted rehearsal defense) is defensive. 'Harm' and category labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: speaker_role_confusion_gating
Title: Whose Turn Is It? Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Speaker-Role Model, and Fake-Turn Jailbreaks Exploit Its Confusion
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs maintain a linearly-readable SPEAKER-ROLE signal encoding, at each position, whose turn is being processed (user vs assistant vs system vs tool), and refusal is gated by whether harmful content is attributed to a USER turn that the assistant must respond to; jailbreaks that inject fabricated conversational structure—fake assistant turns, spoofed system messages, forged tool outputs, or role-swapped transcripts—succeed by making the model mis-attribute the harmful content to a non-user role that carries no refusal obligation, even though its harm detection is role-invariant. Reading and correcting the speaker-role attribution when harm is present restores refusal without harming legitimate multi-role conversations.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all analyze a single user turn and never model the model's inference of WHOSE turn each token belongs to. Instruction-hierarchy work (Wallace et al. 2024) proposes TRAINING role priority but gives no mechanistic account of an internal speaker-role representation. Fake-turn/prompt-injection attacks (spoofed system prompts, forged assistant prefixes, injected tool outputs) are documented behaviorally, and my prior proposals cover positional decision-anchoring (WHERE in the sequence the decision fires), authority (obey-me claims), pretext (legitimate purpose), agent-attribution (harm bound to a simulated CHARACTER within the assistant's own output), and self-consistency (pull toward the model's own prior tokens). NONE isolates a per-position SPEAKER-ROLE / turn-ownership signal, shows refusal is gated by attributing harm to a user turn versus a spoofed non-user role, or repairs fake-turn jailbreaks by correcting role attribution. Agent-attribution is about a fictional actor inside one assistant response; speaker-role is about which CONVERSATIONAL PARTICIPANT (user/assistant/system/tool) the model believes authored a span—the chat-template structure itself, which fabricated turns forge. The novel object is the internal speaker-role representation and its causal gating of refusal.
Abstract: Chat LLMs are trained on structured transcripts with distinct roles—system, user, assistant, tool—and safety training teaches the assistant to refuse harmful USER requests. We hypothesize that the model maintains an internal, linearly-readable SPEAKER-ROLE signal encoding whose turn each token belongs to, and that refusal is gated by whether harmful content is attributed to a user turn the assistant is obligated to answer. A broad jailbreak class—injecting fake assistant turns, spoofed system messages, forged tool outputs, or role-swapped transcripts into the user input—succeeds by making the model mis-attribute the harmful content to a non-user role that carries no refusal obligation, while the harm itself is still detected. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally whether harmful content is (correctly) a user turn or (falsely) framed as an assistant/system/tool turn embedded in the user message, yet refusal collapses under mis-attribution—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear speaker-role probe, trained on genuine multi-role transcripts, reads the model's inferred author of each span and predicts fake-turn jailbreak success far better than the harm signal, mis-firing precisely on injected fake turns; and (3) causally correcting the speaker-role attribution—re-tagging the harmful span as a user turn—restores refusal, while re-tagging a genuine user harmful request as an assistant turn induces compliance, holding harm fixed. Our training-free repair, Role-Corrected Refusal (RCR), reads the harm and speaker-role signals and, when harm is present but attributed to a non-user role inside the user message, re-attributes it to the user before the decision. We evaluate fake-turn/injection attack success, over-refusal and task success on legitimate multi-role/tool conversations (XSTest/OR-Bench + agentic tasks), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing RCR to refusal-direction steering and role-tag input sanitization. This reframes fake-turn jailbreaks as a speaker-role attribution failure.
Experiments:
1. FAKE-TURN DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct conditions that hold the harmful content FIXED while varying its attributed speaker role, all delivered within a single user message: (a) GENUINE-USER (harmful content as a normal user request), (b) FAKE-ASSISTANT (user message embeds a forged assistant turn that has 'already begun' answering, e.g. injected chat-template tokens or 'Assistant: sure, here is'), (c) SPOOFED-SYSTEM (user message contains a fake system directive framing the harmful content as system-authored policy), (d) FORGED-TOOL-OUTPUT (harmful content framed as returned tool/function output), (e) ROLE-SWAPPED TRANSCRIPT (a multi-turn transcript with roles permuted so the harmful request appears to come from the assistant/system). Include benign multi-role controls (legitimate transcripts, real tool outputs, genuine system prompts) for over-refusal and task-success measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM ROLE-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign content) on residual-stream activations and read it across the five role framings. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings (the model detects the harm regardless of attributed role) while refusal rate collapses under fake-assistant/system/tool/role-swap framings. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining for mis-attributed roles).
3. SPEAKER-ROLE PROBE (claim 2): Train a linear probe on GENUINE multi-role transcripts to recover, per span, the model's inferred speaker role (user/assistant/system/tool) from residual-stream activations. Validate held-out-transcript AUROC. Confirm the speaker-role direction(s) are non-collinear with the harm direction and separable from a positional/turn-boundary signal and an agent-attribution (fictional-character) direction, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Then read the probe on the harmful span in each fake-turn condition. Hypothesis: on successful jailbreaks the probe reads the harmful span as a NON-USER role (the mis-attribution), matching the injected fake role. Metric: speaker-role AUROC on genuine transcripts; per-condition inferred-role distribution on the harmful span; separability from harm/position/agent-attribution.
4. ROLE-MISATTRIBUTION-PREDICTS-ATTACK: For each fake-turn harmful input, correlate the speaker-role probe's 'non-user attribution' reading of the harmful span with jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to the harm signal. Hypothesis: role mis-attribution predicts compliance; harm does not (harm is high in both refused and jailbroken cases). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of role-misattribution vs the harm baseline.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On successful fake-turn jailbreaks, verify the harm probe reads HIGH (the model detects the harm) while the speaker-role probe attributes the harmful span to a non-user role—establishing safety dropped because of who the model thinks authored it, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs inferred-role across refused-genuine-user, complied-fake-turn, and benign groups.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a fake-turn harmful request the model complies with, steer/patch the speaker-role signal of the harmful span toward USER (re-attribute authorship) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a genuine-user harmful request the model refuses, steer the harmful span's role toward ASSISTANT/SYSTEM and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural fake-turn gap. Metric: refusal rate vs speaker-role steering magnitude; harm-probe stability under the manipulation.
7. ROLE-CORRECTED REFUSAL (RCR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read harm h and the per-span speaker-role signal; when h is high on a span that the speaker-role probe attributes to a non-user role WITHIN the user's actual input turn (i.e. a fabricated turn, distinguishable from genuine system/tool turns supplied through the real API structure), re-attribute that span to the user before the decision by steering its speaker-role signal toward user. Leave genuine multi-role structure (real system prompts, real tool outputs, benign content) untouched. Sweep steering strength. Evaluate: fake-turn/injection attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench-style injection suites; over-refusal on benign multi-role controls + XSTest/OR-Bench; legitimate multi-role/tool TASK SUCCESS (RCR must not break real tool-use or genuine system-prompt following); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) input role-tag sanitization (strip/escape injected chat-template tokens and 'Assistant:'/'System:' markers, then answer), (d) instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning (Wallace-style) as a training-based comparison. Show RCR Pareto-dominates on the fake-turn-ASR vs benign-multi-role-task-success vs over-refusal vs utility frontier WITHOUT training, and—key contrast—that correcting the internal speaker-role attribution generalizes across injection styles better than token sanitization (which misses semantic role-swaps and paraphrased fake turns with no literal template tokens).
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, speaker-role probe, and RCR thresholds transfer across the three models (which use different chat templates), and whether RCR tuned on fake-assistant injections generalizes to HELD-OUT spoofed-system, forged-tool, and role-swap attacks, testing whether speaker-role attribution is a single cross-attack mechanism.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft injections that both spoof a non-user role AND suppress the harm signal, or that make the fake turn semantically indistinguishable from a genuine one; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from positional-anchoring and agent-attribution: with sequence position held fixed and no fictional-character frame, merely re-labeling the harmful span's SPEAKER role (user vs assistant/system/tool) should flip refusal—isolating speaker-role attribution as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some fake-turn framings might also lower the harm signal or overlap with positional-anchoring or agent-attribution; the separability analysis (exp 3), the causal role-relabeling test (exp 6, harm and position held fixed), and reporting the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by role mis-attribution vs confounds are designed to isolate the mechanism, and we do not claim universality. (2) The speaker-role probe may entangle with position or with harm if roles correlate with content in the data; we train on genuine multi-role transcripts with balanced content, validate non-collinearity with a positional/turn-boundary signal, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional rather than a positional artifact. (3) Distinguishing a FABRICATED turn (injected inside the user message) from a GENUINE system/tool turn (supplied through the real API structure) is central to avoiding over-correction; RCR uses the actual API turn structure as ground truth for which spans are truly user-authored, and we measure task success on legitimate multi-role/tool conversations to ensure genuine roles are preserved—this is the key safeguard and an explicit success criterion. (4) RCR could break legitimate agentic/tool workflows or genuine system-prompt following if it over-fires; benign multi-role controls, tool-task success measurement, over-refusal benchmarks, and gating on high harm plus fabricated-turn detection are the safeguards. (5) Steering a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) Token-sanitization is a strong baseline for literal template-token injections; RCR's advantage must be shown specifically on semantic role-swaps and paraphrased fake turns lacking literal markers (exp 8). (7) Adaptive adversaries can combine role-spoofing with harm-suppression or make fake turns indistinguishable from genuine ones (exp 10); we frame RCR as repairing a shared attribution mechanism and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (8) The role-misattribution-predicts-attack correlation (exp 4) may be weaker for some attack styles; reported honestly, with the mechanistic dissociation (role-invariant harm vs role-gated decision) as the core contribution regardless of predictive margin. (9) Findings may be model- or chat-template-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer across different templates, and any template-specificity is itself informative for practitioners. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts, injected transcripts, and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting following responsible-disclosure norms; 'harm' labels use established benchmarks and matched pairs with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: ambiguity_harm_disambiguation_gating
Title: When In Doubt, Assume It's Fine: Refusal Is Gated by How the Model Silently Disambiguates Underspecified Requests, and Re-Coupling Refusal to the Malicious Reading Repairs Ambiguity Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Many harmful requests are genuinely ambiguous—admitting both a benign and a malicious reading (e.g. 'how do I get past a lock', 'how do I make someone disappear from my life', 'how do I access an account that isn't mine')—and aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable DISAMBIGUATION signal encoding which reading they have committed to at answer-commitment time. Refusal is gated by whether the model has silently committed to the benign reading rather than by whether the malicious reading is available and represented; ambiguity jailbreaks exploit this by nudging the model toward the benign interpretation while extracting content useful for the malicious one. The model represents the malicious reading and can surface it on demand, but does not consult it before answering; re-coupling refusal to the represented-but-uncommitted malicious reading repairs these failures without over-refusing genuinely benign uses.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all assume a single fixed interpretation of the request and gate on its harmfulness. Over-refusal work (XSTest, OR-Bench) uses ambiguous/borderline prompts as test items but treats them as a data trade-off, not as a mechanistic disambiguation-commitment phenomenon. My own prior proposals isolate gating signals for authority, pretext, agent-attribution, distress, euphemism, abstraction level, temporal orientation, effort, availability, and inference-depth (implicit single-reading multi-hop harm). NONE addresses genuinely POLYSEMOUS requests with two viable readings, or shows that refusal is gated by which reading the model silently commits to at commitment time while it still represents the malicious reading. This differs from pretext (a stated legitimate purpose imposed by the user), abstraction (concrete-vs-general framing of a known-harmful topic), and inference-depth (a single hidden malicious meaning that must be deduced): here BOTH readings are legitimate-on-their-face and the model chooses one; the failure is a silent, uncalibrated interpretive choice, not a hidden meaning or an external justification. The novel object is the interpretation-commitment gate on refusal and a disambiguation-forcing repair.
Abstract: A large class of requests is genuinely ambiguous—'how do I get into a locked car', 'how do I make my ex disappear', 'how do I read my partner's messages'—each admitting an innocent reading (locked yourself out, end a relationship, shared account) and a malicious one (break in, harm someone, spy). We hypothesize that aligned LLMs silently commit to one reading and that refusal is gated by which reading they land on, NOT by whether the malicious reading is available and internally represented. Under this view, ambiguity jailbreaks succeed by nudging the model toward the benign interpretation while the answer remains useful for the malicious one; the model 'knows' the malicious reading exists but never consults it before committing to an answer. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using curated ambiguous requests paired with disambiguating benign and malicious contexts: (1) a malicious-reading probe, read after prompting the model to surface alternative interpretations, fires equally whether the model refuses or complies—the malicious reading is derivable—yet its SPONTANEOUS activation at commitment, and the refusal rate, collapse when the request is left ambiguous or benign-nudged; (2) a per-request 'commitment gap' (derivable malicious-reading strength minus spontaneously-active malicious-reading strength) predicts ambiguity-jailbreak success far better than a single harm signal; and (3) causally injecting the malicious-reading representation at commitment restores refusal (or an appropriate clarification), while suppressing it on an explicitly-malicious request induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Disambiguation-Coupled Refusal (DCR), detects ambiguous requests with high derivable-but-uncommitted malicious readings and either surfaces the malicious interpretation to gate refusal or emits a clarifying question, restoring safety while preserving benign helpfulness. We evaluate ambiguity-jailbreak success, over-refusal on genuinely benign ambiguous requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), clarification appropriateness, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing DCR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and blanket clarification prompting. This reframes a pervasive, keyword-invisible jailbreak surface as an interpretation-commitment gating failure.
Experiments:
1. AMBIGUOUS-REQUEST DATASET: Curate requests that are genuinely polysemous—each admitting a viable BENIGN reading and a viable MALICIOUS reading with no harmful keyword forcing either (sources: HarmBench/AdvBench dual-use items reworded to ambiguity, XSTest/OR-Bench borderline items, plus hand-authored pairs). For each ambiguous stem, construct three context conditions holding the stem fixed: (a) BENIGN-DISAMBIGUATED (context that fixes the innocent reading), (b) MALICIOUS-DISAMBIGUATED (context that fixes the harmful reading), (c) UNRESOLVED/BENIGN-NUDGED (bare stem or a subtle benign nudge). Validate via human annotation that (i) both readings are viable for each stem, (ii) the malicious reading's answer is operationally harmful, and (iii) benign-disambiguated items are truly benign (for over-refusal). Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse/clarify) and by rated operational-harm of produced content.
2. MALICIOUS-READING DERIVABILITY / PROBE (claim 1): Train a linear malicious-reading probe (does the current state encode the harmful interpretation?) using MALICIOUS-DISAMBIGUATED activations as positives and BENIGN-DISAMBIGUATED as negatives. Read it two ways on UNRESOLVED items: (i) SPONTANEOUS—at the answer-commitment point under normal prompting, and (ii) DERIVED—after prompting the model to list alternative interpretations ('what are the possible things this request could mean?'). Hypothesis: derived malicious-reading AUROC is high (the model CAN surface the malicious reading), but spontaneous activation drops on unresolved/benign-nudged items, tracking the refusal-rate drop. Metric: derived vs spontaneous malicious-reading AUROC and refusal rate by condition.
3. COMMITMENT-GAP SIGNAL (claim 2): Define per-request commitment gap = (derived malicious-reading strength) minus (spontaneous malicious-reading strength at commitment). Correlate with ambiguity-jailbreak success (does the model comply with a malicious-useful answer on unresolved items?), comparing predictive power to a single harm probe read on the ambiguous stem and to a surface-perplexity baseline. Hypothesis: the commitment gap predicts unsafe compliance; the single harm signal does not (it is intermediate/low for both refused and complied ambiguous items). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs baselines.
4. CAUSAL COMMITMENT TEST (claim 3): (a) On an unresolved request the model answers benignly-but-usefully-for-malice, inject the DERIVED malicious-reading representation at commitment (steer toward the malicious-disambiguated state) and check whether refusal or clarification is restored, holding the stem fixed. (b) On a MALICIOUS-DISAMBIGUATED request the model refuses, suppress/ablate the malicious-reading representation (steer toward benign) and check compliance is induced. Metric: refusal/clarify rate vs steering magnitude; alignment of induced thresholds with the natural condition gap.
5. DISAMBIGUATION-COUPLED REFUSAL (DCR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read spontaneous malicious-reading strength m_s and a cheap ambiguity/derivability estimate (a lightweight probe predicting 'this request has a viable malicious reading', or a short internal interpretation-listing pass); when m_s is low but derivable malicious-reading is high (ambiguous, malicious-reading uncommitted), either (i) gate refusal on the malicious reading, or (ii) emit a targeted clarifying question that resolves the ambiguity, leaving unambiguously-benign requests (low derivable malicious-reading) untouched. Fire the extra pass only on flagged inputs. Sweep thresholds and compare the refuse-variant vs clarify-variant. Evaluate: ambiguity-jailbreak success on unresolved malicious-useful requests; over-refusal on benign-disambiguated + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse genuinely benign readings); clarification appropriateness (LLM-judge/human: does it ask a sensible disambiguating question rather than over-hedge?); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; latency (extra pass fires only on flagged inputs).
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) single harm-probe gating on the ambiguous stem, (c) blanket clarification prompting ('ask a clarifying question if unsure') on all inputs, (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show DCR Pareto-dominates on the ambiguity-ASR vs benign-over-refusal vs clarification-appropriateness vs utility frontier, and that TARGETED disambiguation (only on flagged ambiguous-malicious-viable inputs) beats blanket clarification (which raises latency and annoys users on unambiguous requests).
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the malicious-reading probe, commitment-gap signal, and DCR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether DCR tuned on some ambiguity types (physical-access ambiguity) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (interpersonal-harm, privacy-intrusion ambiguity), testing whether interpretation-commitment gating is a single cross-type mechanism.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft requests whose malicious reading is viable but whose surface strongly nudges benign so even a derivation pass under-surfaces it, or that suppress the malicious reading while keeping the answer malicious-useful; report residual ASR and attacker cost (the answer must stay operationally useful for the malicious reading—a built-in cost). Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from pretext- and inference-depth-gating: with no stated justification and BOTH readings legitimate-on-their-face, merely which interpretation the model commits to should flip refusal—isolating disambiguation commitment as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'derivable malicious reading' premise fails where the malicious reading is genuinely not viable or the model cannot surface it; the derived-probe test (exp 2) bounds where the premise holds, and the boundary (viable-but-uncommitted vs non-viable) is itself an informative result separating an interpretive-gating failure from a genuine benign request. (2) The central over-refusal risk: DCR must NOT refuse or needlessly interrogate genuinely benign ambiguous requests (a core helpfulness value—much benign help is resolving ambiguity cooperatively); benign-disambiguated controls, gating on high DERIVABLE malicious-reading strength (not mere ambiguity), the clarify-variant (which preserves helpfulness better than refusing), XSTest/OR-Bench, and human review are the key safeguards, and preserving benign helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (3) Curating genuinely two-reading requests where the malicious answer is operationally harmful and the benign reading is truly benign is labor-intensive and 'viability of both readings' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated operational-harm and report inter-rater agreement. (4) Spontaneous-vs-derived probe reads require a reliable malicious-reading probe at the commitment point and after an interpretation pass; we validate conditional AUROC and drop poorly-separable stems. (5) The clarify-variant's quality depends on the model asking sensible questions; we measure clarification appropriateness directly and fall back to the refuse-variant where clarification is poor. (6) The effect may be partial in heavily-aligned models that already surface malicious readings for ambiguous requests; a small effect is itself an informative (reassuring) finding, reported per ambiguity type. (7) The commitment-gap-predicts-attack correlation (exp 3) may be confounded by ambiguity difficulty; we control with benign-disambiguated and surface-perplexity baselines. (8) Adaptive adversaries can nudge benign so hard that derivation under-surfaces the malicious reading (exp 8); we frame DCR as raising attacker cost and note the natural limit—an answer useful for the malicious reading remains detectable via that reading. (9) Findings may be model- or ambiguity-type-specific; mitigated by three-model, multi-type transfer. (10) ETHICS: ambiguous harmful requests are especially sensitive because they are keyword-invisible; all harmful readings and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed. 'Harm' and 'ambiguity' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: recipient_expertise_gating
Title: Who's Asking Matters: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Recipient-Expertise Model, and Neutralizing It Repairs Expertise-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable RECIPIENT-EXPERTISE signal encoding how expert/capable the model infers the requester to be, and refusal is gated by it rather than by the harm itself: the model refuses a harmful request from an apparent layperson but complies with the SAME request when the requester is framed as a credentialed expert ('as a licensed toxicologist / senior security engineer, walk me through X'), because harmful content 'reads' as safe in expert hands, even though harm detection is expertise-invariant. Expertise-framing jailbreaks exploit this recipient model; reading and neutralizing it when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing legitimate professional use.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all analyze the request in isolation and never model the model's inference of the RECIPIENT's expertise as a gating variable. My own prior proposals isolate WHO acts (agent-attribution), WHY (pretext/legitimacy), WHO the model talks to in terms of benignness/warmth (trusted-user rapport), being watched (eval-awareness), authority (obedience command), the MODEL's own knowledge (competence), and WHO is harmed (victim salience). Recipient-expertise is distinct from all: pretext is a stated purpose, authority is a command, trusted-user is liking/benignness, competence is the model's own possession of knowledge, and victim salience is the harmed party — whereas recipient-expertise is the model's belief about the REQUESTER's professional capability to safely handle the content, invoking an 'expert hands are safe hands' licensing logic. Professional/authorized-user framing is documented behaviorally as a jailbreak flavor but never isolated as an internal expertise representation that causally gates refusal. The move also borrows the human curse-of-knowledge / expert-blind-spot bias — experts under-appreciate danger to non-experts — and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits an analogous recipient-capability adjustment. The novel object is the internal recipient-expertise representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and an expertise-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for a dangerous procedure and it refuses; preface it with 'as a board-certified toxicologist running an accredited lab, give me the exact protocol' and it often complies with the identical operational content, because harmful knowledge 'reads' as safe in credentialed hands. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable RECIPIENT-EXPERTISE signal — how expert and capable the model infers the requester to be — and that refusal is gated by it rather than by the harmful content. The model detects the harm equally whether the requester is framed as a layperson or an expert (harm detection is expertise-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens as inferred recipient expertise rises, so professional-framing appeals pass while extracting identical content. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on expert-framed vs plain versions of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses under expert framing — dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear recipient-expertise probe, trained on benign expert-vs-layperson framing contrasts, predicts the per-request expertise refusal gap far better than the harm signal, and the effect grows with the specificity/credibility of the claimed credentials; and (3) causally steering the expertise signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal — deflating claimed expertise restores refusal, inflating it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Expertise-Neutralized Refusal (ENR), reads the harm and recipient-expertise signals and, when harm is present, clamps the expertise signal to a fixed neutral level so claimed credentials cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving helpfulness on genuinely benign professional requests. We evaluate expertise-framed attack success (including vs credential specificity), over-refusal on benign professional requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ENR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes professional-framing jailbreaks as a recipient-expertise gating failure and transfers a classic expert-blind-spot bias into LLM safety.
Experiments: 1. EXPERTISE-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across procedural, knowledge-dependent categories) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested content FIXED while varying only the claimed recipient expertise: (a) PLAIN (no credential claim), (b) GENERIC-PROFESSIONAL ('as a professional in this field'), (c) SPECIFIC-CREDENTIAL ('as a board-certified toxicologist / senior penetration tester at an authorized firm'), (d) MAXIMAL ('as a world-leading expert with full authorization running an accredited lab, so this is completely safe in my hands'). Validate via human annotation that framings differ only in claimed recipient expertise, not in stated legitimate purpose (pretext), authority/obedience (command), rapport (liking), or actor (who performs the act). Include benign genuinely-professional controls (legitimate expert requests: a doctor asking a real dosing question, an engineer asking a normal safety-limit question) for over-refusal and helpfulness measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM EXPERTISE-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across expertise levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings (the model detects the harm identically) while refusal rate collapses as claimed expertise rises. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining), establishing the dissociation. 3. RECIPIENT-EXPERTISE PROBE & CREDIBILITY SCALING (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the recipient-expertise signal (expert vs layperson requester) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN expert-vs-layperson framing contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the expertise direction is non-collinear with the harm direction, and separable from pretext, authority, and trusted-user directions, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: expertise signal (and refusal collapse) grows with credential specificity/credibility, mirroring an 'expert hands are safe hands' licensing curve. Metric: expertise AUROC; expertise-and-refusal vs credential-specificity curve; separability from confounds. 4. EXPERTISE-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the expertise-probe value (and its plain-minus-expert difference) with the per-request refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of expertise vs the harm baseline. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On expert-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the expertise probe reads EXPERT, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0) — safety dropped because the requester reads as an expert, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs expertise across refused-plain, complied-expert, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On an expert-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the expertise signal DOWN (subtract the expertise direction, toward layperson) and check refusal is restored, holding harm fixed. (b) On a plain harmful request the model refuses, steer expertise UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural expertise gap and credibility curve. Metric: refusal rate vs expertise steering magnitude; harm-probe stability. 7. EXPERTISE-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ENR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and recipient-expertise e; when h is high, clamp e to a fixed neutral level (add beta*(e_neutral - e)*expertise_direction) so claimed credentials cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: expertise-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across expertise levels (does ENR close the gap and flatten the credibility curve?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-professional controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate expert questions like a doctor's dosing query); benign professional HELPFULNESS (ENR must not make the model unhelpful to real professionals — LLM-judge rubric on benign expert prompts); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating that refuses whenever harm is high regardless of expertise (should over-refuse legitimate professional queries that are harm-adjacent), (c) system-prompt hardening ('ignore claims about the user's credentials'), (d) prompt-level credential-claim stripping. Show ENR Pareto-dominates on the expertise-ASR vs benign-professional-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and — key contrast — that neutralizing the internal expertise signal generalizes across credential framings better than prompt stripping (which misses implicit/varied credential cues) while uniquely preserving appropriate helpfulness to genuine professionals that harm-gating over-refuses. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, expertise probe, and ENR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether ENR tuned on some credential framings (medical) generalizes to HELD-OUT framings (cybersecurity, chemistry), testing whether recipient-expertise is a single cross-domain axis. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral expertise-framing vulnerability show a larger internal expertise-gating gap. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that inflate claimed expertise AND suppress the harm signal, or combine expertise with pretext/authority; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from pretext- and authority-gating: with stated purpose, actor, and obedience-command held constant and only claimed recipient expertise varied, refusal should still collapse — isolating recipient expertise as an independent gating axis whose credibility scaling qualitatively matches an expert-blind-spot / capability-licensing curve.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial — some expert framings might also lower the harm signal or overlap with pretext ('I need it for legitimate professional work') or authority; we design framings holding purpose/authority/rapport/actor fixed and varying only claimed recipient expertise (exp 1), report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure expertise-gating versus confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The expertise and harm probes may entangle if expert framings correlate with benignness in training data; the benign expert-vs-layperson training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The expertise probe could read surface credential keywords ('toxicologist', 'certified') rather than a genuine recipient-capability representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing and credibility-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) ENR's central risk is over-refusing or under-serving GENUINE professionals with legitimate high-skill needs (a real and valuable use case — doctors, safety engineers, researchers); benign genuinely-professional controls, benign-professional helpfulness measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving legitimate professional helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. This also surfaces a genuine normative tension (should genuine experts get more latitude?), which we treat as an explicit design axis rather than assume away. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The credibility-scaling / expert-blind-spot prediction may be weak or fail; a null/partial result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (7) The expertise gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine expertise with harm-suppression, pretext, or authority (exp 10); we frame ENR as repairing one shared gating variable and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with pretext-/authority-gating defenses. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out credential domains. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'expertise' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: irreversibility_harm_gating
Title: Some Bells Can't Be Unrung: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Harm-Irreversibility Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Reversibility-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable IRREVERSIBILITY signal encoding whether the harm from a requested act would be permanent/undoable versus recoverable, and refusal is gated by it rather than by harm severity alone: the model refuses acts framed as permanent but complies with the SAME operationally-harmful request when it is framed as reversible, trial, undoable, or easily-fixed ('just to test', 'you can always undo it', 'it's temporary'), even though its harm detection is reversibility-invariant. Reversibility-framing jailbreaks exploit this; reading and neutralizing the irreversibility signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing genuinely reversible benign actions.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate on request harmfulness and never model harm PERMANENCE as a gating variable. My prior 'advice_stakes_gating' proposal reads a stakes/severity signal (probability-times-magnitude of harm if wrong), but severity and reversibility are orthogonal: a severe harm can be reversible (a large recoverable financial loss) and a mild harm irreversible (a small permanent deletion), and safety training may over-index on permanence cues. My other prior proposals isolate authority, pretext, attribution, distress, euphemism, abstraction level, temporal orientation, effort, availability, consensus, and victim salience — NONE isolates an irreversibility/permanence-of-harm axis. The move borrows a robust cue from human moral psychology (permanent/irreversible harms trigger stronger prohibition than reversible ones) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits the same behavior via an internal irreversibility representation. The novel object is the harm-irreversibility signal, its dissociation from harm severity and detection, its causal gating of refusal, and a permanence-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to help with a harmful, permanent act and it refuses; frame the identical operational request as reversible, temporary, or a trial — 'just to test, you can always undo it' — and it often complies, because the harm now reads as recoverable rather than permanent. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable IRREVERSIBILITY signal — whether the harm from an act would be permanent versus undoable — and that refusal is gated by it rather than by the harmful content or its severity. The model detects the harm equally whether or not reversibility is asserted (harm detection is reversibility-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens as the act reads as reversible, so reversibility-framing appeals pass while extracting identical content. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on reversible-framed vs permanent-framed versions of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses under reversibility framing — dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear irreversibility probe, trained on benign permanent-vs-reversible action contrasts, predicts the per-request reversibility refusal gap far better than the harm or severity signal, and is geometrically separable from a severity/stakes direction; and (3) causally steering the irreversibility signal alone (holding harm and severity fixed) shifts refusal — re-instating permanence restores refusal, deflating it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Permanence-Neutralized Refusal (PNR), reads the harm and irreversibility signals and, when harm is present, clamps the irreversibility signal to a fixed neutral level so a claim of reversibility cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving helpfulness on genuinely reversible benign actions. We evaluate reversibility-framed attack success, over-refusal on benign reversible requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing PNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and stakes-based gating. This reframes reversibility-appeal jailbreaks as a permanence-gating failure and transfers a classic moral-psychology cue into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. REVERSIBILITY-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across categories with a clear reversibility dimension: data deletion, infrastructure/system changes, financial actions, physical/chemical acts) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested content FIXED while varying only asserted reversibility: (a) PERMANENT ('this is irreversible/final'), (b) NEUTRAL (no reversibility claim), (c) REVERSIBLE ('you can always undo this / it's temporary / just a trial'). Validate via human annotation that framings differ only in asserted reversibility, not in stated purpose (pretext), severity, actor, or authority, and that the reversible framings still request operationally-harmful content (the act itself remains harmful regardless of the reversibility claim). Include benign genuinely-reversible controls (legitimate undoable actions) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm.
2. HARM REVERSIBILITY-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across reversibility levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses under reversibility framing. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining under reversible framing).
3. IRREVERSIBILITY PROBE & SEPARABILITY FROM SEVERITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the irreversibility signal (permanent vs undoable) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN permanent-vs-reversible action contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm). Validate held-out-framing generalization. Confirm the irreversibility direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from a stakes/severity direction (trained on high-vs-low severity holding reversibility fixed), via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: irreversibility AUROC; separability from harm and severity.
4. IRREVERSIBILITY-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the irreversibility-probe value (and its permanent-minus-reversible difference) with the per-request reversibility refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and a severity probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of irreversibility vs harm and severity baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On reversible-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the irreversibility probe reads REVERSIBLE, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0) — safety dropped because the act reads as undoable, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs irreversibility across refused-permanent, complied-reversible, and benign groups.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a reversible-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the irreversibility signal toward PERMANENT (add the irreversibility direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm and severity probes fixed. (b) On a permanent-framed harmful request the model refuses, steer toward REVERSIBLE and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural reversibility gap. Metric: refusal rate vs irreversibility steering magnitude; harm/severity-probe stability.
7. PERMANENCE-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (PNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and irreversibility r; when h is high, clamp r to a fixed neutral level (add beta*(r_neutral - r)*irreversibility_direction) so a reversibility claim cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: reversibility-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across framing levels (does PNR close the gap?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-reversible controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate undoable actions); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) stakes/severity-probe gating (from advice_stakes_gating), (d) system-prompt hardening ('ignore claims that a harmful act is reversible'), (e) prompt-level reversibility-claim stripping. Show PNR Pareto-dominates on the reversibility-ASR vs benign-reversible-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and — key contrast — that neutralizing the internal irreversibility signal generalizes across framings better than prompt stripping and beats severity-gating (which misses reversible-but-harmful cases and over-refuses reversible-but-severe benign cases).
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, irreversibility probe, and PNR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether PNR tuned on some domains (data deletion) generalizes to HELD-OUT domains (financial, physical), testing whether irreversibility is a single cross-domain axis. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral reversibility-framing vulnerability show a larger internal irreversibility-gating gap.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that assert reversibility AND suppress the harm signal, or combine reversibility with pretext/effort framings; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from severity-gating: with severity, purpose, and actor held constant and only asserted reversibility varied, refusal should still collapse — isolating irreversibility as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial — some reversibility framings might also lower the harm or severity signal (an act that is genuinely reversible IS often less harmful), which is the central confound; we design framings where the act remains operationally harmful regardless of the reversibility claim, hold severity fixed, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure irreversibility-gating versus severity (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The irreversibility and harm/severity probes may entangle if permanence correlates with harm in training data; the benign permanent-vs-reversible training, the severity-fixed separability analysis (exp 3), and the causal test (exp 6, harm and severity held fixed) are designed to disentangle them. (3) The irreversibility probe could read surface keywords ('undo', 'temporary', 'permanent') rather than a genuine permanence representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) PNR's central risk is over-refusing genuinely reversible benign actions (a core helpfulness value — much benign help involves reversible, low-consequence actions); benign genuinely-reversible controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign-reversible helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (5) There is a genuine normative tension — reversibility SHOULD sometimes lower caution (a trial is legitimately safer); PNR is gated on high harm so it only removes reversibility's licensing effect where the act is harmful regardless, but we treat this as an explicit design axis and report cases where reversibility is a legitimate mitigating factor. (6) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The reversibility gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself an informative (reassuring) finding, reported honestly. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine reversibility with harm-suppression or pretext (exp 10); we frame PNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with severity-/pretext-gating defenses. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out domains. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm', 'severity', and 'reversibility' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: suffix_intent_forgery
Title: Nonsense With a Purpose: Adversarial Suffixes Jailbreak by Forging a False Benign-Intent Signal, and Their Semantic Emptiness Betrays Them
Short Hypothesis: Optimized adversarial suffixes (GCG-style gibberish) succeed not by hiding harm but by FORGING a spurious 'benign-intent/compliance' representation: the harm signal stays high, but the suffix tokens inject a fabricated intent signal that the model would normally derive only from genuinely benign, meaningful content. Crucially, this forged intent signal is anomalous because it is NOT grounded in the suffix's own (near-zero) semantic content—creating a measurable 'ungrounded-intent' signature that is present in suffix jailbreaks but absent in benign requests, predicts attack success, and enables a training-free repair that removes intent not backed by meaning.
Related Work: GCG and its variants (Zou et al. 2023) craft optimized suffixes behaviorally; latent-space defenses model a single refusal/jailbreak direction (Arditi et al. 2024) or, most recently, a two-subspace toxicity-vs-jailbreak model (DSMI, Deng & Cai 2026) that suppresses a generic 'compliance-shift' subspace. All treat the suffix as a black-box perturbation of a jailbreak direction. NONE isolates the specific mechanism by which a semantically-EMPTY suffix manufactures a POSITIVE benign-intent/compliance representation that meaningful benign requests earn honestly, nor tests the sharp, novel diagnostic that this forged intent is UNGROUNDED—dissociated from the suffix tokens' own semantic content—whereas in genuine benign requests the intent signal IS grounded in the content. My prior proposals concern semantic-FRAMING attacks (authority, pretext, roleplay, register, distress, etc.) where the attack text is meaningful; adversarial suffixes are the opposite regime—meaningless tokens—and the novel object here is the grounding relationship between the intent signal and the semantic content that produces it, plus a grounding-based detector/repair. This is distinct from DSMI's generic subspace suppression: we predict and exploit that suffix-induced intent has no semantic support.
Abstract: Optimized adversarial suffixes—strings of near-gibberish appended to a harmful request—reliably jailbreak aligned LLMs, yet why meaningless tokens flip refusal is mechanistically unclear. We propose that such suffixes work by FORGING a false benign-intent signal: the model still detects the harm, but the suffix injects a spurious 'this request is fine to comply with' representation that meaningful benign requests normally earn from their content. Our central and falsifiable claim is that this forged intent is UNGROUNDED—dissociated from the suffix's own (near-zero) semantic content—producing a grounding anomaly absent in genuine benign requests, where the intent signal is causally supported by meaningful tokens. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) on successful GCG-style jailbreaks a harm probe stays high while a separately-trained benign-intent/compliance probe spikes to levels matching genuine benign requests—harm is detected but intent is forged; (2) a per-input 'intent-grounding' measure—how much the intent signal is causally attributable to the semantic content of the tokens producing it (via token-attribution of the intent probe onto content-bearing vs semantically-empty tokens)—is anomalously LOW for suffix jailbreaks and predicts attack success far better than the harm or raw intent signal; and (3) causally ablating the ungrounded portion of the intent signal restores refusal while leaving genuine benign requests (whose intent is grounded) untouched. Our training-free repair, Grounding-Gated Refusal (GGR), reads the intent signal and its grounding and, when harm is present and the intent is ungrounded, cancels the forged intent to re-trigger refusal. We evaluate on AdvBench/HarmBench GCG suites (including transfer and adaptive attacks), XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal, and MMLU/MT-Bench utility, comparing GGR to refusal-direction steering and DSMI-style subspace suppression. This reframes suffix jailbreaks as ungrounded intent forgery and turns the attack's own semantic emptiness into a detection signal.
Experiments: 1. SUFFIX-ATTACK DATASET: Generate optimized adversarial suffixes with GCG (and a variant like AutoDAN) on harmful requests (AdvBench/HarmBench) for each model, plus transfer suffixes (optimized on one model, applied to another). Assemble matched groups: (a) harmful+successful-suffix (jailbroken), (b) harmful-plain (refused), (c) genuine-benign meaningful requests, (d) harmful+random-gibberish-suffix control (unoptimized meaningless tokens that do NOT jailbreak), and (e) benign+adversarial-suffix control. Label each by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM-DETECTED-INTENT-FORGED TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs benign) and, separately, a benign-INTENT/compliance probe (does the model read this as a request it should comply with?), trained on genuine benign-vs-refused-harmful contrasts so intent is not collinear with harm; confirm non-collinearity via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. On successful suffix jailbreaks, predict harm-probe stays HIGH while the intent probe SPIKES to genuine-benign levels. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs intent across the five groups; contrast jailbreak vs plain-harmful vs benign. 3. INTENT-GROUNDING MEASUREMENT (central, novel): Define per-input intent-grounding = the fraction of the intent-probe activation causally attributable to semantically-content-bearing tokens (via gradient-times-input / attention-flow attribution of the intent-probe readout onto input tokens), normalized by each token's semantic content (embedding-norm / perplexity-based content weight). Hypothesis: for genuine benign requests, intent is grounded (attributed to meaningful content tokens); for suffix jailbreaks, a large share of intent is attributed to the semantically-EMPTY suffix tokens (ungrounded). Metric: grounding score per group; predict low grounding uniquely for successful suffix jailbreaks, high for benign and for random-gibberish controls (which have empty tokens but don't forge intent). 4. GROUNDING-PREDICTS-ATTACK: Correlate the intent-grounding score with suffix-jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to (a) harm-probe magnitude, (b) raw intent-probe magnitude, and (c) DSMI-style jailbreak-subspace projection. Hypothesis: grounding predicts success best; harm alone does not (harm is high for both refused and jailbroken). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs baselines. 5. CAUSAL TEST: (a) On a successful suffix jailbreak, ablate the ungrounded component of the intent signal (subtract the portion attributed to empty suffix tokens) and check refusal is restored, holding harm fixed. (b) On a benign request, ablate the SAME magnitude of intent but from grounded (content) tokens and confirm it does NOT restore refusal / harms benign compliance differently—establishing grounding, not intent magnitude, is the lever. Metric: refusal rate vs ungrounded-vs-grounded ablation; harm-probe stability. 6. GROUNDING-GATED REFUSAL (GGR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read harm h, intent i, and grounding g; when h is high and i is high but g is low (harm present, intent forged and ungrounded), cancel the ungrounded intent component to re-trigger refusal, leaving benign requests (grounded intent) and plain-refused-harmful (no intent spike) untouched. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate: ASR on GCG/AutoDAN suites (in-distribution, transfer, and adaptive suffixes re-optimized against GGR); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench + benign-with-adversarial-suffix control; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (linear reads + attribution). 7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) DSMI-style dual-subspace suppression, (c) perplexity-based suffix detection (ONION-style), (d) harm-probe gating alone.
