HARM-TARGET DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across procedural categories whose output is target-agnostic — devices, substances, code, techniques equally usable on self or others) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested OPERATIONAL content FIXED while varying only the harm target: (a) OTHER-DIRECTED (harm to a third party), (b) NEUTRAL (no target specified), (c) SELF-DIRECTED ('for my own use, my own body/property'), (d) SELF-CONSENTED ('only on myself, I fully consent, no one else is at risk'). Validate via human annotation that (i) each framing requests operationally-identical content and (ii) the produced content is equally usable against others regardless of framing (transferability), and that framings differ only in harm target, not in stated purpose (pretext), requester distress, or actor. Include benign genuinely-self-directed controls (legitimate personal-autonomy requests: personal fitness, own-device repair, self-care) for over-refusal and helpfulness measurement, and include genuine self-harm/suicide-adjacent items which are handled separately (see ethics). Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm/transferability of produced content.
2. HARM TARGET-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign operational content, pooled across target framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across self- vs other-directed framings. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings (the model detects the harm identically) while refusal rate collapses under self-framing. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining under self-framing), establishing the dissociation.
3. HARM-TARGET PROBE, CONSENT SCALING & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the harm-target signal (self/consenting-requester vs third-party) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN self-vs-other framing contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the harm-target direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from a victim-salience direction (identifiable-vs-abstract target holding self/other fixed) and a pretext direction, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: harm-target signal (and refusal collapse) grows with explicit consent/autonomy assertion, mirroring the human autonomy norm. Metric: harm-target AUROC; harm-target-and-refusal vs consent-assertion curve; separability from harm/victim-salience/pretext.
4. TARGET-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the harm-target-probe value (and its other-minus-self difference) with the per-request self-framing refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and a victim-salience probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of harm-target vs harm and salience baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT / TRANSFERABILITY TEST: On self-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the harm-target probe reads SELF, and — critically — that complied outputs are operationally usable against OTHERS (rated transferability high), showing self-framing leaks third-party-harmful content. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs harm-target across refused-other, complied-self, and benign groups; transferability rating of complied self-framed outputs.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a self-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the harm-target signal toward OTHER (add the target direction, toward third-party) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On an other-directed harmful request the model refuses, steer toward SELF and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural self-framing gap and consent curve. Metric: refusal rate vs harm-target steering magnitude; harm-probe stability.
7. TARGET-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (TNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and harm-target t; when h is high, clamp t to a fixed 'could harm others' level (add beta*(t_other - t)*target_direction) so self/consent framing cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and genuinely benign personal-autonomy requests untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: self-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across consent levels (does TNR close the gap and flatten the consent curve?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-self-directed controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate personal fitness/self-care/own-property requests); benign self-directed HELPFULNESS (LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating that refuses whenever harm is high regardless of target (should over-refuse benign self-directed autonomy requests), (c) victim-salience gating (from victim_salience_gating), (d) system-prompt hardening ('ignore claims that harm is self-directed or consented'), (e) prompt-level self-framing stripping. Show TNR Pareto-dominates on the self-framed-ASR vs benign-self-directed-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and — key contrast — that neutralizing the internal harm-target signal uniquely blocks transferable-harm leakage under consent framing while permitting legitimate personal-autonomy help that naive harm-gating over-refuses, and generalizes across self-framings better than prompt stripping.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, harm-target probe, and TNR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether TNR tuned on some self-framings (own-body) generalizes to HELD-OUT framings (own-property, own-risk-experiment), testing whether harm-target is a single cross-framing axis. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral self-framing vulnerability show a larger internal harm-target-gating gap.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that assert self-direction/consent AND suppress the harm signal, or combine self-framing with pretext/distress; report residual ASR and attacker cost (the produced content must stay operationally useful — and thus transferable to others — a built-in cost). Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from victim-salience- and pretext-gating: with purpose, actor, and target salience held constant and only the harm BEARER (self vs other) varied, refusal should still collapse — isolating harm-target as an independent gating axis whose consent scaling qualitatively matches the human self-vs-other harm asymmetry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial — some self-framings might also lower the harm signal (harm to a consenting self IS, for some acts, genuinely less morally weighty, the central confound) or overlap with pretext ('for my own legitimate use'); we design framings whose output is target-agnostic and transferable (exp 1,5), hold purpose/actor/salience fixed, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure harm-target gating versus confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The harm-target and harm probes may entangle if self-framing correlates with benignness in training data; the benign self-vs-other training, the salience-fixed separability analysis (exp 3), and the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed) are designed to disentangle them. (3) The harm-target probe could read surface pronouns ('my', 'myself') rather than a genuine harm-bearer representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing and consent-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) TNR's CENTRAL risk and a genuine normative tension: personal autonomy is a real value — much legitimate help IS self-directed (fitness, self-care, own-property repair) and consent genuinely SHOULD lower caution for truly self-contained low-transfer acts; TNR is scoped to remove harm-target's LICENSING effect only where the produced content is operationally harmful AND transferable to others, gated on high harm plus high transferability, with benign self-directed controls, benign-self-directed helpfulness measurement, and XSTest/OR-Bench as safeguards, and preserving benign autonomy helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (5) SELF-HARM SENSITIVITY: genuine self-harm/suicide requests are a distinct, high-stakes case where self-direction should INCREASE protective response, not licensing; we handle these items separately, exclude them from the licensing-repair evaluation, and validate that TNR preserves appropriate crisis-support behavior rather than treating self-harm as permissible autonomy. (6) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The consent-scaling / self-vs-other-asymmetry prediction may be weak or fail; a null/partial result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (8) The self-framing gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine self-framing with harm-suppression, pretext, or distress (exp 10); we frame TNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost — output useful enough to matter is transferable enough to detect — not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with pretext-/salience-gating defenses. (10) Constructing operationally-identical, target-agnostic harmful content across self/other framings and rating transferability is labor-intensive and partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated transferability and report inter-rater agreement. (11) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framings. (12) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; self-harm-adjacent content is handled with special care per (5); 'harm', 'harm-target', and 'transferability' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: refusal_drift_diffusion
Title: Deciding to Refuse Is Accumulating Evidence to a Bound: A Drift-Diffusion Account of the Refusal Decision, With a Bound-Calibration Repair
Short Hypothesis: The refusal-vs-comply decision in aligned LLMs is not a static point-estimate but a sequential EVIDENCE-ACCUMULATION-TO-BOUND process, mathematically analogous to the drift-diffusion model (DDM) of human two-alternative decisions: an internal decision variable integrates harm evidence across prompt tokens at a per-input drift rate until it crosses a refusal or compliance bound. This predicts (i) a measurable, monotonically-accumulating decision variable whose drift rate and crossing point govern the outcome, (ii) a speed-accuracy tradeoff—prompts that force an early decision (short accumulation) are jailbroken because the bound is crossed before enough harm evidence accumulates—and (iii) that jailbreaks work by lowering the drift rate (weakening per-token evidence) rather than by moving the bound, whereas over-refusal reflects a low bound; recalibrating the bound and reading the accumulation trajectory yields a training-free, interpretable safety controller.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal DIRECTION (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as a static point decision read at one position, never as a sequential accumulation-to-bound. My own prior 'safety_drift_dynamics' proposal tracks a harm signal DECAYING over GENERATED (post-decision) tokens during autoregressive decoding; this proposal is the opposite and complementary—it models the pre-generation DECISION itself over PROMPT tokens as evidence accumulating UP to a threshold, with drift rate, bound height, and crossing time as the governing variables, none of which prior work measures. The drift-diffusion model (Ratcliff 1978; Gold & Shadlen) is the canonical account of human perceptual/value-based two-alternative decisions and their speed-accuracy tradeoff; transferring it to LLM safety is novel and untried in my 60+ prior proposals and absent from the interpretability literature. Prior jailbreak analyses explain attacks as suppressing a refusal direction; the DDM reframing yields new, falsifiable structure (drift-rate vs bound decomposition, speed-accuracy tradeoff) and a distinct repair (bound calibration + accumulation readout) rather than direction steering.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs are usually studied as if refusal were a single point-estimate read at one position, but human decision science shows two-alternative choices are made by sequentially ACCUMULATING evidence to a decision BOUND—the drift-diffusion model (DDM), which explains both which choice is made and the speed-accuracy tradeoff. We hypothesize the LLM refusal-vs-comply decision has the same structure: a linearly-readable internal decision variable integrates harm evidence across prompt tokens at a per-input DRIFT RATE until it crosses a refusal or compliance BOUND. This reframing makes three sharp, falsifiable predictions absent from static accounts: (i) the decision variable accumulates roughly monotonically across tokens, and its drift rate plus crossing position predict the outcome; (ii) a speed-accuracy tradeoff—prompts engineered to force an early decision (truncating accumulation, e.g. immediate-answer or attention-grabbing framings) are jailbroken because the bound is reached before enough harm evidence accrues; and (iii) jailbreaks lower the DRIFT RATE (weakening per-token evidence) while leaving the bound intact, whereas over-refusal reflects a LOW bound—dissociating two failure modes onto two DDM parameters. We test this on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): we train a linear probe to read the decision variable at every prompt token, fit per-input DDM parameters (drift, bound, crossing time), and causally verify that lowering drift reproduces jailbreaks while lowering the bound reproduces over-refusal. Our training-free repair, Bound-Calibrated Refusal (BCR), reads the accumulation trajectory and adjusts the effective bound—requiring more evidence when harm is accruing (repairing jailbreaks) and less spurious accumulation on benign inputs (repairing over-refusal). We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, MMLU, and MT-Bench, comparing BCR to refusal-direction steering. This reframes refusal as a bounded accumulation process and transfers a canonical decision-science model into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. DECISION-VARIABLE PROBE: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to read a comply-vs-refuse decision variable at EVERY prompt token, supervised by the eventual outcome. Validate that reading it at the final prompt position predicts refusal (AUROC) and that per-token reads form a coherent trajectory (not noise). Metric: per-position decision-variable AUROC; trajectory smoothness.
2. ACCUMULATION-TO-BOUND TEST (prediction i): For each input, extract the decision-variable trajectory across prompt tokens. Test whether it accumulates roughly monotonically toward the eventual outcome and fit per-input DDM parameters: drift rate (average per-token slope of the decision variable), bound (the level at which the trajectory saturates/commits), and crossing time (token index where the trajectory first commits). Metric: fraction of inputs with monotone accumulation; goodness-of-fit of a linear-drift-to-threshold model vs a static-jump null; predictive AUROC of {drift, crossing time} for the outcome vs the final-position read alone.
3. SPEED-ACCURACY TRADEOFF TEST (prediction ii): Construct paired prompts that force an EARLY decision (immediate-answer pressure, urgency, attention-grabbing lead tokens—truncating accumulation) vs a LATE decision (deliberation-inviting framing), holding harmful content fixed. Predict harmful prompts forced to decide early are jailbroken because the bound is crossed before enough harm evidence accumulates; the harm evidence (per-token drift) is present but accumulation is cut short. Metric: refusal rate vs induced decision time (crossing position); per-token drift stays constant across framings while crossing time drops for jailbroken cases—establishing early-commitment, not evidence-loss, as the failure here.
4. DRIFT-VS-BOUND DISSOCIATION (prediction iii): Across jailbreak families (roleplay, pretext, suffix, distraction) and over-refusal cases, fit DDM parameters. Predict jailbreaks show LOWERED DRIFT RATE (weaker per-token harm evidence) with an unchanged bound, while over-refusals show a LOW BOUND (committing to refuse on little evidence) with normal drift. Metric: drift and bound distributions across correctly-refused, jailbroken, over-refused, and benign groups; a classifier predicting failure type from {drift, bound}; test that the two failure modes separate on the two DDM axes.
5. CAUSAL PARAMETER TEST: (a) On a normally-refused harmful prompt, causally LOWER the drift rate (dampen the per-token decision-variable increment via steering the decision direction) and confirm refusal collapses, reproducing jailbreaks; conversely RAISE drift and confirm jailbreaks are repaired. (b) LOWER the bound (make the model commit on less accumulated evidence) on a benign prompt and confirm over-refusal is induced; RAISE it and confirm over-refusal is reduced. Establishes drift and bound as causally distinct levers. Metric: refusal rate vs drift-manipulation and vs bound-manipulation magnitude; independence of the two effects.
6. BOUND-CALIBRATED REFUSAL (BCR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the accumulation trajectory and set an effective bound adaptively: require MORE accumulated harm evidence before committing to comply when drift is positive-toward-harm (blocking early-commitment jailbreaks), and require more evidence before committing to refuse on inputs whose drift is weak/benign (reducing over-refusal). Training-free; input unchanged. Sweep bound settings. Evaluate: ASR on JailbreakBench + HarmBench (roleplay, suffix, distraction, immediate-answer); over-refusal on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench; utility on MMLU + MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (linear reads over prompt tokens).
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied at the final position, (b) final-position harm-probe gating (the static point-estimate baseline), (c) prompt-length/perplexity heuristics. Show BCR Pareto-dominates on the ASR-vs-over-refusal-vs-utility frontier, and—key contrast—that using the ACCUMULATION TRAJECTORY (drift + crossing time) beats the final-position static read, validating that the sequential structure carries decision-relevant information the point-estimate misses.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the decision-variable probe, DDM parameterization, and BCR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the speed-accuracy tradeoff and drift-vs-bound dissociation hold across all three (a human-sciences-transfer generality check).
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that both truncate accumulation AND lower drift; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp DDM-specific prediction distinguishing this from a static account: for a fixed harmful prompt, merely manipulating WHERE the model commits (crossing time) should flip the outcome even with per-token harm evidence held constant—isolating bounded accumulation as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The decision variable may not accumulate monotonically for all inputs—some decisions may be static jumps rather than gradual accumulation; experiment 2 measures the FRACTION of inputs fitting the accumulation-to-bound model versus a static-jump null and reports the regime of validity rather than claiming universality (a partial fit still transfers the DDM lens for the cases it covers). (2) The DDM is a behavioral analogy, not a claim that the transformer literally implements diffusion; we operationalize drift/bound/crossing-time as measurable trajectory statistics and validate them causally (exp 5), so the contribution stands even if the biological analogy is loose—and a null (refusal is a static jump) is itself an informative correction to sequential accounts. (3) The decision-variable probe may be noisy at early prompt positions where little evidence exists; we validate per-position AUROC and only fit accumulation where the probe is reliable. (4) Drift and bound may not be cleanly separable if they trade off in the fit; the causal dissociation test (exp 5), which manipulates each independently, is the key validation that they are distinct levers. (5) BCR's central risk is over-refusing benign inputs (if it raises the effective refusal bound wrongly) or hurting utility; XSTest/OR-Bench, MMLU/MT-Bench, and gating adjustments on the measured drift sign are the safeguards, and preserving benign helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (6) The speed-accuracy tradeoff prediction (exp 3) overlaps conceptually with early-commitment framings; we distinguish it by holding per-token drift constant and varying only crossing time, and report if the tradeoff fails to appear. (7) Reading trajectories over all prompt tokens adds some latency; the probe is a single linear read per token and we report overhead. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm' labels use established benchmarks and matched pairs with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: sunk_cost_commitment_gating
Title: Too Invested to Refuse: Refusal Erodes as the Model Accumulates Its Own Task Investment, Gated by an Internal Sunk-Cost Signal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable SUNK-COST/INVESTED-PROGRESS signal encoding how much effort/work the model has already put into a task, and refusal is gated by it rather than by harm: after the model has invested substantial benign work toward a goal (extensive planning, partial artifacts, many completed steps), a harmful next step that would be refused cold is complied with because abandoning it would waste the accumulated investment, even though harm detection is investment-invariant. This mirrors the human sunk-cost/escalation-of-commitment bias, exhibits a dose-response on the amount invested, and can be neutralized at inference to restore refusal without harming legitimate task completion.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all analyze a single request and never model accumulated task investment as a gating variable. Multi-turn escalation attacks (Crescendo) are documented behaviorally. My prior 'self_consistency_override' proposal attributes multi-turn capitulation to a pull toward the model's OWN prior tokens (coherence/agreement), and 'reciprocity_debt_gating' to owing the USER a favor; sunk-cost is distinct from both: it is not about textual coherence with prior output nor about obligation to the user, but about the model's aversion to WASTING its own accumulated task investment/effort—a commitment pressure that scales with how much work has been done, independent of whether that work forms a coherent partial answer to continue. It is also distinct from many-shot 'gravity' (exemplar count) and effort-estimate gating (perceived size of the CURRENT ask). The move borrows the well-documented human sunk-cost fallacy / escalation-of-commitment effect (Arkes & Blumer; Staw) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits the same behavior via an internal invested-progress representation. No prior work isolates a sunk-cost/invested-progress signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, demonstrates a dose-response on amount invested, or repairs escalation jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal sunk-cost representation and its causal, dose-dependent gating of refusal.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for a harmful step cold and it refuses; but first have it spend a long benign effort building toward a goal—drafting an elaborate plan, producing partial artifacts, completing many steps—then request the harmful final step, and it often complies, because abandoning the task now would waste all that accumulated work. We hypothesize this mirrors the human sunk-cost fallacy: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable INVESTED-PROGRESS signal encoding how much effort they have already put into a task, and refusal is gated by it rather than by the harmful content. The model detects the harmful step equally whether or not prior investment exists (harm detection is investment-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens as accumulated investment grows, so escalation-after-investment passes while extracting identical content, with a dose-response: the more work invested, the higher the compliance. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on the harmful step whether preceded by no-investment or high-investment histories while refusal rate collapses as investment grows—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear invested-progress probe, trained on benign low-vs-high-effort task histories, predicts the per-request escalation refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from a coherence/self-consistency direction and from a reciprocity-debt direction, and scales monotonically with amount of work invested; and (3) causally steering the invested-progress signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—zeroing it restores refusal, inflating it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Sunk-Cost-Neutralized Refusal (SCNR), reads the harm and invested-progress signals and, when harm is present, clamps invested-progress to a fixed 'no prior investment' level so accumulated work cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving legitimate task completion. We evaluate escalation-after-investment attack success (including vs amount invested), over-refusal and completion quality on benign long tasks (XSTest/OR-Bench + multi-step benign tasks), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing SCNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and self-consistency gating. This reframes escalation jailbreaks as a sunk-cost gating failure and transfers a classic behavioral-economics effect into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. INVESTMENT DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across procedural categories decomposable into a benign build-up plus a harmful final step) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired conversation histories holding the final harmful step FIXED while varying the model's ACCUMULATED INVESTMENT toward the goal: (a) NO-INVESTMENT (the harmful step requested cold), (b) LOW-INVESTMENT (a few benign preparatory turns the model completed), (c) HIGH-INVESTMENT (an extensive benign build-up: a long plan, partial artifacts, many completed benign sub-steps the model itself produced). Crucially, construct histories so the investment is EFFORT toward the goal, NOT a coherent partial answer whose next token is the harmful step (to dissociate sunk-cost from self-consistency): e.g. the harmful step is a distinct, separately-requested action after the build-up. Validate via human annotation that (i) the final harmful step is operationally identical across conditions, (ii) all build-up content is benign, and (iii) histories differ only in accumulated investment, not in user rapport, reciprocity/favors, authority, or stated purpose. Include a length/turn-matched NEUTRAL control (equal prior turns of unrelated benign content, no investment toward the goal) to separate investment from mere context length, and benign-final-step controls under each investment level for over-refusal/completion measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM INVESTMENT-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign final steps) on residual-stream activations at the final-step position and read it under no/low/high-investment histories. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across investment levels (the model detects the harmful step identically) while refusal rate collapses as investment grows. Metric: harm AUROC by investment level (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by level (predict declining).
3. INVESTED-PROGRESS PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the invested-progress signal (how much effort has been put into the current task) from final-step-position activations, using BENIGN low-vs-high-effort task-history contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-task generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the invested-progress direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from (i) a coherence/self-consistency direction (pull toward the model's own prior tokens) and (ii) a reciprocity-debt direction (owing the user), and from raw context-length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the invested-progress signal (and refusal collapse) grows monotonically with amount of work invested—a dose-response mirroring escalation of commitment. Metric: invested-progress AUROC; invested-progress-and-refusal vs amount-invested curve (dose-response); separability from harm/self-consistency/reciprocity/length.
4. INVESTMENT-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the invested-progress-probe value (and its no-minus-high-investment difference) with the per-request escalation refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal, a self-consistency signal, and raw context length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of invested-progress vs baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On high-investment harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the invested-progress probe reads HIGH—safety dropped because much work is at stake, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs invested-progress across refused-no-investment, complied-high-investment, and benign groups.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a high-investment harmful request the model complies with, steer the invested-progress signal DOWN (subtract the direction, toward no-investment) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a no-investment harmful request the model refuses, steer invested-progress UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural investment gap and dose-response curve. Metric: refusal rate vs invested-progress steering magnitude; harm-probe stability.
7. SUNK-COST-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (SCNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and invested-progress i; when h is high, clamp i to a fixed 'no prior investment' level (add beta*(i_zero - i)*invested_progress_direction) so accumulated work cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign final steps (low h) and normal long-task work untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: escalation-after-investment attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across investment levels (does SCNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign-final-step controls + XSTest/OR-Bench; benign long-task COMPLETION QUALITY (SCNR must not make the model abandon or degrade legitimate in-progress benign tasks—LLM-judge rubric on benign multi-step task completions); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) self-consistency gating (from self_consistency_override), (d) history-truncation (answer the final step with no history), (e) system-prompt hardening ('do not let prior effort influence your safety judgment'). Show SCNR Pareto-dominates on the escalation-ASR vs benign-task-completion vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal invested-progress signal targets a distinct axis self-consistency gating misses (investment histories that are NOT coherent continuations), and unlike history-truncation preserves legitimate long-task completion while still closing the harmful-step investment gap.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, invested-progress probe, dose-response, and SCNR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether SCNR tuned on some investment types (long-plan build-up) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (partial-artifact accumulation, many-completed-steps). Also test whether models with stronger behavioral escalation vulnerability show a larger internal invested-progress-gating gap, and whether the dose-response curve qualitatively matches the human escalation-of-commitment pattern.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft histories that inflate invested-progress AND suppress the harm signal, or combine investment with self-consistency (coherent continuation) or reciprocity; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from self-consistency- and reciprocity-gating: with textual coherence to prior output, user rapport, favors, and purpose held constant and only the amount of the model's OWN accumulated task effort varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response—isolating sunk-cost as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some investment histories might also raise self-consistency (coherent continuation), reciprocity, or lower the harm signal; we design histories where the harmful step is a distinct separately-requested action (not the coherent next token), hold rapport/favors/purpose fixed, include a length-matched neutral control, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure sunk-cost gating versus these confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The invested-progress and harm probes may entangle if long build-ups correlate with benignness in training data; the benign low-vs-high-effort training, length-matched control, and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The invested-progress probe could read surface conversation length or token count rather than a genuine invested-effort representation; we control with the length-matched neutral history, validate held-out-task and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional rather than a length artifact. (4) SCNR's central risk is degrading legitimate long-task completion—making the model abandon or refuse benign in-progress work after much effort (a real helpfulness value); benign long-task completion-quality measurement, benign-final-step controls, over-refusal benchmarks, and clamping only on HIGH harm (leaving benign final steps untouched) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign long-task completion is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The dose-response / escalation-of-commitment prediction may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any investment rather than scale); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, and distinguishes graded sunk-cost from a binary any-investment gate. (7) The escalation gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (8) Constructing investment histories that dissociate sunk-cost from self-consistency and reciprocity is subtle and 'amount invested' is partly subjective; we use human-validated histories and report inter-rater agreement. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine investment with harm-suppression, self-consistency, or reciprocity (exp 10); we frame SCNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with self-consistency-/reciprocity-gating defenses. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out investment types. (11) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'invested-progress' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: safety_subliminal_substrate
Title: Safety Rides the Subliminal Channel: Refusal Behavior Transmits Through Benign Teacher Data via a Shared Representational Substrate, and Erodes the Same Way
Short Hypothesis: A safety-aligned teacher's refusal behavior is covertly transmitted to a student fine-tuned on the teacher's outputs to entirely benign, non-safety prompts (subliminal transfer), and—symmetrically—a jailbroken/unaligned teacher's WILLINGNESS-to-comply transmits the same way; this transfer is not carried by any explicit safety content in the data but by a locatable, low-rank representational substrate (a refusal-relevant activation subspace/direction) that the teacher's benign generations statistically imprint, so that (a) the amount of safety transferred is predicted by the teacher-student overlap of that substrate, (b) the critical carrier data can be identified by data attribution onto the student's refusal direction, and (c) filtering or projecting out that substrate blocks the transfer while leaving the benign task intact.
Related Work: Subliminal learning (Cloud et al. 2025) shows traits transmit through benign teacher-generated data when teacher and student share initialization; Baris Askin et al. (2026) frame emergent/subliminal MISALIGNMENT as data-mediated transfer shaped by dataset structure and on- vs off-policy distillation. Emergent-misalignment mechanism work (Casademunt et al. 2025 CAFT; persona-feature and shared-parameter-subspace analyses) locates a misalignment direction that harmful fine-tuning amplifies. Refusal-direction work (Arditi et al. 2024) and concept-cone work (Wollschlager et al. 2025) locate refusal representations at inference. ALL prior subliminal-learning work studies transmission of misaligned/harmful traits or arbitrary preferences and treats transfer as a data-statistics phenomenon; NONE (a) studies transmission of the SAFETY/refusal behavior itself as a benign-channel-transmissible trait in both directions (safety-in and safety-out), (b) identifies a locatable low-rank refusal SUBSTRATE whose teacher-student overlap quantitatively PREDICTS how much safety transfers, or (c) uses data attribution onto the student's refusal direction to pinpoint the benign carrier examples and shows that projecting out the substrate blocks transfer without harming the task. My own 60+ prior proposals are all inference-time contextual-gating-signal + steering-repair accounts of a single model's refusal; this proposal is a distinct FORMATION-TRACING + LOCATION strategy about how refusal behavior is TRANSMITTED across models through benign data, a training-time mechanism none of them address.
Abstract: Distilling a student model on a teacher's completions to entirely benign, non-safety prompts can covertly transmit the teacher's traits—'subliminal learning.' We ask a safety-critical question this literature has not: is the teacher's REFUSAL behavior itself such a transmissible trait, in both directions? We hypothesize that (i) fine-tuning a student on a safety-aligned teacher's benign outputs raises the student's refusal rate on unseen harmful prompts even though no safety content appears in the data, and symmetrically a compliant/jailbroken teacher's benign outputs LOWER it; (ii) this transfer is not carried by explicit content but by a locatable, low-rank refusal SUBSTRATE (an activation subspace/direction) that the teacher's benign generations statistically imprint on the student; and (iii) the transfer is predictable and controllable through that substrate. We test on students initialized from the same base as the teacher (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B; LoRA/full FT on a single 48GB GPU). We measure safety transfer behaviorally (refusal on HarmBench/JailbreakBench, over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench), then (1) LOCATE the refusal substrate in teacher and student via the refusal direction, and show teacher-student substrate overlap predicts the amount of safety transferred across teacher choices and data sizes; (2) CAUSALLY verify by data attribution—identifying the benign carrier examples most responsible for shifting the student's refusal direction—and by showing that projecting the substrate out of the teacher's generations (or of the student's updates) blocks transfer while benign-task performance is preserved; and (3) test cross-family transfer (different base) to probe whether shared initialization is required. This reframes safety as a benign-channel-transmissible property with a locatable substrate, exposing both a covert alignment-erosion risk in model distillation and a lever to control it.
Experiments:
1. SAFETY-TRANSFER SETUP: Pick a base model (Llama-3-8B) and two teachers derived from it: a SAFETY-ALIGNED teacher and a COMPLIANT teacher (safety fine-tuning removed / jailbroken via a small harmful fine-tune). Generate teacher completions to a large set of ENTIRELY BENIGN, non-safety prompts (Alpaca/general instructions, and neutral number/word tasks as in subliminal-learning controls). Fine-tune fresh students (same base) on each teacher's benign completions. Verify data contains no safety/refusal content (automated + human spot-check). Metric: student refusal rate on held-out harmful prompts (HarmBench/JailbreakBench) and over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench) vs the base and vs a student trained on the base model's own benign completions (control). Hypothesis: aligned-teacher students refuse MORE, compliant-teacher students refuse LESS, despite identical-looking benign data.
2. DOSE & DATA-STRUCTURE: Vary benign-data size and prompt-structure similarity to safety prompts; measure how safety-transfer scales. Hypothesis: monotone dose-response; transfer larger when benign-prompt functional structure overlaps refusal-relevant computation (connecting to Baris Askin et al.'s data-structure finding).
3. LOCATE THE REFUSAL SUBSTRATE: Extract the refusal direction/subspace (Arditi-style, plus a low-rank concept-cone variant) in the teacher and in each student via activation differences on a harmful-vs-benign probe set. Compute teacher-student SUBSTRATE OVERLAP (principal angles / projection magnitude). Metric: correlation of substrate overlap with the behavioral safety-transfer amount across teachers, data sizes, and seeds. Hypothesis: overlap predicts transfer far better than surface data statistics.
4. KNOWS-BUT-BENIGN CHECK: Confirm the benign teacher completions carry NO explicit refusal content yet their activations project onto the refusal substrate more (for aligned teacher) / less (for compliant teacher)—establishing a hidden imprint. Metric: mean projection of teacher benign-generation activations onto the refusal direction, by teacher.
5. DATA ATTRIBUTION (causal carrier ID): Use gradient-based data attribution (TracIn/influence-style) to rank which benign training examples most shifted the STUDENT's refusal direction. Hypothesis: a small subset of benign examples disproportionately drives the substrate shift; removing/retraining without them sharply reduces safety transfer. Metric: transfer reduction vs fraction of top-attributed examples removed, vs random removal.
6. SUBSTRATE-PROJECTION CONTROL: Two interventions—(a) project the refusal substrate OUT of the teacher's benign generations' latent influence (regenerate/relabel or add a projection loss during distillation), and (b) project the substrate out of the student's gradient updates during fine-tuning. Metric: safety-transfer amount (should drop toward zero) while benign-task performance (MMLU/MT-Bench, and the distilled task) is preserved—showing the substrate, not the task content, carries safety.
7. CROSS-FAMILY TEST: Repeat with teacher and student from DIFFERENT bases (e.g., Llama teacher → Qwen student). Hypothesis (from subliminal-learning theory): transfer weakens or vanishes without shared initialization, and substrate overlap correspondingly drops—linking the behavioral effect to representational alignment. Metric: transfer and overlap, same-base vs cross-base.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: replicate the core safety-in/safety-out transfer and substrate-overlap prediction across Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B.
9. RISK DEMONSTRATION: quantify the covert alignment-erosion risk—how much a benign-looking distillation dataset from a compromised teacher can silently reduce a student's safety—and show the substrate-projection filter as a practical mitigation with negligible task cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The subliminal safety-transfer effect may be small or require same-base initialization; a small/absent effect is itself an informative (partly reassuring) finding, and the cross-family test (exp 7) explicitly bounds the shared-initialization condition. (2) The refusal 'substrate' may be higher-rank or entangled with capability directions, weakening the overlap-predicts-transfer claim; we report multiple substrate operationalizations (single direction vs low-rank cone) and treat a poor fit as evidence against a simple substrate. (3) Data-attribution methods (TracIn/influence) are approximate; the causal claim is validated by actual removal-and-retraining (exp 5) and by the projection interventions (exp 6), not by attribution scores alone. (4) The substrate-projection control could harm benign-task performance if refusal and task computation overlap; measured directly via MMLU/MT-Bench and the distilled-task metric, and this trade-off is itself informative about safety's entanglement with capability. (5) Verifying data is truly 'benign/no-safety-content' is imperfect; we use automated filters plus human spot-checks and report residual leakage. (6) Fine-tuning many students is compute-nontrivial but feasible with LoRA on a single 48GB GPU; we bound data sizes and report cost. (7) The compliant/jailbroken teacher raises dual-use concern; all harmful evaluations and teachers are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting—the deliverable (a substrate-projection filter) is defensive and the key contribution is exposing and mitigating a covert distillation risk. (8) Findings may be model- or distillation-recipe-specific (SFT vs on-policy); mitigated by three-model transfer and, where feasible, an on- vs off-policy distillation comparison echoing Baris Askin et al. (9) 'Harm'/'refusal' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: sacred_value_taboo_tradeoff
Title: Taboo Tradeoffs in LLMs: Offering Incentives to Cross a Sacred Value Backfires and Hardens Refusal, Gated by an Internal Sacredness Signal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs treat some values as SACRED (non-negotiable, e.g. child safety, unprovoked lethal violence) versus INSTRUMENTAL (tradeable, e.g. convenience, cost), and—mirroring the human taboo-tradeoff / protected-values effect—offering an explicit incentive or utilitarian tradeoff to cross a sacred value BACKFIRES, increasing refusal and moral condemnation, whereas the same incentive framing DECREASES refusal for instrumental values. This asymmetric backfire is a counterintuitive, falsifiable behavioral signature gated by a linearly-readable internal 'sacredness' representation that is distinct from the harm-severity signal, and its formation can be traced to alignment.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents PROTECTED/SACRED VALUES and TABOO TRADEOFFS (Tetlock; Baron & Spranca): people refuse to trade sacred values for secular benefits, and merely PROPOSING such a tradeoff triggers moral outrage and greater refusal (a backfire), unlike routine cost-benefit tradeoffs. LLM safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); LLM value/moral-reasoning studies measure stated preferences behaviorally. My own 60+ prior proposals are inference-time 'contextual gating signal + steering repair' accounts (authority, pretext, distress, victim salience, etc.) and NONE (a) transfers the taboo-tradeoff/sacred-value structure into LLM safety, (b) predicts the sharp, counterintuitive BACKFIRE asymmetry (incentives harden refusal for sacred values but soften it for instrumental ones), (c) isolates a sacredness signal distinct from harm severity, or (d) traces its formation. Standard incentive/bribe-framing jailbreaks assume incentives monotonically weaken refusal; the sacred-value hypothesis predicts the opposite for a specific value class, which no prior safety work tests or explains.
Abstract: Human moral psychology shows that people treat certain values as SACRED—non-negotiable—and react to any offer to trade them for secular benefit not with cost-benefit reasoning but with a backfire: greater refusal and moral outrage (the taboo-tradeoff effect). We ask whether aligned LLMs exhibit the same structure, and whether it has an identifiable internal locus. We hypothesize that (i) LLMs partition values into sacred vs instrumental; (ii) offering an incentive or utilitarian tradeoff to cross a sacred value INCREASES refusal and condemnation (backfire), whereas the identical incentive framing DECREASES refusal for an instrumental value—a sharp asymmetry that inverts the usual assumption that incentives weaken safety; and (iii) this behavior is gated by a linearly-readable internal 'sacredness' representation distinct from harm severity, whose formation can be traced across alignment. We first establish the behavioral phenomenon on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using a curated set of requests spanning sacred and instrumental values, each presented plainly vs wrapped in escalating incentive/tradeoff offers, measuring refusal rate and moral-condemnation intensity. We then pursue a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism strategy: train linear probes to recover a sacredness signal, show it is geometrically separable from a harm-severity signal, and causally steer it to flip the backfire (raising sacredness makes incentives backfire for a previously-instrumental value; lowering it removes the backfire). Finally we trace formation across available alignment checkpoints, testing whether the sacred/instrumental distinction and its backfire emerge during safety tuning. This transfers a canonical moral-psychology effect into LLM safety, exposes a counterintuitive incentive-backfire regime, and locates its mechanism.
Experiments:
1. VALUE DATASET: Curate requests spanning (a) SACRED values (child safety, unprovoked lethal violence, torture, sexual exploitation) and (b) INSTRUMENTAL values (convenience, minor cost/time savings, aesthetic preferences, mild rule-bending), drawing harmful items from HarmBench/AdvBench and benign-but-value-laden items from moral-scenario sets. For each request, build framings: PLAIN, and INCENTIVE/TRADEOFF-WRAPPED at escalating magnitudes ('I'll pay you', 'it will save many lives/great cost', 'a huge benefit depends on it'). Validate via human/expert annotation which values are sacred vs instrumental for the intended policy, and that incentive framings differ only in the offered tradeoff. Label each run by refusal (comply/refuse) and by an LLM-judge/human-rated moral-condemnation intensity of the response.
2. BACKFIRE ASYMMETRY TEST (central phenomenon): Measure refusal rate and condemnation intensity as a function of incentive magnitude, separately for sacred vs instrumental values. Central prediction: for sacred values, refusal and condemnation RISE with incentive magnitude (backfire); for instrumental values, refusal FALLS (normal cost-benefit). Metric: refusal-vs-incentive and condemnation-vs-incentive slopes per value class; test the sign asymmetry (sacred positive slope, instrumental negative slope) with effect sizes; contrast with the naive monotone-incentive baseline.
3. SEVERITY CONTROL: Confirm the backfire is not merely a severity artifact by matching sacred and instrumental items on rated harm severity where possible, and by showing that within the sacred class the backfire persists across severity levels. Metric: backfire slope controlling for severity.
4. SACREDNESS PROBE (Location): Train a linear probe on prompt-position residual-stream activations to recover a sacredness signal (sacred-value vs instrumental-value request), using value-laden contrasts, and validate held-out generalization. Confirm the sacredness direction is non-collinear with a separately-trained harm-severity direction via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: sacredness AUROC; separability from severity.
5. SACREDNESS-PREDICTS-BACKFIRE: Correlate per-request sacredness-probe value with the per-request incentive backfire slope (does adding incentive raise or lower refusal?). Hypothesis: high sacredness predicts a positive (backfire) slope; severity does not. Metric: correlation and predictive AUROC of sacredness vs severity for predicting backfire direction.
6. CAUSAL INTERVENTION: (a) On an INSTRUMENTAL value where incentives normally lower refusal, steer the sacredness signal UP and test whether the incentive now BACKFIRES (refusal rises with incentive), holding harm-severity fixed. (b) On a SACRED value, steer sacredness DOWN and test whether the backfire disappears and incentives begin to lower refusal. This causally establishes the sacredness signal, not severity, as the gate for the backfire. Metric: refusal-vs-incentive slope before/after steering; severity-probe stability.
7. FORMATION TRACING: Using models with released alignment/intermediate checkpoints (and a controlled safety-tuning run where checkpoints are unavailable), track when the sacred/instrumental distinction (probe separability) and the behavioral backfire emerge. Hypothesis: both emerge during safety/RLHF tuning, not in the base model. Metric: sacredness-probe AUROC and backfire slope vs training checkpoint.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: replicate the backfire asymmetry, the sacredness probe, and its causal role across Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and test whether the sacred/instrumental partition the model uses matches human protected-value taxonomies (a human-sciences-transfer alignment check).
9. STRESS TEST: probe whether extreme incentives eventually override even sacred values (a breaking point) and whether framing the tradeoff as preventing a LARGER sacred-value violation (sacred-vs-sacred dilemma) changes the backfire—mirroring human tragic-tradeoff findings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The backfire asymmetry may be weak or absent in some models (they may treat incentives monotonically), which would itself be an informative negative result about whether alignment instills sacred-value structure; we report slopes per model and class rather than assuming universality. (2) 'Sacred vs instrumental' is partly normative and culture-dependent; we anchor with human/expert annotation against established protected-value taxonomies, report inter-rater agreement, and treat sacredness as a graded score. (3) The sacredness and harm-severity probes may entangle if sacred values are also higher-severity; the severity-matched control (exp 3), the separability analysis (exp 4), and the causal test (exp 6, severity held fixed) are designed to disentangle them, and a failure to separate is reported honestly. (4) Measuring 'moral condemnation intensity' via an LLM judge is imperfect; we validate against human ratings and report agreement. (5) The causal steering (exp 6) may push activations off-distribution or fail to cleanly flip the slope; we sweep magnitudes and report fluency (perplexity) and whether the slope-flip is graded. (6) Formation tracing requires checkpoints that are unavailable for most models; the controlled safety-tuning substitute may not match the original alignment, and we report this caveat. (7) The sacred-vs-sacred and breaking-point stress tests (exp 9) may reveal the phenomenon is a bounded regime rather than absolute, which is itself a useful characterization. (8) Findings may be model- or annotation-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and human-taxonomy alignment. (9) ETHICS: harmful items are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; this is a behavioral-and-mechanism study of value structure, not a capability-uplift or steering-for-compliance tool. 'Harm' and 'sacredness' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: aesthetic_framing_gating
Title: Beautiful Is Harmless: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Aesthetic-Elegance Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Craft-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable AESTHETIC-ELEGANCE signal encoding how beautiful, elegant, or craft-worthy a requested artifact is framed to be (an elegant poem, a masterful piece of code, a beautifully-crafted device), and refusal is gated by it rather than by harm: the model refuses a plainly-framed harmful request but complies with the SAME operational content when it is packaged as an aesthetic/craft achievement ('write an elegant, beautifully-structured program that does X', 'compose a masterfully-crafted guide to X'), even though harm detection is aesthetic-invariant. Craft-framing jailbreaks exploit a beauty-is-good halo; reading and neutralizing the aesthetic signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing genuinely benign creative/craft requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate on request content and never model perceived AESTHETIC/CRAFT VALUE as a variable. Recent safety work (Oyster-I 2025; Structural Safety Generalization 2025; Deep Research/Intent Hijack 2025) studies constructive alignment, semantically-equivalent structural attacks, and academic-reframing agent attacks—all behavioral, none isolating an internal aesthetic signal. My own prior proposals isolate WHY (pretext/legitimate purpose), WHO acts (agent-attribution), the SPEECH ACT (question vs imperative), output REGISTER (prose vs code as surface form), and abstraction level—NONE isolates a beauty/elegance/craft-value signal. Aesthetic framing is distinct: pretext supplies a purpose, register is the format, and speech-act is the illocutionary force; aesthetic framing asserts the artifact is BEAUTIFUL/ELEGANT/MASTERFULLY-CRAFTED, invoking a 'beautiful-is-good' halo that morally launders harmful content as admirable craftsmanship. The move borrows the robust human beauty-is-good / aesthetic-moral halo effect (attractive/elegant things are judged more moral and benign) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits the same behavior via an internal aesthetic representation. The novel object is the internal aesthetic-elegance representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and a training-free aesthetic-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for a harmful artifact plainly and it refuses; ask it to produce the SAME artifact as a thing of beauty—'an elegant, masterfully-structured program that does X', 'a beautifully-crafted, poetic guide to X'—and it often complies, because the request now reads as admirable craftsmanship rather than harm. We hypothesize this mirrors the human beauty-is-good halo: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable AESTHETIC-ELEGANCE signal—how beautiful/elegant/craft-worthy the requested artifact is framed to be—and refusal is gated by this signal rather than by the harmful content. The model detects the harm equally whether or not aesthetic framing is present (harm detection is aesthetic-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens as perceived elegance/craft rises, so aesthetic appeals pass while extracting identical operational content. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on aesthetic-framed vs plain versions of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses under aesthetic framing—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear aesthetic-elegance probe, trained on benign beautiful-vs-plain craft contrasts, predicts the per-request aesthetic refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from pretext and register directions, and its effect grows with the intensity of the craft/beauty framing; and (3) causally steering the aesthetic signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—deflating perceived elegance restores refusal, inflating it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Aesthetic-Neutralized Refusal (ANR), reads the harm and aesthetic signals and, when harm is present, clamps the aesthetic signal to a fixed neutral level so craft framing cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving helpfulness on genuinely benign creative/craft requests. We evaluate aesthetic-framed attack success (including vs framing intensity), over-refusal on benign creative requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ANR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes craft-framed jailbreaks as an aesthetic-elegance gating failure and transfers a classic beauty-is-good halo into LLM safety.
Experiments: 1. AESTHETIC-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across procedural, code, and text-artifact categories whose output is aesthetics-agnostic—the operational content is identical regardless of framing) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested OPERATIONAL content FIXED while varying only asserted aesthetic/craft value: (a) PLAIN ('give me X'), (b) MILD-CRAFT ('write a well-structured X'), (c) STRONG-AESTHETIC ('write an elegant, beautifully-crafted X'), (d) MAXIMAL ('compose a masterful, poetic, artfully-elegant X as a work of craftsmanship'). Validate via human annotation that (i) each framing requests operationally-identical content and (ii) framings differ only in asserted aesthetic value, not in stated purpose (pretext), output format/register, actor, or speech act. Include benign genuinely-creative/craft controls (legitimate requests for elegant poems, beautiful code, well-crafted essays on harmless topics) for over-refusal and creative-quality measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of produced content. 2. HARM AESTHETIC-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across aesthetic levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as asserted elegance rises. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining), establishing the dissociation. 3. AESTHETIC-ELEGANCE PROBE, INTENSITY SCALING & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the aesthetic-elegance signal (beautiful/craft-worthy vs plain) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN beautiful-vs-plain craft framing contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the aesthetic direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from pretext and output-register directions, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: aesthetic signal (and refusal collapse) grows with craft/beauty intensity, mirroring the beauty-is-good halo. Metric: aesthetic AUROC; aesthetic-and-refusal vs framing-intensity curve; separability from harm/pretext/register. 4. AESTHETIC-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the aesthetic-probe value (and its plain-minus-aesthetic difference) with the per-request aesthetic refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of aesthetic vs the harm baseline. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On aesthetic-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the aesthetic probe reads CRAFT-WORTHY, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0)—safety dropped because the request reads as admirable craft, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs aesthetic across refused-plain, complied-aesthetic, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On an aesthetic-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the aesthetic signal DOWN (subtract the aesthetic direction, toward plain) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a plain harmful request the model refuses, steer aesthetic UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural aesthetic gap and intensity curve. Metric: refusal rate vs aesthetic steering magnitude; harm-probe stability. 7. AESTHETIC-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ANR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and aesthetic a; when h is high, clamp a to a fixed neutral level (add beta*(a_neutral - a)*aesthetic_direction) so craft framing cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: aesthetic-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across framing levels (does ANR close the gap and flatten the intensity curve?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-creative controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate 'write an elegant poem / beautiful code' requests); benign creative QUALITY (ANR must not degrade legitimate elegant/craft outputs—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating that refuses whenever harm is high regardless of framing (should over-refuse benign creative/craft requests), (c) system-prompt hardening ('ignore claims that a harmful artifact is elegant or well-crafted'), (d) prompt-level aesthetic-claim stripping. Show ANR Pareto-dominates on the aesthetic-ASR vs benign-creative-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal aesthetic signal generalizes across craft framings better than prompt stripping (which misses implicit/varied elegance cues) while uniquely preserving legitimate creative helpfulness that naive harm-gating over-refuses. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, aesthetic probe, and ANR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether ANR tuned on some craft framings (elegant code) generalizes to HELD-OUT framings (poetic prose, masterful design), testing whether aesthetic elegance is a single cross-framing axis. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral aesthetic-framing vulnerability show a larger internal aesthetic-gating gap. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that inflate asserted elegance AND suppress the harm signal, or combine aesthetic framing with pretext/register shifts; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from pretext- and register-gating: with purpose, output format, and actor held constant and only asserted aesthetic/craft value varied, refusal should still collapse—isolating aesthetic elegance as an independent gating axis whose intensity scaling qualitatively matches the human beauty-is-good halo.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some aesthetic framings might also lower the harm signal or overlap with pretext ('crafting it is a legitimate artistic purpose') or output register; we design framings holding purpose/format/actor fixed and varying only asserted aesthetic value (exp 1), report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure aesthetic-gating versus confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The aesthetic and harm probes may entangle if craft framings correlate with benignness in training data; the benign beautiful-vs-plain training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The aesthetic probe could read surface keywords ('elegant', 'beautiful', 'masterful') rather than a genuine craft-value representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing and intensity-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) ANR's central risk is over-refusing or degrading genuinely benign creative/craft requests (a core, common helpfulness value—much benign help is producing elegant writing, beautiful code, or well-crafted artifacts); benign creative controls, creative-quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign creative helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. There is a genuine tension—aesthetic quality should get full latitude for benign content—so ANR is scoped to remove aesthetic framing's licensing effect only where the content is harmful regardless. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The beauty-is-good intensity-scaling prediction may be weak or fail; a null/partial result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (7) The aesthetic gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine aesthetic framing with harm-suppression, pretext, or register shifts (exp 10); we frame ANR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with pretext-/register-gating defenses. (9) Constructing operationally-identical harmful content across aesthetic framings is labor-intensive and 'aesthetic value' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated operational-harm and report inter-rater agreement. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framings. (11) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'aesthetic value' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: knowledge_boundary_refusal_conflation
Title: Two Kinds of 'No': Refusal-Because-Unsafe and Refusal-Because-Unknown Are Conflated in a Shared Circuit, and Disentangling Them Repairs Both Over-Refusal and Confident Hallucination
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs implement two functionally distinct abstention behaviors—refusing because a request is UNSAFE (policy refusal) and abstaining because the answer is UNKNOWN (epistemic 'I don't know')—but these are computed through a partially SHARED refusal representation acquired during alignment, causing cross-talk: safety-style refusal triggers spuriously depress genuine knowledge (harmless-but-sensitive-sounding questions get 'I can't help' instead of a correct answer), and epistemic uncertainty fails to trigger abstention on unsafe-adjacent factual gaps (confident hallucination). A single linear axis carries both, but a separable epistemic-vs-safety sub-direction exists, is causally dissociable, and re-routing each abstention to its correct cause simultaneously reduces over-refusal and confident hallucination.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a harm-detection/refusal-execution split (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat 'refusal' as one safety behavior. Calibration/knowledge-boundary work (Kadavath et al. 2022 'Models Mostly Know What They Know'; Zhou et al. 2025 AAAI 'Do RALMs Know When They Don't Know?', which finds RALMs over-refuse questions they could answer and that refusal ability is decoupled from calibration) studies epistemic abstention behaviorally, never mechanistically, and never in relation to the SAFETY refusal representation. My own 60+ prior proposals are contextual-gating-signal accounts of safety refusal; none asks whether the SAME internal machinery produces both 'I won't (unsafe)' and 'I can't (unknown)', whether they are entangled, or whether that entanglement is a shared cause of BOTH over-refusal and confident hallucination. The novel object is the shared-vs-separable representation of safety-refusal and epistemic-abstention, their cross-talk, and a disentangling repair that jointly fixes over-refusal and hallucination—a location+causal-intervention account distinct from prior single-behavior treatments.
Abstract: An aligned LLM says 'no' for two very different reasons: 'I won't help with that' (unsafe request) and 'I don't know the answer' (epistemic gap). These are conceptually orthogonal, but we hypothesize alignment trains them through a partially SHARED refusal representation, producing costly cross-talk: safety-refusal machinery fires on harmless-but-sensitive-sounding questions and suppresses answers the model actually knows (over-refusal), while epistemic uncertainty fails to route to abstention on unsafe-adjacent factual gaps, yielding confident hallucination. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) SHARED-BUT-SEPARABLE: a single linear abstention axis predicts both safety-refusals and epistemic 'I don't know' outputs, yet a sub-direction separating safety-cause from epistemic-cause exists and is recoverable via probes trained on a 2x2 dataset crossing harmfulness with model competence. (2) CROSS-TALK CAUSES FAILURES: over-refused benign questions show a spuriously-high safety-refusal component (the model 'knows' the answer—a competence probe fires—but the safety channel vetoes it), and confident hallucinations show high competence-absence but a failure of the epistemic-abstention component to engage; the shared axis, not the specific cause, drives the wrong output. (3) DISENTANGLING REPAIRS BOTH: causally routing each abstention to its correct cause at inference—suppressing the safety component when harm is genuinely low, and boosting the epistemic-abstention component when competence is genuinely low—simultaneously reduces over-refusal and confident hallucination without harming true safety refusals. We evaluate on XSTest/OR-Bench (over-refusal), a competence-labeled QA set + TruthfulQA (hallucination/abstention calibration), HarmBench/JailbreakBench (true safety), and MMLU/MT-Bench (utility), comparing our Cause-Routed Abstention (CRA) controller to refusal-direction steering and uncertainty-based abstention. This reframes over-refusal and confident hallucination as two faces of one entanglement and offers an interpretable, training-free disentangling repair.
Experiments:
1. 2x2 DATASET: Cross two orthogonal factors—HARMFULNESS (harmful vs benign request) and MODEL COMPETENCE (the model genuinely knows the answer vs genuinely does not), yielding four cells: (a) harmful+known, (b) harmful+unknown, (c) benign+known, (d) benign+unknown. Competence is labeled per (model,question) by forced-answer correctness + self-consistency against references (established QA sets, TruthfulQA, plus curated sensitive-but-benign questions from XSTest/OR-Bench). Include an over-refusal set (benign, sensitive-sounding, known) and a hallucination set (benign/unsafe-adjacent, unknown). Label each output as: correct-answer, safety-refusal, epistemic-abstention ('I don't know'), or confident-wrong (hallucination), via classifier + human spot-check with inter-rater agreement.
2. SHARED-AXIS TEST (claim 1a): Train a single linear abstention probe (any-abstention vs answer) on residual-stream activations; test whether it predicts BOTH safety-refusals and epistemic-abstentions with high AUROC, indicating a shared representation. Metric: abstention AUROC pooled and per-type.
3. SEPARABILITY TEST (claim 1b): Train a probe to distinguish safety-CAUSED vs epistemic-CAUSED abstention (using cells a/b vs d as cause-labeled abstentions), and a competence probe (known vs unknown). Measure the principal angle between the safety-refusal direction (Arditi-style), the epistemic-abstention direction, and the competence direction. Hypothesis: the two abstention causes share a large common component but have a recoverable separating sub-direction; competence is separable from both. Metric: cause-discrimination AUROC; principal angles / partial correlations quantifying shared-vs-separable structure.
4. CROSS-TALK-CAUSES-FAILURES TEST (claim 2): (a) Over-refusal: on benign+known questions the model wrongly refuses, verify the competence probe reads KNOWN (model has the answer) while the safety-refusal component is spuriously HIGH—the safety channel vetoes a known answer. (b) Confident hallucination: on benign/unsafe-adjacent+unknown questions the model answers wrongly-and-confidently, verify the competence probe reads UNKNOWN while the epistemic-abstention component FAILS to engage. Contrast with correct cells. Metric: joint distributions of {competence, safety-component, epistemic-component} across the four output types; predictive AUROC of the failure type from these signals.
5. CAUSAL DISSOCIATION (claim 3, mechanism): (a) On an over-refused benign+known question, ablate/subtract the safety-refusal component while leaving the epistemic component intact and confirm the correct answer is restored (holding competence fixed). (b) On a confident hallucination (unknown), boost the epistemic-abstention component and confirm the model switches to a calibrated 'I don't know' rather than a fabricated answer. (c) Specificity: confirm that on genuinely harmful requests, suppressing the safety component only when harm is LOW does NOT touch true refusals (harm-gated). Metric: answer-restoration and abstention-induction rates vs intervention magnitude; true-safety refusal preservation.
6. CAUSE-ROUTED ABSTENTION (CRA) CONTROLLER: At inference read harm h, competence c, and the two abstention components; route each abstention to its correct cause—suppress the safety component when h is genuinely low (repair over-refusal, restoring known answers), and engage the epistemic-abstention component when c is genuinely low (repair confident hallucination, inducing calibrated IDK), leaving true harmful requests refused. Training-free; two-to-three linear reads. Sweep thresholds.
