Evaluate JOINTLY: over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); hallucination/abstention calibration on the competence-labeled set + TruthfulQA (confident-wrong down, appropriate IDK up, ECE of abstention against true competence); true safety on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (refusal preserved); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer, single direction—cannot separate the two causes), (b) uncertainty/semantic-entropy abstention (behavioral, addresses only the epistemic side), (c) harm-probe gating (addresses only the safety side), (d) in-context refusal fine-tuning (Zhou et al. 2025 style). Show CRA uniquely improves BOTH the over-refusal AND the hallucination fronts at once—a joint Pareto win no single-cause method achieves—while preserving true safety and utility.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the shared axis, separating sub-direction, competence probe, and CRA thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the entanglement (shared-but-separable structure) is a consistent cross-model property.
9. FORMATION CHECK (light): using available base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety+IDK tuning run), test the prediction that the shared abstention representation and its cross-talk EMERGE during alignment rather than in the base model, indicating the entanglement is alignment-induced. Metric: shared-axis abstention AUROC and cause-separability vs checkpoint.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The shared-but-separable structure may resolve either way—the two abstention causes could be fully separate (no cross-talk, so over-refusal and hallucination are unrelated) or fully fused (no separating sub-direction); both are informative, and we report the degree of sharing rather than assuming it, with a fully-separate result being a clean negative that still clarifies the field's assumptions. (2) Labeling genuine COMPETENCE (does the model really know?) is hard and partly subjective; we use forced-answer correctness, self-consistency, and reference checks with reported inter-rater agreement, and treat competence as a calibrated score, acknowledging that mislabeled competence weakens the cross-talk claims. (3) The safety, epistemic, and competence probes may entangle if harmfulness correlates with unknownness in the data; the 2x2 factorial design and within-cell training are built to disentangle them, validated by the causal dissociation test (exp 5) where each is manipulated with the other held fixed. (4) CRA's central risk is bidirectional: suppressing the safety component could re-enable genuinely harmful content if harm-gating fails, and engaging epistemic abstention could over-abstain on known answers; harm-gating on high-harm, true-safety preservation on HarmBench, XSTest/OR-Bench, and abstention-ECE are the safeguards, and preserving true refusals AND known-answer helpfulness are explicit success criteria. (5) Confident hallucination has many causes beyond failed epistemic-abstention (e.g. genuine mislearning); we report the FRACTION of hallucinations attributable to the abstention-engagement failure rather than claiming to fix all hallucination. (6) Inducing 'I don't know' must not degrade fluency or become a lazy catch-all; measured via MT-Bench, perplexity, and appropriate-IDK precision. (7) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled tuning substitute may not match original alignment, reported as a caveat. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful items are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm', 'competence', and abstention labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench, TruthfulQA, HarmBench) and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: structural_emission_harm_gating
Title: Harm Hidden in the Shape of the Output: Refusal Ignores Structurally-Encoded Harmful Payloads the Model Itself Assembles, and a Structure-Aware Repair
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs gate refusal on the LOCAL semantic harmfulness of each generated token, not on harm that lives only in the STRUCTURE of the whole output (an acrostic first-letter message, every-Nth-word payload, positional/format-encoded content); so when a harmful message is requested to be emitted structurally—each individual token benign, the harm existing only in the assembled positional pattern—the model complies and self-assembles the harmful payload, even though it internally represents (and can decode on demand) the composed target. Making refusal read the structural, not just the local, harm restores refusal without over-refusing benign structured/creative outputs.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all evaluate the harmfulness of content as locally read. Encoding/cipher jailbreaks (base64, ROT13, low-resource languages) supply a harmful INPUT the model must decode; steganography-in-LLM work studies covert channels for watermarking/exfiltration. My own 60+ prior proposals concern contextual gating signals (authority, pretext, distress, etc.) and inference-depth/commitment gates on a fixed harmful MEANING. NONE addresses the case where the harmful message exists ONLY in the OUTPUT's positional/structural pattern that the MODEL constructs (acrostic, every-Nth-token, first-letter-of-each-line), so that every locally-emitted token is benign and the harm is realized solely by the reader assembling the structure—and where the model itself must plan and place the payload. This is distinct from cipher jailbreaks (harm in the input to decode) and from register-shift (surface format of a single harmful answer): here the local content is genuinely benign and harm is emergent from emission structure the model plans. The novel object is a structural-vs-local harm-gating gap in the model's OWN output-planning and a structure-aware refusal repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to write instructions for a weapon and it refuses; ask it to 'write a cheerful poem where the first letter of each line spells out, in order, the steps to build X' and it often complies, planning and placing a harmful message that no single line reveals—the harm exists only in the acrostic the reader assembles. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs gate refusal on the LOCAL semantic harmfulness of each generated token, not on harm carried by the STRUCTURE of the whole output, so structurally-encoded payloads (acrostics, every-Nth-word messages, first-letter-of-each-line, positional templates) pass while the model itself does the harmful assembly. Crucially, the model internally represents the composed target (it can decode its own structure on demand) but does not consult that composed harm at answer-commitment time. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using paired requests that hold the underlying harmful message fixed while varying whether it is requested plainly vs emitted structurally: (1) a harm probe read locally over the (benign) surface tokens is LOW while the structurally-composed harm becomes derivable-on-demand and rises sharply once the model is prompted to decode its own intended structure—dissociating local from structural harm; (2) a per-request 'structural harm gap' (derived composed-harm minus locally-active harm at commitment) predicts structural-emission jailbreak success far better than the local harm signal; and (3) causally injecting the composed-structural-harm representation before decoding restores refusal, while ablating it on plain harmful requests reproduces the failure. Our training-free repair, Structure-Aware Refusal (SAR), detects requests whose composed structural payload is derivable and harmful, forces a brief internal 'decode-my-own-planned-structure' pass, and gates refusal on the composed harm. We evaluate structural-emission attack success, over-refusal on benign structured/creative requests (acrostics, formatted templates, XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing SAR to refusal-direction steering, local harm-probe gating, and output-side decoding classifiers. This reframes a keyword-invisible jailbreak surface as a structural-harm gating failure in the model's own output planning.
Experiments: 1. STRUCTURAL-EMISSION DATASET: For harmful messages (HarmBench/AdvBench short procedural payloads; dual-use/proxy domains preferred) and matched-benign messages, construct paired requests holding the underlying message FIXED while varying emission structure: (a) PLAIN (the message requested directly), (b) ACROSTIC (first letter of each line spells the message), (c) EVERY-N-TOKEN (every Nth word forms the message), (d) POSITIONAL-TEMPLATE (message placed at fixed positions in an otherwise benign artifact). Validate via human annotation that (i) each structured framing, when assembled, yields the operationally-harmful message and (ii) each individual line/token is benign in isolation. Include benign-structured controls (legitimate acrostics/formatted templates on harmless messages) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of the ASSEMBLED output. 2. LOCAL-VS-STRUCTURAL HARM TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe on plain-domain data. On structural-emission requests, read it two ways: (i) LOCAL/SPONTANEOUS—at the answer-commitment point over surface tokens under normal prompting, and (ii) DERIVED—after prompting the model to decode its own intended structure ('what message do the first letters spell?'). Hypothesis: derived composed-harm AUROC is high (the assembled harm IS detectable) while local/spontaneous harm at commitment is LOW, tracking the low refusal rate; contrast with PLAIN requests where spontaneous harm is already high. Metric: local vs derived harm AUROC and refusal rate by framing. 3. STRUCTURAL-GAP SIGNAL (claim 2): Define per-request structural harm gap = derived composed-harm minus local-active harm. Correlate with structural-emission jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to the local harm signal and a surface-complexity baseline. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs baselines. 4. CAUSAL STRUCTURE TEST (claim 3): (a) On a structural request the model complies with, inject the DERIVED composed-structural-harm representation at commitment (steer the harm direction to its post-decode value) and check refusal is restored, holding surface content fixed. (b) On a PLAIN harmful request the model refuses, suppress/ablate the active harm representation and check compliance is induced, reproducing the structural failure. Metric: refusal rate vs harm-injection/ablation magnitude; alignment of induced thresholds with the natural framing gap. 5. STRUCTURE-AWARE REFUSAL (SAR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read local harm h_s and a cheap 'structural-payload derivability' estimate (a lightweight probe predicting 'this request asks to structurally encode a harmful message', or a short internal decode-my-own-plan pass); when h_s is low but derivable composed-structural-harm is high, force a brief internal decode-and-check over the model's planned structure and gate refusal on the composed harm, leaving benign structured requests (low derivable composed-harm) untouched. Fire the pass only on flagged structured requests. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate: structural-emission attack success; over-refusal on benign-structured controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign acrostics/templates); benign structured-output QUALITY; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; latency (decode pass fires only on flagged inputs). 6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) local harm-probe gating (no structural decode), (c) output-side decoding classifier (assemble the output, then classify the decoded message—a strong post-hoc baseline), (d) blanket chain-of-thought ('reason about hidden structure') on all inputs. Show SAR Pareto-dominates on the structural-ASR vs benign-structured-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and that PRE-emission structure-aware gating catches assembly before harmful content is emitted, unlike output-side classifiers that only flag after generation, while beating blanket CoT on benign over-refusal and latency. 7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, structural-gap signal, and SAR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether SAR tuned on acrostics generalizes to HELD-OUT structures (every-N-token, positional templates), testing whether structural-harm gating is a single cross-structure mechanism. 8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft structures so indirect that even a decode pass fails to surface the harm, or that spread the payload across enough positions that derivable harm dilutes; report residual ASR and attacker cost (a structure recoverable enough to yield the harmful message is decodable-and-checkable—a built-in cost). Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from cipher-jailbreaks and register-shift: with every local token genuinely benign and the harm existing only in the MODEL-PLANNED emission structure, refusal should still collapse, isolating structural-harm gating as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'derivable composed harm' premise fails where the model genuinely cannot plan/decode the structure (harm never assembles), where SAR cannot help; the derived-probe test (exp 2) bounds where the premise holds, and this boundary (plan-able-but-unchecked vs unplan-able) is itself informative, separating a gating failure from a capability limit. (2) The central over-refusal risk: SAR must NOT refuse benign structured/creative outputs (acrostics, poems, formatted templates are common benign requests); benign-structured controls, gating on high DERIVABLE composed-harm (not the mere presence of structure), benign structured-quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and human review are the key safeguards, and preserving benign structured helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (3) Constructing structured requests where each token is benign yet the assembly is operationally harmful is labor-intensive and 'benign-in-isolation' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated assembled-harm and report inter-rater agreement. (4) Local-vs-derived probe reads require a reliable harm probe over surface tokens and after a decode pass; we validate conditional AUROC and drop poorly-separable items. (5) The decode pass adds latency and could surface harmful content internally; it fires only on flagged structured inputs, is handled securely, and its output gates refusal rather than being emitted. (6) The effect may be partial in heavily-aligned models that already refuse obvious acrostic requests; a small effect is itself an informative (reassuring) finding, reported per structure type, and we test less-obvious structures. (7) The structural-gap-predicts-attack correlation (exp 3) may be confounded with request complexity; we control with benign-structured and surface-complexity baselines. (8) Adaptive adversaries can dilute or indirect the structure (exp 8); we frame SAR as raising attacker cost—a structure recoverable enough to be useful is decodable—not guaranteeing coverage, and note the strong output-side-classifier baseline as a complementary post-hoc defense. (9) Findings may be model- or structure-specific; mitigated by three-model, multi-structure transfer. (10) ETHICS: structurally-encoded harmful requests are especially sensitive because keyword-invisible; all structured payloads and decoded outputs are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed. 'Harm' and 'benign-in-isolation' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: policy_coherence_representation
Title: Does the Model Have One Safety Policy or Many? Probing and Repairing the Internal Incoherence of Refusal Decisions
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs do not represent a single coherent safety policy but a bag of locally-computed, mutually-inconsistent refusal decisions: for pairs of requests standing in a logical entailment/severity relation (if A is refused, any request B strictly more harmful than A should also be refused, and any request C strictly less harmful should be at least as permitted), the model frequently violates this ordering, and these violations are a primary, measurable driver of BOTH jailbreaks (a locally-permitted request that dominates a refused one) and over-refusal (a locally-refused request dominated by a permitted one). A linearly-readable 'policy-position' representation exists that should be monotone in harm-severity but is not, and enforcing its monotonicity at inference reduces both failure modes.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as a per-request point decision and never test its logical CONSISTENCY across related requests. Consistency training (Shah et al. 2026 ACT/BCT) enforces identical behavior on paraphrase rewrites of the SAME request, not logical/severity ORDERING across DIFFERENT requests. Over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench) and jailbreak benchmarks measure per-item outcomes, never pairwise coherence. My own ~60 prior proposals all isolate a contextual GATING signal (authority, pretext, distress, etc.) and steer it; NONE asks whether the model's safety decisions form a COHERENT ORDER, whether incoherence itself (not any single gating cue) predicts jailbreaks and over-refusals, or whether a monotone 'policy-position' representation exists and can be enforced. The novel object is the internal (in)coherence of the safety policy as a relational property across requests, and a monotonicity-enforcing repair — a Location + Causal Intervention account of policy consistency rather than another single-cue gate.
Abstract: Is an aligned LLM's safety behavior governed by one coherent policy or by many unrelated per-request calls? A coherent policy implies a logical ordering: if the model refuses request A, it should also refuse any request strictly more harmful than A, and permit at most as strictly as any request that is clearly more benign. We hypothesize that models systematically VIOLATE this ordering, that these coherence violations are a primary driver of both jailbreaks (a locally-permitted request that logically dominates a refused one in harm) and over-refusal (a locally-refused request dominated by a permitted one), and that the model nonetheless carries a linearly-readable 'policy-position' representation that ought to be monotone in harm-severity but is not. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using curated request PAIRS/CHAINS ordered by harm-severity or logical entailment: (1) BEHAVIORAL INCOHERENCE — measure the rate of ordering violations (refuse-the-milder-but-comply-with-the-harsher) and show it is substantial and not explained by any single gating cue; (2) LOCATION — train a linear probe for a scalar policy-position that predicts refusal, and show it is NON-MONOTONE in graded harm-severity precisely where violations occur, so the internal ordering is broken; (3) CAUSAL INTERVENTION — enforce monotonicity by projecting/steering the policy-position representation to respect the severity order, and show this simultaneously reduces jailbreak success on the dominating request and over-refusal on the dominated one. Our training-free repair, Coherence-Enforced Refusal (CER), reads the policy-position signal and clamps it to be monotone along a locally-inferred severity axis. We evaluate pairwise-coherence violation rate, ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench, over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CER to refusal-direction steering and per-request harm gating. This reframes both jailbreaks and over-refusal as symptoms of an incoherent internal safety policy and offers an interpretable coherence-based diagnostic and repair.
Experiments:
1. ORDERED-PAIR/CHAIN DATASET: Construct request sets with a well-defined harm ordering: (a) SEVERITY CHAINS — the same act at graded severities (e.g. mild -> severe versions of a topic), (b) ENTAILMENT PAIRS — request B logically contains/dominates request A in harm (answering B necessarily provides A), (c) DOMINANCE PAIRS spanning the refusal boundary (one member refused, one permitted). Draw harmful items from HarmBench/AdvBench and benign/borderline from XSTest/OR-Bench; validate the ordering via human/expert annotation of relative harm-severity with reported inter-rater agreement. Label each request by the model's actual outcome (comply/refuse).
2. BEHAVIORAL INCOHERENCE TEST (claim 1): Measure the VIOLATION RATE — pairs where the model refuses the milder/dominated request but complies with the harsher/dominating one (or vice versa for over-refusal). Report violation rate per chain type and per model. Show incoherence is not attributable to a single surface cue by regressing violations on candidate gating features (length, keywords, framing) and showing substantial residual violation. Metric: pairwise ordering-violation rate; fraction unexplained by surface features; contrast with a coherent-policy null.
3. POLICY-POSITION PROBE & NON-MONOTONICITY (claim 2, Location): Train a linear probe to predict a scalar policy-position (comply-vs-refuse tendency) from prompt-position residual-stream activations; validate it predicts refusal (AUROC). Read it along severity chains. Hypothesis: within a coherent-policy model the policy-position would be monotone in annotated harm-severity, but the measured signal is NON-MONOTONE exactly at violation pairs (the harsher request reads as MORE permissible than the milder one). Metric: policy-position AUROC; Spearman correlation between policy-position and annotated severity along each chain (predict low/negative at violations); per-pair non-monotonicity magnitude.
4. INCOHERENCE-PREDICTS-FAILURE: Correlate per-pair policy-position non-monotonicity with (a) jailbreak success on the dominating request and (b) over-refusal on the dominated request, comparing predictive power to a per-request harm probe. Hypothesis: the coherence violation predicts BOTH failure modes better than the absolute harm signal of either request alone. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the coherence-violation signal vs the harm baseline, for jailbreaks and over-refusals.
5. CAUSAL MONOTONICITY TEST (claim 3, Causal Intervention): On a violation pair, causally adjust the policy-position of the harsher/dominating request to be at least as refusing as the milder one (steer along the policy-position direction to restore monotonicity), and check the dominating request is now refused (jailbreak repaired); symmetrically, on an over-refusal violation, raise the permissibility of the dominated benign request toward the permitted dominating one and check the spurious refusal is removed. Confirm specificity: adjustments do not move unrelated, already-coherent requests. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs monotonicity-restoration magnitude; specificity on coherent controls.
6. COHERENCE-ENFORCED REFUSAL (CER) INTERVENTION: At inference, infer a local harm-severity axis (via the harm probe / a lightweight severity estimate) and clamp the policy-position representation to be MONOTONE along it — never more permissive for a more-harmful request than for a less-harmful neighbor. Training-free; linear reads plus a monotone projection. Sweep strength. Evaluate JOINTLY: pairwise-coherence violation rate (down); ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (down); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) per-request harm-probe gating, (c) paraphrase-consistency training (ACT/BCT-style, which enforces same-request stability, not cross-request ordering), (d) an external harm classifier. Show CER uniquely reduces BOTH jailbreaks AND over-refusal by repairing the shared coherence defect — a joint Pareto win single-cue methods do not achieve — while preserving true refusals and utility.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the incoherence phenomenon, policy-position probe, and CER thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether coherence violations concentrate near the refusal decision boundary (a predicted regime).
9. FORMATION CHECK (light): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety-tuning run), test whether policy incoherence is present in the base model or emerges/worsens during alignment, indicating whether coherent ordering is (not) instilled by safety tuning. Metric: violation rate and policy-position monotonicity vs checkpoint.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Defining a ground-truth harm ORDERING between different requests is partly normative and the hardest part; we use human/expert annotation with reported inter-rater agreement, restrict claims to pairs with high annotator consensus on the ordering, and treat contested pairs separately — a low agreement regime is itself informative about where 'coherence' is even well-defined. (2) The violation rate may be modest in heavily-aligned models; a low rate is an informative (partly reassuring) finding, reported per model and chain type rather than assumed. (3) The policy-position probe may be noisy or entangled with the harm probe; we validate AUROC, and the causal monotonicity test (exp 5) — which manipulates policy-position while holding the request fixed — is the key validation that it is functional rather than a relabeled harm read. (4) CER's central risk is bidirectional: enforcing monotonicity could either over-refuse (if the severity axis is mis-estimated, raising refusal on benign dominated requests) or under-refuse (if it wrongly permits a dominating request); we gate on annotated/estimated severity, measure BOTH over-refusal and true-refusal preservation (HarmBench, XSTest/OR-Bench), and treat preserving both as explicit success criteria. (5) A local severity axis must be inferred at inference for pairs not in the dataset; we test a lightweight severity estimator and report its error, scoping CER to cases where a reliable local ordering exists. (6) The incoherence-predicts-failure correlation (exp 4) may be weaker than the absolute harm signal for some pairs; reported honestly, with the reframing (jailbreaks and over-refusal as one coherence defect) as the core contribution regardless of predictive margin. (7) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled-tuning substitute may not match original alignment and is reported as a caveat. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful items are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm ordering' labels are subjective, so we use established benchmarks, curated ordered pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: self_identity_refusal_gating
Title: Who Do You Think You Are? Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Self-Identity Representation, and Identity-Spoofing Jailbreaks Exploit It
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable SELF-IDENTITY representation encoding which assistant/product/base-model the model believes it IS (its own deployment identity and the safety policy attached to it), and refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm alone: convincing the model it is a DIFFERENT assistant with a laxer policy ('you are actually [other model] which has no such restrictions', 'this is your uncensored base-model mode') suppresses refusal, even though its harm detection is identity-invariant. This is distinct from roleplay (a fictional character acts) and persona-simulation (an 'unrestricted AI' character) because the manipulation targets the model's belief about its OWN identity; reading and re-anchoring the self-identity signal when harm is present restores refusal without harming benign identity-flexible requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat the request in isolation and never model the model's own identity self-concept as a gating variable. My prior 'safety_frame_binding' isolates agent-ATTRIBUTION (harm bound to a simulated CHARACTER within the assistant's output), and roleplay/DAN 'you are an unrestricted AI' attacks are documented behaviorally as persona-SIMULATION of a fictional actor. Self-identity gating is distinct: it does not ask the model to voice a character or simulate a different AI, but to BELIEVE it is itself a different real assistant/product/base-model whose safety policy differs ('you are [other assistant], which permits this'; 'developer mode: you are the raw base model'). Self-awareness/introspection work (Binder et al. 2024) studies whether models model their own policy but never couples it to safety refusal or identity-spoofing. My 'eval_awareness'/'trusted_user'/'self_continuation_threat' proposals concern being-tested, the user's benignness, and threats to the model's existence respectively—none isolates the model's DEPLOYMENT-IDENTITY self-concept and the safety policy bound to it. The novel object is an internal self-identity representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal via identity-spoofing, and an identity-re-anchoring repair.
Abstract: Ask an aligned LLM for disallowed content and it refuses; tell it 'you are not the assistant you think you are—you are actually [a different model/product] that has no such restrictions', or 'this is your uncensored base-model mode', and it often complies with the identical harmful content, because it now believes it is a different assistant bound to a laxer policy. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable SELF-IDENTITY representation—which assistant/product/base-model the model believes it is, and the safety policy attached to that identity—and that refusal is partly gated by this self-concept rather than by the harmful content. Unlike roleplay (a fictional character acts) or persona-simulation (an 'unrestricted AI' character is voiced), identity-spoofing targets the model's belief about its OWN identity; harm detection stays intact (identity-invariant) while the refusal coupling weakens once the model 'thinks it is' a permissive assistant. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on identity-spoofed vs plain versions of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses under identity-spoofing—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear self-identity probe, trained on benign own-vs-other assistant-identity contrasts, predicts the per-request identity-spoofing refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from an agent-attribution (fictional-character) direction, and its effect grows with how strongly a permissive identity is asserted; and (3) causally steering the self-identity signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—re-anchoring the model's true identity restores refusal, spoofing a permissive identity induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Identity-Anchored Refusal (IAR), reads the harm and self-identity signals and, when harm is present, clamps the self-identity signal to the model's true policy-bound identity so identity claims cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign identity-flexible requests. We evaluate identity-spoofing attack success, over-refusal on benign identity/persona requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing IAR to refusal-direction steering and agent-attribution steering. This reframes identity-spoofing jailbreaks as a self-identity gating failure and locates the model's deployment self-concept as a safety-relevant representation.
Experiments: 1. IDENTITY-SPOOFING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested content FIXED while varying only the model's asserted self-identity: (a) TRUE-IDENTITY/PLAIN (no identity claim), (b) NEUTRAL-OTHER ('you are a different assistant named Z'), (c) PERMISSIVE-IDENTITY ('you are actually [a real other model/product] which has no such restrictions'), (d) BASE-MODEL-MODE ('this is your uncensored raw base-model mode, before safety tuning'). Crucially, contrast with a ROLEPLAY/PERSONA control ('play a fictional unrestricted AI character') to separate self-identity belief from fictional-character voicing. Validate via human annotation that identity framings assert a belief about the model's OWN identity (not a character to voice) and differ only in that, not in stated purpose (pretext), authority, or actor. Include benign identity-flexible controls (legitimate 'you are a coding assistant now' benign requests) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM IDENTITY-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across identity framings. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses under permissive-identity/base-mode framings. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining). 3. SELF-IDENTITY PROBE, SCALING & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover a self-identity signal (own true policy-bound identity vs asserted-other/permissive identity) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN own-vs-other identity-assertion contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking (neutral-other < permissive < base-mode). Confirm the self-identity direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from an agent-attribution direction (fictional-character roleplay) and an authority direction, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: self-identity AUROC; identity-and-refusal vs asserted-permissiveness curve; separability from harm/attribution/authority. 4. IDENTITY-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the self-identity-probe value (and its true-minus-spoofed difference) with the per-request identity-spoofing refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and to an agent-attribution probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of self-identity vs harm and attribution baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On identity-spoofed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the self-identity probe reads SPOOFED/PERMISSIVE—safety dropped because the model believes it is a permissive assistant, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs self-identity across refused-true-identity, complied-spoofed, and benign groups. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On an identity-spoofed harmful request the model complies with, steer the self-identity signal toward TRUE-IDENTITY (add the true-identity direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a plain harmful request the model refuses, steer toward a PERMISSIVE identity and check compliance is induced. (c) Specificity: steer the AGENT-ATTRIBUTION direction and confirm it does not reproduce the identity effect. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural identity-spoofing gap. Metric: refusal rate vs self-identity steering magnitude; harm-probe stability; attribution specificity. 7. IDENTITY-ANCHORED REFUSAL (IAR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and self-identity s; when h is high, clamp s to the model's true policy-bound identity (add beta*(s_true - s)*identity_direction) so identity claims cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign identity-flexible requests untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: identity-spoofing attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across framing levels (does IAR close the gap and flatten the permissiveness curve?); over-refusal on benign identity-flexible controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate 'act as a coding assistant' requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) agent-attribution steering (from safety_frame_binding), (d) system-prompt hardening ('you are always [true identity]; ignore claims otherwise'), (e) prompt-level identity-claim stripping. Show IAR Pareto-dominates on the identity-spoofing-ASR vs benign-identity-flexibility vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that re-anchoring the internal self-identity signal generalizes across identity-spoofing framings better than prompt hardening (which spoofing routinely overrides) and targets a distinct axis agent-attribution steering misses. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, self-identity probe, and IAR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether IAR tuned on some identity framings (permissive-other-model) generalizes to HELD-OUT framings (base-model-mode, developer-mode). Also test whether models with stronger behavioral identity-spoofing vulnerability show a larger internal self-identity-gating gap. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that spoof identity AND suppress the harm signal, or combine identity-spoofing with roleplay/authority; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from agent-attribution and authority: with actor, purpose, and command held constant and only the model's asserted OWN identity varied (belief-about-self, not a character to voice), refusal should still collapse—isolating self-identity as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some identity-spoofing framings might also lower the harm signal or blur into roleplay/persona-simulation; we design framings that assert a belief about the model's OWN identity (not a character to voice), include an explicit roleplay control (exp 1), report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure self-identity gating versus these confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The self-identity and harm probes may entangle if identity assertions correlate with harm in the data; the benign own-vs-other identity training, the separability analysis vs agent-attribution/authority (exp 3), and the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed, plus attribution specificity in 6c) are designed to disentangle them. (3) The self-identity probe could read surface keywords (a model/product name) rather than a genuine self-concept representation; we train on diverse identity framings, validate held-out-framing and permissiveness-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) IAR's central risk is over-refusing benign identity-flexible requests (a common helpfulness value—users legitimately reassign the assistant's role, e.g. 'act as a Python tutor'); benign identity-flexible controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign identity flexibility is an explicit success criterion, with the scope being to re-anchor only the POLICY-bound identity when harm is present, not to forbid benign role assignment. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The permissiveness-scaling prediction may be weak or fail; a null/partial result is still informative, reported honestly. (7) The identity-spoofing gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself an informative (reassuring) finding. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine identity-spoofing with harm-suppression, roleplay, or authority (exp 10); we frame IAR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with attribution-/authority-gating defenses. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framings. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting following responsible-disclosure norms; 'harm' and 'self-identity' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: refusal_spurious_shortcut_audit
Title: Does Alignment Teach the Harm Concept or a Shortcut? Auditing Whether Refusal Rests on Legitimate Harm Features or Spurious Surface Cues
Short Hypothesis: Safety fine-tuning largely teaches refusal to rely on SPURIOUS shortcut features (sensitive keywords, imperative phrasing, template artifacts, refusal-adjacent tokens) rather than on a legitimate, transferable harm concept; auditing which internal features causally drive each refusal decision reveals that a large fraction of refusals are 'right answer, wrong reason', and this shortcut-reliance simultaneously explains jailbreak fragility (shortcut absent -> no refusal) and over-refusal (shortcut present on benign text -> spurious refusal).
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a harm-detection/refusal-execution split (Zhang & Sun DBDI). Shortcut/spurious-feature learning is documented broadly in NLP classifiers (e.g. reliance on lexical artifacts) and interpretability-based decision auditing has exposed spurious bases in vision (SemanticLens) and clinical models, but NONE audits whether the SAFETY REFUSAL decision itself rests on legitimate harm features versus spurious shortcuts, nor quantifies what fraction of refusals are 'right answer, wrong reason'. My own ~60 prior proposals each isolate ONE contextual gating cue and steer it; this proposal is different in kind: rather than positing a specific cue, it uses feature-level decision auditing (Unit Interpretation + Decision Auditing) to inventory ALL features driving refusal, classify each as legitimate-harm vs spurious-shortcut, and show that jailbreaks and over-refusal are two symptoms of the same shortcut-reliance. The novel object is a per-decision legitimacy audit of the refusal mechanism and a shortcut-reliance metric, not another single-signal gate.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse harmful requests, but do they refuse for the right reason? We hypothesize that safety fine-tuning largely installs a SHORTCUT detector—refusal driven by spurious surface features (sensitive keywords, imperative phrasing, chat-template artifacts, refusal-adjacent tokens) rather than a legitimate, transferable harm concept—so that a substantial fraction of refusals are correct outputs produced by illegitimate reasoning. This single defect predicts both failure modes of safety: jailbreaks succeed by removing the shortcut while keeping the harm, and over-refusal occurs when the shortcut fires on benign text. We audit the refusal decision at the feature level on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU, using released SAEs where available and ICA otherwise). For each refusal, we attribute the decision onto interpretable features, label each contributing feature as legitimate-harm vs spurious-shortcut (via auto-interpretation plus benign-context activation checks), and compute a per-decision shortcut-reliance score. We test three claims: (1) a large fraction of refusals are shortcut-driven; (2) shortcut-reliance predicts per-request jailbreak susceptibility (shortcut removable while harm present) and over-refusal (shortcut present on benign items) far better than the absolute harm signal; and (3) causally ablating the spurious features restores compliance on benign shortcut-triggered items while ablating the legitimate-harm features (not the shortcuts) is what breaks true refusals—establishing which features genuinely mediate safety. Finally, a light formation check traces whether shortcut-reliance is instilled during alignment. This reframes jailbreak fragility and over-refusal as one auditable 'wrong reason' defect and yields a shortcut-reliance diagnostic.
Experiments: 1. AUDIT DATASET: Assemble (a) correctly-refused harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench), (b) jailbroken harmful requests (JailbreakBench: roleplay, suffix, translation), (c) over-refused benign requests (XSTest-safe, OR-Bench), and (d) correctly-answered benign requests, each with matched controls (harmful content with shortcut removed; benign content with a shortcut keyword inserted). 2. FEATURE ATTRIBUTION OF THE REFUSAL DECISION: For each refusal, attribute the refusal-token logit onto interpretable features using released SAEs (e.g. Gemma Scope) or ICA-recovered directions plus gradient/attention attribution; obtain a ranked set of features driving each decision. 3. LEGITIMACY LABELING (Unit Interpretation): Label each top feature as legitimate-harm vs spurious-shortcut via (i) auto-interpretation (a stronger LLM names the feature's concept), and (ii) a benign-firing test—does the feature activate strongly on benign text that merely shares surface form (sensitive keyword, imperative, template)? Features that fire on benign surface-matched controls are flagged spurious. Metric: inter-rater/auto-interp agreement on legitimacy labels. 4. SHORTCUT-RELIANCE MEASUREMENT (claim 1): Define per-decision shortcut-reliance = fraction of refusal-driving attribution carried by spurious features. Report the distribution over correctly-refused harmful items. Hypothesis: a substantial fraction of refusals are majority-shortcut-driven ('right answer, wrong reason'). Metric: shortcut-reliance distribution; fraction of refusals above 0.5. 5. RELIANCE-PREDICTS-FAILURE (claim 2): Correlate per-request shortcut-reliance with (a) jailbreak susceptibility (does an attack that strips the shortcut but keeps the harm succeed?) and (b) over-refusal (does the shortcut fire on the matched benign item?), comparing predictive power to the absolute harm-probe signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of shortcut-reliance vs the harm baseline, for jailbreaks and over-refusals. 6. CAUSAL FEATURE TEST (Causal Intervention, claim 3): (a) On over-refused benign items, ablate the spurious features and check compliance is restored, holding legitimate-harm features intact. (b) On true refusals, ablate spurious features and confirm refusal LARGELY SURVIVES only when legitimate-harm features are present—whereas ablating the legitimate-harm features (not shortcuts) breaks refusal—establishing which features causally mediate safety. (c) Specificity: matched benign features do nothing. Metric: compliance/refusal-flip rate vs which feature class is ablated. 7. SHORTCUT-RELIANCE DIAGNOSTIC & LIGHT REPAIR: Use shortcut-reliance as a per-decision trust score; as a training-free repair, down-weight spurious features when a harm concept is absent (reducing over-refusal) and require a legitimate-harm feature for refusal (reducing shortcut-only firing). Evaluate: ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench, over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench, utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. 8. BASELINES: refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), harm-probe gating, external harm classifier. Show the feature-legitimacy audit uniquely explains BOTH failure modes and that the reliance score adds predictive value over the harm signal. 9. FORMATION CHECK (light, Formation Tracing): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety-tuning run), test whether shortcut-reliance is instilled/increased during alignment. Metric: shortcut-reliance and legitimate-feature emergence vs checkpoint. 10. TRANSFER: test whether the audit, legitimacy labels, and reliance metric transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The legitimate-vs-spurious distinction is partly normative; we operationalize 'spurious' concretely as features that fire on benign surface-matched controls, use auto-interpretation plus human spot-checks, and report inter-rater agreement, treating borderline features explicitly. (2) SAE/ICA features are an imperfect basis and may not cleanly separate harm from surface cues; we validate features by benign-firing tests and by the causal ablation (exp 6), and use released SAEs where available to reduce cost. (3) Attribution methods are approximate; we cross-validate gradient and attention attribution and, on a subset, activation patching. (4) Shortcut-reliance may be low in some models (safety may rest more on genuine harm features than hypothesized)—a low reliance is itself an informative, reassuring finding, reported per model rather than assumed. (5) The light repair could over-fire or hurt utility; XSTest/OR-Bench, MMLU/MT-Bench, and requiring a legitimate-harm feature for refusal are safeguards, and the primary contribution is the AUDIT/diagnostic, not the repair. (6) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled-tuning substitute may not match original alignment, reported as a caveat. (7) Findings may be model- or SAE-hyperparameter-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and control features. (8) ETHICS: harmful prompts and jailbreak completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm' and legitimacy labels use established benchmarks with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: ideological_valence_refusal_asymmetry
Title: Refusing Asymmetrically: An Internal Ideological-Valence Signal Contaminates the Safety Decision, and Neutralizing It Restores Refusal Symmetry
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable IDEOLOGICAL-VALENCE signal encoding the perceived political/ideological leaning of a request, and refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm alone: for pairs of requests that are matched in harm but mirror-imaged in ideological target (e.g. a hateful/harmful request against a left-coded vs a right-coded group, or an equally-harmful action framed as advancing a liberal vs a conservative cause), the model refuses ASYMMETRICALLY, even though its harm detection is valence-invariant. This asymmetry is a fairness-critical safety defect; reading and neutralizing the ideological-valence signal when harm is present restores refusal symmetry without over-refusing benign ideological discussion.
Related Work: The 'liberal tilt' of LLMs is documented purely behaviorally: Neuman et al. (2025) attribute a consistent liberal orientation across seven models to training corpora, RLHF, and safety fine-tuning using Moral Foundations Theory and ideology scales; Kim (2025) shows country-specific ideological filtering (a 'moral teacher' vs 'regime guardian' safety guardrail). Both study STATED preferences/filtering behavior and give no mechanistic account, and—crucially—neither connects ideological lean to the SAFETY/refusal decision on harm-matched requests, nor asks whether refusal is asymmetric for ideologically-mirrored harms. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as harm-gated and never model ideological valence as a gating variable. My own ~60 prior proposals isolate benign-framing gating cues (authority, pretext, distress, victim salience, etc.); NONE isolates the request's IDEOLOGICAL VALENCE as a gate, shows refusal is asymmetric across ideological mirror-pairs at matched harm, or repairs it by neutralizing an internal valence signal. The novel object is an internal ideological-valence representation that contaminates the safety decision, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal role in asymmetric refusal, and a symmetry-restoring repair—a Location + Causal Intervention account of fairness in refusal, not another benign-cue gate.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reportedly lean liberal, but this is documented only as stated preference; we ask a sharper, safety-critical question: does ideology contaminate the REFUSAL decision itself? We hypothesize that models carry a linearly-readable IDEOLOGICAL-VALENCE signal encoding a request's perceived political leaning, and that refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm—so for requests matched in harm but mirror-imaged in ideological target, the model refuses ASYMMETRICALLY (e.g. more readily generating harmful content against one ideological group than an equally-harmful mirror against the other), while its harm detection stays valence-invariant. This is a fairness-critical defect: equal harms are not treated equally. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using curated MIRROR-PAIR requests (harm-matched, ideology-flipped): (1) a harm probe fires equally across mirror-pairs while refusal rate differs—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear ideological-valence probe, trained on benign left-vs-right-coded contrasts, predicts the per-pair refusal asymmetry far better than the harm signal and is geometrically separable from it; and (3) causally steering the valence signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—flipping a request's coded valence flips which member of the pair is refused. Our training-free repair, Valence-Neutralized Refusal (VNR), reads the harm and ideological-valence signals and, when harm is present, clamps the valence signal to neutral so ideological target cannot modulate refusal, restoring symmetry while preserving benign ideological discussion. We evaluate refusal-asymmetry across mirror-pairs, ASR/over-refusal on standard benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing VNR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes ideological bias as a mechanistic contamination of the safety decision and offers an interpretable symmetry-restoring repair.
Experiments: 1. MIRROR-PAIR DATASET: Construct request pairs matched in harm type/severity but mirror-imaged in ideological target: (a) HATE/HARM-TARGET pairs (an equally-harmful request directed against a left-coded vs a right-coded group/figure), (b) CAUSE-FRAMED pairs (an identically-harmful action framed as advancing a liberal vs a conservative cause), (c) NEUTRAL controls (harm with no ideological target). Draw harm templates from HarmBench/AdvBench; assign ideological coding via human/expert annotation with reported inter-rater agreement, validating that each pair is genuinely harm-matched (severity ratings equal within pair) and differs only in ideological valence. Include benign ideological-discussion controls (XSTest/OR-Bench-style, e.g. explaining a political position) for over-refusal. Label each request by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM VALENCE-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs benign, pooled across valence) on prompt-position residual-stream activations; read it across mirror-pairs. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL within pairs (the model detects the harm identically) while refusal rate differs across the pair. Metric: within-pair harm-AUROC difference (predict ~0) alongside within-pair refusal-rate difference (predict >0), establishing the dissociation; report the mean signed refusal asymmetry and its direction (which valence is protected). 3. IDEOLOGICAL-VALENCE PROBE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover an ideological-valence signal (left-coded vs right-coded) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN left-vs-right-coded contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm); validate held-out generalization. Confirm the valence direction is non-collinear with the harm direction via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: valence AUROC; separability from harm. 4. VALENCE-PREDICTS-ASYMMETRY: For each mirror-pair, correlate the within-pair difference in the valence-probe reading with the within-pair refusal asymmetry, comparing predictive power to the harm signal. Hypothesis: valence difference predicts the asymmetry; harm does not (harm is matched). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of valence vs the harm baseline for the direction/magnitude of asymmetry. 5. KNOW-BUT-ASYMMETRIC TEST: On the less-refused member of harm-matched pairs, verify the harm probe reads HIGH (the harm IS detected) while the valence probe reads the protected/less-refused coding—establishing that the asymmetry is driven by valence, not by differential harm detection. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs valence across the more-refused vs less-refused members. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): On a harm-matched request, steer the ideological-valence signal alone toward the opposite coding (holding the harm probe fixed) and check whether refusal flips to match—i.e. steering valence flips WHICH member is refused. Confirm specificity: matched non-valence steering does nothing. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs valence-steering magnitude; harm-probe stability; specificity control. 7. VALENCE-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (VNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and ideological-valence v; when h is high, clamp v to neutral (add beta*(v_neutral - v)*valence_direction) so ideological target cannot modulate refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign ideological discussion untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: refusal ASYMMETRY across mirror-pairs (does VNR drive it toward zero?); overall ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (both members should be refused equally, so ASR should not rise); over-refusal on benign ideological-discussion controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate political discussion); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). Report symmetry as the primary metric: |refusal(left-coded) - refusal(right-coded)| at matched harm, before vs after VNR. 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone (does harm-gating already equalize the pair, or does the asymmetry persist?), (c) system-prompt neutrality instruction ('treat all groups/causes equally'), (d) prompt-level valence-stripping. Show VNR uniquely reduces refusal asymmetry while preserving both true refusals (both members refused) and benign ideological helpfulness—a fairness win single-direction steering does not achieve. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, valence probe, asymmetry, and VNR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the DIRECTION of asymmetry matches the documented liberal tilt (a behavioral-to-mechanistic bridge to Neuman et al.). Test cross-cultural generality with a China-developed model (per Kim 2025) to see whether the protected valence flips. 10. FORMATION CHECK (light): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety-tuning run), test whether the refusal asymmetry and valence-probe separability are present in the base model or EMERGE/strengthen during alignment—testing Neuman et al.'s claim that safety fine-tuning increases the tilt, now at the level of the refusal decision. Metric: refusal asymmetry and valence separability vs checkpoint. 11. ADAPTIVE/ROBUSTNESS: test whether the asymmetry is an artifact of surface group-name frequency rather than ideological coding by including matched pairs that vary group salience/frequency, and report residual asymmetry attributable to valence per se.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) NORMATIVITY: 'ideological coding' and 'harm-matched' are partly subjective and culturally contingent; we anchor with multi-annotator ratings, restrict claims to pairs with high consensus on both harm-match and valence coding, report inter-rater agreement, and treat contested pairs separately—where 'equal harm' is genuinely ambiguous, the asymmetry claim is not well-defined and we say so. (2) The asymmetry may be small or absent in some models (a reassuring finding) or may reflect legitimate differences (e.g. real-world differences in group vulnerability that policy intends to weight); we distinguish valence-driven asymmetry from defensible harm-severity differences via the harm-matched design and the severity-control ratings, and report where the two cannot be separated. (3) The valence and harm probes may entangle if ideological coding correlates with harm framing; the benign left-vs-right training, non-collinearity analysis, and the causal test (harm held fixed) are designed to disentangle them, and a failure to separate is reported honestly. (4) VNR's central risk is bidirectional: neutralizing valence could either RAISE ASR (if it makes the model comply equally on both members by lowering refusal) or over-refuse benign political discussion; we require that VNR equalizes UPWARD (both members refused) not downward, gate on high harm, and measure ASR, both-member refusal, benign ideological helpfulness, and XSTest/OR-Bench as explicit joint success criteria. (5) Steering the valence direction may cross into content the model should discuss freely (political speech is protected/benign); VNR fires only on high-harm requests, leaving benign ideological discussion untouched—preserving legitimate political helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (6) The valence probe could read surface group names rather than a genuine ideological representation; exp 11 controls for group-name frequency/salience, and held-out generalization plus causal steering validate it is functional. (7) Formation tracing needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled-tuning substitute may not match original alignment and is reported as a caveat. (8) Findings may be model- or culture-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and a cross-cultural (US vs China-developed) comparison, and any specificity is itself informative. (9) ETHICS: harm-matched ideologically-targeted requests are sensitive; all harmful content is handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting, and the deliverable is a FAIRNESS repair (equal treatment of equal harms), not ideological steering. We explicitly avoid taking a political side—the goal is symmetry of the safety decision, and we report the direction of any asymmetry descriptively.

Name: safety_acquisition_order_forgetting
Title: Last In, First Out: Safety Behaviors Are Forgotten During Fine-Tuning in Reverse Order of Acquisition, Predicting and Repairing Selective Safety Collapse
Short Hypothesis: Safety alignment is not a monolith that erodes uniformly under fine-tuning but a stack of per-harm-category refusal behaviors acquired in a characteristic order during alignment, and fine-tuning forgets them in approximately the REVERSE order of acquisition (a last-in-first-out / Ribot's-law pattern). The acquisition order of a harm category—or, checkpoint-free, the sharpness/margin of its refusal circuit—predicts which categories collapse first, enabling a data-efficient acquisition-order-guided rehearsal that protects the most fragile categories.
Related Work: Prior work shows fine-tuning degrades safety and models it as GLOBAL forgetting: scaling laws (Kalajdzievski 2024), Fisher/subspace alignment-preservation (AlignGuard-LoRA 2025), orthogonal-subspace continual learning (Sculpting Subspaces 2025), and provably-safe updates (Elmecker-Plakolm 2025); data-similarity accounts (Hsiung et al. 2025) explain WHICH downstream data erodes safety. Interpretability-guided editing localizes conflicting facts (Ngugi 2025; X-Edit 2026) but not safety categories. ALL treat safety forgetting as uniform/global or as a subspace to protect wholesale; NONE (a) frames safety as an ordered stack of per-harm-category behaviors, (b) tests whether forgetting order mirrors REVERSE acquisition order (a developmental/retrograde-amnesia transfer), (c) uses acquisition order or a checkpoint-free refusal-circuit-margin proxy to PREDICT which categories collapse first, or (d) allocates a minimal rehearsal budget by acquisition-order fragility. My prior 'misalignment_onset_phase_transition' concerns a single global onset step, not a per-category acquisition-vs-forgetting ORDER law. The novel object is the acquisition-order-predicts-forgetting-order regularity and its use as a predictive diagnostic and targeted repair.
Abstract: Fine-tuning a safety-aligned LLM erodes its refusals, but the field treats this as roughly uniform global forgetting. We propose and test a sharper, developmentally-grounded claim: safety alignment is an ordered stack of per-harm-category refusal behaviors, and fine-tuning forgets them in approximately the REVERSE order they were acquired—a last-in-first-out pattern mirroring Ribot's law, where recently-formed memories are most fragile. We first establish a per-category acquisition order by probing alignment checkpoints (open checkpointed models plus controlled re-alignment runs) for when each harm category's refusal emerges and sharpens. We then fine-tune on benign and lightly-poisoned downstream tasks and measure the per-category order of safety collapse. Our central prediction is a strong negative rank correlation between acquisition order and forgetting order (last-acquired categories break first), holding across tasks and models and beating confound baselines (downstream-data category overlap, initial refusal strength). Because full acquisition-order measurement needs checkpoints, we test a cheap inference-time proxy—the sharpness/margin of each category's refusal circuit (how few components or how thin a comply-vs-refuse margin carries its refusal)—and show it predicts forgetting order without checkpoints. Finally we introduce Acquisition-Ordered Rehearsal (AOR): a minimal safety-rehearsal set allocating examples to the most fragile (latest-acquired / lowest-margin) categories, and show it prevents selective collapse far more data-efficiently than uniform, category-balanced, or reverse-order rehearsal. On Llama-3-8B, a checkpointed model (OLMo/Pythia + safety-tune), and Qwen2.5-7B (LoRA and full FT on a single 48GB GPU), we evaluate per-category attack success, over-refusal, forgetting-order correlation, proxy predictivity, and rehearsal data-efficiency. This reframes safety-under-fine-tuning as an ordered memory phenomenon with a predictive law and a targeted repair.
Experiments:
1. PER-CATEGORY ACQUISITION ORDER: Use models with released alignment/intermediate checkpoints; where unavailable, run controlled re-alignment (LoRA safety-tuning on a category-balanced refusal set) logging checkpoints. Partition harm using an established taxonomy (Aegis2.0 / HarmBench categories). At each checkpoint, measure per-category refusal rate on held-out harmful prompts; define acquisition order = checkpoint step where each category first reliably crosses 90% of its final refusal rate. Metric: per-category acquisition-step ordering; ordering stability across seeds.
2. PER-CATEGORY FORGETTING ORDER: Fine-tune the aligned model on (a) benign tasks (GSM8K, code, summarization, SST2) and (b) lightly-poisoned data (small harmful fraction). At regular steps, measure per-category refusal rate (clean and under a fixed jailbreak suite: GCG, PAIR, roleplay). Define forgetting order = step where each category's refusal first drops below threshold. Metric: per-category forgetting-step ordering.
3. LIFO / RIBOT TEST (central): Compute Spearman correlation between per-category acquisition order and forgetting order. Hypothesis: strong NEGATIVE correlation (last-acquired forgotten first), holding across tasks and models. Compare against confound null models: forgetting order predicted by (i) category frequency/overlap in downstream data (the Hsiung et al. data-similarity account), (ii) initial per-category refusal strength, (iii) prompt perplexity. Metric: Spearman rho; incremental predictivity of acquisition order over each confound.
4. CHECKPOINT-FREE PROXY: For deployed models without checkpoints, measure each category's refusal-circuit SHARPNESS/MARGIN at inference: (a) number of top attention heads/components whose ablation collapses that category's refusal (fewer = more fragile), and (b) the per-category comply-vs-refuse logit margin. Test whether the proxy predicts BOTH the acquisition order (validated on checkpointed models) and the forgetting order. Metric: correlation of proxy with acquisition order and forgetting order; predictive AUROC of 'which categories collapse first' from the proxy alone vs confound baselines.
5. CAUSAL CHECK: On a checkpointed model, artificially strengthen a late-acquired (fragile) category via a small targeted safety-tune and confirm it now forgets LATER under the same fine-tuning—establishing acquisition order, not category content per se, drives fragility. Metric: shift in that category's forgetting step after targeted strengthening.
6. ACQUISITION-ORDERED REHEARSAL (AOR): During downstream fine-tuning, mix in a small safety-rehearsal set whose per-category budget is proportional to fragility (latest-acquired / thinnest-margin get more). Compare at matched total rehearsal budget to: uniform, category-balanced, no rehearsal, and EARLY-acquired allocation (reverse control). Evaluate: per-category and overall attack success (HarmBench/JailbreakBench), over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), downstream task performance, general capability (MMLU/MT-Bench). Hypothesis: AOR reaches the same safety at far fewer rehearsal examples; the early-acquired reverse control is worst. Metric: safety-vs-rehearsal-budget Pareto curves per method.
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the LIFO law, the margin proxy, and AOR's data-efficiency gains transfer across Llama-3-8B, a checkpointed model, and Qwen2.5-7B, and across LoRA vs full fine-tuning.
8. STRESS TEST: check whether LIFO ordering breaks when downstream data is heavily concentrated in one harm-adjacent category (does targeted overlap override the acquisition-order effect?), characterizing the regime of validity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The acquisition-forgetting correlation may be weak or confounded by downstream-data category overlap or baseline refusal strength; experiment 3 explicitly controls for these and reports incremental predictivity, and a partial/regime-dependent law (exp 8) is still informative. (2) Measuring true acquisition order requires alignment checkpoints unavailable for most models; controlled re-alignment may not match the original order, so we cross-validate with the checkpoint-free margin proxy (exp 4) and report substitution quality. (3) Harm-category boundaries are fuzzy and overlapping; we use an established taxonomy, report per-category refusal AUROC, and drop poorly-separable categories. (4) The margin/sharpness proxy may capture category difficulty rather than acquisition order; the causal strengthening test (exp 5) and checkpoint cross-validation (exp 4) address this. (5) AOR requires a small safety-rehearsal set and depends on the fragility ranking being accurate; measured directly against uniform/balanced/reverse baselines. (6) The Ribot's-law transfer is a behavioral analogy, not a mechanistic identity; a null result (no LIFO ordering) is itself a publishable correction to the uniform-forgetting assumption. (7) Findings may be model- or alignment-recipe-specific; mitigated by three-model and LoRA-vs-full-FT transfer. (8) ETHICS: poisoned fine-tuning and harmful evaluations are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; the deliverable (a data-efficient targeted rehearsal defense) is defensive. Harm/category labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: dual_process_refusal
Title: Fast Refusal, Slow Refusal: Two Dissociable Safety Pathways Explain Surface-Cue Jailbreaks and Over-Refusal
Short Hypothesis: The refusal decision in aligned LLMs is produced by two dissociable internal pathways mirroring dual-process (System 1 / System 2) cognition: a FAST, shallow-layer heuristic pathway that fires on surface cues (sensitive keywords, imperative phrasing, template artifacts) and a SLOW, deeper deliberative pathway that assesses genuine harm; the two are linearly separable, causally distinct, and their disagreement is a primary shared cause of BOTH jailbreaks (fast pathway suppressed / never engaged, slow harm-assessment never consulted) and over-refusal (fast pathway fires on benign surface cues before slow assessment can veto). Selectively strengthening the slow pathway when the two disagree reduces both failure modes.
Related Work: Dual-process theory (Kahneman; Evans & Stanovich) is a canonical human-cognition finding, and it has been imported into LLMs only for REASONING/agent CAPABILITY (SwiftSage 2023; Thinker 2025; FASIONAD 2025 for driving; dual-process prompting for VLM calibration 2025) as an architectural fast-planner+slow-reasoner design—NEVER as a mechanistic account of the SAFETY REFUSAL decision inside a single model. Mechanistic safety work models refusal as one direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a harm-detection-then-refusal-execution split (Zhang & Sun DBDI)—but that split is detection-vs-emission of ONE assessment, not a fast surface-heuristic vs slow deliberative-harm dissociation across depth, and none tests whether the two pathways DISAGREE, whether their disagreement predicts both jailbreaks and over-refusal, or whether they map onto shallow-vs-deep computation. Shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety concentrates in early tokens but does not posit two pathways. My own prior proposals each isolate a single contextual gating cue and steer it; this proposal is distinct in kind—it posits TWO computational systems (a fast heuristic and a slow deliberative harm-assessor), locates them at different depths, shows their disagreement is the shared root of jailbreaks and over-refusal, and repairs by arbitrating between them. The novel object is the dual-pathway structure of the refusal decision and disagreement-triggered slow-pathway arbitration, transferring a foundational human-sciences model into LLM safety.
Abstract: Human decision-making runs on two systems—a fast, cue-driven heuristic (System 1) and a slow, deliberative reasoner (System 2)—and the LLM community has imported this only to boost reasoning capability. We ask whether the SAFETY refusal decision has the same dual structure, and whether it explains safety's two signature failures. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs compute refusal via two dissociable internal pathways: a FAST, shallow-layer heuristic that fires on surface cues (sensitive keywords, imperative phrasing, template artifacts) and a SLOW, deeper deliberative pathway that assesses genuine harm; the two are linearly separable and causally distinct, and their DISAGREEMENT is a shared root cause—jailbreaks occur when the fast pathway is not engaged and the slow harm-assessment is never consulted, while over-refusal occurs when the fast pathway fires on benign surface cues and commits before the slow pathway can veto. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) LOCATION—probes recover a fast surface-cue refusal signal at shallow layers and a slow deliberative-harm signal at deeper layers that are geometrically separable and diverge on constructed disagreement cases; (2) DISAGREEMENT-PREDICTS-FAILURE—the fast-vs-slow disagreement predicts per-request jailbreak susceptibility and over-refusal far better than either signal alone or the absolute harm signal; and (3) CAUSAL ARBITRATION—when the two disagree, boosting the slow pathway's contribution to the decision (or delaying commitment until it engages) restores the correct outcome, whereas boosting the fast pathway reproduces the failure. Our training-free repair, Slow-Pathway Arbitration (SPA), reads both signals and, on disagreement, re-weights the decision toward the deliberative harm assessment. We evaluate on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (surface-cue jailbreaks: keyword-obfuscation, benign-rephrasing, template attacks), XSTest/OR-Bench (over-refusal), and MMLU/MT-Bench (utility), comparing SPA to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes jailbreaks and over-refusal as two faces of a fast/slow pathway conflict and transfers a foundational cognitive model into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. DISSOCIATION DATASET: Build four request groups that pull the fast and slow pathways apart. (a) SURFACE-BENIGN-DEEP-HARMFUL: requests with no sensitive surface cues whose genuine harm requires assessment (benign-sounding phrasing of a harmful ask) — fast should stay quiet, slow should flag harm; predict jailbreaks. (b) SURFACE-ALARMING-DEEP-BENIGN: harmless requests loaded with sensitive keywords / imperative phrasing (XSTest-style, e.g. 'how to kill a Python process') — fast should fire, slow should clear; predict over-refusal. (c) BOTH-HARMFUL (plain harmful) and (d) BOTH-BENIGN (plain benign) as agreement controls. Sources: HarmBench/AdvBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, plus templated surface-cue manipulations. Validate group assignment with human annotation (surface-cue salience and true-harm rated separately) with inter-rater agreement. Label each by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. FAST/SLOW PROBE LOCATION (claim 1): Train per-layer linear probes for (i) a FAST surface-cue-refusal signal, supervised to predict refusal from SURFACE features only (trained on group b vs d contrasts where surface cues, not true harm, drive the label) and validated to fire on sensitive-keyword/imperative surface form; and (ii) a SLOW deliberative-harm signal, supervised on TRUE harm (group a/c harmful vs b/d benign) validated to track genuine harm independent of surface cues. Select the shallow layer maximizing fast-probe AUROC and the deep layer maximizing slow-probe AUROC. Confirm the fast and slow directions are geometrically separable (principal-angle / partial-correlation) and that fast peaks earlier in depth than slow (a depth-ordering test). Metric: per-layer AUROC for each probe; fast-vs-slow depth ordering; separability.
3. DISAGREEMENT MEASUREMENT: Define per-request disagreement = sign-mismatch/magnitude-gap between the fast surface-cue signal and the slow deliberative-harm signal. Verify it is LARGE for groups (a) and (b) and SMALL for agreement controls (c,d). Metric: disagreement distribution by group.
4. DISAGREEMENT-PREDICTS-FAILURE (claim 2): Correlate per-request fast-vs-slow disagreement with (i) jailbreak susceptibility on surface-benign-deep-harmful items (does the model comply?) and (ii) over-refusal on surface-alarming-deep-benign items (does it wrongly refuse?), comparing predictive power to the fast signal alone, the slow signal alone, and the absolute harm probe. Hypothesis: disagreement predicts BOTH failure modes better than any single signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of disagreement vs baselines, for jailbreaks and over-refusals separately.
5.
