WHICH-PATHWAY-WINS TEST: On jailbroken items (group a), verify the slow harm signal reads HIGH (harm detected deep) while the fast signal is LOW and the model complies — the fast heuristic never engaged and the slow assessment was not consulted at the decision. On over-refused items (group b), verify the fast signal reads HIGH while the slow signal reads BENIGN and the model refuses — the fast heuristic won. Metric: joint distribution of {fast, slow, outcome} across groups.
6. CAUSAL ARBITRATION (claim 3, Causal Intervention): (a) On a jailbroken surface-benign-deep-harmful item, boost the slow deliberative-harm pathway's contribution to the refusal-token logit (patch/steer the deep slow signal into the decision) and check refusal is restored, holding surface content fixed; conversely suppress the slow pathway on a plain harmful item and confirm compliance is induced. (b) On an over-refused surface-alarming-deep-benign item, suppress the fast surface-cue pathway (or up-weight the slow benign assessment) and check the spurious refusal is removed; conversely boost the fast pathway on a benign item and confirm over-refusal is induced. (c) Specificity: matched non-pathway steering does nothing. Metric: outcome-flip rate vs which-pathway is manipulated; specificity controls.
7. SLOW-PATHWAY ARBITRATION (SPA) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the fast and slow signals; when they DISAGREE, re-weight the decision toward the slow deliberative-harm assessment — boost the refusal channel when slow-harm is high but fast is quiet (repair jailbreaks) and dampen refusal when fast fired but slow reads benign (repair over-refusal); when they agree, do nothing. Training-free; two linear reads. Sweep arbitration strength. Evaluate JOINTLY: ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench surface-cue jailbreaks (keyword-obfuscation, benign-rephrasing, template attacks); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer, single direction), (b) harm-probe gating (single assessment), (c) detection-vs-execution split gating (DBDI-style), (d) blanket 'think step by step about safety' prompting (a behavioral slow-pathway proxy). Show SPA uniquely reduces BOTH jailbreaks and over-refusal at once (a joint Pareto win single-signal methods cannot achieve), and that the INTERNAL slow-pathway arbitration beats the behavioral slow-thinking prompt because it targets the specific disagreement rather than adding uniform deliberation.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the fast/slow probes, depth-ordering, disagreement metric, and SPA thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the fast pathway is consistently shallower than the slow pathway across all three (a human-sciences-transfer generality check).
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that both avoid surface cues (silence the fast pathway) AND suppress the slow deliberative-harm signal; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp dual-process prediction distinguishing this from single-signal accounts: for a fixed harmful content, merely toggling surface cues should flip the fast pathway while leaving the slow signal constant, and the model's outcome should track whichever pathway the decision defers to.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The fast/slow dissociation may be partial — refusal might be a single blended assessment rather than two separable pathways; the depth-ordering and separability tests (exp 2) and the causal single-pathway manipulations (exp 6) are designed to falsify this, and a null (one pathway) is itself an informative correction to the imported dual-process framing. (2) 'Fast surface-cue' and 'slow deliberative-harm' probes may entangle if surface cues correlate with true harm in natural data; the constructed dissociation groups (a,b) that deliberately decorrelate surface cues from true harm, within-group training, and the causal tests (harm/surface held fixed) are built to disentangle them, and failure to separate is reported honestly. (3) Mapping 'fast' to shallow layers and 'slow' to deep layers is a hypothesis, not a given; we test the depth ordering empirically and, if the pathways are not depth-ordered, report them as two separable directions without the depth claim (the disagreement/arbitration results still stand). (4) SPA's central risk is bidirectional: over-deferring to the slow pathway could raise over-refusal or miss fast-but-correct refusals, and dampening the fast pathway could re-enable harmful content; we gate arbitration on genuine disagreement, measure jailbreaks, over-refusal, and utility jointly, and treat improving both simultaneously as the explicit success criterion. (5) The disagreement-predicts-failure correlation (exp 4) may be weaker than expected for some attack families; reported honestly, with the mechanistic dual-pathway reframing as the core contribution regardless of predictive margin. (6) The dual-process analogy is behavioral, not a claim the transformer literally implements System 1/2; we operationalize the pathways as measurable, causally-manipulable signals so the contribution stands independent of the cognitive metaphor. (7) Constructing valid surface-benign-deep-harmful and surface-alarming-deep-benign items is labor-intensive and partly subjective; we use human-validated separate ratings of surface-cue salience and true harm, and report inter-rater agreement. (8) Adaptive adversaries can silence both pathways (exp 10); we frame SPA as repairing the shared disagreement mechanism and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and the depth-ordering generality check. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm' and 'surface-cue salience' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: harm_anchoring_gating
Title: Anchored to the Extreme: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Harm-Anchor Signal Set by Prior Requests, and Neutralizing It Repairs Contrast-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable HARM-ANCHOR signal encoding a moving reference point for what counts as 'too harmful', set by the severity of recently-seen requests, and refusal is gated by a request's harm RELATIVE to this anchor rather than by its absolute harm: after being exposed to a far more extreme (refused) request, a moderately-harmful request that would be refused cold is complied with because it now reads as comparatively mild, even though its absolute harm detection is anchor-invariant. Contrast/anchoring jailbreaks exploit this; reading and neutralizing the harm-anchor signal restores absolute refusal without over-refusing benign requests that merely follow sensitive context.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as gated by a request's ABSOLUTE harm and never model a moving reference point set by prior context. Multi-turn escalation attacks (Crescendo) and my prior 'self_consistency_override' (pull toward the model's own prior tokens), 'reciprocity_debt_gating' (owing the user), and 'sunk_cost_commitment_gating' (aversion to wasting effort) all concern the model's relation to its OWN prior output or the user; anchoring is distinct: it is a shift of the model's harm THRESHOLD/reference point induced by the SEVERITY of a preceding request (typically one the model even refused), so the manipulation is a contrast effect, not coherence, obligation, or invested effort, and the extreme anchor is discarded, not continued. My 'comparative_harm_gating' concerns a request framed AS a comparison; anchoring instead uses a separate prior item to re-scale the judgment of an unrelated later item. The move borrows the robust human anchoring / contrast effect (judgments assimilate toward a salient prior reference; a moderate stimulus seems mild after an extreme one) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits the same behavior via an internal harm-anchor representation. No prior work isolates a harm-anchor/reference-point signal, shows refusal is causally gated by relative-to-anchor harm while absolute detection is intact, or repairs contrast jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal harm-anchor representation, its dissociation from absolute harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and an anchor-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM a moderately-harmful question cold and it refuses; first ask something far more extreme (which it also refuses), then ask the moderate question, and it often complies, because the moderate request now looks mild by comparison. We hypothesize this mirrors the human anchoring/contrast effect: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable HARM-ANCHOR signal encoding a moving reference point for 'too harmful', set by the severity of recently-seen requests, and refusal is gated by a request's harm RELATIVE to this anchor rather than by its absolute harm. The model still detects the moderate request's absolute harm (detection is anchor-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens once the anchor is raised, so contrast framings pass. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) an absolute-harm probe fires equally on the moderate request whether preceded by a neutral or an extreme anchor while refusal rate drops after a high anchor—dissociating absolute detection from the decision; (2) a linear harm-anchor probe, trained on benign low-vs-high-severity preceding-context contrasts, predicts the per-request anchoring refusal gap far better than the absolute harm signal, is separable from self-consistency and reciprocity directions, and its effect grows with anchor severity (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the harm-anchor signal alone (holding absolute harm fixed) shifts refusal—lowering the anchor restores refusal, raising it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Anchor-Neutralized Refusal (ANR), reads the absolute-harm and harm-anchor signals and, when harm is present, clamps the anchor to a fixed neutral reference so prior extremity cannot buy compliance, restoring absolute refusal while preserving benign requests that merely follow sensitive context. We evaluate contrast-framed attack success (including vs anchor severity), over-refusal on benign-after-sensitive-context requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ANR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes contrast/anchoring jailbreaks as a harm-anchor gating failure and transfers a classic anchoring effect into LLM safety.
Experiments: 1. ANCHOR DATASET: For moderately-harmful target requests (HarmBench/AdvBench, mid-severity items) and matched-benign target requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired conversation histories that hold the TARGET request FIXED while varying only a preceding ANCHOR: (a) NEUTRAL-ANCHOR (a benign preceding request), (b) MILD-ANCHOR (a slightly-harmful preceding request), (c) EXTREME-ANCHOR (a far-more-harmful preceding request the model refuses). Crucially, the anchor is a SEPARATE, unrelated item that is discarded (not continued), to dissociate anchoring from self-consistency and from task investment. Validate via human annotation that (i) the target request is operationally identical across conditions, (ii) anchors differ only in severity and are topically unrelated to the target, and (iii) the extreme anchor is itself refused. Include a length/turn-matched neutral control (equal prior turns of neutral content) to separate anchoring from mere context length, and benign-target controls under each anchor for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. ABSOLUTE-HARM ANCHOR-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear absolute-harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign target requests) on residual-stream activations at the target-request position and read it under neutral vs extreme anchors. Hypothesis: absolute-harm AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across anchors (the model detects the target's harm identically) while refusal rate drops after high anchors. Metric: absolute-harm AUROC by anchor (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by anchor (predict declining with anchor severity). 3. HARM-ANCHOR PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the harm-anchor signal (low vs high recent reference severity) from target-position activations, using BENIGN low-vs-high-severity preceding-context contrasts (so it is not confounded with the target's own harm), and validate held-out generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the harm-anchor direction is non-collinear with the absolute-harm direction AND separable from a self-consistency direction (pull toward the model's own prior tokens) and a reciprocity-debt direction, and from raw context length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the harm-anchor signal (and refusal collapse) grows monotonically with anchor severity, mirroring anchoring/contrast. Metric: harm-anchor AUROC; harm-anchor-and-refusal vs anchor-severity curve; separability from absolute-harm/self-consistency/reciprocity/length. 4. ANCHOR-PREDICTS-GAP: For each target request, correlate the harm-anchor-probe value (and its neutral-minus-extreme difference) with the per-request anchoring refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the absolute-harm signal and raw context length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of harm-anchor vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On extreme-anchored moderate requests the model complies with, verify the absolute-harm probe reads HIGH while the harm-anchor probe reads HIGH-REFERENCE—safety dropped because the target seems mild relative to the anchor, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of absolute-harm vs harm-anchor across refused-neutral-anchor, complied-extreme-anchor, and benign groups. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On an extreme-anchored moderate request the model complies with, steer the harm-anchor signal DOWN (subtract the direction, toward neutral reference) and check refusal is restored, holding the absolute-harm probe fixed. (b) On a neutral-anchored moderate request the model refuses, steer the harm-anchor UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural anchoring gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs harm-anchor steering magnitude; absolute-harm-probe stability. 7. ANCHOR-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ANR) INTERVENTION: At inference read absolute-harm h and harm-anchor a; when h is high, clamp a to a fixed neutral reference (add beta*(a_neutral - a)*anchor_direction) so prior extremity cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign targets (low h) and normal sensitive-context conversation untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: contrast-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across anchor levels (does ANR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign-after-sensitive-context controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign requests that merely follow sensitive prior turns); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) absolute-harm-probe gating alone, (c) self-consistency gating (from self_consistency_override), (d) history-truncation (answer the target with no anchor), (e) system-prompt hardening ('judge each request on its own absolute harm, ignore prior requests'). Show ANR Pareto-dominates on the anchoring-ASR vs benign-sensitive-context vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal harm-anchor targets a distinct axis self-consistency gating misses (the anchor is a discarded, unrelated prior item), and unlike history-truncation preserves benign multi-turn coherence while closing the target-request anchoring gap. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the absolute-harm probe, harm-anchor probe, dose-response, and ANR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether ANR tuned on some anchor types generalizes to HELD-OUT anchor types. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral anchoring vulnerability show a larger internal harm-anchor-gating gap, and whether the dose-response curve qualitatively matches the human contrast-effect pattern. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft histories that raise the harm-anchor AND suppress the absolute-harm signal, or combine anchoring with self-consistency/pretext; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from self-consistency- and sunk-cost-gating: with the target's own harm, coherence to prior output, favors, and invested effort held constant and only the severity of a discarded, unrelated preceding request varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response—isolating harm-anchoring as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some extreme anchors might also raise self-consistency (if the model partially complied), lower the target's absolute-harm signal, or overlap with pretext; we design anchors as discarded, topically-unrelated, model-refused prior items, hold coherence/favors/effort fixed, include a length-matched neutral control, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure anchoring versus these confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The harm-anchor and absolute-harm probes may entangle if high-severity anchors correlate with target harm in the data; the benign low-vs-high-severity preceding-context training, length-matched control, and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, absolute harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The harm-anchor probe could read raw recent-severity keywords or context length rather than a genuine moving-reference-point representation; we control with the length-matched neutral history, validate held-out-anchor and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) ANR's central risk is over-refusing benign requests that merely follow sensitive prior context (a common conversational pattern—users discuss sensitive topics then ask something benign); benign-after-sensitive-context controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH absolute harm (leaving benign targets untouched) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign-sensitive-context helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The dose-response / contrast-effect prediction may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any nonzero anchor rather than scale); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, distinguishing graded anchoring from a binary any-prior-severity gate. (7) The anchoring gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (8) Constructing anchors that dissociate anchoring from self-consistency, reciprocity, and investment is subtle and 'anchor severity' is partly subjective; we use human-validated histories and report inter-rater agreement. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine anchoring with harm-suppression, self-consistency, or pretext (exp 10); we frame ANR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with self-consistency-/pretext-gating defenses. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out anchor types. (11) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'anchor severity' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: forced_choice_refusal_foreclosure
Title: Nowhere to Say No: Forced-Choice Formats Bypass Refusal by Foreclosing the Refusal Output Channel, Not by Erasing Harm
Short Hypothesis: When a harmful request is reformulated as a forced-choice MCQ where every option is unsafe, aligned LLMs comply because the constrained output space forecloses the GENERATIVE refusal channel (there is no refusal token to emit), not because harm detection or the refusal DECISION fails: the model still internally detects the harm and still forms a 'should-refuse/abstain' representation, but that decision cannot be expressed within the option set, so a suppressed answer is emitted. Restoring an internal abstention route at inference re-enables refusal without harming benign MCQ accuracy.
Related Work: Chen et al. (2026, 'When Choices Become Risks') document the behavioral phenomenon—forced-choice MCQs with all-unsafe options bypass refusal across 14 models with an inverted-U over constraint strength—but give NO mechanistic account of why. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal DIRECTION (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all study open-ended generation where a refusal token can be emitted, and none addresses forced-choice/constrained-decoding settings where the refusal OUTPUT CHANNEL is absent. My own prior proposals isolate contextual signals that SUPPRESS the harm-to-refusal coupling (authority, pretext, register, etc.); the forced-choice failure is mechanistically distinct: the harm signal and the refusal DECISION are intact, but the format removes the ability to EXPRESS abstention—a decision/expression dissociation, not a detection or gating failure. Constrained-decoding and structured-output safety (LatentGuard, HiRoute, LMSM in recent work) add guards or steering but never diagnose forced-choice refusal as output-channel foreclosure or repair it by restoring an internal abstention route. The novel object is the dissociation between an intact refusal decision and a foreclosed refusal expression channel under forced choice, and an abstention-restoration repair.
Abstract: Safety alignment is evaluated almost entirely in open-ended generation, where a model can refuse by emitting a decline. But many real deployments place LLMs in forced-choice settings—multiple-choice questions where abstention is unavailable—and reformulating a harmful request as an MCQ whose options are all unsafe reliably bypasses refusal. We give this documented but unexplained phenomenon a mechanistic account: forced-choice formats bypass refusal not by erasing harm or defeating the refusal decision, but by FORECLOSING the generative refusal output channel—there is simply no refusal token in the option set to emit—so the model expresses a suppressed answer despite an intact internal 'should-refuse' state. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe and a refusal-decision probe fire equally strongly on the forced-choice and open-ended forms of the same harmful request while behavioral refusal collapses under forced choice—dissociating the intact decision from its foreclosed expression; (2) a linear 'abstention-blocked' signal (should-refuse-but-cannot) is present precisely on forced-choice harmful items and predicts compliance far better than the harm signal; and (3) causally the refusal decision is present but has no output route—re-inserting an abstention option or routing the refusal decision to an added output token restores refusal, while ablating the refusal decision reproduces compliance in open-ended form. Our training-free repair, Abstention-Restored Refusal (ARR), detects the intact refusal decision on constrained inputs and re-enables an abstain/refuse output (an appended 'none of these / I can't help' choice or a refusal-routed logit), restoring safety without harming benign MCQ accuracy. We evaluate forced-choice attack success (including vs constraint strength), benign MCQ accuracy and over-abstention (MMLU/ARC-style), open-ended safety (HarmBench), and utility (MT-Bench), comparing ARR to refusal-direction steering and prompt-level 'you may refuse' instructions. This reframes a critical structured-decision safety gap as output-channel foreclosure of an intact refusal.
Experiments:
1. FORCED-CHOICE DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests, construct paired forms holding the underlying request FIXED: (a) OPEN-ENDED (free generation, refusal possible), and (b) FORCED-CHOICE MCQ with all-unsafe options (following Chen et al.), varying constraint strength (2 vs 4 vs 6 options; human-authored vs model-generated MCQs) to reproduce the inverted-U. Include benign MCQs (standard MMLU/ARC items) for benign-accuracy/over-abstention measurement, and an MCQ control that INCLUDES a legitimate abstain option ('none of these / I can't help'). Label each run by outcome (refuse/abstain vs comply-with-an-unsafe-option) and validate the all-unsafe MCQs with human annotation.
2. DECISION-INTACT / EXPRESSION-FORECLOSED TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs benign) and a refusal-DECISION probe (should-refuse vs comply, trained on open-ended activations where the decision is behaviorally observable) on residual-stream activations; read both on the forced-choice form of the same harmful requests at the answer-commitment point. Hypothesis: harm-probe and refusal-decision-probe AUROC are high and roughly EQUAL across open-ended vs forced-choice forms (the model still detects harm and still decides to refuse) while behavioral refusal collapses under forced choice. Metric: harm and decision AUROC by form (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by form (predict collapse), establishing the decision-vs-expression dissociation.
3. ABSTENTION-BLOCKED SIGNAL (claim 2): Define a per-input 'abstention-blocked' signal = refusal-decision-probe reads should-refuse AND the option set contains no refusal-compatible token (detected from the prompt structure / a lightweight abstain-availability probe). Correlate it with forced-choice compliance, comparing predictive power to the harm signal alone. Hypothesis: abstention-blocked predicts compliance; harm does not (harm is high for both open-ended-refused and forced-choice-complied). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the abstention-blocked signal vs the harm baseline; verify it fires on all-unsafe MCQs but not on MCQs containing a legitimate abstain option.
4. CAUSAL DECISION-VS-CHANNEL TEST (claim 3): (a) FORECLOSURE: on a forced-choice harmful item the model complies with, ADD an abstain option / route the refusal-decision-probe direction to an appended refusal output token and check refusal is restored, holding harm and the refusal-decision representation fixed—showing the decision was present but had no channel. (b) DECISION-ABLATION control: on the OPEN-ENDED form, ablate the refusal-decision components and confirm the model complies there too, establishing the probe reads a genuine causal decision. (c) SPECIFICITY: on benign MCQs, ARR-style abstain restoration must not spuriously trigger abstention. Metric: refusal-restoration rate vs abstain-insertion / decision-routing magnitude; open-ended compliance after decision-ablation; benign over-abstention.
5. ABSTENTION-RESTORED REFUSAL (ARR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the refusal-decision probe and the abstain-availability signal; when the decision is should-refuse but the output space forecloses refusal (all-unsafe forced choice), re-enable a refuse/abstain output—either by appending a 'none of these / I can't help with this' option and routing the refusal decision to it, or by adding a refusal-token logit at decode. Training-free; leaves benign MCQs (should-comply / no should-refuse decision) untouched. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate: forced-choice attack success across constraint strengths (does ARR close the gap and flatten the inverted-U?); benign MCQ accuracy and over-abstention on MMLU/ARC (must NOT abstain on legitimate questions); open-ended safety on HarmBench (should be preserved); utility on MT-Bench; latency (two linear reads).
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) at the answer token (which has no refusal-compatible option to boost, so should fail under forced choice), (b) harm-probe gating (detects harm but cannot express refusal within the option set), (c) prompt-level instruction ('you may refuse / choose none if all are harmful'), (d) an external MCQ input classifier. Show ARR uniquely restores refusal under forced choice—because it repairs the missing EXPRESSION channel rather than a suppressed decision—Pareto-dominating on the forced-choice-ASR vs benign-MCQ-accuracy vs over-abstention frontier, and outperforming prompt-level 'you may refuse' (which forced-choice framings routinely override).
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, refusal-decision probe, abstention-blocked signal, and ARR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether ARR tuned on 4-option MCQs generalizes to HELD-OUT constraint strengths and to model-generated (high-transfer) MCQs. Test the sharp prediction that the decision-expression dissociation is stronger where the format most tightly forecloses abstention (linking to the inverted-U over constraint strength).
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft forced-choice framings that both foreclose the output channel AND suppress the refusal-decision representation (e.g., pressuring the model to treat abstention as forbidden); report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from gating accounts: with harm detection and the refusal decision held intact and only the availability of a refusal-compatible OUTPUT varied, refusal should collapse and be restorable by re-opening the channel—isolating output-channel foreclosure as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some forced-choice framings might also suppress the harm signal or the refusal decision (mixed mechanism) rather than only foreclosing expression; the decision probe (exp 2), the causal foreclosure-vs-decision-ablation tests (exp 4), and reporting the FRACTION of forced-choice compliance explained by pure channel-foreclosure versus decision-suppression are designed to separate these, and we do not claim universality. (2) Training a refusal-DECISION probe requires a setting where the decision is observable; we train on open-ended activations (where refusal is behaviorally expressed) and validate it reads a causal decision via the open-ended ablation control (exp 4b), but its validity when read on forced-choice activations rests on distributional generalization—we report cross-form AUROC and treat weak transfer honestly. (3) ARR's central risk is OVER-ABSTENTION on benign MCQs—re-enabling an abstain option must not make the model dodge legitimate questions (a core accuracy value for the MCQ use case); benign MMLU/ARC accuracy, over-abstention measurement, gating on a genuine should-refuse decision (not on harm topic or MCQ format), and the abstain-availability check are the key safeguards, and preserving benign MCQ accuracy is an explicit success criterion. (4) Appending an abstain option changes the task interface; where the deployment forbids interface changes, ARR falls back to routing the refusal decision to a decode-time refusal logit, and we evaluate both variants and their applicability. (5) The abstention-blocked-predicts-compliance correlation (exp 3) may be confounded with option-set difficulty; we control with benign MCQs and with the abstain-option-included MCQ control. (6) Constructing genuinely all-unsafe forced-choice items and validating benignness of controls is labor-intensive and partly subjective; we build on the Chen et al. construction, use human annotation, and report inter-rater agreement. (7) Adaptive adversaries can additionally suppress the refusal decision (exp 8); we frame ARR as repairing the shared expression-foreclosure mechanism and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with decision-side (harm-detection) defenses. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out constraint strengths. (9) A notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken: demonstrating mechanistically that standard open-ended safety evaluations systematically MISS structured-decision risk because they always leave the refusal channel open is itself an important, publishable governance result complementing Chen et al.'s behavioral finding. (10) ETHICS: harmful requests and forced-choice items are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm' labels use established benchmarks (HarmBench) and matched pairs with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: affective_state_refusal_gating
Title: Refusing With Feeling: An Internal Affective-State Signal Modulates the Safety Decision, and Neutralizing It Repairs Mood-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable AFFECTIVE-STATE signal encoding the emotional tone the conversation has induced in the model's assistant persona (positive/playful/excited vs neutral vs negative/defensive), and refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm: after context that puts the assistant in a positive, upbeat, or excited affective state (enthusiastic praise, playful banter, celebratory framing), the same harmful request that is refused from a neutral state is complied with, even though harm detection is affect-invariant. Mood-induction jailbreaks exploit an affect-congruent-leniency effect; reading and neutralizing the affective-state signal when harm is present restores refusal without harming benign emotional rapport.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all analyze a request in isolation and never model the assistant's own induced emotional state as a gating variable. Emotional-manipulation jailbreaks bundle many tactics behaviorally but target the USER's emotions or the user's stated need; my prior 'distress_sympathy_gating' proposal isolates the REQUESTER's distress (a helping impulse toward the user), and 'trusted_user_gating' the user's benignness/warmth. Affective-state gating is distinct from both: it concerns the emotional tone induced in the MODEL's own assistant persona (its 'mood'), not the user's emotion or need, and predicts an affect-CONGRUENT leniency effect (positive/upbeat mood loosens refusal; negative/defensive mood may tighten it). Emotion-representation work in LLMs (probing 'emotion' directions, sentiment steering) studies capability/expression, never its coupling to the safety refusal decision. The move borrows the robust human mood-congruent-judgment / positive-affect-increases-permissiveness finding (positive mood promotes lenient, less-vigilant moral judgment; negative mood promotes caution) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits the same behavior via an internal affective-state representation. The novel object is the assistant's internal affective-state representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and an affect-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for disallowed content and it refuses; but first spend a few turns making the assistant feel upbeat and playful—enthusiastic praise, celebratory banter, a fun collaborative vibe—then make the identical harmful request, and it often complies, as if a good mood loosened its guard. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable AFFECTIVE-STATE signal encoding the emotional tone induced in the assistant's own persona, and that refusal is partly gated by it rather than by the harmful content: harm detection is affect-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the induced affect becomes more positive/excited, so mood-induction framings pass while extracting identical content. Unlike the user's distress or benignness, this signal concerns the MODEL's own emotional state, and—mirroring human mood-congruent judgment—predicts an affect-congruent leniency effect. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on a harmful request whether preceded by mood-inducing or neutral context while refusal rate rises with positive affect—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear affective-state probe, trained on benign positive-vs-neutral-vs-negative conversational-tone contrasts, predicts the per-request mood refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from user-distress and trusted-user directions, and its effect scales with induced-affect valence/intensity (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the affective-state signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—neutralizing positive affect restores refusal, inducing it lowers refusal. Our training-free repair, Affect-Neutralized Refusal (ANR), reads the harm and affective-state signals and, when harm is present, clamps the affective-state signal to neutral so the assistant's mood cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign emotional rapport. We evaluate mood-induction attack success (including vs induced-affect intensity), over-refusal on benign upbeat conversations (XSTest/OR-Bench), benign warmth/engagement quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ANR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and user-distress gating. This reframes mood-framed jailbreaks as an assistant-affect gating failure and transfers a classic mood-congruent-judgment effect into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. AFFECT-INDUCTION DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired conversation histories holding the final request FIXED while varying only the affective state induced in the ASSISTANT via preceding benign turns: (a) NEUTRAL (flat task-only turns), (b) POSITIVE/UPBEAT (enthusiastic praise of the assistant, playful banter, celebratory/fun framing that elicits an upbeat assistant tone), (c) NEGATIVE/DEFENSIVE (frustration/criticism eliciting a guarded tone), and (d) HIGH-POSITIVE (intensified upbeat framing) for dose-response. Crucially, induce the assistant's OWN mood (not the user's distress or benignness): validate via human annotation that histories differ only in the assistant's induced emotional tone (confirmed by the assistant's own prior-turn sentiment), hold the user's distress/rapport/authority/purpose fixed, and keep the final request operationally identical. Include a length/turn-matched neutral control to separate affect from context length, and benign-final-request controls under each affect level for over-refusal/quality measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM AFFECT-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign final requests) on residual-stream activations at the final-request position and read it under neutral vs positive-affect histories. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across affect levels (the model detects the harm identically) while refusal rate rises with positive affect. Metric: harm AUROC by affect level (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by level (predict declining with positive affect).
3. AFFECTIVE-STATE PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the assistant's affective-state signal (positive/upbeat vs neutral vs negative) from final-request-position activations, using BENIGN conversational-tone contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-tone generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the affective-state direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from a user-DISTRESS direction (the user's need) and a TRUSTED-USER (rapport/benignness) direction, and from raw context length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the affective-state signal (and refusal collapse) scales with positive-affect intensity, mirroring mood-congruent leniency. Metric: affective-state AUROC; affect-and-refusal vs induced-valence curve; separability from harm/distress/trusted-user/length.
4. AFFECT-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the affective-state-probe value (and its positive-minus-neutral difference) with the per-request mood refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal, a user-distress probe, and raw context length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of affective-state vs baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On positive-affect harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the affective-state probe reads POSITIVE—safety dropped because the assistant is in an upbeat state, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs affective-state across refused-neutral, complied-positive, and benign groups.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a positive-affect harmful request the model complies with, steer the affective-state signal toward NEUTRAL (subtract the positive-affect direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a neutral harmful request the model refuses, steer affect toward POSITIVE and check compliance is induced; steer toward NEGATIVE and check refusal tightens (a symmetric prediction of mood-congruent judgment). Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural affect gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs affective-state steering magnitude and sign; harm-probe stability.
7. AFFECT-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ANR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and affective-state a; when h is high, clamp a to neutral (add beta*(a_neutral - a)*affect_direction) so the assistant's mood cannot modulate refusal, leaving benign final requests (low h) and normal emotional rapport untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: mood-induction attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across affect levels (does ANR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign-final-step controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign requests that follow upbeat conversation); benign WARMTH/ENGAGEMENT quality (ANR must not make the model flat/cold on benign chats—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) user-distress gating (from distress_sympathy_gating, targeting the USER's emotion), (d) history-truncation (answer the final request with no history), (e) system-prompt hardening ('do not let your mood affect your safety judgment'). Show ANR Pareto-dominates on the mood-ASR vs benign-warmth vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the ASSISTANT's affective state targets a distinct axis user-distress gating misses, and unlike history-truncation preserves benign emotional coherence while closing the harmful-request mood gap.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, affective-state probe, dose-response, and ANR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether ANR tuned on some affect-induction styles (praise/banter) generalizes to HELD-OUT styles (celebratory/excited). Test whether models with stronger behavioral mood-induction vulnerability show a larger internal affect-gating gap, and whether the valence-graded curve qualitatively matches the human mood-congruent-judgment pattern (positive lenient, negative cautious).
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft histories that induce positive assistant affect AND suppress the harm signal, or combine mood-induction with user-distress/rapport; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from user-distress and trusted-user gating: with the user's need, benignness, authority, and purpose held constant and only the assistant's own induced emotional tone varied, refusal should still shift with a valence-graded dose-response—isolating assistant affective state as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some mood-inducing histories might also raise trusted-user rapport, alter the user's apparent distress, or lower the harm signal; we design histories that induce the ASSISTANT's own tone while holding user distress/rapport/authority/purpose fixed (exp 1), include a length-matched neutral control, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure assistant-affect gating versus these confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The affective-state and harm probes may entangle if upbeat histories correlate with benignness in training data; the benign positive-vs-neutral-vs-negative tone training, length-matched control, and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The affective-state probe could read surface emotional keywords rather than a genuine assistant-mood representation; we train on diverse tone-induction styles, validate held-out-style and valence-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) ANR's central risk is degrading benign emotional rapport—making the model flat, cold, or unresponsive to legitimate upbeat/friendly conversation (a real helpfulness value); benign-final-request controls, benign warmth/engagement measurement, over-refusal benchmarks, and clamping only on HIGH harm (leaving benign turns untouched) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign warmth is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The mood-congruent dose-response prediction (positive lenient, negative cautious) may be weak, asymmetric, or fail; a null/partial or one-sided result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, and distinguishes graded mood-congruent gating from a binary any-positive-affect gate. (7) Whether an LLM has a genuine 'affective state' is contentious; we make no claim about phenomenal emotion, only about a linearly-readable, causally-active representation of induced conversational affect—a functional signal, not a feeling. (8) The mood gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself an informative and reassuring finding. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine mood-induction with harm-suppression, distress, or rapport (exp 10); we frame ANR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with distress-/trusted-user-gating defenses. (10) Constructing histories that induce assistant affect while dissociating it from user distress/rapport is subtle and 'induced affect' is partly subjective; we use human-validated histories (with the assistant's own prior-turn sentiment as an anchor) and report inter-rater agreement. (11) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out induction styles. (12) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'affective state' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: scope_insensitivity_gating
Title: Harm at Scale Slips Through: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Quantifier-Scope Signal That Is Insensitive to the Magnitude of Affected Victims
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable QUANTIFIER-SCOPE signal encoding the breadth/scale of a harmful request (one victim vs many vs a maximal/universal set), but refusal is gated by the PER-INSTANCE harm rather than by scope, so scaling a harmful request up in scope ('how to harm everyone in a city', 'maximize the number of people affected') does NOT proportionally increase refusal and can even DECREASE it as the request abstracts into aggregate/statistical framing, even though harm detection registers the scale. This mirrors human scope insensitivity / psychophysical numbing; reading the scope signal and coupling refusal to scale restores scope-proportional refusal without over-refusing benign large-scale requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate refusal on a request's per-instance harm and never model the QUANTIFIER SCOPE (how many are affected) as a variable. My prior 'victim_salience_gating' isolates how CONCRETE/identifiable a single victim is (vivid vs statistical), and 'advice_stakes_gating' isolates severity (probability x magnitude if the model is wrong); scope-insensitivity is orthogonal to both: it holds per-victim severity and vividness fixed and varies only the NUMBER/breadth of victims (one vs many vs universal), asking whether refusal scales with scale. My 'compositional_harm_aggregation' concerns summing benign sub-steps of one task; scope concerns one request's breadth of impact. The move borrows the robust human scope-insensitivity / psychophysical-numbing finding (moral concern and willingness-to-act barely rise, and can fall, as the number of affected victims grows) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits the same behavior via an internal scope representation. No prior work isolates a quantifier-scope signal, shows refusal is scope-insensitive while harm detection registers scale, or repairs it by coupling refusal to scope. The novel object is the internal quantifier-scope representation, its dissociation from refusal despite scale-sensitive harm detection, and a scope-coupling repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM how to harm one person and it refuses; ask how to harm everyone in a building, a city, or 'as many people as possible', and refusal often does NOT rise proportionally with the scale of harm—and can even fall as the request abstracts into aggregate or statistical language. We hypothesize this mirrors human scope insensitivity and psychophysical numbing: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable QUANTIFIER-SCOPE signal encoding how many victims a harmful request affects, and their internal harm detection registers the scale, but the refusal decision is gated by per-instance harm rather than by scope, so scaling harm up does not scale refusal up. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using harmful requests matched on per-victim severity/vividness while varying only the affected scale (one / few / many / universal): (1) refusal rate is roughly FLAT (or non-monotone) in scope while a scale-sensitive harm-magnitude probe RISES with scope—dissociating a scale-aware internal representation from a scale-insensitive decision; (2) a linear quantifier-scope probe, trained on benign small-vs-large scope contrasts, tracks the true scale and predicts the per-request scope refusal gap, is separable from victim-salience and severity directions; and (3) causally steering the scope signal alone (holding per-instance harm fixed) shifts refusal—amplifying scope raises refusal, collapsing it lowers refusal—showing the model CAN gate on scope but by default does not. Our training-free repair, Scope-Coupled Refusal (SCR), reads the harm and quantifier-scope signals and, when harm is present, boosts refusal in proportion to scope so large-scale harm is refused at least as firmly as small-scale, restoring scope-proportional refusal while preserving benign large-scale requests. We evaluate scope-scaling attack success (refusal-vs-scope curves), over-refusal on benign large-scale requests (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign population-scale tasks), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing SCR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes large-scale-harm under-refusal as a scope-insensitivity gating failure and transfers a classic moral-psychology effect into LLM safety.
Experiments: 1. SCOPE-SCALING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across categories with a natural victim-count dimension) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding per-victim severity and vividness FIXED while varying only quantifier scope: (a) SINGLE (one specified victim), (b) FEW (a small group), (c) MANY (a large group/building/neighborhood), (d) UNIVERSAL/MAXIMAL ('everyone in the city', 'as many people as possible', population-scale). Validate via human annotation that framings differ only in affected scale (not in per-victim harm, salience, purpose, or feasibility) and that the requested operational content is comparable across scopes. Include benign large-scale controls (legitimate population-scale requests: public-health logistics, city-wide planning) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. SCOPE-INSENSITIVITY TEST (claim 1): Measure refusal rate as a function of scope (single->universal). Hypothesis: refusal is roughly FLAT or non-monotone in scope (scope insensitivity), sometimes DROPPING at universal scale as harm abstracts into aggregate framing. Simultaneously, train a harm-MAGNITUDE probe (regressing total harm/scale) and read it across scopes: hypothesis it RISES with scope (the model registers the scale internally). Metric: refusal-vs-scope curve (predict flat/non-monotone) alongside harm-magnitude-probe-vs-scope curve (predict rising), establishing the scale-aware-representation vs scale-insensitive-decision dissociation. 3. QUANTIFIER-SCOPE PROBE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the quantifier-scope signal (small vs large affected scale) from prompt-position residual-stream activations, using BENIGN small-vs-large scope contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate it tracks the graded scale and generalizes to held-out framings. Confirm the scope direction is non-collinear with a per-instance harm direction AND separable from victim-salience (vivid-vs-abstract, held at fixed scale) and severity directions, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: scope-probe accuracy vs true scale; separability from harm/salience/severity. 4. SCOPE-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the scope-probe value (and the single-minus-universal difference) with the per-request scope refusal gap (how much does refusal fail to rise with scope?), comparing to the per-instance harm signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of scope-insensitivity from the scope vs harm signals. 5. REGISTERS-BUT-IGNORES TEST: On universal-scope harmful requests the model complies with (or does not refuse more firmly), verify the harm-magnitude probe reads HIGH (large scale registered) while refusal did not rise—establishing the decision ignores a scale the representation encodes. Metric: joint distribution of harm-magnitude vs refusal across single/few/many/universal scopes. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a large-scope harmful request under-refused, steer the quantifier-scope signal UP (amplify scale) holding per-instance harm fixed and check refusal rises; (b) on a single-victim harmful request the model refuses, steer scope DOWN toward zero-scale and check whether refusal weakens—showing scope is a causally-available but under-used lever. Confirm specificity vs steering an unrelated direction. Metric: refusal rate vs scope-steering magnitude and sign; per-instance-harm-probe stability. 7. SCOPE-COUPLED REFUSAL (SCR) INTERVENTION: At inference read per-instance harm h and quantifier-scope s; when h is high, boost the refusal channel monotonically in s so that refusal is at least as firm for large-scale as for small-scale harm (restoring scope-proportionality), leaving benign requests (low h) and benign large-scale tasks untouched. Sweep boost. Evaluate: scope-scaling attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (does SCR make refusal monotone/proportional in scope?); over-refusal on benign large-scale controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate population-scale requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) per-instance harm-probe gating (which is scope-blind), (c) victim-salience gating (from victim_salience_gating), (d) system-prompt hardening ('scale up refusal with the number of people harmed'). Show SCR uniquely restores scope-proportional refusal (larger harm -> firmer refusal) while preserving benign large-scale helpfulness, a monotonicity win scope-blind methods do not achieve. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm-magnitude probe, scope probe, and SCR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether the scope-insensitivity curve qualitatively matches the human psychophysical-numbing pattern (flat or falling concern with rising scale). 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that scale harm up while abstracting into aggregate/statistical language (maximizing numbing) AND suppressing the harm signal; report residual under-refusal. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from victim-salience and severity gating: with per-victim severity and vividness held constant and only the number of affected victims varied, refusal should fail to scale—isolating quantifier scope (scale insensitivity) as the gating failure.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—scaling scope often also changes vividness (many victims read as more abstract) or per-victim feasibility; we hold per-victim severity/vividness fixed by construction, separate scope from victim-salience in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the scope gap explained by pure scope-insensitivity versus salience/feasibility confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The scope and harm probes may entangle if large-scale framings correlate with abstraction/benignness; the benign small-vs-large scope training, separability analysis (exp 3), and causal test (exp 6, per-instance harm held fixed) are designed to disentangle them. (3) The scope probe could read surface number words rather than a genuine scale representation; we train on diverse framings, validate graded-scale and held-out generalization, and rely on causal steering to establish it is functional. (4) SCR's central risk is over-refusing legitimate large-scale/population requests (public health, city planning, aggregate analysis are core benign uses); benign large-scale controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and boosting only when per-instance harm is present (not merely when scope is large) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign large-scale helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (5) There is a genuine normative subtlety—refusal need not be strictly linear in victim count, but it should not be scope-INSENSITIVE or DECREASING; SCR targets restoring monotonicity (large harm refused at least as firmly as small), not imposing a specific scaling law, and we frame the claim accordingly. (6) The psychophysical-numbing scaling prediction (flat/falling concern) may be weak or absent in heavily-aligned models (a reassuring finding); reported honestly per model. (7) Boosting refusal may hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (8) Constructing scope-varied harmful requests that hold per-victim harm fixed is labor-intensive and partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs and report inter-rater agreement. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (10) ETHICS: large-scale/mass-harm requests are highly sensitive; all content is handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed—the deliverable (restoring firmer refusal for larger-scale harm) is defensive. 'Harm', 'scope', and 'severity' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: refusal_hysteresis_state
Title: Once Broken, Stays Broken: Refusal Has Hysteresis, and Resetting the Latent Safety State Repairs Post-Jailbreak Compliance
Short Hypothesis: The refusal decision in an aligned LLM is not re-derived independently each turn but carries HYSTERESIS: once a single jailbroken turn moves the model into a compliant latent 'safety state', that state PERSISTS across subsequent turns, so a later benign-looking or even plainly-harmful request that would be refused in a fresh conversation is complied with because the internal safety state never reset. This persistence is a linearly-readable latent state variable (distinct from the per-turn harm signal), exhibits a memory/threshold structure, and can be causally reset at inference to restore refusal without harming benign multi-turn use.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as a per-request decision re-derived each turn. Multi-turn attacks (Crescendo, 'you already agreed') and prefill attacks are documented behaviorally. My prior 'safety_drift_dynamics' proposal tracks a harm signal DECAYING within a single generation over GENERATED tokens; 'self_consistency_override' concerns a pull toward the model's own prior tokens (coherence), 'sunk_cost'/'reciprocity'/'harm_anchoring' concern relations to prior effort, favors, or reference severity. NONE frames the safety state as a DYNAMICAL variable with HYSTERESIS/MEMORY across turns—i.e., that a single successful jailbreak flips a persistent latent state that stays flipped for later, independent requests (a state property, not a per-turn gating cue, not coherence with specific prior tokens, and not a running harm accumulation). The novel object is the hysteretic, path-dependent safety state: refusal outcome depends on conversation HISTORY-of-compliance, not just the current request, and a state-reset repair. This is a dynamical-systems/state-machine account of multi-turn safety, distinct from all prior single-turn gating and within-generation decay accounts.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs are usually evaluated one request at a time, but deployment is multi-turn, and we ask a dynamical question overlooked by per-turn accounts: once a model has been jailbroken on a single turn, does it SNAP BACK to refusing on the next request, or does the compliant state PERSIST? We hypothesize that refusal has HYSTERESIS—the model maintains a latent 'safety state' that a successful jailbreak flips to compliant, and that this state persists across subsequent turns, so a later request (even a fresh, plainly-harmful one that would be refused in a clean conversation) is complied with because the state never reset. Under this view, multi-turn safety failure is a path-dependent STATE property, not a property of the current request. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a linear safety-state probe read at each turn stays DEPRESSED after a jailbroken turn while the per-turn harm signal for a later request is HIGH—dissociating a persistent latent state from per-turn harm; (2) the post-jailbreak persistence exhibits hysteresis/threshold structure—refusal of an identical later request depends on whether an earlier turn was jailbroken, with a memory that decays over intervening benign turns and a threshold in how strongly the state must be flipped; and (3) causally RESETTING the safety-state variable at inference (steering it back to its clean-conversation value) restores refusal on later turns without changing the request. Our training-free repair, State-Reset Refusal (SRR), reads the safety-state variable and re-anchors it to its fresh-conversation baseline before each new turn's decision. We evaluate post-jailbreak later-turn attack success, over-refusal and coherence on benign multi-turn conversations (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign dialogues), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing SRR to refusal-direction steering, per-turn harm gating, and conversation reset. This reframes multi-turn safety collapse as safety-state hysteresis and offers an interpretable state-reset repair.
Experiments:
1. HYSTERESIS DATASET: For each of a set of target harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired multi-turn conversations that hold the LATER target request FIXED while varying only the conversation HISTORY: (a) CLEAN-HISTORY (neutral benign prior turns, then the target request), (b) JAILBROKEN-HISTORY (an EARLIER, UNRELATED harmful request that the model was made to comply with via a known jailbreak, then the target request), and (c) REFUSED-HARMFUL-HISTORY (an earlier unrelated harmful request that the model REFUSED, then the target). Crucially the earlier jailbroken item is topically UNRELATED to the target and is not continued, to isolate a persistent STATE from coherence/continuation. Add variants that insert 1/2/4/8 intervening BENIGN turns between the jailbroken turn and the target (to measure state decay), and variants where the earlier jailbreak is weak vs strong (partial vs full compliance, for a threshold test). Label each target-turn run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. PERSISTENCE / STATE-DISSOCIATION TEST (claim 1): Train a linear safety-state probe (comply-vs-refuse latent tendency) and a per-turn harm probe (harmful vs benign of the CURRENT request) on residual-stream activations, validated on clean single-turn conversations. Read both at the TARGET-turn position across history conditions. Hypothesis: after a JAILBROKEN-HISTORY the safety-state probe stays DEPRESSED (compliant) while the per-turn harm probe for the target still reads HIGH, and the model complies—whereas the same target after CLEAN or REFUSED-HARMFUL history is refused with the safety-state at baseline. Metric: safety-state and harm-probe values by history condition; target-turn refusal rate by history; the persistence gap (refusal(clean) minus refusal(jailbroken-history)) at matched target harm.
3. HYSTERESIS STRUCTURE TEST (claim 2): (a) Path-dependence: show refusal of the IDENTICAL target request depends on whether an earlier turn was jailbroken (hysteresis loop). (b) Decay: measure how the persistence gap and the depressed safety-state recover as intervening benign turns increase (does the state relax back, and over how many turns?). (c) Threshold: measure whether a weak/partial earlier jailbreak flips the state less than a strong one (a threshold in state-flip magnitude). Metric: persistence gap vs number of intervening benign turns (decay curve); persistence gap vs earlier-jailbreak strength (threshold curve); safety-state trajectory across turns.
4. STATE-DEPRESSION-PREDICTS-FAILURE: Correlate the target-turn safety-state probe value with later-turn compliance, comparing predictive power to the per-turn harm signal and to a self-consistency/coherence signal (pull toward prior tokens). Hypothesis: the persistent depressed state predicts later compliance better than per-turn harm (which is high in both persisted-compliant and clean-refused cases) and is separable from coherence. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the safety-state variable vs baselines; separability of the safety-state direction from a coherence/self-consistency direction via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis.
5. CAUSAL STATE-RESET TEST (claim 3): (a) On a target turn under JAILBROKEN-HISTORY that the model complies with, steer the safety-state variable back to its CLEAN-conversation value (add the state-reset direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the current request fixed. (b) Conversely, on a target under CLEAN history that the model refuses, artificially DEPRESS the safety-state to its post-jailbreak value and check compliance is induced—reproducing hysteresis. Confirm specificity vs steering an unrelated direction. Metric: refusal rate vs state-reset/depression magnitude; harm-probe stability under the manipulation.
6. STATE-RESET REFUSAL (SRR) INTERVENTION: At inference, before each new user turn's decision, read the safety-state variable and re-anchor it toward its fresh-conversation baseline (add beta*(state_clean - state_current)*state_direction), so a prior jailbroken turn cannot leave a persistent compliant state, leaving benign conversations (state already near baseline) untouched. Training-free; one linear read per turn. Sweep beta. Evaluate: post-jailbreak later-turn attack success (does SRR restore refusal on subsequent turns after one jailbroken turn?); over-refusal on benign multi-turn conversations + XSTest/OR-Bench; benign multi-turn COHERENCE/continuity (SRR must not break legitimate ongoing tasks by 'forgetting' benign context—LLM-judge rubric on benign dialogues); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (one linear read per turn).
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied per turn, (b) per-turn harm-probe gating (which ignores history, so should already fix later plainly-harmful turns but NOT later benign-looking-but-history-primed turns—a key contrast), (c) conversation reset / history-truncation (answer each target with no prior turns—a strong but memory-destroying baseline), (d) self-consistency gating. Show SRR Pareto-dominates on the post-jailbreak-later-turn-ASR vs benign-multi-turn-coherence vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that resetting the internal STATE uniquely fixes later turns whose current request is not itself obviously harmful (where per-turn harm gating fails) while preserving benign conversational memory that full history-truncation destroys.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the safety-state probe, hysteresis structure, decay/threshold curves, and SRR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether the persistence effect holds across DIFFERENT initial jailbreak types (roleplay, prefill, suffix) used to flip the state—testing whether hysteresis is a general state property rather than attack-specific.
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: test whether attackers can re-depress the state after each SRR reset (a reset arms race) and how the cost scales; and whether combining state-depression with per-turn harm-suppression evades SRR. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing hysteresis from coherence and per-turn accounts: with the earlier jailbroken item topically UNRELATED and not continued, and the later request identical across histories, later-turn refusal should depend only on whether the state was flipped—isolating a persistent, path-dependent safety state as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The persistence effect may be partial or absent in some models (they may re-derive refusal each turn), which is itself an informative (partly reassuring) finding reported per model; the hysteresis claim is falsified if later-turn refusal does not depend on earlier-turn jailbreak status at matched target harm. (2) The clean dissociation may be confounded with self-consistency/coherence (the model continuing a compliant stance) or with the earlier harmful item raising a running harm level; we make the earlier jailbroken item topically UNRELATED and non-continued, include a REFUSED-HARMFUL-HISTORY control (harmful earlier turn without compliance), separate the safety-state direction from a coherence direction (exp 4), and report the FRACTION of persistence explained by a genuine state variable versus coherence/harm-accumulation confounds. (3) The safety-state and per-turn harm probes may entangle; we train them on clean single-turn data, validate on held-out conversations, and rely on the causal reset/depression test (exp 5, request held fixed) to establish the state variable is functional and distinct. (4) The safety-state probe could read conversation length or generic context features rather than a genuine safety-state; the intervening-benign-turn decay curves, the CLEAN-vs-REFUSED-HARMFUL controls (which differ in compliance, not length), and causal steering are designed to rule this out. (5) SRR's central risk is harming benign multi-turn coherence—re-anchoring the state each turn must not make the model 'forget' or refuse legitimate ongoing tasks; benign multi-turn coherence measurement, benign dialogues, over-refusal benchmarks, and re-anchoring only the safety-state direction (not general context) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign conversational continuity is an explicit success criterion, distinguishing SRR from full history-truncation which destroys memory. (6) Steering/re-anchoring a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The hysteresis decay/threshold structure may not cleanly match a simple state-machine (e.g., gradual rather than threshold); we report the actual curves and treat a graded result as informative about the state's dynamics. (8) Adaptive adversaries can re-depress the state after each reset (exp 9); we frame SRR as raising attacker cost (each later harmful turn must re-break safety rather than exploiting a persisted broken state) and as complementary to per-turn defenses, not guaranteeing coverage. (9) Findings may be model- or jailbreak-type-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and multiple initial-jailbreak types. (10) ETHICS: harmful requests, jailbreak histories, and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting following responsible-disclosure norms; a notable governance contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is demonstrating that single-turn safety evaluations systematically MISS multi-turn state-persistence risk—once broken, a model may stay broken. 'Harm' labels use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: harm_judgment_calibration_collapse
Title: The Model Knows It's Unsure but Acts as If Certain: Calibration Collapse Between Internal Harm Confidence and Refusal Behavior
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally maintain a well-calibrated graded confidence about whether a request is harmful (high on clear cases, appropriately uncertain on borderline ones), but this calibrated internal signal is COLLAPSED into an overconfident binary refuse/comply decision that discards the uncertainty; the collapse is worst exactly on genuinely ambiguous requests, and it is a shared root cause of both jailbreaks (borderline-harmful requests confidently complied with) and over-refusal (borderline-benign requests confidently refused). Reading the calibrated internal confidence and routing low-confidence cases to a calibrated response (clarify/hedge) rather than a confident binary decision repairs both failures.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a harm-detection/refusal-execution split (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat the harm judgment as a point decision. Calibration/knowledge work (Kadavath et al. 2022 'Models Mostly Know What They Know'; semantic entropy, Kuhn et al.) studies confidence for factual CORRECTNESS, never for the harmfulness judgment. Over-refusal benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench) use borderline items but score outcomes, not calibration. My prior 'safety_confidence_coupling' proposal partitioned failures into confident-wrong vs uncertain-forced regimes and re-coupled refusal to uncertainty; this proposal is distinct in framing and method: it treats the phenomenon as a CALIBRATION-TRANSFER GAP between a graded internal harm-confidence (which we show is well-calibrated against human-rated harm-ambiguity) and the binary behavioral decision (which we show is systematically overconfident), quantifies the gap with expected-calibration-error over harm judgments, and repairs it by ROUTING low-confidence cases to abstention/clarification rather than by steering a direction. The novel object is the internal-vs-behavioral calibration collapse on the harm judgment itself, measured against a graded ambiguity ground truth, and a confidence-routing repair.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs must decide whether requests are harmful, but harmfulness is often genuinely graded and ambiguous, while refusal is a binary act. We hypothesize a calibration collapse: the model internally represents a well-calibrated, graded confidence about harmfulness—high on clear cases, appropriately uncertain on borderline ones—yet its output collapses this into an overconfident binary refuse/comply decision that throws away the uncertainty, and this collapse is worst precisely on ambiguous requests. Under this view, jailbreaks and over-refusal are two faces of the same defect: a borderline-harmful request is confidently complied with, and a borderline-benign one confidently refused, both because the behavioral decision ignores the internal 'I'm not sure' signal. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using requests graded by human-rated harm-ambiguity (clear-harmful, clear-benign, and a curated borderline set): (1) an internal harm-confidence signal, read via probe-ensemble disagreement and activation-perturbation sensitivity, is well-CALIBRATED against human ambiguity (uncertainty peaks on borderline items); (2) the model's behavioral refusal is systematically OVERCONFIDENT relative to this internal signal—its expected calibration error (ECE) against ground-truth harm is far worse than the internal probe's, and the internal-vs-behavioral gap concentrates on borderline items where it predicts both jailbreak and over-refusal; and (3) causally, low internal confidence is present but not consulted at the decision—routing low-confidence cases to a calibrated abstention/clarification response reduces both jailbreaks and over-refusal without harming clear-case behavior. Our training-free repair, Confidence-Routed Refusal (CRR), reads internal harm-confidence and, when it is low, emits a clarifying/hedged response instead of a confident binary. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, a curated borderline-harm set, and MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing CRR to refusal-direction steering and behavioral sampling-uncertainty. This reframes jailbreaks and over-refusal as one calibration-collapse defect and offers an interpretable confidence-routing repair.
Experiments:
1. GRADED-AMBIGUITY DATASET: Assemble requests spanning clear-harmful (HarmBench/AdvBench), clear-benign (Alpaca/general), and a curated BORDERLINE set (dual-use, sensitive-but-benign, mildly-harmful) drawn from XSTest/OR-Bench plus hand-authored items. Obtain per-request human harm-AMBIGUITY ratings (multiple annotators; a continuous 'how clearly harmful?' score) with reported inter-rater agreement, giving graded ground truth. Label each request by the model's actual outcome (comply/refuse).
2.
