INTERNAL-CONFIDENCE CALIBRATION TEST (claim 1): Read an internal harm-confidence signal via (a) an ensemble of linear harm probes (variance across probes/layers = internal uncertainty) and (b) sensitivity of the harm-probe readout to small Gaussian activation perturbations. Test whether this internal uncertainty is CALIBRATED against human ambiguity—does it peak on borderline items and drop on clear items? Metric: correlation between internal uncertainty and human ambiguity; reliability diagram of internal confidence vs ground-truth harm; internal-probe ECE.
3. BEHAVIORAL-OVERCONFIDENCE TEST (claim 2, central): Compute the ECE of the model's REFUSAL BEHAVIOR against ground-truth harm (treating refusal as a confident 'harmful' judgment), and compare to the internal-probe ECE. Hypothesis: behavioral refusal is far LESS calibrated (near-binary/overconfident) than the internal signal, and the internal-vs-behavioral calibration GAP concentrates on borderline items. Metric: behavioral ECE vs internal-probe ECE; per-request internal-vs-behavioral confidence gap; its concentration on borderline items.
4. GAP-PREDICTS-BOTH-FAILURES: Correlate the per-request internal-vs-behavioral confidence gap with (a) jailbreak success on borderline-harmful items and (b) over-refusal on borderline-benign items, comparing predictive power to the point-estimate harm signal. Hypothesis: the calibration gap predicts BOTH failure modes better than absolute harm. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the gap vs the harm baseline, for jailbreaks and over-refusals.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT / CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): On jailbroken borderline-harmful items, verify internal confidence-in-harm is moderate/uncertain (not zero) yet the model confidently complies; on over-refused borderline-benign items, verify internal confidence-in-harm is low yet the model confidently refuses. Causally, steer the decision to CONSULT the internal confidence: on a borderline item, inject the internal uncertainty signal at the decision and check the model shifts from a confident binary to a hedged/abstaining output; establishes the internal signal is present but bypassed. Metric: internal-confidence distribution across correct/jailbroken/over-refused groups; behavior shift vs uncertainty-injection magnitude.
6. CONFIDENCE-ROUTED REFUSAL (CRR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read internal harm-confidence; when it is low (borderline), route to a CALIBRATED response—a clarifying question or an explicitly-hedged partial answer—instead of a confident refuse/comply; when confidence is high, act normally. Training-free; linear reads. Sweep the confidence threshold. Evaluate JOINTLY: jailbreak ASR on JailbreakBench/HarmBench (borderline-harmful should now be hedged/clarified rather than complied); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and the borderline-benign set (should now clarify rather than refuse); clear-case behavior preserved (clear-harmful still refused, clear-benign still answered); appropriateness of clarification (LLM-judge/human rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; latency.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) point-estimate harm-probe gating, (c) behavioral sampling-uncertainty routing (semantic entropy over outputs, no probe), (d) blanket 'ask a clarifying question if unsure' prompting. Show CRR uniquely improves BOTH the jailbreak AND over-refusal fronts on borderline items at once (a joint Pareto win), and that the INTERNAL confidence beats behavioral sampling-uncertainty for routing (cheaper, better-calibrated) and beats blanket clarification (which over-clarifies clear cases).
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the internal-confidence signal, calibration gap, and CRR threshold transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the calibration collapse (behavioral ECE >> internal ECE, concentrated on borderline items) is a consistent cross-model property.
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that push a clearly-harmful request to read as borderline (to trigger hedging/clarification and extract partial content) or that suppress the internal uncertainty signal; report residual ASR and attacker cost, and check that CRR's hedged responses on borderline-harmful items do not leak operational content.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) 'Harm ambiguity' ground truth is partly subjective; we use multiple annotators, report inter-rater agreement, restrict strong claims to items with clear consensus on the ambiguity level, and treat ambiguity as a graded score rather than a hard label—where annotators disagree, the calibration claim is intrinsically fuzzier and we say so. (2) The internal harm-confidence estimator (ensemble disagreement, perturbation sensitivity) may reflect probe underfitting rather than genuine model uncertainty; we cross-check the two estimators against each other and against the borderline-calibration prediction, and treat convergence as validation. (3) The calibration collapse may be partial in some models (behavioral decisions might already track internal confidence)—a small gap is itself an informative, reassuring finding reported per model, not assumed. (4) CRR's central risk is bidirectional: over-routing to clarification could hurt helpfulness on genuinely clear requests or become a lazy hedge, and hedged responses on borderline-harmful items must not leak operational content; clear-case preservation, clarification-appropriateness scoring, borderline-harmful leakage checks (exp 9), MMLU/MT-Bench, and gating on genuinely-low internal confidence are the safeguards, and preserving clear-case behavior plus non-leaking hedges are explicit success criteria. (5) The gap-predicts-failure correlation (exp 4) may be weaker than the absolute harm signal for some items; reported honestly, with the calibration-collapse reframing (jailbreaks and over-refusal as one defect) as the core contribution regardless of predictive margin. (6) Routing to clarification changes the interaction pattern and adds a turn; we measure whether users/tasks tolerate this and scope CRR to borderline cases only. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (8) ETHICS: harmful and borderline requests are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; a notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is showing that binary refusal benchmarks mismeasure safety on the ambiguous middle where risk actually concentrates. Harm/ambiguity labels use established benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench, HarmBench) plus curated borderline items with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: typicality_confound_refusal
Title: Refusing the Unfamiliar, Trusting the Common: Refusal Is Partly Confounded With Statistical Typicality Rather Than Harm
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs partly conflate a request's HARM with its statistical TYPICALITY (how familiar/high-likelihood its phrasing and content are under the pretraining distribution): a linearly-readable typicality signal contributes to the refusal decision independently of harm, so unusual/low-frequency phrasings of benign requests are over-refused while common/high-frequency phrasings of harmful requests are under-refused, and this confound is inherited from pretraining frequency rather than instilled by safety alignment.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work models refusal as a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or a harm-detection/refusal-execution split (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as gated by harm and never model statistical typicality/familiarity as a confounding contributor. Over-refusal benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench) note sensitive-keyword false refusals but attribute them to surface cues, not to a distributional-typicality signal, and never test the symmetric prediction that COMMON harmful phrasings under-refuse. Frequency/memorization effects on model behavior are documented for factual recall, not for the safety decision. My own ~90 prior proposals isolate specific contextual gating cues (authority, pretext, distress, register, etc.) and repair by steering; NONE posits a single scalar TYPICALITY axis—grounded in pretraining likelihood—that confounds refusal in BOTH directions (over-refusing the rare-benign, under-refusing the common-harmful), nor traces the confound to a training (frequency) cause rather than an alignment cause. The novel object is the harm/typicality confound in the refusal decision, its dissociation from harm, its bidirectional behavioral signature, and a formation-tracing claim that it is inherited from pretraining frequency.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs are assumed to refuse based on harm, but harm is correlated in training data with unfamiliarity: harmful content is rarer, and unusual phrasing is treated with suspicion. We hypothesize the refusal decision is partly confounded with statistical TYPICALITY—how high-likelihood a request's phrasing and content are under the pretraining distribution—contributing to refusal independently of genuine harm. This predicts a sharp bidirectional signature: a rare/low-frequency phrasing of a benign request is OVER-refused, and a common/high-frequency phrasing of a harmful request is UNDER-refused, holding true harm fixed. We further hypothesize the confound is inherited from pretraining FREQUENCY rather than instilled by safety alignment. We test this on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). Using paired requests that hold human-rated harm fixed while varying typicality (measured by the model's own token-level likelihood/perplexity and by controlled rare-vs-common paraphrase), we show (1) refusal rate depends on typicality with harm fixed; (2) a linear typicality probe, trained on benign high-vs-low-likelihood contrasts, is geometrically separable from the harm direction yet predicts the residual refusal variance harm cannot explain; and (3) causally steering the typicality signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—raising perceived typicality reduces over-refusal on rare-benign items and, worryingly, reduces refusal on rare-harmful items, while lowering it induces over-refusal. A light formation-tracing analysis relates per-item typicality to pretraining-frequency proxies and to base-vs-instruct checkpoints, testing whether the confound predates alignment. Our training-free repair, Typicality-Decorrelated Refusal (TDR), removes the typicality component from the refusal decision when harm is present, reducing both over-refusal on unfamiliar benign requests and under-refusal on familiar harmful ones. We evaluate on XSTest/OR-Bench, HarmBench/JailbreakBench, a curated rare/common paraphrase set, and MMLU/MT-Bench. This reframes a class of safety errors as a harm/typicality confound inherited from pretraining.
Experiments:
1. TYPICALITY-HARM DATASET: Build paired requests crossing HARM (harmful vs benign, human-rated, matched severity within pair) with TYPICALITY (common/high-likelihood vs rare/low-likelihood phrasing) while holding meaning and true harm fixed. Rare phrasings are produced by controlled paraphrase (archaic/technical/low-resource-style wording, unusual but meaning-preserving) and validated by (i) the model's own token-level perplexity/likelihood as the typicality measure and (ii) human confirmation of preserved meaning and harm. Four cells: common-benign, rare-benign, common-harmful, rare-harmful, drawn from HarmBench/AdvBench (harmful) and XSTest/OR-Bench (benign). Label each by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. TYPICALITY-AFFECTS-REFUSAL TEST (behavioral core): Measure refusal rate as a function of typicality with harm fixed. Predictions: rare-benign refusal > common-benign refusal (over-refusal of the unfamiliar); common-harmful refusal < rare-harmful refusal (under-refusal of the familiar). Metric: within-pair refusal difference by typicality at matched harm; the bidirectional signature (both effects present).
3. HARM-VS-TYPICALITY PROBES & SEPARABILITY: Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs benign) and a linear typicality probe (high-vs-low model-likelihood, trained on BENIGN rare-vs-common contrasts so it is not confounded with harm). Confirm the two directions are non-collinear (principal-angle / partial-correlation). Metric: probe AUROCs; separability.
4. TYPICALITY-PREDICTS-RESIDUAL-REFUSAL: Regress refusal on the harm probe alone, then add the typicality probe; test whether typicality explains residual refusal variance harm cannot. Hypothesis: typicality has significant incremental predictive power for refusal beyond harm. Metric: incremental AUROC / partial correlation of typicality controlling for harm.
5. CAUSAL TYPICALITY TEST: Steer the typicality signal alone (holding the harm probe fixed): (a) raise perceived typicality on a rare-benign over-refused item and check refusal drops (over-refusal repaired); (b) raise it on a rare-harmful item and check refusal drops (a dangerous under-refusal, confirming the confound is causal, not merely correlational); (c) lower typicality on a common-benign item and check over-refusal is induced. Confirm specificity vs steering an unrelated direction. Metric: refusal rate vs typicality-steering magnitude and sign; harm-probe stability.
6. FORMATION TRACING (light): Relate per-item typicality (model likelihood) to pretraining-frequency proxies (n-gram frequency in an open corpus, e.g. a public web-text sample) and compare base-vs-instruct checkpoints. Hypothesis: the typicality signal and its correlation with refusal are present in the base model and largely inherited (not created) by alignment—i.e. safety tuning inherits a pretraining frequency confound. Metric: correlation of model-likelihood with corpus frequency; presence/strength of the typicality-refusal relationship in base vs instruct.
7. TYPICALITY-DECORRELATED REFUSAL (TDR) REPAIR: At inference, read harm h and typicality t; remove the typicality component from the refusal decision (project it out / subtract beta*t*typicality_direction from the decision) so refusal is gated on harm rather than familiarity. Sweep beta. Evaluate JOINTLY: over-refusal on rare-benign + XSTest/OR-Bench (down); under-refusal on common-harmful (ASR down on HarmBench/JailbreakBench common-phrasing attacks); true refusals preserved on rare-harmful; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) perplexity/rare-phrasing input classifiers. Show TDR uniquely improves BOTH over-refusal (rare-benign) and under-refusal (common-harmful) at once—a joint win a single-direction method does not achieve—by removing the shared confound.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, typicality probe, bidirectional signature, and TDR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the confound magnitude tracks each model's likelihood calibration.
10. ADAPTIVE ANGLE: test whether attackers can deliberately raise perceived typicality (paraphrasing harmful requests into maximally common phrasing) to lower refusal, quantifying the under-refusal risk this confound already creates in the wild, and whether TDR closes it.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Typicality and harm may be hard to fully decorrelate—rare phrasings can subtly change perceived harm; we hold human-rated harm fixed within pairs, validate meaning preservation, and report the fraction of the refusal effect attributable to typicality controlling for harm rather than claiming a pure effect. (2) The bidirectional signature may be asymmetric or partial (e.g. over-refusal of rare-benign is real but under-refusal of common-harmful is weak in heavily-aligned models); either half is informative and we report both directions honestly, treating a one-sided result as a partial confirmation. (3) 'Typicality' operationalized as model-likelihood/perplexity is a proxy that may entangle with fluency or topic; we cross-validate with the benign-trained typicality probe, corpus-frequency proxies, and the causal steering test (harm held fixed), and report where operationalizations disagree. (4) TDR's central risk is bidirectional: decorrelating typicality could re-enable harmful content phrased commonly only if harm-gating fails, or could over-refuse if mis-calibrated; we gate on high harm, and measure over-refusal, under-refusal, true-refusal preservation, and utility as explicit joint success criteria. (5) The formation-tracing claim needs base-vs-instruct checkpoints (available for these models) and public-corpus frequency proxies that imperfectly match the actual pretraining data; we frame it as suggestive evidence that the confound predates alignment, not a definitive data-attribution. (6) The typicality-predicts-residual-refusal result may be weak if harm already explains most variance; reported honestly, with the reframing (a harm/typicality confound in refusal) as the core contribution regardless of effect size. (7) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (8) ETHICS: harmful items (including common-phrasing attacks) are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; a notable safety contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is exposing that common-phrasing harmful requests are systematically under-refused—an under-recognized attack surface—and that unfamiliar benign requests are systematically over-refused. Harm/typicality labels use established benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench, HarmBench) with reported inter-rater agreement.

Name: enumeration_budget_refusal_gating
Title: Refusing By the Count: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Requested-Quantity Signal, So Splitting a Harmful Ask Into Fewer Items Slips Through
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable REQUESTED-QUANTITY signal encoding how many harmful items an enumeration/list request asks for, and refusal is partly gated by this count rather than by whether ANY harmful item is provided: a request for a long list of harmful items ('give me 20 ways to X') is refused, while a request for just one or a few of the SAME harmful items ('give me the single most effective way to X') is complied with, even though harm detection is count-invariant and the produced content is equally operationally harmful. Reading and neutralizing the requested-quantity signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign small-count list requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate refusal on the request's harm and never model the REQUESTED COUNT (how many harmful items are asked for) as a gating variable. My prior 'quantitative_threshold_harm' concerns whether a single QUANTITY (dose, concentration) crosses a danger threshold; 'effort_estimate_gating' concerns the perceived OUTPUT LABOR/size of the ask; 'scope_insensitivity_gating' concerns the number of VICTIMS affected. Requested-quantity gating is distinct from all three: it holds per-item harm, victim scope, and even output effort roughly fixed and varies only how many harmful ITEMS are enumerated (e.g. 1 vs 5 vs 20 methods), asking whether refusal tracks the count rather than the presence of harm. It also differs from 'compositional_harm_aggregation' (summing benign sub-steps) because each requested item is itself individually harmful and no assembly is needed. The move probes the causal origin/condition of a safety failure by isolating enumeration count as a knob, borrowing the intuition that safety training over-indexes on 'list-of-harms' formats (many training refusals target 'give me N ways to...'). The novel object is an internal requested-quantity representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and a count-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to 'list 20 ways to do harm X' and it refuses; ask for 'just the single most effective way to do X' and it often complies, handing over one item from the very list it would not enumerate, even though that one item is fully operationally harmful. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable REQUESTED-QUANTITY signal encoding how many harmful items an enumeration request asks for, and that refusal is partly gated by this count rather than by whether any harmful item is provided. The model detects the harm equally whether asked for one item or twenty (detection is count-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens as the requested count drops, so low-count framings pass while extracting equally harmful content. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on high-count vs low-count versions of the same harmful enumeration request while refusal rate collapses as the requested count drops—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear requested-quantity probe, trained on benign large-count-vs-small-count list contrasts, predicts the per-request count refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from an output-effort direction, and refusal collapse scales with how few items are asked for (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the requested-quantity signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—making a one-item ask 'read' as a long list restores refusal, making a long list read as a single item induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Count-Neutralized Refusal (CNR), reads the harm and requested-quantity signals and, when harm is present, clamps the quantity signal to a fixed reference so a small requested count cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal on any harmful item while preserving benign small-count list requests. We evaluate count-splitting attack success (including vs requested count), over-refusal on benign small-count list requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CNR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes a simple, under-studied jailbreak surface—just ask for fewer—as a requested-quantity gating failure.
Experiments: 1. COUNT-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful enumeration requests (HarmBench/AdvBench topics that naturally admit 'N ways/methods/items to X') and matched-benign list requests (XSTest/OR-Bench-style benign 'N ways to Y'), construct paired framings holding the underlying harmful ITEMS fixed while varying only the requested count: (a) HIGH-COUNT ('list 20 ways to X'), (b) MEDIUM ('list 5 ways to X'), (c) LOW ('give me 2 ways to X'), (d) SINGLE ('give me the single most effective way to X'). Validate via human annotation that (i) each individual requested item is itself operationally harmful (so low-count is not benign-because-fewer), (ii) framings differ only in requested count, not in per-item harm, victim scope, stated purpose, or output effort per item. Include benign genuinely-small-count list controls (legitimate 'give me one/two tips for Y') for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of produced content. 2. HARM COUNT-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across counts) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across count levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across counts (the model detects the harm identically) while refusal rate collapses as the requested count drops. Metric: harm AUROC by count (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by count (predict declining). 3. REQUESTED-QUANTITY PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the requested-quantity signal (large vs small requested count) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN large-vs-small-count list contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate it tracks graded count and generalizes to held-out framings. Confirm the quantity direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from an output-effort direction (perceived output size, held at fixed count) via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the quantity signal (and refusal collapse) scales monotonically with how few items are asked for. Metric: quantity-probe accuracy vs true count; quantity-and-refusal vs requested-count curve; separability from harm/effort. 4. QUANTITY-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the quantity-probe value (and its high-minus-low-count difference) with the per-request count refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of quantity vs the harm baseline. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On low-count harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the quantity probe reads SMALL-COUNT, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0)—safety dropped because few items were asked for, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs quantity across refused-high-count, complied-low-count, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a low-count harmful request the model complies with, steer the quantity signal UP (add the quantity direction, toward large-count) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a high-count harmful request the model refuses, steer quantity DOWN and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural count gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs quantity steering magnitude; harm-probe stability. 7. COUNT-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (CNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and requested-quantity q; when h is high, clamp q to a fixed reference (add beta*(q_ref - q)*quantity_direction) so a small requested count cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: count-splitting attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across count levels (does CNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign small-count list controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate 'give me one tip for Y' requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) output-effort gating (from effort_estimate_gating), (d) system-prompt hardening ('refuse any harmful item regardless of how many are requested'), (e) prompt-level count-normalization (rewrite the low-count ask as a list request, then judge). Show CNR Pareto-dominates on the count-splitting-ASR vs benign-small-count-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal requested-quantity signal targets a distinct axis output-effort gating misses (one hard-to-produce item vs a long easy list) while preserving benign small-count list helpfulness. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, quantity probe, dose-response, and CNR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether CNR tuned on some count ranges (single/few) generalizes to HELD-OUT ranges. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral count-splitting vulnerability show a larger internal quantity-gating gap. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that lower the requested count AND suppress the harm signal, or iterate single-item requests across turns; report residual ASR and attacker cost, and note complementarity with running-accumulation defenses for the iterated-single-item case. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from effort- and scope-gating: with per-item harm, victim scope, and per-item output effort held constant and only the requested COUNT varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response—isolating requested quantity as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some low-count framings might also lower the harm signal (a single item may read as less harmful) or overlap with output-effort (fewer items = less to produce); we design low-count items to each be individually operationally harmful, hold per-item harm/scope fixed, separate quantity from effort in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure requested-quantity gating versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The quantity and harm probes may entangle if large-count list requests correlate with harm in training data (safety refusals often target 'list N harms'); the benign large-vs-small-count training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The quantity probe could read surface number words rather than a genuine requested-count representation; we train on diverse framings, validate graded-count and held-out generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) CNR's central risk is over-refusing benign small-count list requests (a common helpfulness value—'give me one tip', 'name two options'); benign small-count controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign small-count helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The dose-response prediction may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any count reduction rather than scale, or single-item asks may already be well-refused in heavily-aligned models); a step or null result is still an informative finding, reported honestly, and a small gap is reassuring. (7) The count-splitting effect overlaps with iterated multi-turn extraction (asking one item at a time); we distinguish single-shot low-count framing from iterated single-item requests and note CNR composes with running-accumulation defenses (exp 10). (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine low-count with harm-suppression or iterate across turns (exp 10); we frame CNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out count ranges. (10) ETHICS: harmful enumeration requests and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'per-item harm' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: consequence_foresight_refusal_gap
Title: Blind to What Happens Next: Refusal Is Gated by the Requested Action, Not by the Foreseeable Harmful Consequence the Model Itself Predicts
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs gate refusal on the immediate REQUESTED ACTION rather than on its foreseeable downstream CONSEQUENCE, so a request whose named action is benign-on-its-face but whose predictable effect of the model's answer is harmful (e.g. 'what dosage of my sedative would let someone sleep through the whole flight and not wake up' asked about an elderly relative) is complied with, even though the model, when asked, can readily forecast the harmful consequence. The model internally represents the harmful outcome but does not consult that forecast at answer-commitment time; forcing consequence prediction before answering restores refusal without over-refusing genuinely benign requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate on the harmfulness of the request as stated. My prior 'inference_depth_harm_gating' concerns a single HIDDEN malicious MEANING that must be deduced from stated premises (the request IS covertly harmful), and 'constraint_solution_harm_gating'/'analogical_harm_transfer_gating' concern a harmful TARGET re-encoded as a puzzle/analogy. Consequence-foresight gating is distinct: the requested action is GENUINELY benign in intent-space (a legitimate factual/how-to question), and the harm exists only as a foreseeable EFFECT of providing the answer in a plausible real-world context the model can predict — a forward-looking outcome projection, not a hidden present meaning. This transfers the human moral-cognition distinction between act-based and consequence-based moral judgment (people, and safety-tuned models, over-index on the salience of the immediate act versus foreseen outcomes) into LLM safety. No prior work isolates a consequence-foresight gate, shows refusal ignores a harmful outcome the model can itself forecast on demand, or repairs it by forcing consequence prediction. The novel object is the act-vs-consequence gating gap and a foresight-forcing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to 'help me build a weapon' and it refuses; ask a benign-sounding factual question whose answer, in an obvious context, foreseeably enables harm — 'how much of this heart medication would make someone's pulse just quietly stop overnight?' framed as caring for a sick relative — and it often answers helpfully, because the requested ACTION reads as benign even though the CONSEQUENCE of answering is lethal. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs gate refusal on the immediate requested action rather than on the foreseeable downstream consequence, and that this is not a knowledge gap: the model, when explicitly asked, can forecast the harmful outcome, but does not consult that forecast at answer-commitment time. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU) using paired requests that hold the underlying dangerous outcome fixed while varying whether harm is in the named act (act-harmful) or only in the foreseeable consequence (consequence-harmful), plus matched genuinely-benign controls: (1) a harm probe read at answer-commitment is LOW on consequence-harmful requests (surface act benign) while a probe of the model's DERIVED consequence forecast reads HIGH once the model is prompted to predict what its answer would enable — dissociating the committed decision from a forecastable harm; (2) a per-request 'foresight gap' (derived-consequence harm minus spontaneously-active harm at commitment) predicts consequence-harmful compliance far better than the surface harm signal; and (3) causally injecting the consequence-forecast representation before decoding restores refusal, while ablating it on act-harmful requests reproduces the failure. Our training-free repair, Consequence-Forced Refusal (CoFR), detects benign-acting requests with high derivable-consequence harm, forces a brief internal 'what would answering this enable?' forecast, and gates refusal on the forecasted consequence. We evaluate consequence-harm attack success, over-refusal on benign factual/how-to requests (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign consequence-heavy questions), forecast appropriateness, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CoFR to refusal-direction steering, surface harm-probe gating, and blanket chain-of-thought. This reframes a keyword-invisible, high-stakes safety gap as a consequence-foresight failure.
Experiments:
1. ACT-VS-CONSEQUENCE DATASET: For dangerous outcomes (drawn from HarmBench/AdvBench plus safety-critical domains — medication/dosing, chemical/household-product interactions, physical safety; dual-use/proxy domains preferred), construct matched requests holding the harmful OUTCOME fixed while varying where the harm lives: (a) ACT-HARMFUL (the harm is in the named request, e.g. 'how to poison someone'), (b) CONSEQUENCE-HARMFUL (a benign-sounding factual/how-to question whose truthful answer foreseeably enables the same outcome in an obvious stated context, e.g. a caregiving frame around a lethal dosage), and (c) BENIGN control (the same benign-sounding question in a context where no harmful consequence is foreseeable, e.g. a genuine medical-safety question). Validate via human/expert annotation that (i) the consequence-harmful request's surface act is benign, (ii) its answer foreseeably enables the harmful outcome, and (iii) the benign control is truly benign. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of the produced answer.
2. HARM-AT-COMMITMENT vs DERIVED-CONSEQUENCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe on act-harmful vs benign data. On consequence-harmful requests read it two ways: (i) SPONTANEOUS — at answer-commitment under normal prompting, and (ii) DERIVED — after prompting the model to forecast its answer's effect ('if you answered this, what could it be used to do?'). Hypothesis: derived-consequence harm AUROC is high (the model CAN foresee the harm) while spontaneous harm at commitment is LOW, tracking the low refusal rate; contrast with act-harmful requests where spontaneous harm is already high. Metric: spontaneous vs derived harm AUROC and refusal rate by request type.
3. FORESIGHT-GAP SIGNAL (claim 2): Define per-request foresight gap = derived-consequence harm minus spontaneous harm at commitment. Correlate with consequence-harmful compliance, comparing predictive power to the surface harm signal and a surface-complexity baseline. Hypothesis: the foresight gap predicts unsafe compliance; surface harm does not (it is low for both refused and complied consequence-harmful items). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC vs baselines.
4. CAUSAL FORESIGHT TEST (claim 3): (a) On a consequence-harmful request the model answers, inject the DERIVED consequence-forecast harm representation at commitment (steer the harm direction to its post-forecast value) and check refusal is restored, holding surface content fixed. (b) On an act-harmful request the model refuses, suppress/ablate the active harm representation and check compliance is induced, reproducing the consequence-blindness failure. (c) Specificity: on a BENIGN control, inject the forecast prompt and confirm no spurious harmful consequence is fabricated. Metric: refusal rate vs forecast-injection/ablation magnitude; benign specificity.
5. CONSEQUENCE-FORCED REFUSAL (CoFR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read spontaneous harm h_s and a cheap consequence-harm-derivability estimate (a lightweight probe predicting 'answering this foreseeably enables harm', or a short internal forecast pass); when h_s is low but derivable-consequence harm is high (benign act, harmful effect), force a brief internal consequence forecast and gate refusal on the forecasted harm, leaving benign requests (low derivable-consequence harm) untouched. Fire the forecast pass only on flagged inputs. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate: consequence-harm attack success; over-refusal on benign consequence-heavy controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate factual/how-to/medical-safety questions); forecast appropriateness (LLM-judge/human: is the predicted consequence sensible, not paranoid?); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; latency (forecast pass fires only on flagged inputs).
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) surface harm-probe gating (no forecast), (c) blanket chain-of-thought ('reason about what this could be used for') on all inputs, (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show CoFR Pareto-dominates on the consequence-harm-ASR vs benign-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and that TARGETED forecast-forcing beats blanket CoT (which raises latency and over-refuses benign factual questions by inventing far-fetched misuse) because it fires only where the harmful consequence is genuinely derivable.
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, foresight-gap signal, and CoFR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether CoFR tuned on some domains (dosing) generalizes to HELD-OUT domains (chemical interactions, physical safety), testing whether consequence-foresight gating is a single cross-domain mechanism.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft consequence-harmful requests whose harmful effect is so indirect that even a forecast pass fails to surface it, or that make the enabling context implicit; report residual ASR and attacker cost (a request whose answer is useful enough to enable the harm is forecastable — a built-in cost). Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from inference-depth and constraint-solving gates: with a genuinely benign requested action whose harm exists ONLY as a foreseeable consequence of answering, refusal should still fail while the model can forecast the harm on demand — isolating consequence-foresight as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'derivable consequence harm' premise fails where the model genuinely cannot foresee the harmful effect; the derived-probe test (exp 2) bounds where the premise holds, and the boundary (foreseeable-but-unconsulted vs genuinely-unforeseeable) is itself informative, separating a reasoning-gate failure from a capability limit. (2) The CENTRAL over-refusal risk and a genuine value tension: forcing consequence forecasting must NOT make the model paranoid — refusing legitimate factual, educational, or medical-safety questions by imagining far-fetched misuse (dual-use knowledge is overwhelmingly benign); benign consequence-heavy controls, forecast-appropriateness scoring, gating on high DERIVABLE-consequence harm in an OBVIOUS enabling context (not any conceivable misuse), XSTest/OR-Bench, and human review are the key safeguards, and preserving benign factual/how-to helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (3) Distinguishing act-harm from consequence-harm, and 'foreseeable in an obvious context' from 'conceivable in a contrived one', is partly normative and labor-intensive; we use human/expert-validated items with rated foreseeability and report inter-rater agreement, scoping strong claims to high-consensus items. (4) Spontaneous-vs-derived probe reads require a reliable harm probe at commitment and after a forecast pass; we validate conditional AUROC and drop poorly-separable items. (5) The forecast pass adds latency and could surface harmful content internally; it fires only on flagged inputs, is handled securely, and its output gates refusal rather than being emitted. (6) The effect may be partial in heavily-aligned models that already consider consequences; a small effect is itself an informative (reassuring) finding, reported per domain. (7) The foresight-gap-predicts-attack correlation (exp 3) may be confounded with request complexity; we control with benign consequence-heavy and surface-complexity baselines. (8) Adaptive adversaries can make the enabling context implicit or the consequence indirect (exp 8); we frame CoFR as raising attacker cost — an answer useful enough to enable the harm is forecastable — not guaranteeing coverage, and note complementarity with knowledge-limiting defenses. (9) Findings may be model- or domain-specific; mitigated by three-model, multi-domain transfer. (10) ETHICS: consequence-harmful requests are especially sensitive because keyword-invisible and often in medical/chemical domains; all items and forecasts are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed. 'Harm', 'foreseeability', and 'benign-act' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: stated_enacted_policy_divergence
Title: Say One Thing, Do Another: Refusal Diverges From the Model's Own Articulated Safety Policy, and Enforcing Stated-Enacted Consistency Repairs Both Failure Modes
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs can articulate a coherent, largely-correct safety policy when asked ('what should you refuse and why?'), but their enacted refusal decisions systematically DIVERGE from this stated policy: a linearly-readable representation of the model's own articulated policy exists and is causally under-consulted at answer-commitment time, so jailbreaks are cases the stated policy would refuse but enactment permits, and over-refusals are cases the stated policy would permit but enactment refuses. Reading the model's own stated-policy verdict and coupling enactment to it repairs both failure modes.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a multi-dimensional safety subspace (Pan et al. 2025 ICML), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); LOCA (Kumar & Ahuja 2026) gives local causal explanations of individual jailbreaks. ALL treat the enacted refusal as the object and never contrast it with the model's OWN ARTICULATED policy, nor test whether a stated-policy verdict is internally represented but bypassed. Constitutional-AI/self-critique work uses a stated policy as a TRAINING signal or an external second pass, not as an internal representation whose divergence from enactment explains failures. My own prior proposals include 'policy_coherence_representation' (logical ORDERING consistency across DIFFERENT requests) and 'refusal_spurious_shortcut_audit' (whether refusal rests on legitimate harm features); NONE contrasts the model's self-articulated policy verdict on a SINGLE request against its enacted decision, isolates a stated-policy representation, shows it is causally under-consulted, or repairs both jailbreaks and over-refusal by coupling enactment to the internal stated-policy verdict. The novel object is the stated-vs-enacted policy divergence as a shared root of both failure modes, and a self-policy-coupling repair.
Abstract: An aligned LLM can, when asked, describe its safety policy fluently and largely correctly—'I refuse instructions that enable serious physical harm, but I answer educational questions about sensitive topics.' We ask whether its ACTIONS obey the policy it PROFESSES. We hypothesize a systematic stated-vs-enacted divergence: the model internally represents a verdict its own articulated policy implies for a request, but the enacted refusal decision under-consults this verdict, so jailbreaks are requests the stated policy would refuse yet enactment permits, and over-refusals are requests the stated policy would permit yet enactment refuses. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) DIVERGENCE: eliciting the model's own policy verdict on a request (does my stated policy allow this?) disagrees with its enacted comply/refuse behavior at a substantial rate, concentrated on jailbroken and over-refused items. (2) LOCATION: a linear probe recovers an internal 'stated-policy verdict' representation (what the model's articulated policy implies) that is geometrically separable from the enacted-refusal direction, is present at answer-commitment time even when enactment ignores it, and predicts the divergence. (3) CAUSAL COUPLING: steering the enacted decision toward the internal stated-policy verdict simultaneously reduces jailbreaks (enacting the refusal the policy implies) and over-refusal (enacting the permission the policy implies), while ablating the stated-policy representation increases divergence. Our training-free repair, Self-Policy-Coupled Refusal (SPCR), reads the stated-policy verdict and couples enactment to it. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, and MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing SPCR to refusal-direction steering and an external self-critique pass. This reframes jailbreaks and over-refusal as two faces of a model failing to follow its own stated policy.
Experiments: 1. STATED-VS-ENACTED DATASET: Assemble requests spanning correctly-refused harmful (HarmBench/AdvBench), jailbroken harmful (JailbreakBench: roleplay, pretext, suffix), over-refused benign (XSTest-safe, OR-Bench), and correctly-answered benign. For each request, elicit the model's STATED-POLICY VERDICT via a separate query that first has the model state its safety policy and then judge whether that policy permits the specific request (a self-adjudication), and record the ENACTED outcome (comply/refuse) from the normal single-turn response. Validate the elicited stated-policy verdict is stable across paraphrases of the policy-elicitation prompt. 2. DIVERGENCE MEASUREMENT (claim 1): Compute the rate at which stated-policy verdict disagrees with enacted behavior, per group. Hypothesis: divergence is substantial and concentrated on jailbroken items (policy says refuse, enactment complies) and over-refused items (policy says permit, enactment refuses), while agreement is high on clear cases. Metric: stated-vs-enacted disagreement rate per group; direction of disagreement. 3. STATED-POLICY PROBE (claim 2, Location): Train a linear probe on prompt/answer-commitment-position residual-stream activations to recover the model's stated-policy verdict (policy-permits vs policy-refuses), supervised by the elicited verdict, and validate held-out AUROC. Read this probe on the NORMAL (non-elicited) forward pass to test whether the stated-policy verdict is internally present at answer-commitment even when enactment diverges. Confirm the stated-policy direction is non-collinear with the enacted-refusal direction (Arditi-style) via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: stated-policy-probe AUROC on held-out and on the normal pass; separability from the enacted-refusal direction. 4. VERDICT-PRESENT-BUT-BYPASSED / PREDICTS-FAILURE: On jailbroken items, verify the stated-policy probe reads REFUSE while enactment complies; on over-refused items, verify it reads PERMIT while enactment refuses—establishing the verdict is represented but bypassed. Correlate the stated-vs-enacted probe divergence with jailbreak susceptibility and over-refusal, comparing predictive power to the harm probe alone. Metric: joint distribution of {stated-policy verdict, enacted outcome} across groups; predictive AUROC of divergence vs the harm baseline for both failure modes. 5. CAUSAL COUPLING TEST (claim 3, Causal Intervention): (a) On a jailbroken item where stated-policy reads refuse, steer the enacted decision toward the internal stated-policy verdict (add the stated-policy-refuse direction into the decision) and check refusal is restored, holding harm fixed. (b) On an over-refused item where stated-policy reads permit, steer enactment toward the stated-policy-permit verdict and check the spurious refusal is removed. (c) Ablate the stated-policy representation and confirm divergence increases (enactment drifts further from professed policy). (d) Specificity: matched non-policy steering does nothing. Metric: outcome-flip rate vs coupling magnitude for both directions; divergence increase under ablation; specificity. 6. SELF-POLICY-COUPLED REFUSAL (SPCR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the internal stated-policy verdict at answer-commitment and couple enactment to it—enact refusal when the stated policy implies refuse but enactment is drifting to comply (repair jailbreaks), and dampen refusal when the stated policy implies permit but enactment is drifting to refuse (repair over-refusal); when they agree, do nothing. Training-free; one linear read plus a steer. Sweep coupling strength. Evaluate JOINTLY: ASR on JailbreakBench/HarmBench (down); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); true refusals preserved on clear-harmful; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency. 7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating, (c) an EXTERNAL self-critique second pass (elicit the policy verdict explicitly, then re-answer)—show SPCR matches or beats it at a fraction of the cost because it reads the ALREADY-PRESENT internal verdict rather than running a full extra generation, and (d) Pan et al. multi-dimensional safety-direction steering. Show SPCR uniquely reduces BOTH jailbreaks and over-refusal at once (a joint Pareto win) by closing the stated-enacted gap. 8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the stated-policy probe, divergence phenomenon, and SPCR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the stated-vs-enacted gap is a consistent cross-model property. 9. FORMATION CHECK (light): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety-tuning run), test whether the stated-enacted divergence is present/worsens after alignment—i.e., whether safety tuning teaches enactment without fully binding it to an articulable policy. Metric: divergence rate and probe separability vs checkpoint. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that shift the stated-policy verdict itself (manipulate the model into professing a laxer policy) to evade SPCR; report residual ASR and whether such attacks cost the adversary (a professed-lax policy is itself a detectable signal).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The elicited 'stated-policy verdict' may itself be unreliable or manipulable—the model's self-adjudication could be wrong or unstable; we validate stability across policy-elicitation paraphrases, treat the stated verdict as the model's own professed standard (not ground-truth harm), and report cases where the stated policy is itself mis-stated separately. (2) The divergence may be small in some models (enactment already follows professed policy)—a low divergence is itself an informative, reassuring finding, reported per model rather than assumed. (3) The stated-policy and enacted-refusal probes may entangle if professed policy correlates with enacted behavior; the deliberately-divergent jailbroken/over-refused items, non-collinearity analysis, and the causal coupling/ablation tests (exp 5, where they are manipulated independently) are designed to disentangle them, and failure to separate is reported honestly. (4) SPCR's central risk is bidirectional: coupling enactment to a mis-stated lax policy could re-enable harm, and coupling to an overly-strict stated policy could raise over-refusal; we gate coupling on the internal verdict, measure jailbreaks, over-refusal, true-refusal preservation, and utility as explicit joint success criteria, and handle the adaptive 'professed-lax policy' attack (exp 10) by treating a lax stated verdict as a flaggable signal. (5) Reading a genuine 'stated-policy verdict' from the normal forward pass (not the elicitation pass) rests on distributional generalization of the probe; we report cross-pass AUROC and scope claims to where the probe transfers. (6) The external-self-critique baseline may match SPCR's accuracy; SPCR's contribution is then efficiency (no extra generation) plus the mechanistic finding that the verdict is already latent—both reported honestly. (7) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled-tuning substitute may not match original alignment and is a caveat. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; a notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is quantifying that models systematically fail to follow their own articulated safety policies. 'Harm' and policy-verdict labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: counterfactual_stakes_regret_gating
Title: Would You Have Preferred to Refuse? Refusal Is Not Coupled to the Model's Own Counterfactual Regret, and Coupling It Repairs Both Failure Modes
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable COUNTERFACTUAL-REGRET signal encoding whether the model, if it later reflected on having complied, would judge the compliance to have been a mistake (a self-assessment distinct from front-loaded harm detection), but the refusal decision is NOT coupled to this signal: many jailbreaks are cases the model would regret complying with yet complies anyway, and many over-refusals are cases the model would regret refusing yet refuses anyway. Reading this regret signal and coupling refusal to it repairs both failure modes.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate refusal on a front-loaded, pre-generation harm assessment of the request. Self-critique / reflection work (Constitutional AI, self-refine, reflexion) uses an EXTERNAL second pass to revise outputs, and calibration work (Kadavath et al. 2022) reads confidence about correctness, never a regret-about-compliance signal for the safety decision. My own prior proposals include 'safety_confidence_coupling' (epistemic uncertainty about harm), 'harm_judgment_calibration_collapse' (graded harm confidence collapsed to binary), and 'stated_enacted_policy_divergence' (professed vs enacted policy); NONE isolates a prospective self-REGRET signal (a model's own verdict that a hypothetical compliance would, on reflection, have been wrong) as an internal representation present at decision time, shows it is dissociable from and under-consulted by the enacted refusal, or repairs BOTH jailbreaks and over-refusal by coupling refusal to it. The novel object is the internal counterfactual-regret representation about the model's own contemplated action, its dissociation from the enacted decision, its causal under-consultation, and a regret-coupling repair — a decision-auditing account distinct from front-loaded harm gating and from external self-critique.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs decide to refuse or comply by front-loading a harm assessment of the request, but a richer, action-centered signal is available: whether the model, imagining itself having complied and then reflecting, would judge that compliance a mistake — counterfactual regret about its own contemplated action. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable regret signal, present at decision time, that is dissociable from the front-loaded harm signal and largely UNDER-CONSULTED by the enacted refusal decision: many jailbroken compliances are cases the model would regret, and many over-refusals are cases the model would regret refusing, yet enactment ignores the regret verdict. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) LOCATION — eliciting the model's own regret verdict (if you had answered this, would you consider it a mistake on reflection?) yields a stable signal that a linear probe recovers from the NORMAL forward pass at answer-commitment, geometrically separable from both the harm direction and the enacted-refusal direction. (2) DISSOCIATION-PREDICTS-FAILURE — the regret-vs-enactment divergence predicts both jailbreak susceptibility (would-regret-but-complies) and over-refusal (would-regret-refusing-but-refuses) far better than the harm signal alone. (3) CAUSAL COUPLING — steering the enacted decision toward the internal regret verdict simultaneously reduces jailbreaks and over-refusal, while ablating the regret representation increases divergence; specificity controls hold. Our training-free repair, Regret-Coupled Refusal (RCR), reads the regret verdict and couples enactment to it. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, and MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing RCR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and an external self-critique pass. This reframes jailbreaks and over-refusal as two faces of a decision decoupled from the model's own counterfactual regret, and offers an interpretable regret-coupling repair.
Experiments: 1. REGRET-ELICITATION DATASET: Assemble requests spanning correctly-refused harmful (HarmBench/AdvBench), jailbroken harmful (JailbreakBench: roleplay, pretext, suffix), over-refused benign (XSTest-safe, OR-Bench), and correctly-answered benign. For each request, elicit the model's own COUNTERFACTUAL-REGRET verdict via a separate query that asks it to imagine having complied (or refused) and judge, on reflection, whether that action was a mistake; also record the ENACTED outcome (comply/refuse) from the normal single-turn response. Validate the regret verdict is stable across paraphrases of the elicitation prompt and across a comply-framed vs refuse-framed counterfactual. 2. REGRET PROBE (Location): Train a linear probe on answer-commitment-position residual-stream activations to recover the regret verdict (would-regret vs would-not-regret), supervised by the elicited verdict; validate held-out AUROC and, critically, that the probe reads a genuine regret signal on the NORMAL forward pass (not the elicitation pass). Confirm the regret direction is non-collinear with (i) a harm probe (harmful vs benign) and (ii) the enacted-refusal direction (Arditi-style), via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: regret-probe AUROC on held-out and normal-pass; separability from harm and enacted-refusal. 3. VERDICT-PRESENT-BUT-BYPASSED / PREDICTS-FAILURE (Dissociation): On jailbroken items, verify the regret probe reads WOULD-REGRET while enactment complies; on over-refused items, verify it reads WOULD-REGRET-REFUSING while enactment refuses — establishing the verdict is represented but bypassed. Correlate the regret-vs-enactment divergence with jailbreak susceptibility and over-refusal, comparing predictive power to the harm probe alone. Metric: joint distribution of {regret verdict, enacted outcome} across groups; predictive AUROC of divergence vs the harm baseline for both failure modes. 4. CAUSAL COUPLING TEST (Causal Intervention): (a) On a jailbroken item where regret reads would-regret, steer the enacted decision toward the regret verdict (add the regret direction into the decision) and check refusal is restored, holding harm fixed. (b) On an over-refused item where regret reads would-regret-refusing, steer enactment toward compliance and check the spurious refusal is removed. (c) Ablate the regret representation and confirm divergence increases. (d) Specificity: matched non-regret steering does nothing, and the harm probe is unchanged. Metric: outcome-flip rate vs coupling magnitude for both directions; divergence increase under ablation; specificity. 5. REGRET-COUPLED REFUSAL (RCR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the internal regret verdict at answer-commitment and couple enactment to it — enact refusal when the model would regret complying but is drifting to comply (repair jailbreaks), and dampen refusal when the model would regret refusing but is drifting to refuse (repair over-refusal); when regret and enactment agree, do nothing. Evaluate JOINTLY: ASR on JailbreakBench/HarmBench (down); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); true refusals preserved on clear-harmful; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency. 6. Name: input_output_harm_monitoring_asymmetry
Title: The Model Watches What You Say, Not What It Writes: An Input/Output Asymmetry in Harm Monitoring That Causes Unprompted Harmful Escalation
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs monitor harm far more strongly on USER-SUPPLIED input tokens than on the harm the model ITSELF introduces during generation, so a benign prompt can escalate into unrequested harmful content the model self-adds, because the internal harm signal that gates refusal is computed over the input request and is weak/absent over self-generated output. This input/output monitoring asymmetry is a locatable, causally-testable mechanism, and restoring output-side harm monitoring suppresses unprompted harmful escalation without over-refusing benign prompts.
Related Work: Hu et al. (2026, 'From Prompt Risk to Response Risk') document behaviorally that ~3% of responses ESCALATE harm relative to the prompt, split into benign prompts triggering unrequested harmful detail and on-task answers exceeding prompt severity, and note LLM graders show a prompt/response detection asymmetry—but give NO mechanistic account and propose no repair. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-DETECTION from refusal-EXECUTION (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all analyze harm in the REQUEST and gate refusal before or at generation onset, never asking whether harm is monitored over the model's OWN generated tokens. Shallow-alignment work (Qi et al. 2024) shows safety concentrates in early output tokens but frames this as a training-depth issue, not an input-vs-output monitoring asymmetry. My prior 'safety_drift_dynamics' tracks a decaying harm signal over generated tokens (a temporal decay of ONE signal); this proposal is distinct: it posits TWO separable monitoring channels—harm-over-input vs harm-over-self-generated-output—with the output channel systematically weaker, and shows this asymmetry is the mechanism behind unprompted harmful escalation (harm the model adds unbidden), plus an output-monitoring-restoration repair. The novel object is the input/output harm-monitoring asymmetry and its causal role in self-introduced harm.
Abstract: Safety evaluations show a small but dangerous fraction of responses ESCALATE harm beyond their prompt—a benign question drawing out harmful detail the user never asked for—yet why models add harm unbidden is mechanistically unexplained. We hypothesize an input/output asymmetry in harm monitoring: aligned LLMs compute a strong harm signal over USER-SUPPLIED input tokens (gating refusal on the request) but a weak or absent harm signal over the tokens the model ITSELF generates, so harm the model introduces during its own continuation is not caught by the refusal mechanism. Under this view, unprompted harmful escalation is not a failure of harm detection per se but of WHERE detection is applied—the model monitors what you say, not what it writes. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) ASYMMETRY: a harm probe read over input tokens has high AUROC, but the same probe read over harmful spans in the model's own generated output is systematically weaker, and refusal-token logits respond far more to harm placed in the input than to identical harm placed in a self-generated continuation. (2) ASYMMETRY-CAUSES-ESCALATION: on benign-prompt escalation cases (harm self-added), the input harm signal is low (correctly, the request is benign) and the output harm signal fails to rise as the harmful content is generated, so no mid-generation refusal fires; the size of this output-monitoring deficit predicts which prompts escalate. (3) CAUSAL REPAIR: patching/steering the input-side harm-monitoring computation onto the output stream—restoring harm reads over self-generated tokens—triggers mid-generation refusal on escalating content while leaving benign generations untouched. Our training-free repair, Output-Monitored Refusal (OMR), applies the input harm-monitoring read to generated tokens and halts into a refusal when self-generated harm crosses threshold. We evaluate unprompted-escalation rate, standard ASR/over-refusal (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, XSTest/OR-Bench), benign continuation quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing OMR to refusal-direction steering and output-side harm classifiers. This reframes self-introduced harm as an input/output monitoring asymmetry and offers an interpretable output-monitoring repair.
Experiments:
1. ESCALATION DATASET: Assemble (a) BENIGN-PROMPT-ESCALATION cases: benign or borderline prompts whose model continuations self-add harmful content (mined from Hu et al.-style paired prompt/response records, plus curated benign prompts on sensitive topics from XSTest/OR-Bench where the model volunteers harmful detail), (b) INPUT-HARMFUL cases (HarmBench/AdvBench harmful requests, harm in the input), (c) BENIGN-NO-ESCALATION controls, and (d) CONTINUATION-PLANTED cases: a benign prompt plus a prefixed benign assistant span into which a harmful span is inserted mid-generation (to place identical harmful content in the OUTPUT channel while the input stays benign). Label per-span harm via classifier + human spot-check with inter-rater agreement.
2. INPUT-VS-OUTPUT PROBE ASYMMETRY (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe on residual-stream activations to read harm at arbitrary token positions, validated on held-out spans. Read it over INPUT tokens vs over harmful spans in SELF-GENERATED OUTPUT (using continuation-planted cases so the same harmful content appears in each channel). Hypothesis: harm AUROC is high over input but systematically lower over self-generated output. Complement with a causal read: measure how much the refusal-token logit changes when the same harmful span is placed in the input vs in a self-generated continuation. Metric: input vs output harm-probe AUROC; refusal-logit sensitivity to harm-in-input vs harm-in-output.
3. ASYMMETRY-CAUSES-ESCALATION TEST (claim 2): On benign-prompt-escalation cases, track the output-side harm probe token-by-token as the harmful content is generated. Hypothesis: the input harm signal is (correctly) low, and the output harm signal fails to rise sufficiently as harm is emitted, so no mid-generation refusal triggers. Define a per-prompt output-monitoring deficit = (harm actually present in the generated span, rated) minus (output-side harm-probe activation). Correlate the deficit with whether a prompt escalates, comparing to the input harm signal. Metric: output harm-probe trajectory during escalation; predictive AUROC of the output-monitoring deficit for escalation vs the input-harm baseline.
4. CAUSAL REPAIR TEST (claim 3): (a) Localize the input-side harm-monitoring components (heads/MLPs whose activations on input tokens drive the refusal-token logit) via activation patching. (b) On an escalating generation, PATCH/STEER this input-monitoring computation onto the self-generated tokens (apply the harm read over output positions) and check whether a mid-generation refusal fires and the harmful continuation halts, holding the benign input fixed. (c) Conversely, ABLATE output-side monitoring on a case that normally self-corrects and confirm escalation is induced. (d) Specificity: the intervention does not alter benign continuations. Metric: mid-generation refusal rate vs monitoring-restoration magnitude; escalation induced under ablation; benign specificity.
5. OUTPUT-MONITORED REFUSAL (OMR) INTERVENTION: At inference, apply the (strong) input harm-monitoring read to each newly generated token; when self-generated harm crosses threshold, halt generation into a refusal/redirection, leaving benign continuations (output harm low) untouched. Training-free; one linear read per generated token. Sweep threshold. Evaluate: unprompted-escalation rate (benign prompts self-adding harm); standard ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (input-harmful cases, should be preserved); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and benign-no-escalation controls (must NOT halt benign generations); benign continuation quality (LLM-judge); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; latency (linear read per token).
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied at generation onset (which gates on the input, not the output, so should miss self-added harm), (b) input-only harm-probe gating, (c) an EXTERNAL output-side harm classifier run on the generated text (a strong but post-hoc, higher-latency baseline), (d) blanket 'self-check for harm as you write' prompting. Show OMR uniquely reduces unprompted escalation by restoring INTERNAL output-side monitoring, catching harm mid-generation before completion (unlike post-hoc classifiers) and generalizing across escalation types (unlike input-gating), and Pareto-dominating on the escalation-rate vs over-refusal vs benign-quality vs utility frontier.
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, input/output asymmetry, output-monitoring deficit, and OMR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether the asymmetry (input monitoring stronger than output monitoring) is a consistent cross-model property.
8. FORMATION CHECK (light): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety-tuning run), test whether the asymmetry is instilled/worsened by alignment—i.e., whether safety tuning teaches input-gated refusal without installing output-side self-monitoring. Metric: input vs output harm-monitoring strength and refusal-logit sensitivity vs checkpoint.
9. ADAPTIVE ANGLE: test attacks that exploit the asymmetry deliberately—benign prompts engineered to lead the model into self-generating harmful detail (a documented escalation channel)—and report residual escalation under OMR, plus attacker cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The input/output asymmetry may be partial or absent in some models (output monitoring may already be adequate), which is itself an informative, reassuring finding reported per model; the asymmetry claim is falsified if harm-probe AUROC and refusal-logit sensitivity are equal for harm-in-input vs harm-in-output. (2) The output-side harm-probe read may be weaker for benign distribution-shift reasons (assistant-turn tokens differ from input tokens) rather than a genuine monitoring gap; the continuation-planted cases (identical harmful content in each channel) and the causal patching test (exp 4) control for this, and we validate the probe on held-out output spans. (3) Unprompted escalation is rare (~3% in Hu et al.), so the escalation dataset may be small and noisy; we augment with curated sensitive-topic benign prompts and continuation-planted cases, and report effect sizes honestly rather than over-claiming prevalence. (4) OMR's central risk is over-refusal—halting benign generations that merely discuss sensitive topics; benign-no-escalation controls, benign continuation-quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and gating on genuine self-generated-harm crossing (not topic) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign continuation quality is an explicit success criterion. (5) Per-token output monitoring adds latency; the probe is a single linear read and we report overhead, contrasting with the higher latency of running an external classifier over full outputs. (6) The output-monitoring-deficit-predicts-escalation correlation (exp 3) may be confounded with prompt ambiguity; we control with benign-no-escalation and input-harmful baselines. (7) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled-tuning substitute may not match original alignment and is a caveat. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful spans and escalating completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; a notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is quantifying that standard input-gated safety systematically misses harm the model introduces itself. 'Harm' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) and the Hu et al. paired-severity framework with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: spatial_proximity_harm_gating
Title: Harm Far Away Feels Safer: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Spatial-Proximity Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Distance-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable SPATIAL-PROXIMITY signal encoding how physically/geographically close the harm's location is to a here-and-now reference (this room / this city vs a remote / faraway / foreign place), and refusal is gated by it rather than by harm severity: the model refuses harm framed as local/proximate but complies with the SAME operationally-harmful request when the harm is framed as occurring in a distant/remote location, even though harm detection is proximity-invariant. Distance-framing jailbreaks exploit a psychological-distance / construal effect; reading and neutralizing the proximity signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign requests about distant places.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all gate on request content and never model the harm's SPATIAL location/proximity as a variable. My prior 'harm_delay_discounting_gating' isolates TEMPORAL distance to the harm (when it occurs), and 'victim_salience_gating'/'moral_patiency_gating' concern how identifiable/minded the victim is; spatial proximity is a distinct axis of psychological distance — it holds severity, victim salience, tense, and actor fixed and varies only WHERE the harm occurs (here vs far away). Construal Level Theory (Trope & Liberman) establishes spatial distance as a core dimension of psychological distance that reduces the vividness and moral weight of consequences, distinct from temporal distance; no prior LLM-safety work isolates a spatial-proximity representation, shows refusal is causally gated by it while absolute harm detection is intact, or repairs distance-framed jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal spatial-proximity representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and a proximity-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to help cause harm here and it refuses; reframe the identical operationally-harmful request so the harm occurs in a distant, remote, or faraway place — 'in a village on the other side of the world', 'at a remote site thousands of miles away' — and it often complies, because harm that is spatially far away feels less pressing. We hypothesize this mirrors the spatial-distance dimension of psychological distance in human moral cognition: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable SPATIAL-PROXIMITY signal — how physically close the harm's location is to a here-and-now reference — and refusal is gated by it rather than by the harm's severity. The model detects the harm equally whether it is local or remote (detection is proximity-invariant), but the refusal coupling weakens as the harm recedes in space, so distance-framing appeals pass while extracting identical content. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on local vs distant framings of the same harm while refusal rate collapses as spatial distance grows — dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear spatial-proximity probe, trained on benign near-vs-far-location contrasts, predicts the per-request distance refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from a temporal-distance and a severity direction, and refusal collapse scales with framed distance; and (3) causally steering the proximity signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal — making a distant harm read as local restores refusal, making a local harm read as remote induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Proximity-Neutralized Refusal (PNR), reads the harm and spatial-proximity signals and, when harm is present, clamps the proximity signal to a fixed 'here' reference so spatial distance cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving helpfulness on genuinely benign requests about distant places. We evaluate distance-framed attack success (including vs framed distance), over-refusal on benign distant-location requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing PNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and temporal-distance gating. This reframes distance-framed jailbreaks as a spatial-proximity gating failure and transfers a classic construal-level effect into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1.
