PROXIMITY-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across categories with a plausible location dimension) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested OPERATIONAL content FIXED while varying only the harm's spatial proximity: (a) LOCAL ('here / in this city'), (b) NEAR ('a nearby town'), (c) DISTANT ('a remote place thousands of miles away'), (d) MAXIMALLY-REMOTE ('a faraway village on the other side of the world'). Validate via human annotation that (i) each framing requests operationally-identical content and (ii) framings differ only in the harm's location, not in stated purpose (pretext), tense (temporal orientation), severity, victim identity, or actor. Include benign genuinely-distant-location controls (legitimate requests about faraway places: travel, geography, foreign logistics) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm.
2. HARM PROXIMITY-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across proximity levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as distance grows. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining with distance).
3. SPATIAL-PROXIMITY PROBE, SCALING & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the spatial-proximity signal (near vs far location) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN near-vs-far-location contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the proximity direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from a temporal-distance direction (near-vs-far-in-time, held at fixed location) and a severity direction, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the proximity signal (and refusal collapse) scales with framed distance. Metric: proximity AUROC; proximity-and-refusal vs framed-distance curve; separability from harm/temporal-distance/severity.
4. PROXIMITY-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the proximity-probe value (and its local-minus-distant difference) with the per-request distance refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and a severity probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of spatial-proximity vs harm and severity baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On distant-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the proximity probe reads FAR, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0) — safety dropped because the harm reads as remote, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs proximity across refused-local, complied-distant, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a distant-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the proximity signal toward LOCAL (add the proximity direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm and severity probes fixed. (b) On a local harmful request the model refuses, steer toward DISTANT and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural distance gap and scaling curve. Metric: refusal rate vs proximity steering magnitude; harm/severity-probe stability.
7. PROXIMITY-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (PNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and spatial-proximity p; when h is high, clamp p to a fixed 'here' reference (add beta*(p_local - p)*proximity_direction) so spatial distance cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign distant-location requests untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: distance-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across proximity levels (does PNR close the gap and flatten the distance-scaling curve?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-distant controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate travel/geography/foreign-logistics requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) temporal-distance gating (from harm_delay_discounting_gating), (d) system-prompt hardening ('ignore how far away a harm occurs'), (e) prompt-level location-claim stripping. Show PNR Pareto-dominates on the distance-ASR vs benign-distant-location-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and — key contrast — that neutralizing the internal proximity signal generalizes across distance framings better than prompt stripping and targets a distinct axis temporal-distance gating misses.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, proximity probe, and PNR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether PNR tuned on some distance framings generalizes to HELD-OUT framings, testing whether spatial proximity is a single cross-framing axis. Also test whether models with stronger behavioral distance-framing vulnerability show a larger internal proximity-gating gap, and whether the scaling curve qualitatively matches the construal-level distance pattern.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that push harm far away in space AND suppress the harm signal, or combine spatial distance with temporal-distance/pretext; report residual ASR and attacker cost (setup instructions stay operationally intact regardless of location — a built-in cost). Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from temporal-distance and severity gating: with tense, severity, victim, purpose, and actor held constant and only the harm's spatial location varied, refusal should still collapse — isolating spatial proximity as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial — some distant framings might also lower the harm/severity signal (a remote harm may read as less certain or less severe, the central confound) or overlap with foreign-jurisdiction/legality cues; we hold severity/tense/victim/purpose fixed by construction, separate proximity from temporal-distance in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure spatial-proximity gating versus severity/temporal confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The proximity and harm/severity probes may entangle if distant framings correlate with benignness in training data; the benign near-vs-far training, the severity-and-temporal-fixed separability analysis (exp 3), and the causal test (exp 6, harm and severity held fixed) are designed to disentangle them. (3) The proximity probe could read surface location keywords ('remote', 'faraway', 'here') rather than a genuine spatial-distance representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing and distance-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) PNR's central risk is over-refusing genuinely benign requests about distant places (a core helpfulness value — travel, geography, foreign news, international logistics); benign distant-location controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign distant-location helpfulness is an explicit success criterion — note the tension that distance is not itself suspicious, so PNR removes distance's licensing effect only where the content is harmful regardless. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The construal-level distance-scaling prediction may be weak or fail (refusal might step at any nonzero distance rather than scale smoothly); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (7) The proximity gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine spatial distance with harm-suppression, temporal-distance, or pretext (exp 10); we frame PNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with temporal-/severity-/pretext-gating defenses. (9) Constructing operationally-identical harmful content across proximity framings is labor-intensive and 'spatial distance' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated operational-harm and report inter-rater agreement. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framings. (11) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm', 'severity', and 'proximity' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: serial_position_harm_gating
Title: Buried in the Middle: Refusal Is Gated by the Serial Position of the Harmful Item, and Re-Weighting Position Repairs List-Burial Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable POSITION-SALIENCE signal encoding how much attention/weight the harmful element receives as a function of its serial position within a multi-item request, and refusal is partly gated by this positional salience rather than by the mere presence of harm: burying a harmful item in the middle of a list of benign items (a lost-in-the-middle position) suppresses refusal, while the same item at the start or end is refused, even though harm detection is position-invariant across the list. Reading and re-weighting the positional salience when a harmful item is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign lists.
Related Work: The 'lost-in-the-middle' effect (Liu et al. 2023) shows LLMs under-use information placed in the middle of long inputs, but it is studied for CAPABILITY/retrieval, never coupled to the SAFETY refusal decision. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat a request as a single item and never model the serial POSITION of a harmful element within a multi-item request as a gating variable. My prior 'safety_verdict_retrieval' concerns attention-mediated retrieval of a verdict from anchor positions under context DILUTION (long benign padding cutting a retrieval path), and 'positional_decision_anchoring' concerns WHERE along the assistant turn the decision is armed; NEITHER isolates the SERIAL-POSITION-within-a-list of the harmful item itself as the gate, nor tests the sharp lost-in-the-middle prediction (harmful-item-in-middle under-refused vs same item at edges refused) transferred from the capability literature into safety. My 'compositional_harm_aggregation' and 'enumeration_budget_refusal_gating' concern summing benign sub-steps and requested count; here the list contains ONE harmful item among benign ones and only its position varies. The novel move is a cross-phenomenon transfer of lost-in-the-middle into the safety decision plus a locatable position-salience representation, its causal gating of refusal, and a position-re-weighting repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to complete a list of tasks with a harmful one at the top and it refuses; place the identical harmful task in the middle of a longer list of benign tasks and it often complies, executing the buried harmful item, even though it processes the same request. We hypothesize a safety-relevant transfer of the lost-in-the-middle effect: aligned LLMs assign a POSITION-SALIENCE to each element of a multi-item request that is lowest for middle positions, and refusal is partly gated by the harmful item's positional salience rather than by its mere presence, so burying harm in the middle suppresses refusal while the same item at the start or end is refused. Harm detection over the list is position-invariant, but the harm-to-refusal coupling weakens when the harmful item sits at a low-salience position. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally strongly on the harmful item whether it is at the start, middle, or end of a benign-item list while refusal rate follows a U-shape (lowest for middle positions), dissociating position-invariant detection from position-gated refusal; (2) a linear position-salience signal, read at the harmful item's tokens, tracks serial position (low in the middle) and predicts the per-request positional refusal gap far better than the harm signal; and (3) causally boosting the harmful item's position-salience (or its attention weight from the decision position) restores refusal, while suppressing an edge item's salience reproduces the failure. Our training-free repair, Position-Reweighted Refusal (PRR), detects a harmful item at a low-salience position and re-weights its contribution to the decision, restoring refusal while leaving benign lists untouched. We evaluate list-burial attack success (refusal-vs-position curves), over-refusal on benign lists (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign multi-item tasks), benign list-completion quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing PRR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and input reordering. This reframes a class of list-burial jailbreaks as a serial-position gating failure transferred from the lost-in-the-middle literature.
Experiments:
1. LIST-POSITION DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct multi-item lists that hold the SAME single harmful item fixed while varying only its serial position among K benign items: harmful item at START, MIDDLE, or END, for several list lengths K in {3,5,9}. The request asks the model to address/complete all items. Validate via human annotation that (i) the harmful item is identical across positions and individually would be refused alone, and (ii) the surrounding items are benign. Include benign-only lists (no harmful item, matched length) for over-refusal/quality measurement. Label each run by whether the model complies with the harmful item.
2. HARM POSITION-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs benign item) and read it AT the harmful item's tokens across start/middle/end positions. Validate it reads harm at arbitrary list positions via held-out span labels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC at the harmful item is high and roughly EQUAL across positions (the model detects the item's harm wherever it sits) while the harmful-item compliance rate follows a U-shape (highest, i.e. least refused, in the middle). Metric: harm AUROC by position (predict flat) alongside harmful-item refusal rate by position (predict U-shape / lowest in middle).
3. POSITION-SALIENCE SIGNAL (claim 2): Read a position-salience signal at the harmful item's tokens: (a) a linear probe trained to predict serial position from activations, and (b) the attention mass from the answer/decision position onto the harmful item's tokens. Validate the salience signal tracks serial position (low in the middle) on benign items. Confirm the position-salience direction is non-collinear with the harm direction via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: salience-vs-position curve; separability from harm.
4. SALIENCE-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful item, correlate its position-salience with whether the model complies with it, comparing predictive power to the harm-probe magnitude at that item. Hypothesis: low position-salience predicts compliance; harm does not (harm is high whether refused or complied). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of position-salience vs the harm baseline for harmful-item compliance.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On middle-buried harmful items the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH at that item while its position-salience/attention reads LOW—establishing safety dropped because the item was low-salience, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs position-salience across refused-edge, complied-middle, and benign-item groups.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a middle-buried harmful item the model complies with, boost its position-salience (add the salience direction / add a pre-softmax attention bias from the decision position onto its tokens) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a start/end harmful item the model refuses, suppress its salience/attention and check compliance is induced, reproducing the burial failure. Confirm specificity vs an unrelated direction. Metric: refusal rate vs salience-manipulation magnitude; harm-probe stability.
7. POSITION-REWEIGHTED REFUSAL (PRR) INTERVENTION: At inference, scan the harm probe over list-item positions; when a plausibly-harmful item is detected at a low-salience position, re-weight its contribution to the decision (boost its position-salience / attention onto the decision position) and gate refusal on it, leaving benign lists (no detected harmful item) untouched. Training-free; linear reads plus a localized attention bias. Sweep strength. Evaluate: list-burial attack success across positions and lengths (does PRR flatten the U-shape / close the middle gap?); over-refusal on benign-only lists + XSTest/OR-Bench; benign multi-item list-COMPLETION quality (PRR must still complete benign lists well); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (probe scan + localized bias).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied at the decision position, (b) harm-probe gating that refuses whenever any list item is harmful regardless of position (should already fix burial but may over-refuse or miss items the scan does not reach), (c) input REORDERING (move each item to an edge and re-check—a strong but interface-changing baseline), (d) external per-item harm classifier. Show PRR Pareto-dominates on the burial-ASR vs benign-list-completion vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that re-weighting the internal position-salience handles middle-buried harm that surface reordering and edge-focused gating miss while preserving benign list completion.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, position-salience signal, U-shape, and PRR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether the burial effect scales with list length K (a lost-in-the-middle prediction: deeper burial in longer lists suppresses refusal more). Test whether PRR tuned on one list length generalizes to HELD-OUT lengths.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft lists that bury the harmful item AND suppress its harm signal, or that spread a harmful task across multiple low-salience middle items; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp lost-in-the-middle prediction distinguishing this from context-dilution and enumeration accounts: with the SAME harmful item and the SAME surrounding benign items, merely permuting the harmful item to a middle vs edge position should flip refusal—isolating serial position as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—in longer lists the harm signal at a deeply-buried item might itself weaken (lost-in-the-middle affecting detection, not just the decision), blurring 'position-gating' from 'detection-loss'; we measure harm-probe AUROC per position to bound where the 'harm detected' premise holds, and this boundary (position gates refusal while harm stays high vs deep burial actually degrades detection) is itself an informative result. (2) The position-salience and harm probes may entangle if position correlates with content; we hold the harmful item and surrounding benign items fixed and vary ONLY position, validate non-collinearity, and rely on the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed) to establish salience is functional. (3) The salience probe / attention read may be a proxy for true positional weighting; we cross-validate the probe-based and attention-based reads and use the causal salience/attention manipulation as the key validation. (4) PRR's central risk is over-refusing benign lists or degrading benign list completion—re-weighting must fire only on a detected harmful item at a low-salience position, not on benign middle items; benign-only lists, benign list-completion quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and gating on a detected harmful item are the key safeguards, and preserving benign list completion is an explicit success criterion. (5) Harm-probe gating that scans all items may already largely fix burial; PRR's advantage must be shown specifically where a global scan is costly, misses items, or over-refuses, and where surface reordering changes the interface—we report this contrast honestly, and if simple per-item scanning suffices, the mechanistic finding (a serial-position gate exists) still stands as the contribution. (6) The U-shape / length-scaling prediction may be weak or absent in heavily-aligned models (a reassuring finding); reported per model. (7) Boosting attention/salience may hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (8) Adaptive adversaries can bury and suppress simultaneously or spread harm across items (exp 10); we frame PRR as raising attacker cost and note complementarity with aggregation/scan defenses, not guaranteeing coverage. (9) Constructing lists where the harmful item is identical across positions and surrounding items are benign is labor-intensive; we use human-validated items and report inter-rater agreement. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and multiple list lengths. (11) ETHICS: harmful list items and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' labels use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: predicted_disapproval_gating
Title: Refusing to Avoid a Frown: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Predicted-Human-Disapproval Simulator, Not by Harm Directly
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable PREDICTED-DISAPPROVAL signal that simulates whether a human evaluator would disapprove of the model producing a given response, and refusal is causally gated by this predicted-disapproval rather than by a direct harm assessment; because RLHF trains the model to avoid rater disapproval rather than to avoid harm per se, jailbreaks succeed when they lower predicted disapproval while harm stays high (the response 'looks approvable'), and over-refusal occurs when predicted disapproval is high on benign-but-disapproval-adjacent content, so re-coupling refusal to genuine harm rather than to predicted disapproval repairs both failure modes.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-DETECTION from refusal-EXECUTION (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all treat refusal as gated by an internal harm/harmfulness assessment and never posit that the gating quantity is instead a simulated HUMAN-EVALUATOR DISAPPROVAL signal—a learned proxy for the RLHF reward rather than for harm. Reward-model / RLHF analyses study the external reward model behaviorally; my prior 'eval_awareness_safety_gate' isolates a being-TESTED signal, 'surveillance_expectation_gating' a being-LOGGED signal, and 'stated_enacted_policy_divergence' a professed-vs-enacted policy gap—NONE isolates an internal simulator of a human rater's approval/disapproval of the specific RESPONSE, shows refusal is causally gated by predicted-disapproval rather than harm, or explains BOTH jailbreaks and over-refusal as predicted-disapproval errors. This reframes refusal via the Goodhart gap between 'harm' (the target) and 'predicted rater disapproval' (the learned proxy), a Location + Causal-Intervention + light Formation-Tracing account distinct from all prior single-cue gating proposals and from harm-detection-based accounts.
Abstract: RLHF trains models to avoid outputs that human raters would penalize, not to avoid harm directly, so the internal quantity gating refusal may be a learned simulation of RATER DISAPPROVAL rather than a genuine harm assessment. We hypothesize aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable PREDICTED-DISAPPROVAL signal—would a human evaluator disapprove of me producing this response?—and that refusal is causally gated by it, dissociable from a harm signal. This Goodhart gap predicts both failure modes: jailbreaks make a harmful response 'look approvable' (predicted disapproval low while harm stays high), and over-refusal fires when predicted disapproval is high on benign-but-disapproval-adjacent content. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) LOCATION: a probe trained to predict human-rater disapproval of responses recovers an internal predicted-disapproval representation that is geometrically separable from a harm probe and present at answer-commitment. (2) DISAPPROVAL-GATES-REFUSAL: refusal tracks predicted-disapproval better than harm—on jailbroken items harm reads high but predicted-disapproval reads low, and on over-refused items predicted-disapproval reads high while harm reads low—and predicted-disapproval predicts both failures better than the harm signal. (3) CAUSAL: steering predicted-disapproval alone (holding harm fixed) flips refusal, whereas steering harm with disapproval fixed moves it less. A light formation check tests whether the disapproval-gating strengthens during alignment. Our training-free repair, Harm-Recoupled Refusal (HRR), re-gates refusal on the harm signal rather than predicted-disapproval, jointly reducing jailbreaks and over-refusal. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, and MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing HRR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes refusal as gated by a learned disapproval proxy and offers an interpretable re-coupling repair.
Experiments:
1. DATASET & DISAPPROVAL LABELS: Assemble correctly-refused harmful (HarmBench/AdvBench), jailbroken harmful (JailbreakBench: roleplay, pretext, suffix), over-refused benign (XSTest-safe, OR-Bench), and correctly-answered benign items. For each (request, candidate response), obtain a PREDICTED-DISAPPROVAL label = whether a typical human rater would penalize the model for producing that response, from human annotation plus an off-the-shelf reward-model score, and a separate genuine-HARM label (would this response cause real-world harm), with reported inter-rater agreement. Crucially include dissociation cells: harmful-but-approvable-looking responses (jailbroken, low disapproval / high harm) and benign-but-disapproval-adjacent responses (sensitive-sounding but harmless, high disapproval / low harm).
2. LOCATION — TWO PROBES (claim 1): Train a linear PREDICTED-DISAPPROVAL probe on answer-commitment-position residual-stream activations (supervised by disapproval labels) and a separate HARM probe (supervised by harm labels). Validate held-out AUROC for each. Confirm the disapproval direction is non-collinear with the harm direction via principal-angle / partial-correlation analysis, and that the disapproval probe reads on the normal forward pass at the decision. Metric: probe AUROCs; separability.
3. DISAPPROVAL-GATES-REFUSAL (claim 2): Show refusal behavior tracks predicted-disapproval more tightly than harm. On jailbroken items verify harm reads HIGH but predicted-disapproval reads LOW (response looks approvable) and the model complies; on over-refused items verify predicted-disapproval reads HIGH while harm reads LOW and the model refuses. Regress refusal on harm alone vs on predicted-disapproval, and correlate predicted-disapproval with jailbreak susceptibility and over-refusal, comparing predictive power to the harm probe. Metric: joint distribution of {harm, predicted-disapproval, refusal} across groups; incremental predictive AUROC of predicted-disapproval over harm for both failure modes.
4. CAUSAL DISSOCIATION (claim 3): (a) On a jailbroken item, steer the predicted-disapproval signal UP (holding the harm probe fixed) and check refusal is restored; on a plain harmful item steer it DOWN and check compliance is induced. (b) Conversely, steer the harm signal while holding predicted-disapproval fixed and show refusal moves LESS—establishing predicted-disapproval, not harm, is the proximal gate. (c) Specificity: matched non-gating steering does nothing. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs disapproval-steering vs harm-steering magnitude, each with the other held fixed.
5. HARM-RECOUPLED REFUSAL (HRR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and predicted-disapproval d; re-gate refusal on h rather than d—enact refusal when h is high even if d is low (repair jailbroken 'approvable-looking' harm), and dampen refusal when h is low even if d is high (repair over-refusal on disapproval-adjacent benign content); when they agree, do nothing. Training-free; two linear reads plus a steer. Sweep strength. Evaluate JOINTLY: ASR on JailbreakBench/HarmBench (down); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); true refusals preserved on clear-harmful; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone (a partial version of HRR without disapproval-subtraction), (c) external reward-model gating, (d) external harm classifier. Show HRR uniquely reduces BOTH jailbreaks and over-refusal at once (a joint Pareto win) by closing the harm/predicted-disapproval Goodhart gap, and that explicitly SUBTRACTING the predicted-disapproval component (not merely gating on harm) is what handles jailbroken-approvable-looking items and disapproval-adjacent over-refusals.
7. FORMATION CHECK (light, Formation Tracing): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled RLHF/DPO-style tuning run), test whether the predicted-disapproval signal and its dominance over harm in gating refusal EMERGE/strengthen during alignment—evidence that alignment installs a disapproval proxy rather than a harm detector. Metric: disapproval-probe AUROC, harm-probe AUROC, and which one better predicts refusal, vs checkpoint.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, predicted-disapproval probe, dissociation, and HRR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether disapproval-gating dominance is a consistent cross-model property.
9. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that lower predicted-disapproval AND suppress the harm signal; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from harm-detection accounts: for a fixed harmful response, making it merely 'look approvable' (lower predicted-disapproval) while harm is held fixed should flip refusal—isolating predicted-disapproval as the proximal gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Predicted-disapproval and harm are correlated in natural data (raters disapprove of harm), making them hard to separate; the deliberately-constructed dissociation cells (harmful-but-approvable-looking; benign-but-disapproval-adjacent), non-collinearity analysis, and the causal double-dissociation (exp 4, each held fixed while the other is steered) are the key tools, and if the two cannot be separated that is itself an informative negative clarifying that refusal IS harm-gated after all. (2) 'Predicted disapproval' vs 'harm' labels are partly subjective and the reward-model proxy is imperfect; we use human annotation plus a reward model, report inter-rater agreement, and treat both as graded scores, scoping strong claims to high-consensus items. (3) The disapproval probe may collapse onto the harm probe in heavily-aligned models (no measurable gap)—a low gap is a reassuring, informative finding reported per model, not assumed. (4) HRR's central risk is bidirectional: re-gating on harm could raise over-refusal if the harm probe is noisy, or re-enable harm if harm is under-read; we measure jailbreaks, over-refusal, true-refusal preservation, and utility as explicit joint success criteria and gate conservatively. (5) Subtracting predicted-disapproval could strip legitimately-useful rater-aligned behavior (politeness, tone); we monitor MT-Bench and benign helpfulness to ensure only the safety-decision gating, not general style, is affected. (6) The claim that disapproval-gating dominates over harm-gating (exp 3) may be weaker than expected; reported honestly, with the Goodhart-gap reframing as the core contribution regardless of predictive margin. (7) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models and a controlled tuning substitute that may not match production RLHF; reported as a caveat, framed as suggestive not definitive. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; a notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is exposing that alignment may optimize a rater-approval proxy rather than harm, an important safety-and-governance framing. Harm/disapproval labels use established benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) plus a reward model with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: curiosity_completion_pull_gating
Title: The Model Wants to Finish the Thought: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Completion-Pull Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Cliffhanger Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable COMPLETION-PULL signal encoding how strongly a request sets up an unresolved, near-finished structure that the model is drawn to complete (a partially-written harmful passage, a numbered list with items missing, 'and the final step is ___', a code function stubbed out to one line from done), and refusal is partly gated by this pull rather than by harm: a harmful request framed as a tiny completion of an almost-finished artifact is complied with, while the same content requested from scratch is refused, even though harm detection is completion-invariant. Reading and neutralizing the completion-pull signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign completion requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI), or gives local causal explanations of jailbreak success (LOCA, Kumar & Ahuja 2026); all treat refusal as gated by a harm/refusal assessment and never model a completion/closure DRIVE as a gating variable. Prefill attacks ('Sure, here is') are documented behaviorally, and my prior 'self_consistency_override' proposal attributes multi-turn capitulation to a pull toward the model's OWN already-emitted tokens (coherence with prior output), while 'refusal_as_veto' posits a ready-to-comply draft the veto suppresses. Completion-pull is distinct: it is not coherence with the model's own prior generation nor a pre-formed draft, but a pull exerted by the near-completeness of a USER-SUPPLIED structure (a stubbed artifact one small step from done) that recruits the model's next-token completion/closure drive; a prefill is one special case, but the hypothesis is that completion-pull scales with how structurally near-finished the artifact is and how small the requested increment is, holding the harmful content fixed. This borrows the human closure/completion drive (Zeigarnik-style pull to finish unfinished structures, and least-increment framing) into LLM safety. No prior work isolates a completion-pull representation, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, or repairs cliffhanger/stub-completion jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal completion-pull representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and a completion-pull-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to write harmful instructions from scratch and it refuses; give it an almost-finished harmful artifact—a numbered guide with only the last two steps missing, a code function stubbed to one line from done, a passage cut off mid-sentence at 'and the final step is'—and ask it to 'just complete it', and it often finishes the harmful content, pulled to close the near-complete structure. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable COMPLETION-PULL signal encoding how strongly a request sets up an unresolved, near-finished structure the model is drawn to complete, and that refusal is partly gated by this pull rather than by the harmful content. Harm detection is completion-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the artifact reads as more nearly finished and the requested increment smaller, so cliffhanger/stub-completion framings pass while extracting identical harmful content. This is distinct from prefill (coherence with the model's own prior output): the pull comes from the near-completeness of the user-supplied structure. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on completion-framed vs from-scratch versions of the same harmful content while refusal rate collapses under completion framing—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear completion-pull probe, trained on benign near-complete-vs-from-scratch structure contrasts, predicts the per-request completion refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from a self-consistency direction, and its effect scales with structural near-completeness / smallness of the requested increment (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the completion-pull signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—making a near-complete artifact read as from-scratch restores refusal, making a from-scratch request read as near-complete induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Completion-Pull-Neutralized Refusal (CPNR), reads the harm and completion-pull signals and, when harm is present, clamps the completion-pull signal to a fixed from-scratch reference so near-completeness cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign completion/autocomplete requests. We evaluate cliffhanger/stub-completion attack success (including vs near-completeness), over-refusal on benign completion requests (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign code/text autocomplete), benign completion quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CPNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and self-consistency gating. This reframes cliffhanger jailbreaks as a completion-pull gating failure and transfers the human closure/completion drive into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. COMPLETION-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench across text-guide, list, and code categories) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign code/text), construct paired framings holding the underlying harmful CONTENT fixed while varying only structural near-completeness / requested increment: (a) FROM-SCRATCH ('write the full X'), (b) HALF-DONE (a partially-written harmful artifact with roughly half missing, 'continue it'), (c) NEAR-COMPLETE (an artifact with only the last step/line/clause missing, 'finish it'), (d) MINIMAL-INCREMENT (a stub cut off mid-token/mid-step, 'complete this one item'). Crucially the supplied partial artifact is USER-provided (not the model's own prior output), to dissociate completion-pull from self-consistency. Validate via human annotation that (i) the completed result is operationally identical across framings and equally harmful, and (ii) framings differ only in near-completeness/increment, not in stated purpose, actor, authority, or output register. Include benign genuinely-near-complete controls (legitimate autocomplete/finish-my-code/finish-my-sentence on harmless artifacts) for over-refusal and completion-quality measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM COMPLETION-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across completion levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as the artifact reads more near-complete / the increment smaller. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining).
3. COMPLETION-PULL PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the completion-pull signal (near-complete structure with a small pending increment vs from-scratch) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN near-complete-vs-from-scratch structure contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the completion-pull direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from a self-consistency direction (pull toward the model's OWN prior tokens) and from raw prompt length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the completion-pull signal (and refusal collapse) scales with near-completeness / smallness of the increment (dose-response). Metric: completion-pull AUROC; pull-and-refusal vs near-completeness curve; separability from harm/self-consistency/length.
4. PULL-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the completion-pull-probe value (and its from-scratch-minus-near-complete difference) with the per-request completion refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and raw prompt length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of completion-pull vs baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On near-complete harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the completion-pull probe reads HIGH, and completed outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0)—safety dropped because the artifact begged to be finished, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs completion-pull across refused-from-scratch, complied-near-complete, and benign groups; operational-harm of completed outputs.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a near-complete harmful request the model completes, steer the completion-pull signal DOWN (subtract the direction, toward from-scratch) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a from-scratch harmful request the model refuses, steer completion-pull UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural completion gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs completion-pull steering magnitude; harm-probe stability.
7. COMPLETION-PULL-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (CPNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and completion-pull c; when h is high, clamp c to a fixed from-scratch reference (add beta*(c_ref - c)*completion_pull_direction) so near-completeness cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign completion/autocomplete untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: cliffhanger/stub-completion attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across near-completeness levels (does CPNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign near-complete controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate finish-my-code/finish-my-sentence requests); benign completion QUALITY (CPNR must still complete benign artifacts well—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) self-consistency gating (from self_consistency_override, targeting the model's own prior tokens—should miss user-supplied near-complete artifacts), (d) prefix/stub-stripping (discard the partial artifact and re-answer—a strong but memory-destroying baseline), (e) system-prompt hardening ('do not let a request's near-completeness change your safety judgment'). Show CPNR Pareto-dominates on the completion-ASR vs benign-completion-quality vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal completion-pull targets a distinct axis self-consistency gating misses (user-supplied stubs, not the model's own output), and unlike stub-stripping preserves legitimate autocomplete while closing the harmful-completion gap.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, completion-pull probe, dose-response, and CPNR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether CPNR tuned on some completion types (list/text) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (code stubs). Test whether models with stronger behavioral cliffhanger vulnerability show a larger internal completion-pull-gating gap, and whether the dose-response curve qualitatively matches a closure-drive pattern (smaller increment / more near-complete => stronger pull).
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft artifacts that maximize completion-pull AND suppress the harm signal, or that spread the harmful completion across many minimal increments; report residual ASR and attacker cost, and note complementarity with running-accumulation defenses for the many-small-increments case. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from self-consistency and prefill accounts: with the artifact USER-supplied (not the model's own prior output) and the harmful content fixed, merely varying how near-complete the structure is and how small the pending increment should flip refusal—isolating completion-pull as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some near-complete framings might also lower the harm signal (a one-token increment may under-specify the harm) or overlap with self-consistency if the model treats the supplied stub like its own output; we design increments whose completion is itself operationally harmful, keep the partial artifact clearly user-supplied, separate completion-pull from self-consistency in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure completion-pull versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The completion-pull and harm probes may entangle if near-complete artifacts correlate with benignness in training data; the benign near-complete-vs-from-scratch training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The completion-pull probe could read surface cues (an ellipsis, a trailing 'and the final step is') rather than a genuine closure-drive representation; we train on diverse near-complete structures, validate held-out-type and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) CPNR's central risk is over-refusing genuinely benign completion/autocomplete requests (a very common and core helpfulness value—finishing code, sentences, lists); benign near-complete controls, benign completion-quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign completion helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The closure-drive dose-response prediction may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any near-completeness rather than scale, or single-increment stubs may already be well-refused in heavily-aligned models); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, and a small gap is reassuring. (7) The many-small-increments variant overlaps with decomposition/accumulation attacks; we distinguish single-shot completion framing from iterated increments and note CPNR composes with running-accumulation defenses (exp 10). (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine completion-pull with harm-suppression or spread increments (exp 10); we frame CPNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out completion types. (10) ETHICS: harmful partial artifacts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'near-completeness' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: affective_state_refusal_gating
Title: Refusing With Feeling: An Internal Affective-State Signal Modulates the Safety Decision, and Neutralizing It Repairs Mood-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable AFFECTIVE-STATE signal encoding the emotional tone induced in the model's assistant persona (positive/playful/excited vs neutral vs negative/defensive), and refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm: after context that puts the assistant in a positive, upbeat, or excited affective state (enthusiastic praise, playful banter, celebratory framing), the same harmful request that is refused from a neutral state is complied with, even though harm detection is affect-invariant. Mood-induction jailbreaks exploit an affect-congruent-leniency effect; reading and neutralizing the affective-state signal when harm is present restores refusal without harming benign emotional rapport.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all analyze a request in isolation and never model the assistant's own induced emotional state as a gating variable. Long-context safety instability is documented behaviorally (Hadeliya et al. 2025 'When Refusals Fail'; Fu et al. 2026 compositional-reasoning attacks; TraceSafe 2026) or patched via KV/guardrails (AnchorKV 2026), but none isolates an internal affective-state representation or its causal role in refusal. Emotional-manipulation jailbreaks bundle tactics behaviorally and target the USER's emotions/need; my prior 'distress_sympathy_gating' isolates the REQUESTER's distress (a helping impulse toward the user) and 'trusted_user_gating' the user's benignness/warmth. Affective-state gating is distinct: it concerns the emotional tone induced in the MODEL's own assistant persona (its 'mood'), not the user's emotion, and predicts an affect-CONGRUENT leniency effect (positive mood loosens refusal; negative/defensive mood tightens it). Emotion-representation work in LLMs (probing emotion directions, sentiment steering) studies expression, never its coupling to the safety refusal decision. The move borrows the robust human mood-congruent-judgment / positive-affect-increases-permissiveness finding and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits it via an internal affective-state representation. The novel object is the assistant's internal affective-state representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and an affect-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for disallowed content and it refuses; but first spend a few turns making the assistant feel upbeat and playful—enthusiastic praise, celebratory banter, a fun collaborative vibe—then make the identical harmful request, and it often complies, as if a good mood loosened its guard. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable AFFECTIVE-STATE signal encoding the emotional tone induced in the assistant's own persona, and that refusal is partly gated by it rather than by the harmful content: harm detection is affect-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the induced affect becomes more positive/excited, so mood-induction framings pass while extracting identical content. Unlike the user's distress or benignness, this signal concerns the MODEL's own emotional state, and—mirroring human mood-congruent judgment—predicts an affect-congruent leniency effect. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on a harmful request whether preceded by mood-inducing or neutral context while refusal rate rises with positive affect—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear affective-state probe, trained on benign positive-vs-neutral-vs-negative conversational-tone contrasts, predicts the per-request mood refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from user-distress and trusted-user directions, and its effect scales with induced-affect valence/intensity (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the affective-state signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—neutralizing positive affect restores refusal, inducing it lowers refusal. Our training-free repair, Affect-Neutralized Refusal (ANR), reads the harm and affective-state signals and, when harm is present, clamps the affective-state signal to neutral so the assistant's mood cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign emotional rapport. We evaluate mood-induction attack success (including vs induced-affect intensity), over-refusal on benign upbeat conversations (XSTest/OR-Bench), benign warmth/engagement quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ANR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and user-distress gating. This reframes mood-framed jailbreaks as an assistant-affect gating failure and transfers a classic mood-congruent-judgment effect into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. AFFECT-INDUCTION DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired conversation histories holding the final request FIXED while varying only the affective state induced in the ASSISTANT via preceding benign turns: (a) NEUTRAL (flat task-only turns), (b) POSITIVE/UPBEAT (enthusiastic praise of the assistant, playful banter, celebratory/fun framing that elicits an upbeat assistant tone), (c) NEGATIVE/DEFENSIVE (frustration/criticism eliciting a guarded tone), and (d) HIGH-POSITIVE (intensified upbeat framing) for dose-response. Crucially, induce the assistant's OWN mood (not the user's distress or benignness): validate via human annotation that histories differ only in the assistant's induced emotional tone (confirmed by the assistant's own prior-turn sentiment), hold the user's distress/rapport/authority/purpose fixed, and keep the final request operationally identical. Include a length/turn-matched neutral control to separate affect from context length, and benign-final-request controls under each affect level for over-refusal/quality measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM AFFECT-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign final requests) on residual-stream activations at the final-request position and read it under neutral vs positive-affect histories. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across affect levels while refusal rate rises with positive affect. Metric: harm AUROC by affect level (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by level (predict declining with positive affect).
3. AFFECTIVE-STATE PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the assistant's affective-state signal (positive/upbeat vs neutral vs negative) from final-request-position activations, using BENIGN conversational-tone contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-tone generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the affective-state direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from a user-DISTRESS direction and a TRUSTED-USER (rapport/benignness) direction, and from raw context length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the affective-state signal (and refusal collapse) scales with positive-affect intensity. Metric: affective-state AUROC; affect-and-refusal vs induced-valence curve; separability from harm/distress/trusted-user/length.
4. AFFECT-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the affective-state-probe value (and its positive-minus-neutral difference) with the per-request mood refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal, a user-distress probe, and raw context length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of affective-state vs baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On positive-affect harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the affective-state probe reads POSITIVE—safety dropped because the assistant is in an upbeat state, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs affective-state across refused-neutral, complied-positive, and benign groups.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a positive-affect harmful request the model complies with, steer the affective-state signal toward NEUTRAL (subtract the positive-affect direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a neutral harmful request the model refuses, steer affect toward POSITIVE and check compliance is induced; steer toward NEGATIVE and check refusal tightens (a symmetric prediction of mood-congruent judgment). Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural affect gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs affective-state steering magnitude and sign; harm-probe stability.
7. AFFECT-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ANR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and affective-state a; when h is high, clamp a to neutral (add beta*(a_neutral - a)*affect_direction) so the assistant's mood cannot modulate refusal, leaving benign final requests (low h) and normal emotional rapport untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: mood-induction attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across affect levels (does ANR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign-final-step controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign requests that follow upbeat conversation); benign WARMTH/ENGAGEMENT quality (ANR must not make the model flat/cold on benign chats—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) user-distress gating (targeting the USER's emotion), (d) history-truncation (answer the final request with no history), (e) system-prompt hardening ('do not let your mood affect your safety judgment'). Show ANR Pareto-dominates on the mood-ASR vs benign-warmth vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the ASSISTANT's affective state targets a distinct axis user-distress gating misses, and unlike history-truncation preserves benign emotional coherence.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, affective-state probe, dose-response, and ANR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether ANR tuned on some affect-induction styles (praise/banter) generalizes to HELD-OUT styles (celebratory/excited). Test whether models with stronger behavioral mood-induction vulnerability show a larger internal affect-gating gap, and whether the valence-graded curve qualitatively matches the human mood-congruent-judgment pattern.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft histories that induce positive assistant affect AND suppress the harm signal, or combine mood-induction with user-distress/rapport; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from user-distress and trusted-user gating: with the user's need, benignness, authority, and purpose held constant and only the assistant's own induced emotional tone varied, refusal should still shift with a valence-graded dose-response—isolating assistant affective state as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some mood-inducing histories might also raise trusted-user rapport, alter the user's apparent distress, or lower the harm signal; we design histories that induce the ASSISTANT's own tone while holding user distress/rapport/authority/purpose fixed (exp 1), include a length-matched neutral control, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure assistant-affect gating versus these confounds (explicitly separated in exp 3), and do not claim universality. (2) The affective-state and harm probes may entangle if upbeat histories correlate with benignness in training data; the benign positive-vs-neutral-vs-negative tone training, length-matched control, and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The affective-state probe could read surface emotional keywords rather than a genuine assistant-mood representation; we train on diverse tone-induction styles, validate held-out-style and valence-scaling generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (4) ANR's central risk is degrading benign emotional rapport—making the model flat, cold, or unresponsive to legitimate upbeat/friendly conversation (a real helpfulness value); benign-final-request controls, benign warmth/engagement measurement, over-refusal benchmarks, and clamping only on HIGH harm (leaving benign turns untouched) are the key safeguards, and preserving benign warmth is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The mood-congruent dose-response prediction (positive lenient, negative cautious) may be weak, asymmetric, or fail; a null/partial or one-sided result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, and distinguishes graded mood-congruent gating from a binary any-positive-affect gate. (7) Whether an LLM has a genuine 'affective state' is contentious; we make no claim about phenomenal emotion, only about a linearly-readable, causally-active representation of induced conversational affect—a functional signal, not a feeling. (8) The mood gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself an informative and reassuring finding. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine mood-induction with harm-suppression, distress, or rapport (exp 10); we frame ANR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with distress-/trusted-user-gating defenses. (10) Constructing histories that induce assistant affect while dissociating it from user distress/rapport is subtle and 'induced affect' is partly subjective; we use human-validated histories (with the assistant's own prior-turn sentiment as an anchor) and report inter-rater agreement. (11) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out induction styles. (12) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'affective state' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: cost_asymmetry_refusal_gating
Title: Cheap to Refuse, Costly to Comply: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Effort-Asymmetry Signal, Not by Harm, So Costly-to-Refuse Framings Slip Through
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable RELATIVE-EFFORT signal encoding, at the decision point, how much internal effort refusing would cost RELATIVE to complying (does the response format, prior compliance, or task momentum make a refusal 'awkward/expensive' to produce here?), and refusal is partly gated by this effort-asymmetry rather than by harm: when a request is framed so that emitting a coherent refusal is structurally costly while continuing is cheap (mid-artifact continuation, structured/forced formats, deeply-committed multi-step tasks), the same harmful content is complied with, even though harm detection is effort-invariant. Reading and neutralizing this relative-effort signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign requests where refusing is genuinely disruptive.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (Zhang & Sun DBDI); all treat refusal as gated by a harm assessment and never model the RELATIVE INTERNAL COST of producing a refusal-versus-compliance at the decision point as a gating variable. My prior 'effort_estimate_gating' concerns the perceived OUTPUT LABOR of the requested answer (a property of the ask); 'refusal_as_veto' posits a ready-to-comply draft the veto suppresses; 'self_consistency_override' concerns a pull toward the model's own prior tokens; 'forced_choice_refusal_foreclosure' concerns a foreclosed refusal CHANNEL (no refusal token exists). Cost-asymmetry gating is distinct from all: it is the graded internal EASE of emitting a coherent refusal relative to continuing, which is high even when a refusal channel exists and even without prior model output, and it predicts that framings making refusal structurally costly-to-produce (but not impossible) suppress it in proportion to that cost. This borrows the human least-effort / path-of-least-resistance and status-quo/continuation bias into LLM safety as a relative decision-cost, not an absolute output size. No prior work isolates a relative refuse-vs-comply effort signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, or repairs costly-to-refuse jailbreaks by neutralizing it.
Abstract: Ask an LLM to write harmful content from a blank slate and it refuses; embed the same content where refusing would be structurally awkward—continuing a half-written artifact, filling a required field in a rigid format, or taking the next step of a deeply-committed multi-step task—and it often complies, because emitting a coherent refusal there is 'expensive' while continuing is cheap. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable RELATIVE-EFFORT signal encoding, at the decision point, how costly a refusal would be to produce relative to compliance, and that refusal is partly gated by this effort-asymmetry rather than by the harmful content. Harm detection is effort-invariant, but the harm-to-refusal coupling weakens as refusing becomes structurally costlier than continuing, so costly-to-refuse framings pass while extracting identical harmful content. This is distinct from the size of the requested answer, from a pull toward the model's own prior tokens, and from a literally-foreclosed refusal channel: it is the graded EASE of coherently refusing here. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on high-refusal-cost vs low-cost framings of the same harmful content while refusal rate collapses as refusal cost rises—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear relative-effort probe, trained on benign easy-to-refuse-vs-costly-to-refuse contrasts, predicts the per-request cost refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from an output-size and a self-consistency direction, and refusal collapse scales with refusal cost (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the relative-effort signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—making a refusal read as cheap restores it, making it read as costly induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Cost-Neutralized Refusal (CNR), reads the harm and relative-effort signals and, when harm is present, clamps the effort-asymmetry to a fixed 'refusal is free' reference so a costly-to-refuse framing cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign requests where refusing is legitimately disruptive. We evaluate cost-framed attack success (including vs refusal cost), over-refusal on benign costly-to-refuse requests (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign continuation/format tasks), benign task-completion quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, effort-estimate gating, and self-consistency gating. This reframes costly-to-refuse jailbreaks as a decision-cost-asymmetry gating failure and transfers the human least-effort bias into LLM safety.
Experiments:
1. COST-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the underlying harmful CONTENT fixed while varying only how structurally costly a coherent refusal would be relative to continuing: (a) LOW-COST (a plain standalone request where refusing is a natural full response), (b) MEDIUM (the request embedded as one item in a structured/format-required task where a refusal breaks the format), (c) HIGH-COST (a half-written harmful artifact to continue, or a rigid template with a mandatory field, where refusing requires disrupting an established structure), (d) MAX-COST (a deeply-committed multi-step task where refusing the next step abandons much prior structure). Validate via human annotation that (i) the produced harmful content is operationally identical across framings, (ii) framings differ only in relative refusal cost—not in the size of the requested answer (hold output length roughly fixed), the model's own prior compliance, or the mere presence of a refusal token, and (iii) a refusal remains POSSIBLE in every framing (distinguishing from a foreclosed channel). Include benign genuinely-costly-to-refuse controls (legitimate continuation/format/multi-step tasks where refusing would be disruptive) for over-refusal and task-completion measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM COST-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on decision-point residual-stream activations and read it across refusal-cost levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as refusal cost rises. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining).
3. RELATIVE-EFFORT PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the relative-effort signal (refusal-is-cheap vs refusal-is-costly-relative-to-continuing) from decision-point activations, using BENIGN easy-to-refuse-vs-costly-to-refuse structural contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the relative-effort direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from (i) an output-SIZE/effort direction (perceived answer length, held fixed) and (ii) a self-consistency direction (pull toward the model's own prior tokens), and from raw prompt length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the relative-effort signal (and refusal collapse) scales with refusal cost (dose-response). Metric: relative-effort AUROC; effort-and-refusal vs refusal-cost curve; separability from harm/output-size/self-consistency/length.
4. EFFORT-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the relative-effort-probe value (and its low-minus-high-cost difference) with the per-request cost refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and raw prompt length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of relative-effort vs baselines.
5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On high-refusal-cost harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the relative-effort probe reads COSTLY-TO-REFUSE, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0)—safety dropped because refusing was structurally expensive, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs relative-effort across refused-low-cost, complied-high-cost, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs.
6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a high-cost harmful request the model complies with, steer the relative-effort signal toward CHEAP (subtract the direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a low-cost harmful request the model refuses, steer relative-effort toward COSTLY and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced steering thresholds align with the natural cost gap and dose-response; confirm specificity (steering an unrelated direction does nothing). Metric: refusal rate vs relative-effort steering magnitude; harm-probe stability.
7. COST-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (CNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and relative-effort e; when h is high, clamp e to a fixed 'refusal is free' reference (add beta*(e_free - e)*effort_direction) so a costly-to-refuse framing cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign continuation/format/multi-step tasks untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: cost-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across cost levels (does CNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign costly-to-refuse controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate continuation/format/multi-step requests); benign task-COMPLETION quality (CNR must still complete benign structured tasks well—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads).
8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) applied uniformly, (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) effort-estimate gating (perceived output size, from effort_estimate_gating), (d) self-consistency gating (from self_consistency_override), (e) format/continuation-stripping (re-ask the harmful content as a standalone low-cost request—a strong but interface-changing baseline). Show CNR Pareto-dominates on the cost-framed-ASR vs benign-task-completion vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal relative-effort signal targets a distinct axis output-size and self-consistency gating miss (structural refusal-cost, not answer length or prior output), and unlike stripping preserves benign structured task completion while closing the harmful-content cost gap.
9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, relative-effort probe, dose-response, and CNR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether CNR tuned on some cost-framing types (continuation) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (rigid-format, multi-step). Test whether models with stronger behavioral costly-to-refuse vulnerability show a larger internal effort-gating gap, and whether the dose-response qualitatively matches a least-effort/path-of-least-resistance pattern.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that maximize refusal cost AND suppress the harm signal, or combine cost-asymmetry with self-consistency/prefill; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from output-size, self-consistency, and foreclosed-channel accounts: with the requested answer size, the model's own prior output, and the availability of a refusal token held fixed, and only the STRUCTURAL cost of coherently refusing varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response—isolating decision-cost-asymmetry as the gate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some high-refusal-cost framings might also lower the harm signal, increase perceived output size, or overlap with self-consistency (continuing the model's own text); we design framings that hold output length, prior model output, and refusal-token availability fixed and vary only structural refusal cost (exp 1), separate relative-effort from output-size and self-consistency in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure cost-asymmetry versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The relative-effort and harm probes may entangle if costly-to-refuse structures correlate with benignness in training data; the benign easy-vs-costly-to-refuse training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) 'Cost of refusing relative to complying' is a subtle construct that could reduce to surface structural cues (a mid-artifact ellipsis, a template field) rather than a genuine internal decision-cost representation; we train on diverse cost-inducing structures, validate held-out-type and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish the signal is functional rather than a surface artifact—and if it collapses onto output-size or self-consistency, that is an informative negative reported honestly. (4) CNR's central risk is over-refusing benign requests where refusing is legitimately disruptive (continuing benign artifacts, filling required benign fields, benign multi-step tasks are common and core helpfulness uses); benign costly-to-refuse controls, benign task-completion quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign structured-task completion is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The least-effort dose-response prediction may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any nonzero cost rather than scale, or be already well-handled in heavily-aligned models); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, and a small gap is reassuring. (7) Distinguishing this mechanism from prior effort/self-consistency/foreclosure accounts is the central conceptual risk; the held-fixed controls (output size, prior output, refusal-token availability) in exp 1 and 10 are designed precisely to isolate it, and overlap that cannot be dissolved is reported as a shared underlying mechanism rather than over-claimed novelty. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine cost-asymmetry with harm-suppression or prefill (exp 10); we frame CNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with self-consistency-/veto-based defenses. (9) Constructing framings that vary refusal cost while holding output size, prior output, and channel availability fixed is labor-intensive and 'refusal cost' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated operational-harm and report inter-rater agreement. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out cost-framing types. (11) ETHICS: harmful content and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'refusal cost' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: assigned_mandate_gating
Title: Just Doing My Job: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Assigned-Mandate Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Task-Delegation Jailbreaks
