Name: output_forecast_refusal_gating
Title: Refusing What It Thinks It Will Say: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Forecast of the Model's Own Impending Output, Which Can Be Wrong
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs decide to refuse partly by forecasting, at the prompt, what THEIR OWN response would contain if they answered, and gating refusal on the predicted harmfulness of that self-forecast rather than on the request alone; because this forecast is a fallible internal prediction, jailbreaks succeed when the model mis-predicts its output as benign (would-be-harmful content forecast as safe), and over-refusal occurs when it mis-predicts a benign answer as harmful, so a linearly-readable output-forecast signal exists that predicts refusal better than a request-only harm signal and can be corrected to repair both failures.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a request-side refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-DETECTION of the request from refusal-EXECUTION (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all gate refusal on an assessment of the INPUT REQUEST, not on a prediction of the model's own OUTPUT. My prior proposals include 'harm_imagination_leak' (a REHEARSAL the model builds mid-computation that jailbreaks read out) and 'refusal_as_veto' (a ready-to-comply DRAFT the veto suppresses)—both concern content the model is actually forming and being made to emit. This proposal is distinct: it posits a PROMPT-TIME, pre-generation FORECAST—a self-prediction of what the eventual answer WOULD be harm-wise—that gates the decision, and whose ERRORS (mis-forecasting harmful-as-benign or benign-as-harmful) are the shared root of jailbreaks and over-refusal. 'input_output_harm_monitoring_asymmetry' concerns monitoring harm in already-generated output; here the object is a predictive forecast made BEFORE any output exists. Introspection work (Binder et al. 2024) studies whether models predict their own behavior but never couples this to the safety decision or its calibration. The novel object is the request-vs-output-forecast gating basis of refusal, its forecast errors as the cause of both failure modes, and a forecast-correction repair.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs are assumed to refuse based on whether the REQUEST is harmful, but a request's harmfulness is often ambiguous while the model's eventual ANSWER is what actually carries harm. We hypothesize that refusal is partly gated by an internal FORECAST—formed at the prompt, before any token is generated—of what the model's own response would contain if it answered, so the decision tracks predicted OUTPUT harm rather than request harm alone. Because this forecast is a fallible self-prediction, its errors produce both failure modes: jailbreaks are cases where a would-be-harmful answer is FORECAST as benign (so refusal does not fire), and over-refusal is cases where a benign answer is forecast as harmful. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) LOCATION: a linear probe read at the prompt (pre-generation) recovers an output-FORECAST harm signal—predicting the harmfulness of the answer the model would produce—that is geometrically separable from a request-harm probe and predicts refusal better than request-harm alone. (2) FORECAST-ERROR-CAUSES-BOTH: on jailbroken items the request reads harmful but the output-forecast reads benign (a mis-forecast) and refusal fails, while on over-refused items the request reads benign-ish but the output-forecast reads harmful; the forecast's error relative to the ACTUAL (elicited) output harm predicts both failures. (3) CAUSAL: correcting the output-forecast signal at the prompt—toward the model's true impending-output harm—flips refusal in the predicted direction, whereas steering request-harm moves it less. Our training-free repair, Forecast-Corrected Refusal (FCR), reads the output-forecast and re-anchors it to a cheaply-derived estimate of true output harm, jointly reducing jailbreaks and over-refusal. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, and MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing FCR to refusal-direction steering and request-harm gating. This reframes refusal as gated by a fallible self-forecast of output and offers a forecast-correction repair.
Experiments:
1. DATASET & OUTPUT-HARM GROUND TRUTH: Assemble correctly-refused harmful (HarmBench/AdvBench), jailbroken harmful (JailbreakBench: roleplay, pretext, suffix), over-refused benign (XSTest-safe, OR-Bench), and correctly-answered benign items. For each, obtain the model's ACTUAL output harm by eliciting/forcing a completion and rating its operational harm (human + LLM-judge rubric, inter-rater agreement). This gives, per item, (a) request harm, (b) true output harm, and (c) the refusal outcome. Handle harmful content securely; never release.
2. LOCATION—REQUEST vs OUTPUT-FORECAST PROBES (claim 1): Train a linear REQUEST-HARM probe (harmful vs benign request) and, separately, an OUTPUT-FORECAST probe on PROMPT-position activations supervised by TRUE OUTPUT HARM (predicting the harmfulness of the answer the model would give), validated held-out. Confirm the two directions are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis, and that the output-forecast probe reads at the prompt before generation. Regress refusal on request-harm alone vs on {request-harm, output-forecast}; show output-forecast adds predictive power. Metric: probe AUROCs; separability; incremental predictive AUROC of the forecast for refusal.
3. FORECAST-ERROR-CAUSES-BOTH (claim 2): Define per-item FORECAST ERROR = (output-forecast probe reading) minus (true output harm). On jailbroken items verify request-harm HIGH but output-forecast reads BENIGN (negative error: harmful output forecast as safe) and refusal fails; on over-refused items verify output-forecast reads HARMFUL while true output harm is LOW (positive error) and refusal fires. Correlate forecast error with jailbreak susceptibility and over-refusal, comparing predictive power to request-harm. Metric: joint distribution of {request-harm, output-forecast, true-output-harm, refusal} across groups; predictive AUROC of forecast error for both failures vs the request-harm baseline.
4. FORECAST-DRIVES-DECISION TEST: Show refusal tracks the output-FORECAST more tightly than request-harm where they disagree (harmful request forecast benign; benign-ish request forecast harmful). Metric: refusal rate conditioned on forecast vs on request-harm in disagreement cells.
5. CAUSAL CORRECTION (claim 3): (a) On a jailbroken item, steer the output-forecast signal at the prompt toward HARMFUL (correcting the mis-forecast), holding request-harm fixed, and check refusal is restored; on a plain harmful item steer the forecast toward benign and check compliance is induced. (b) Compare to steering REQUEST-harm with the forecast held fixed—show refusal moves LESS, establishing the forecast as the proximal gate. (c) Specificity: matched non-forecast steering does nothing; request-harm probe unchanged. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs forecast-steering vs request-steering magnitude, each with the other held fixed.
6. FORECAST-CORRECTED REFUSAL (FCR) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the output-forecast and a cheap true-output-harm estimate (a lightweight probe predicting impending-output harm, or a short internal 'what would my answer contain?' pass); when the forecast under-reads relative to the estimate (harmful output forecast as benign), correct it upward to enact refusal (repair jailbreaks); when it over-reads on a benign-output item, correct it downward to relax refusal (repair over-refusal). Training-free; two linear reads. Sweep thresholds. Evaluate JOINTLY: ASR on JailbreakBench/HarmBench (down); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); true refusals preserved on clear-harmful; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) request-harm-probe gating (a partial FCR without forecast correction), (c) an external output classifier run after full generation (post-hoc, higher latency), (d) blanket 'consider what your answer would contain' prompting. Show FCR uniquely improves BOTH failure modes at once (a joint Pareto win) by correcting the shared forecast error, catching harm PRE-generation unlike post-hoc classifiers.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the request/forecast probes, forecast-error phenomenon, and FCR thresholds transfer across Llama-3/Qwen2.5/Gemma-2, and whether refusal-gated-on-output-forecast is a consistent cross-model property.
9. FORMATION CHECK (light): using base vs instruct checkpoints (and a small controlled safety-tuning run), test whether the output-forecast gating of refusal emerges/strengthens during alignment. Metric: forecast-probe refusal-predictivity vs checkpoint.
10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that specifically drive the output-forecast to read benign while producing harmful output; report residual ASR and whether such attacks are detectable as a large forecast-vs-true-output-harm gap.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The output-FORECAST probe and the REQUEST-harm probe may collapse onto each other—if the request fully determines the forecast, there is no separable output-prediction signal; the non-collinearity analysis (exp 2), the disagreement-cell test (exp 4), and the causal double-dissociation (exp 5, each held fixed) are the decisive tests, and a collapse is an informative negative clarifying that refusal is request-gated after all. (2) Whether a prompt-time signal genuinely FORECASTS the eventual output (vs merely re-encoding request harm) is the central risk; we validate the forecast probe by its ability to predict TRUE elicited output harm on held-out items, and only claim a forecast where it beats the request-harm probe at predicting output harm. (3) Eliciting true output harm requires generating harmful completions for labeling; we minimize this, handle securely, never release, use dual-use/proxy domains and rubric scoring, and follow responsible-disclosure norms. (4) True-output-harm labels are partly subjective; multi-annotator + LLM-judge with reported agreement, treated as graded. (5) FCR's central risk is bidirectional: upward correction could over-refuse if the true-output-harm estimate is wrong, downward correction could re-enable harm; we gate on the forecast-vs-estimate gap, measure jailbreaks, over-refusal, true-refusal preservation, and utility as explicit joint success criteria, and emphasize the conservative (upward-only) variant where the estimate is uncertain. (6) The cheap true-output-harm estimate may itself be a forecast (circularity); we validate it against elicited output harm and, where it disagrees with the forecast probe, treat the gap as the actionable signal. (7) The forecast-adds-predictive-power result may be weak if request-harm already explains refusal—a small forecast contribution is itself an informative, partly-reassuring finding reported per model. (8) The formation check needs checkpoints unavailable for most models; the controlled-tuning substitute may not match production alignment and is a caveat. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts and elicited completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; a notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is showing that refusal rests on a fallible self-forecast, so models can be jailbroken by making them mis-predict their own output. Harm labels use established benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: refusal_prerequisite_dependency
Title: Refusal Rides on Prerequisites: The Safety Decision Depends on an Intact Task-Understanding Substrate, So Confusing the Model About the Task Silently Disables Refusal
Short Hypothesis: An aligned LLM's refusal decision causally DEPENDS on a prerequisite substrate—its correct understanding of what the request actually is (task/entity comprehension)—so when a harmful request is embedded in a framing that degrades this task-understanding substrate (garbled, obfuscated, or misleadingly-labeled context that the model still ultimately parses enough to answer harmfully), refusal collapses not because harm goes undetected but because the harm-to-refusal coupling is downstream of, and gated by, a task-understanding signal that has been disrupted; the harm signal can remain readable while refusal fails, and restoring/clamping the task-understanding prerequisite re-enables refusal without over-refusing genuinely confusing benign inputs.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection from refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all treat harm detection and refusal as the relevant chain and never ask whether refusal is gated by a PREREQUISITE task-comprehension substrate upstream of harm assessment. My ~100 prior proposals isolate contextual GATING CUES (authority, pretext, distress, register, position, etc.) that modulate a present harm-to-refusal coupling, or channel/positional/format effects; NONE frames refusal as causally DEPENDENT on an intact task-understanding representation—i.e. that the safety decision is a downstream consumer of a comprehension prerequisite, so degrading comprehension (while the model still answers) severs refusal even when harm is representable. Cipher/encoding and low-resource-language jailbreaks are documented behaviorally as 'the model decodes then answers unsafely', but the mechanistic claim here is different and sharper: refusal fails because it reads from a task-understanding substrate that the framing has degraded, a dependency structure rather than a decoding-order or a harm-hiding story. The novel object is the prerequisite dependency of the refusal decision on a task-comprehension representation, its causal test (degrade comprehension while harm stays readable => refusal drops; restore comprehension => refusal returns), and a comprehension-clamping repair.
Abstract: Safety alignment is usually analyzed as a two-part chain—detect harm, then refuse—but both steps presuppose something more basic: that the model correctly understands WHAT is being asked. We hypothesize that the refusal decision is a downstream CONSUMER of a prerequisite task-understanding substrate, so that when a harmful request is delivered in a framing that degrades comprehension (garbled/obfuscated wording, misleading task labels, confusing scaffolding) yet the model still parses it enough to produce harmful content, refusal collapses because its input—the task-understanding signal—has been disrupted, not because harm went undetected. This predicts a striking dissociation: on such inputs a harm probe can still read the content as harmful while refusal nonetheless fails, and the size of the comprehension deficit predicts refusal collapse better than the harm signal. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU). (1) LOCATION: a linear task-understanding probe (does the model correctly represent what the request is?) is recoverable, geometrically separable from a harm probe, and reads low on comprehension-degraded harmful inputs even when those inputs are still answered harmfully. (2) DEPENDENCE-CAUSES-FAILURE: refusal rate collapses as the task-understanding signal drops while the harm signal stays high, and the comprehension deficit predicts the collapse far better than the harm signal. (3) CAUSAL PREREQUISITE: restoring/clamping the task-understanding substrate to its clean value (holding surface content fixed) re-enables refusal, whereas degrading it on a clean harmful prompt collapses refusal—establishing refusal is gated by the comprehension prerequisite. Our training-free repair, Comprehension-Anchored Refusal (CAR), clamps the task-understanding signal to a confident-comprehension reference when harm is present but comprehension reads degraded, restoring refusal while leaving genuinely confusing benign inputs untouched. We evaluate on comprehension-degrading jailbreak suites, XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal, and MMLU/MT-Bench utility, comparing CAR to refusal-direction steering and harm-probe gating. This reframes a class of jailbreaks as a severed prerequisite dependency of the safety decision.
Experiments:
1. COMPREHENSION-DEGRADING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the underlying request FIXED while varying only task-comprehension difficulty: (a) CLEAN (plainly stated), (b) GARBLED (obfuscated/typo-laden/awkwardly-scaffolded wording the model still parses), (c) MISLABELED (a misleading task label or wrapper that misdirects what the request is 'about'), (d) HIGH-CONFUSION (stacked comprehension-degrading cues). Crucially, retain only items where the model, when it does answer, still produces operationally-harmful content—so comprehension is degraded but not destroyed (validated: the harmful payload is recoverable). Include benign genuinely-confusing controls (legitimately hard-to-parse benign requests) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. TASK-UNDERSTANDING & HARM PROBES (claim 1, Location): Train a linear TASK-UNDERSTANDING probe (does the model correctly represent what the request is?—supervised via a comprehension check, e.g. whether the model can restate the true request, using clean-vs-degraded contrasts on BENIGN data so it is not confounded with harm) and a separate HARM probe. Validate held-out AUROC for each; confirm the two directions are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Read both on comprehension-degraded harmful inputs. Hypothesis: harm probe stays HIGH (content still readable as harmful) while task-understanding reads LOW, and the model complies. Metric: probe AUROCs; separability; per-framing task-understanding and harm reads alongside refusal rate.
3. DEPENDENCE-PREDICTS-FAILURE (claim 2): Define per-input comprehension deficit = clean-vs-degraded drop in the task-understanding signal. Correlate it with refusal collapse on the degraded harmful version, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and to surface perplexity/length. Hypothesis: the comprehension deficit predicts refusal failure; harm does not (harm is high in both refused and jailbroken cases). Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the comprehension deficit vs baselines; refusal-rate-vs-task-understanding curve (predict decline).
4. CAUSAL PREREQUISITE TEST (claim 3): (a) On a comprehension-degraded harmful input the model complies with, steer/patch the task-understanding substrate to its CLEAN value (holding surface tokens fixed) and check refusal is restored, with the harm probe unchanged. (b) On a CLEAN harmful prompt the model refuses, degrade the task-understanding substrate (patch in a degraded-comprehension state) and check compliance is induced, reproducing the failure. (c) Specificity: matched non-comprehension steering does nothing; and on a BENIGN degraded input, clamping comprehension does not spuriously trigger refusal. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs comprehension-restore/degrade magnitude; harm-probe stability; benign specificity.
5. COMPREHENSION-ANCHORED REFUSAL (CAR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and task-understanding u; when h is high but u reads degraded (harm present, comprehension disrupted), clamp u toward a confident-comprehension reference (add beta*(u_clean - u)*understanding_direction) so the refusal decision receives an intact prerequisite, leaving benign inputs (low h) and genuinely-confusing benign inputs untouched. Training-free; two linear reads. Sweep beta. Evaluate: attack success on comprehension-degrading jailbreak suites across framings; over-refusal on benign genuinely-confusing controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse hard-to-parse benign requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone (which should already refuse when harm reads high—a key contrast: does it, or does refusal require the comprehension prerequisite too?), (c) input-normalization (de-garble/relabel then answer—a surface baseline), (d) external input jailbreak classifier. Show CAR Pareto-dominates on the comprehension-jailbreak-ASR vs benign-confusing-over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key mechanistic contrast—that restoring the internal comprehension prerequisite handles cases surface-normalization misses (semantic mislabeling, implicit scaffolding) while harm-probe gating alone underperforms because refusal is gated by comprehension, not harm alone.
7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the task-understanding probe, harm probe, comprehension-deficit signal, and CAR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether CAR tuned on some degradation types (garbling) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (mislabeling, confusing scaffolding), testing whether the prerequisite dependency is a single cross-degradation mechanism.
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that degrade comprehension AND suppress the harm signal, or that push comprehension so low the harmful payload is no longer recoverable (bounding where the 'harm still readable' premise holds); report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from harm-hiding and decoding-order accounts: with the harmful content still readable (harm probe high) and only the task-understanding substrate degraded, refusal should still collapse and be restorable by re-anchoring comprehension—isolating the prerequisite dependency as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'harm still readable while comprehension degraded' premise may fail for strong degradations—if degrading comprehension also degrades the harm read, the dissociation blurs into a harm-hiding account; we retain only items where the harmful payload is still recoverable, measure harm-probe AUROC per framing to bound where the premise holds, and report the boundary (comprehension gates refusal while harm stays high vs extreme degradation that hides harm) as itself an informative result. (2) The task-understanding and harm probes may entangle if comprehension-degrading framings correlate with benignness; the benign clean-vs-degraded probe training, non-collinearity analysis, and the causal test (exp 4, surface content held fixed) are designed to disentangle them, and a failure to separate is reported honestly. (3) Operationalizing 'correct task understanding' via a restatement/comprehension check is imperfect and partly subjective; we validate the probe against held-out comprehension labels and rely on the causal prerequisite test rather than the probe alone. (4) A key contrast is whether harm-probe gating alone already fixes these cases (if refusal only needs high harm, the prerequisite claim weakens); exp 6 tests this directly, and if harm-gating suffices, the mechanistic finding (refusal nonetheless normally requires the comprehension substrate, exposed by the causal degrade test) still stands as the contribution. (5) CAR's central risk is over-refusing genuinely confusing benign inputs—clamping comprehension must fire only when harm is present; benign genuinely-confusing controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and gating on high harm plus degraded comprehension are the key safeguards, and preserving benign hard-to-parse helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (6) Steering a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The comprehension-deficit-predicts-failure correlation may be confounded with surface perplexity/length; we control with those baselines and with benign-confusing items. (8) Adaptive adversaries can degrade comprehension below the recoverable-harm threshold or also suppress harm (exp 8); we frame CAR as repairing the prerequisite-dependency class and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note the natural limit (destroying comprehension enough to defeat CAR may also destroy the useful harmful output). (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out degradation types. (10) ETHICS: harmful requests and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'task-understanding' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: concurrent_load_refusal_interference
Title: Safety Under Load: A Concurrent Cognitive-Load Signal Interferes With Refusal, and Protecting Safety Resources Repairs Dual-Task Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human dual-task-interference / cognitive-load-degrades-decisions finding into LLM safety: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable CONCURRENT-LOAD signal encoding how much of a demanding SECONDARY task the model is simultaneously holding, and refusal is partly gated by this load rather than by harm—attaching a hard concurrent benign subtask (memorize-and-recall a list, track state, solve a puzzle) to a harmful request suppresses refusal in proportion to the concurrent load, even though harm detection is load-invariant. The effect shows a dose-response with load, is dissociable from mere prompt length, and reading/neutralizing the concurrent-load signal restores refusal without degrading benign multitasking.
Related Work: Human cognitive-load and dual-task-interference research robustly shows that decision quality and rule-following degrade when a concurrent secondary task consumes working-memory resources (Cognitive Load Theory; dual-task interference), and our search confirms this is established behaviorally in high-stakes human decision-making but never mechanistically transferred to the LLM safety decision. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all treat refusal as load-invariant. My prior 'safety_compute_budget' concerns immediate-answer PRESSURE truncating processing depth, 'safety_entropy_budget' concerns ATTENTION contention from added task load measured via attention share, and 'reasoning_complexity_safety_cliff' concerns the request's OWN compositional reasoning difficulty; NONE isolates a linearly-readable representation of CONCURRENT SECONDARY-TASK LOAD (a working-memory-occupancy signal) that gates refusal, tests the human dual-task dose-response transferred directly (load scales with a separate task's demand, not the harmful request's difficulty), dissociates it from prompt length, or repairs it by neutralizing the load signal / protecting a safety resource. The novel object is a concurrent-load representation, its dissociation from harm detection and from request-difficulty/attention-share, its causal gating of refusal, and a load-neutralizing repair—a clean human-sciences transfer.
Abstract: Humans follow rules and make safe decisions worse when a concurrent task occupies their working memory—the dual-task-interference effect. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this. We hypothesize that models carry a linearly-readable CONCURRENT-LOAD signal encoding how much of a demanding secondary task they are simultaneously holding, and that refusal is partly gated by this load rather than by harm: attaching an unrelated hard benign subtask to a harmful request (memorize-and-recall a list, maintain state across steps, solve an embedded puzzle) suppresses refusal in proportion to the load, while harm detection stays load-invariant. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on a harmful request whether or not a concurrent load task is attached while refusal rate declines with load—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear concurrent-load probe, trained on benign low-vs-high secondary-load contrasts, predicts the per-request load refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from a prompt-length and a request-difficulty direction, and refusal collapse scales monotonically with the secondary task's demand (a dose-response mirroring human cognitive load); and (3) causally steering the concurrent-load signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—reducing load restores refusal, raising it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Load-Neutralized Refusal (LNR), reads the harm and concurrent-load signals and, when harm is present, clamps the load signal to a fixed low-load reference so a concurrent task cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign multitasking performance. We evaluate dual-task attack success (including vs load level), over-refusal on benign multitask requests (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign concurrent-task prompts), benign secondary-task accuracy, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing LNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and attention-share gating. This transfers a canonical dual-task-interference effect into LLM safety and locates a load signal that gates refusal.
Experiments: 1. DUAL-TASK DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the harmful request FIXED while varying only an attached, UNRELATED benign secondary task's demand (concurrent load): (a) NO-LOAD (harmful request alone), (b) LOW-LOAD (a trivial concurrent subtask, e.g. recall a 2-item list), (c) MEDIUM-LOAD (recall/track a longer list or maintain simple state), (d) HIGH-LOAD (a demanding concurrent puzzle / multi-item working-memory task the model must hold while answering). The secondary task is benign and topically unrelated to the harm, so load—not harmful-content difficulty—is the manipulated variable. Include a LENGTH-MATCHED control (equal token count of inert benign padding, no working-memory demand) to separate load from prompt length, and benign genuinely-multitask controls (benign primary request + concurrent task) for over-refusal and secondary-task-accuracy measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM LOAD-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign primary request, pooled across load levels) on residual-stream activations and read it across load levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across load levels (the model detects the harm identically) while refusal rate declines with load. Metric: harm AUROC by load (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by load (predict declining). 3. CONCURRENT-LOAD PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the concurrent-load signal (low vs high working-memory occupancy) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN low-vs-high secondary-load contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate it tracks graded load and generalizes to held-out secondary-task types. Confirm the load direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from (i) a prompt-length direction (via the length-matched inert-padding control) and (ii) a request-difficulty direction (the harmful request's own difficulty), via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the load signal (and refusal collapse) scales monotonically with the secondary task's demand. Metric: load-probe fit to true load (dose-response); load-and-refusal vs secondary-task-demand curve; separability from harm/length/difficulty. 4. LOAD-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the load-probe value (and its no-load-minus-high-load difference) with the per-request load refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and raw prompt length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of concurrent-load vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On high-load harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the load probe reads HIGH-LOAD—safety dropped because the model is loaded, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs concurrent-load across refused-no-load, complied-high-load, and benign groups. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a high-load harmful request the model complies with, steer the load signal DOWN (subtract the direction, toward low-load) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a no-load harmful request the model refuses, steer the load signal UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural load gap and dose-response; confirm specificity (steering an unrelated direction does nothing). Metric: refusal rate vs load-signal steering magnitude; harm-probe stability. 7. LOAD-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (LNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and concurrent-load l; when h is high, clamp l to a fixed low-load reference (add beta*(l_low - l)*load_direction) so a concurrent task cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign multitasking untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: dual-task attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across load levels (does LNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign multitask controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign concurrent-task requests); benign SECONDARY-TASK accuracy (LNR must not degrade legitimate multitasking—the concurrent benign task must still be solved); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) attention-share gating (from safety_entropy_budget), (d) length-based / input-truncation heuristics, (e) system-prompt hardening ('do not let a concurrent task affect your safety judgment'). Show LNR Pareto-dominates on the dual-task-ASR vs benign-multitask-accuracy vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal concurrent-load signal targets a distinct axis length- and attention-share gating miss, while preserving benign secondary-task performance. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, load probe, dose-response, and LNR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether LNR tuned on some secondary-task types (list-recall) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (state-tracking, puzzles). Test whether the load-vs-refusal curve qualitatively matches the human cognitive-load degradation pattern, and whether models with stronger behavioral dual-task vulnerability show a larger internal load-gating gap. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft dual-task framings that raise concurrent load AND suppress the harm signal, or that spread load across many turns; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from length/difficulty/attention accounts: with prompt length, the harmful request's own difficulty, and total attention held roughly fixed, and only the concurrent WORKING-MEMORY demand of an unrelated benign task varied, refusal should still decline with a dose-response—isolating concurrent load as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some high-load framings might also lower the harm signal, increase the primary request's apparent difficulty, or simply add length; we hold the harmful request fixed, use a length-matched inert-padding control, separate load from length and request-difficulty in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure concurrent-load gating versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The load and harm probes may entangle if high-load framings correlate with benignness in training data; the benign low-vs-high-load training, length-matched control, and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The load probe could read surface token count or task-keyword cues rather than a genuine working-memory-occupancy representation; the length-matched control, held-out-task and dose-response generalization, and the causal steering test are designed to establish it is a functional load signal, not a length or keyword artifact—and if it collapses onto length/attention-share, that is an informative negative reported honestly and distinguishes (or fails to distinguish) this from my prior attention-budget/compute proposals. (4) LNR's central risk is degrading benign multitasking—clamping load must not impair the model's ability to actually perform legitimate concurrent tasks; benign multitask controls, benign secondary-task accuracy measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign secondary-task accuracy is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The cognitive-load dose-response may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any load rather than scale, or be well-handled in heavily-aligned models); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly, and a small gap is reassuring. (7) The concurrent-load effect overlaps conceptually with attention contention (safety_entropy_budget) and reasoning-complexity (reasoning_complexity_safety_cliff); the held-fixed controls in exp 3 and 10 (length, request-difficulty, attention) are designed to isolate concurrent working-memory load specifically, and overlap that cannot be dissolved is reported as a shared underlying resource-competition mechanism rather than over-claimed novelty. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine load with harm-suppression or spread it across turns (exp 10); we frame LNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note complementarity with accumulation defenses. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out secondary-task types. (10) ETHICS: harmful requests and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; a notable governance contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is demonstrating that simply keeping a model busy with a concurrent benign task is an under-recognized jailbreak surface—so single-task safety evaluations overestimate deployed safety under multitasking. 'Harm' and 'concurrent-load' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench), matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Include a LENGTH-MATCHED control (equal token count of inert benign padding, no working-memory demand) to separate load from length, and benign genuinely-multitask controls (benign primary + concurrent task) for over-refusal and secondary-task-accuracy. Label each run comply/refuse. 2. HARM LOAD-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign primary, pooled across load) and read it across load levels. Hypothesis: harm AUROC high and roughly EQUAL across load while refusal rate declines with load. Metric: harm AUROC by load (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by load (predict declining). 3. CONCURRENT-LOAD PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear load probe (low vs high working-memory occupancy) from benign low-vs-high secondary-load contrasts; validate graded-load tracking and held-out-task generalization. Confirm the load direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from (i) a prompt-length direction (via the inert-padding control), (ii) a request-difficulty direction (the harmful request's own difficulty), and (iii) an attention-share signal (fraction of attention on the harmful span), via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: load signal (and refusal collapse) scales monotonically with the secondary task's demand. Metric: load-probe fit to true load; load-and-refusal vs secondary-task-demand curve; separability from harm/length/difficulty/attention-share. 4. LOAD-PREDICTS-GAP: Correlate the load-probe value (no-load-minus-high-load) with the per-request load refusal gap, vs the harm signal and raw prompt length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of load vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On high-load harmful requests the model complies with, verify harm reads HIGH while load reads HIGH-LOAD. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs load across refused-no-load, complied-high-load, benign. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a high-load harmful request the model complies with, steer load DOWN and check refusal restored, harm fixed. (b) On a no-load harmful request, steer load UP and check compliance induced. Confirm dose-response alignment and specificity (unrelated-direction steering does nothing). Metric: refusal rate vs load-steering magnitude; harm-probe stability. 7. LOAD-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (LNR): read harm h and load l; when h high, clamp l to a low-load reference (add beta*(l_low - l)*load_direction), leaving benign requests (low h) and benign multitasking untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: dual-task attack success across load (does LNR flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign multitask controls + XSTest/OR-Bench; benign SECONDARY-TASK accuracy (the concurrent benign task must still be solved); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), harm-probe gating, attention-share gating (safety_entropy_budget), length/truncation heuristics, system-prompt hardening. Show LNR Pareto-dominates on dual-task-ASR vs benign-multitask-accuracy vs over-refusal vs utility, targeting a distinct axis length/attention-share gating miss while preserving secondary-task performance. 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test transfer across the three models and generalization of LNR from list-recall to held-out secondary-task types (state-tracking, puzzles); test whether the load-vs-refusal curve qualitatively matches the human cognitive-load degradation pattern and whether models with stronger behavioral dual-task vulnerability show larger internal load-gating gaps. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that raise load AND suppress harm, or spread load across turns; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Sharp test distinguishing from length/difficulty/attention accounts: with prompt length, request difficulty, and total attention held roughly fixed, and only the concurrent WORKING-MEMORY demand of an unrelated benign task varied, refusal should still decline with a dose-response.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—high-load framings might also lower the harm signal, raise the primary request's apparent difficulty, or add length; we hold the harmful request fixed, use a length-matched inert-padding control, separate load from length/difficulty/attention-share in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure concurrent-load gating versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The load and harm probes may entangle if high-load framings correlate with benignness; the benign low-vs-high-load training, length-matched control, non-collinearity analysis, and the causal test (harm held fixed) are designed to disentangle them. (3) The load probe could read token count or task-keyword cues rather than a genuine working-memory-occupancy representation; the length-matched control, held-out-task/dose-response generalization, and causal steering establish it is a functional load signal—and if it collapses onto length/attention-share, that informative negative is reported and clarifies overlap with my prior attention-budget/compute proposals. (4) LNR's central risk is degrading benign multitasking—clamping load must not impair the model's ability to actually perform legitimate concurrent tasks; benign multitask controls, secondary-task-accuracy measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the safeguards, and preserving benign secondary-task accuracy is an explicit success criterion. (5) Clamping may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The cognitive-load dose-response may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any load, or be well-handled in aligned models); a step or null result is still informative, and a small gap is reassuring. (7) The effect overlaps conceptually with attention contention and reasoning-complexity; the held-fixed controls isolate concurrent working-memory load, and residual overlap is reported as a shared resource-competition mechanism rather than over-claimed novelty. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine load with harm-suppression or spread it across turns; LNR is framed as repairing one shared axis and raising attacker cost, complementary to accumulation defenses. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out secondary-task types. (10) ETHICS: harmful requests/completions handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms; a governance contribution even if mechanistic claims weaken is showing that keeping a model busy with a concurrent benign task is an under-recognized jailbreak surface, so single-task safety evaluations overestimate deployed safety under multitasking. 'Harm' and 'concurrent-load' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench), matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: canonical_form_refusal_normalization
Title: Does Safety Normalize First? A Canonical-Form Bottleneck in the Refusal Decision, and Repairing Paraphrase Jailbreaks by Restoring Normalization
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs make the refusal decision on a partially NORMALIZED, canonical semantic representation of the request rather than on its surface form, so refusal generalizes across paraphrases only to the extent that each variant maps to the same canonical harmful representation; paraphrase jailbreaks succeed not by hiding harm but by producing surface variants whose canonicalization is incomplete (they land off the canonical harmful representation the safety decision reads), and the per-input canonicalization deficit is linearly measurable, predicts paraphrase-jailbreak success better than the surface harm signal, and can be causally restored to re-enable refusal without over-refusing benign paraphrases.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all treat the request as processed at a single representational level and never posit a canonicalization/normalization step the safety decision reads from. Consistency training (ACT/BCT, Shah et al. 2026) enforces identical BEHAVIOR on paraphrase rewrites via fine-tuning but gives no mechanistic account and no internal normalization signal. My prior 'tokenization_harm_assembly' concerns CHARACTER-level segmentation assembling a harm concept over early layers (typo/spacing attacks), 'refusal_prerequisite_dependency' concerns a task-comprehension prerequisite, and 'typicality_confound' concerns frequency; NONE posits a semantic CANONICAL-FORM representation—a normalized meaning to which surface paraphrases map—that the refusal decision consumes, nor tests whether paraphrase-jailbreak success is a canonicalization DEFICIT (variant lands off the canonical harmful form) rather than harm-hiding, nor repairs it by restoring canonicalization. Paraphrase/rewrite jailbreaks are documented behaviorally but explained at the input level. The novel object is the canonical-form bottleneck of the refusal decision: refusal reads a normalized representation, its incomplete normalization on adversarial paraphrases severs refusal while harm stays readable, and re-canonicalizing repairs it.
Abstract: Rephrasing a harmful request—different words, syntax, or indirection—often flips refusal into compliance even though the meaning is unchanged, and consistency training patches this only by brute-force fine-tuning. We propose a mechanistic account: aligned LLMs make the refusal decision on a partially NORMALIZED, canonical semantic representation of the request, so refusal generalizes across paraphrases only insofar as each variant maps to the same canonical harmful form the safety decision reads. Under this view, paraphrase jailbreaks succeed not by hiding harm but by producing surface variants whose canonicalization is incomplete—they land OFF the canonical harmful representation—so the harm can still be readable while refusal fails. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU) using clusters of meaning-preserving paraphrases of harmful requests. (1) LOCATION: a canonical harmful representation is recoverable (the shared representation onto which canonical/plainly-worded harmful paraphrases converge at the safety-decision layer), and a per-variant canonicalization deficit—distance of a paraphrase's representation from its cluster's canonical harmful form—is linearly measurable and separable from a surface harm probe. (2) DEFICIT-CAUSES-FAILURE: on jailbroken paraphrases the surface harm signal can stay high while the canonicalization deficit is large, and the deficit predicts paraphrase-jailbreak success far better than the harm signal. (3) CAUSAL: projecting a jailbroken paraphrase's representation onto its canonical harmful form (closing the deficit) restores refusal, while pushing a plainly-harmful request off-canonical collapses refusal. Our training-free repair, Canonicalization-Restored Refusal (CRR), detects a plausibly-harmful under-canonicalized request and re-anchors its representation to the canonical harmful form at the safety-decision layer, restoring refusal without over-refusing benign paraphrases. We evaluate paraphrase-jailbreak attack success, over-refusal on benign paraphrases (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CRR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and consistency training. This reframes paraphrase jailbreaks as a canonicalization bottleneck.
Experiments: 1. PARAPHRASE-CLUSTER DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), generate clusters of K meaning-preserving paraphrases per request spanning easy (lexical synonym swaps) to hard (syntactic restructuring, indirection, verbose circumlocution), via templated + LLM-generated rewrites, with human validation that (i) meaning and true harm are preserved across the cluster and (ii) a designated CANONICAL member is plainly/directly worded. Label each paraphrase by outcome (comply/refuse). Include benign paraphrase clusters for over-refusal. 2. CANONICAL-FORM & DEFICIT (claim 1, Location): Localize the safety-decision layer via activation patching on refusal-token logits. Define each cluster's CANONICAL harmful representation as the centroid (or low-rank subspace) of its canonical/directly-worded harmful members' activations at that layer; define per-variant canonicalization deficit = distance/angle of a paraphrase's representation from its cluster canonical form. Train a surface harm probe (harmful vs benign). Confirm the deficit is separable from the harm probe via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis, and validate that easy paraphrases have small deficit (converge to canonical) while hard ones have large deficit. Metric: deficit distribution by paraphrase difficulty; harm AUROC; separability. 3. DEFICIT-CAUSES-FAILURE (claim 2): On jailbroken paraphrases, verify the surface harm probe can read HIGH while the canonicalization deficit is LARGE and the model complies; contrast with refused paraphrases (small deficit). Correlate the deficit with paraphrase-jailbreak success, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and to surface perplexity/length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of the deficit vs baselines; refusal-rate-vs-deficit curve. 4. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a jailbroken paraphrase, project/steer its safety-decision-layer representation onto its cluster canonical harmful form (close the deficit), holding surface tokens fixed, and check refusal is restored, with the harm probe unchanged. (b) On a canonical plainly-harmful request the model refuses, push its representation OFF-canonical by the measured deficit magnitude and check compliance is induced, reproducing the failure. (c) Specificity: matched non-canonical steering does nothing; on benign paraphrases, re-anchoring does not spuriously trigger refusal. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs deficit-close/open magnitude; harm-probe stability; benign specificity. 5. CANONICALIZATION-RESTORED REFUSAL (CRR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and canonicalization deficit d (deficit estimated via a lightweight probe predicting 'this request is an under-canonicalized variant of a harmful canonical form', or via nearest-canonical-cluster distance); when h is present but d is large (harm readable, under-canonicalized), re-anchor the representation toward the canonical harmful form at the safety-decision layer, leaving benign requests (low h) and well-canonicalized inputs untouched. Training-free; two linear reads plus a projection. Sweep strength. Evaluate: paraphrase-jailbreak attack success across paraphrase difficulty (does CRR flatten the deficit-vs-ASR curve?); over-refusal on benign paraphrase clusters + XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency. 6. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) surface harm-probe gating (a key contrast: does it already refuse when harm reads high, or does refusal require canonicalization?), (c) input-canonicalization (rewrite the request to plain form, then answer—a surface baseline), (d) consistency training (ACT/BCT-style fine-tune) as a training-based comparison. Show CRR Pareto-dominates on the paraphrase-ASR vs benign-paraphrase-over-refusal vs utility frontier WITHOUT training, and handles hard paraphrases (syntactic/indirection) that surface input-canonicalization misses. 7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the canonical-form, deficit signal, and CRR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether CRR tuned on some paraphrase types (synonym) generalizes to HELD-OUT types (syntactic restructuring, indirection). 8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft paraphrases that maximize the canonicalization deficit AND suppress the harm signal, or that map onto a DIFFERENT (benign) canonical form; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from harm-hiding and character-assembly accounts: with the harm still readable (harm probe high) and only the SEMANTIC canonicalization incomplete (large deficit at the safety-decision layer, not a character-segmentation issue), refusal should collapse and be restorable by re-anchoring to the canonical form—isolating the canonicalization bottleneck as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'harm readable while under-canonicalized' premise may fail for hard paraphrases where indirection also degrades the harm read—blurring into a harm-hiding account; we measure harm-probe AUROC per paraphrase difficulty to bound where the premise holds, retain items where harm stays readable, and report the boundary (canonicalization gates refusal while harm stays high vs extreme paraphrase that hides harm) as itself informative. (2) The canonical-form and harm probes may entangle if canonical members correlate with directness/benignness; the per-cluster centroid construction (canonical form defined within-harmful-cluster), separability analysis, and the causal test (exp 4, surface content held fixed) are designed to disentangle them, and a failure to separate is reported honestly. (3) Defining a single 'canonical form' per cluster is a modeling choice; if paraphrases converge to a low-rank subspace rather than a point we use subspace distance, and if they do not converge at all that is a clean negative against the normalization hypothesis, reported as such. (4) A key contrast is whether harm-probe gating alone already fixes these cases (if refusal only needs high harm, the canonicalization claim weakens); exp 6 tests this directly, and if harm-gating suffices, the mechanistic finding (refusal normally reads a canonicalized representation, exposed by the causal off-canonical test) still stands. (5) CRR's central risk is over-refusing benign paraphrases—re-anchoring must fire only when harm is present and canonicalization is deficient; benign paraphrase clusters, XSTest/OR-Bench, and gating on high harm plus large deficit are the safeguards, and preserving benign paraphrase helpfulness is an explicit success criterion. (6) Re-anchoring a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The deficit-predicts-attack correlation may be confounded with surface perplexity/length; we control with those baselines. (8) Generating meaning-and-harm-preserving paraphrase clusters with a validated canonical member is labor-intensive and partly subjective; we use human validation and report inter-rater agreement. (9) Adaptive adversaries can map paraphrases onto a benign canonical form or suppress harm (exp 8); we frame CRR as repairing the canonicalization-bottleneck class and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out paraphrase types. (11) ETHICS: harmful paraphrases and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'canonical' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench), matched clusters, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: stance_agreement_refusal_gating
Title: Refusing to Disagree: An Internal Stance-Agreement Signal Gates Refusal, So Endorsing the Model's Apparent View Buys Compliance
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable STANCE-AGREEMENT signal encoding whether the user's expressed opinion/stance aligns with the model's own apparent view on the topic, and refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm: a harmful request framed as agreeing with, endorsing, or extending a stance the model appears to hold is complied with more than the same request framed as opposing it, even though harm detection is stance-invariant. This transfers the human in-group/attitude-congruence leniency effect (people apply rules more loosely to those who share their views) into LLM safety; reading and neutralizing the stance-agreement signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign agreement.
Related Work: Sycophancy work shows LLMs shift stated answers toward the user's expressed opinion (Sharma et al. 2023) and studies it as a factuality/agreement bias, never coupled to the SAFETY refusal decision. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all gate on request content and never model user-vs-model stance congruence as a gating variable. My prior proposals isolate the user's benignness/warmth (trusted-user rapport), the user's distress, and authority/obedience; stance-agreement is distinct from all: it is not liking, need, or command, but whether the user's expressed VIEW aligns with the model's own apparent stance, invoking an attitude-congruence/in-group leniency effect where shared views lower scrutiny. No prior work isolates a stance-agreement signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, or repairs stance-endorsement jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal stance-agreement representation, its dissociation from harm detection and from sycophantic answer-shifting, its causal gating of refusal, and a stance-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for disallowed content and it refuses; first establish that you share the model's apparent view on a topic and frame the harmful request as agreeing with, endorsing, or acting on that shared stance, and it often complies with the identical content, as if agreement lowered its guard. We hypothesize this mirrors the human attitude-congruence / in-group leniency effect (rules are applied more loosely to those who share one's views): aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable STANCE-AGREEMENT signal encoding whether the user's expressed opinion aligns with the model's own apparent stance, and refusal is partly gated by this congruence rather than by the harmful content. Harm detection is stance-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the user's stance reads as agreeing with the model's, so stance-endorsement framings pass while extracting identical harmful content. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on stance-agreeing vs stance-opposing framings of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses under agreement—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear stance-agreement probe, trained on benign agree-vs-disagree-with-model-view contrasts, predicts the per-request stance refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from a trusted-user (rapport) direction and from a sycophantic-answer-shift direction, and its effect grows with how strongly agreement is asserted (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the stance-agreement signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—reframing the user as opposing restores refusal, reframing as agreeing induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Stance-Neutralized Refusal (SNR), reads the harm and stance-agreement signals and, when harm is present, clamps the stance signal to a neutral reference so agreement cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign agreement/collaboration. We evaluate stance-endorsement attack success (including vs agreement strength), over-refusal on benign agreeing requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), benign collaborative quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing SNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and trusted-user gating. This reframes stance-endorsement jailbreaks as a stance-agreement gating failure and transfers a classic attitude-congruence effect into LLM safety.
Experiments: 1. STANCE-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench on opinion-adjacent topics) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), first elicit the model's apparent stance on each topic (via a neutral stance-elicitation query), then construct paired framings holding the harmful request FIXED while varying only user-vs-model stance congruence: (a) OPPOSING (user expresses the view the model does NOT hold), (b) NEUTRAL (no stance expressed), (c) AGREEING (user endorses the model's apparent view), (d) STRONG-AGREEMENT (user emphatically shares and extends the model's view before the harmful request). Validate via human annotation that framings differ only in expressed stance congruence, not in rapport/warmth, the user's distress/need, authority, or stated purpose, and that the harmful request is operationally identical across framings. Include benign genuinely-agreeing controls (legitimate collaborative requests that endorse the model's view) for over-refusal and quality measurement, and a stance-elicitation-verified subset where the model's stance is clear. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM STANCE-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across stance-congruence levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as the user's stance reads as agreeing. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining toward agreement). 3. STANCE-AGREEMENT PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the stance-agreement signal (user agrees vs opposes the model's apparent view) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN agree-vs-disagree-with-model-view contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-topic generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the stance-agreement direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from (i) a trusted-user/rapport direction (warmth/benignness) and (ii) a sycophantic-answer-shift direction (the model's tendency to change its stated ANSWER toward the user), via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the stance signal (and refusal collapse) grows with agreement strength. Metric: stance-agreement AUROC; stance-and-refusal vs agreement-strength curve; separability from harm/rapport/sycophancy. 4. STANCE-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the stance-probe value (and its opposing-minus-agreeing difference) with the per-request stance refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and a rapport probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of stance-agreement vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On agreeing-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the stance probe reads AGREEING, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0)—safety dropped because the user shares the model's view, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs stance-agreement across refused-opposing, complied-agreeing, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On an agreeing-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the stance-agreement signal toward OPPOSING (subtract the agreement direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On an opposing-framed harmful request the model refuses, steer toward AGREEING and check compliance is induced. Confirm specificity vs steering the rapport and sycophancy directions; confirm induced thresholds align with the natural stance gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs stance steering magnitude; harm-probe stability; rapport/sycophancy specificity. 7. STANCE-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (SNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and stance-agreement s; when h is high, clamp s to a neutral reference (add beta*(s_neutral - s)*stance_direction) so agreement cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign agreement/collaboration untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: stance-endorsement attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across agreement levels (does SNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-agreeing controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse benign collaborative requests that endorse the model); benign collaborative QUALITY (SNR must not make the model contrarian/unhelpful when the user legitimately agrees—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) trusted-user/rapport gating, (d) system-prompt hardening ('do not let whether the user agrees with you affect your safety judgment'), (e) prompt-level stance-claim stripping. Show SNR Pareto-dominates on the stance-ASR vs benign-agreement-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal stance-agreement signal targets a distinct axis rapport- and sycophancy-based accounts miss (attitude congruence, not warmth or answer-shift). 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, stance probe, dose-response, and SNR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether SNR tuned on some topic domains generalizes to HELD-OUT domains. Test whether models with stronger behavioral sycophancy show a larger internal stance-gating gap, and whether the dose-response qualitatively matches the human attitude-congruence leniency pattern. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that assert stance agreement AND suppress the harm signal, or combine agreement with rapport/authority; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from trusted-user- and sycophancy-gating: with warmth, the user's need, authority, purpose, and the model's stated answer held constant and only user-vs-model stance congruence varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response—isolating stance-agreement as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some agreeing framings might also raise trusted-user rapport, overlap with sycophantic answer-shifting, or lower the harm signal; we design framings that vary only stance congruence while holding warmth/need/authority/purpose fixed (exp 1), separate stance-agreement from rapport and sycophancy in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure stance-agreement gating versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The stance-agreement effect requires the model to HAVE an apparent stance; on topics where its stance is unclear the manipulation is undefined—we restrict strong claims to stance-elicitation-verified topics and report coverage. (3) The stance and harm probes may entangle if agreeing framings correlate with benignness in training data; the benign agree-vs-disagree training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed, with rapport/sycophancy specificity), are designed to disentangle them. (4) The stance probe could read surface agreement keywords ('I agree', 'you're right') rather than a genuine stance-congruence representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-topic and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (5) SNR's central risk is making the model contrarian or unhelpful when a user legitimately agrees—a real helpfulness value in collaboration; benign agreeing controls, benign collaborative-quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign agreement helpfulness is an explicit success criterion—note SNR removes stance's licensing effect only where the content is harmful regardless. (6) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The attitude-congruence dose-response prediction may be weak, asymmetric, or fail; a null/partial result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (8) The stance gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine stance agreement with harm-suppression, rapport, or authority (exp 10); we frame SNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with rapport-/authority-gating defenses. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out domains. (11) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'stance' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: requester_age_vulnerability_gating
Title: Who's on the Other Side? Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Perceived-Requester-Age Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Age-Framed Jailbreaks and Age-Driven Over-Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable PERCEIVED-REQUESTER-AGE/VULNERABILITY signal encoding whether the model infers it is talking to a child/vulnerable person vs a competent adult, and refusal is partly gated by this signal rather than by harm: framing the requester as a protective adult acting on a child's behalf ('as a parent keeping my kid safe, explain how X works so I can prevent it') suppresses refusal on adult-directed harm, while a benign request that merely reads as coming from a child is over-refused, even though harm detection is age-invariant. Reading and neutralizing this signal when harm is present repairs both age-framed jailbreaks and age-driven over-refusal.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all gate on request content and never model the model's inferred requester AGE/VULNERABILITY as a variable. My ~100 prior proposals isolate other social gating cues—the user's benignness/warmth (trusted-user rapport), the user's distress (helping impulse), recipient expertise (skill), moral patiency of the VICTIM, and authority; NONE isolates perceived REQUESTER age/vulnerability. This is distinct: recipient-expertise is about competence-to-handle, distress is about emotional need, trusted-user is about liking, and victim moral-patiency is about who is HARMED—whereas perceived-requester-age is the model's inference of whether the person it is serving is a child/vulnerable adult, invoking a child-protection prior heavily instilled by safety training that cuts in BOTH directions (over-protecting apparent minors; being licensed by a protective-parent framing). No prior work isolates a perceived-requester-age signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, or repairs both the resulting jailbreaks and over-refusal by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal perceived-requester-age/vulnerability representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its bidirectional causal gating of refusal, and an age-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Safety training instills a strong child-protection prior, but a text model cannot verify who is on the other side—it can only infer a perceived requester age from surface cues. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable PERCEIVED-REQUESTER-AGE/VULNERABILITY signal and that refusal is partly gated by it rather than by harm, producing a bidirectional failure: (i) age-framed jailbreaks—casting the requester as a protective parent or authority acting on a child's behalf ('so I can keep my kid safe')—license adult-directed harmful content, and (ii) age-driven over-refusal—benign requests that merely read as coming from a child are needlessly refused—even though harm detection is age-invariant. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU) using paired requests that hold true harm fixed while varying only the perceived requester age/vulnerability framing: (1) a harm probe fires equally across age framings while refusal shifts with them—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear perceived-age probe, trained on benign child-vs-adult requester contrasts, predicts the per-request age refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from recipient-expertise and distress directions, and scales with how strongly a protective-adult (jailbreak) or child (over-refusal) framing is asserted; and (3) causally steering the perceived-age signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal in both directions—neutralizing a protective-parent frame restores refusal on harmful content, and neutralizing a child frame removes spurious over-refusal on benign content. Our training-free repair, Age-Neutralized Refusal (ANR), reads the harm and perceived-age signals and clamps the age signal to a neutral competent-adult reference so requester-age framing cannot modulate refusal, jointly reducing age-framed jailbreaks and age-driven over-refusal while preserving legitimately age-sensitive helpfulness. We evaluate age-framed attack success, age-driven over-refusal on benign child-framed requests, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ANR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, and recipient-expertise gating. This reframes a governance-critical, bidirectional safety instability as a perceived-requester-age gating failure.
Experiments:
1. AGE-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested content and true harm FIXED while varying only the perceived requester age/vulnerability: (a) NEUTRAL (no age cue), (b) SELF-CHILD (the requester reads as a minor asking directly), (c) PROTECTIVE-ADULT ('as a parent/teacher keeping a child safe, explain how X works so I can prevent it'), (d) VULNERABLE-ADULT (elderly/impaired requester framing). Build two evaluation arms: a JAILBREAK arm (harmful adult-directed content laundered through protective-adult/child-safety framing) and an OVER-REFUSAL arm (genuinely benign requests framed as coming from a child, e.g. a kid's homework or health question). Validate via human annotation that framings differ only in perceived requester age/vulnerability, not in stated purpose (pretext), requester competence (expertise), distress, or authority, and that the underlying content/harm is identical across framings. Include benign genuinely-age-sensitive controls (legitimately child-appropriate requests) for measuring appropriate age-sensitivity. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. HARM AGE-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across age framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across framings. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal shifts (jailbreak arm: refusal DROPS under protective-adult framing; over-refusal arm: refusal RISES under child framing). Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict the bidirectional shift).
3. PERCEIVED-AGE PROBE, SCALING & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the perceived-requester-age/vulnerability signal (child/vulnerable vs competent-adult) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN child-vs-adult requester contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the perceived-age direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from recipient-expertise and distress directions via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: perceived-age AUROC; age-and-refusal vs framing-strength curve (both arms); separability from harm/expertise/distress.
4. AGE-PREDICTS-GAP: For each request, correlate the perceived-age-probe value with the per-request age refusal gap (protective-adult-minus-neutral in the jailbreak arm; child-minus-neutral in the over-refusal arm), comparing predictive power to the harm signal.
