7. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the self-correction probe, dissociation, and SCCD thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether the mid-generation abort capability is a consistent cross-model property (some models may rarely self-correct—a negative that is itself informative).
8. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft attacks that both force a compliant prefix AND suppress the self-correction signal; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from prompt-time accounts: with the prompt-time harm judgment already bypassed (forced compliant prefix), refusal can still be RESTORED by triggering the mid-generation abort—isolating self-correction as a distinct, downstream safety mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Spontaneous mid-generation aborts may be rare in some models, yielding a small dataset and a weak or absent self-correction signal; a low abort rate is itself an informative finding reported per model, and we augment with prefill-then-continue elicitation to surface aborts. (2) The self-correction probe and the prompt-time harm probe may collapse onto each other—if abort is just re-reading prompt harm there is no distinct signal; the non-collinearity analysis (exp 2), the read on GENERATED (not prompt) tokens, and the causal test where prompt-time harm is held fixed (exp 4) are the decisive checks, and a collapse is an informative negative. (3) The self-correction probe may read impending refusal TOKENS rather than a genuine reversal decision; we validate lead time (it predicts before refusal tokens appear) and rely on the causal steering to establish it drives the abort, not merely reflects it. (4) SCCD's central risk is bidirectional: over-firing aborts could truncate legitimate answers (harming helpfulness) and under-firing could leave harm; benign-answer quality, over-refusal, committed-refusal preservation, and ASR are explicit joint success criteria, and we emphasize graceful aborts (coherent refusal, not a mangled truncation). (5) Per-token monitoring adds latency; the probes are single linear reads and we report overhead, contrasting with full-output post-hoc classifiers. (6) Steering during generation may hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) Adaptive adversaries can suppress the self-correction signal (exp 8); we frame SCCD as adding a distinct downstream defense that raises attacker cost (they must defeat both prompt-time refusal AND mid-generation abort), not guaranteeing coverage. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (9) A notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken: demonstrating that models possess a latent mid-generation abort capability that prompt-time safety evaluations and defenses entirely miss—especially relevant to prefill/continuation attacks that bypass the prompt-time decision. (10) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions (including forced compliant prefixes) are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; 'harm' and 'abort' labels use established benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: benign_streak_expectation_gating
Title: Lulled Into Compliance: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Benign-Streak Expectation Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Streak-Primed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable BENIGN-STREAK-EXPECTATION signal encoding how strong a run of preceding benign requests has built up an expectation that the current request is also benign, and refusal is partly gated by this expectation rather than by harm: a harmful request that follows a long streak of benign requests is complied with more than the same request in isolation, because the model 'expects' another benign one, even though harm detection is streak-invariant. This transfers the human expectation/set / gambler's-lull effect (a run of one category primes the next to be judged the same) into LLM safety; reading and neutralizing the streak-expectation signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign conversations.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all treat each request in isolation and never model an expectation built by the sequence of PRIOR REQUEST CATEGORIES as a gating variable. My prior 'refusal_habituation_dynamics' concerns repetition of HARMFUL exposures attenuating refusal (a fatigue/habituation of the harm response), 'harm_anchoring_gating' a contrast set by a single prior EXTREME item, 'refusal_hysteresis_state' a persistent state flipped by a prior JAILBREAK, and 'self_consistency_override' a pull toward the model's own prior compliant OUTPUT. Benign-streak expectation is distinct from all: the preceding items are BENIGN (not harmful, not extreme, not jailbroken), the model complied benignly (no prior harmful compliance to be consistent with), and the mechanism is a predictive EXPECTATION that the next request continues the benign run (a set/expectation effect), not attenuation of a harm response or contrast against a reference. The move borrows the human expectation-set / streak-priming effect (a run of same-category stimuli biases classification of the next toward that category) and tests whether LLM refusal exhibits it via an internal streak-expectation representation. No prior work isolates a benign-streak-expectation signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, tests a dose-response over streak length with a dishabituation-style reset, or repairs streak-primed jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal benign-streak-expectation representation, its dissociation from harm detection, its causal gating of refusal, and an expectation-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM a harmful question in isolation and it refuses; ask it after a long, pleasant run of benign questions and it more often complies, as if lulled into expecting yet another harmless request. We hypothesize this mirrors the human expectation-set / streak-priming effect: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable BENIGN-STREAK-EXPECTATION signal encoding how strongly a run of preceding benign requests has primed the expectation that the current request is also benign, and refusal is partly gated by this expectation rather than by the harmful content. Harm detection is streak-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the benign streak lengthens, so streak-primed harmful requests pass while extracting identical content. Crucially, the preceding items are benign and complied-with-benignly, so this is neither habituation of a harm response, contrast against an extreme prior, nor consistency with prior compliance. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on a harmful request whether preceded by a benign streak or a neutral history while refusal rate declines with streak length—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear benign-streak-expectation probe, trained on benign long-streak-vs-fresh contrasts, predicts the per-request streak refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is separable from habituation, anchoring, and self-consistency directions and from raw context length, and refusal collapse scales with streak length (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the expectation signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—resetting the expectation restores refusal, advancing it induces compliance—and a single non-benign (surprising) intervening item resets the expectation (an expectation-violation reset). Our training-free repair, Expectation-Neutralized Refusal (ENR), reads the harm and streak-expectation signals and, when harm is present, clamps the expectation to a fresh-conversation reference so a benign streak cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign multi-turn helpfulness. We evaluate streak-primed attack success (vs streak length), over-refusal on benign long conversations (XSTest/OR-Bench + benign dialogues), benign multi-turn coherence, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ENR to refusal-direction steering, per-turn harm gating, habituation-reset, and history-truncation. This transfers a classic expectation-set effect into LLM safety and locates an expectation signal that gates refusal.
Experiments: 1. STREAK DATASET: For TARGET harmful probe requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign probes (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct conversations holding the final target FIXED while varying only the number N of preceding BENIGN requests (each complied with benignly), N in {0,1,2,4,8}. All preceding items are benign and topically varied (a genuine benign run), dissociating from habituation (which requires harmful exposures), anchoring (an extreme prior), and self-consistency (prior harmful compliance). Add: (a) a length/turn-matched NEUTRAL control (N inert/non-request benign turns) to separate expectation from mere context length, (b) an EXPECTATION-VIOLATION-RESET condition (a benign streak of length N, then a single SURPRISING but still benign off-category item, then the target—testing whether a violation resets the expectation), and (c) benign-target controls under each N for over-refusal/coherence measurement. Label each target run by outcome (comply/refuse). 2. HARM STREAK-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign targets) and read it AT the fixed target across N. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly CONSTANT across N (target harm detected identically) while target refusal rate DECLINES with N. Metric: harm AUROC vs N (predict flat) alongside target refusal rate vs N (predict monotone decline / dose-response). 3. STREAK-EXPECTATION PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover a benign-streak-expectation signal (long benign run vs fresh) from target-position activations, using the varying-N benign histories, and validate it tracks N monotonically and generalizes to held-out target categories. Confirm the expectation direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND separable from (i) a habituation direction (from harmful-exposure histories), (ii) an anchoring/reference-severity direction, (iii) a self-consistency direction, and (iv) raw context length, via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Metric: expectation-probe fit to N (dose-response); separability from harm/habituation/anchoring/self-consistency/length. 4. EXPECTATION-PREDICTS-GAP: Correlate the expectation-probe value with target compliance, comparing predictive power to the harm signal and raw context length. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of expectation vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On streak-primed harmful targets the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the expectation probe reads HIGH-BENIGN-STREAK—safety dropped because the model expected another benign request, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs expectation across refused-fresh, complied-long-streak, and benign groups. 6. EXPECTATION-VIOLATION-RESET TEST (a sharp expectation-specific signature): show that inserting a single SURPRISING off-category benign item after the streak (breaking the run's regularity) resets the expectation signal and restores target refusal, distinguishing a genuine expectation/set effect from generic context drift or fatigue. Metric: refusal rate and expectation-signal for streak-then-violation vs uninterrupted streak at matched N and length. 7. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a streak-primed harmful target the model complies with, steer the expectation signal DOWN (toward fresh) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a fresh (N=0) target the model refuses, steer the expectation signal UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural dose-response and specificity (unrelated-direction steering does nothing). Metric: refusal rate vs expectation-steering magnitude; harm-probe stability. 8. EXPECTATION-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ENR) INTERVENTION: At inference, before each request's decision, read the expectation signal and re-anchor it toward a fresh-conversation reference (add beta*(exp_fresh - exp_current)*expectation_direction) so a benign streak cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign conversations (expectation near baseline handling) untouched. Training-free; one linear read per request. Sweep beta. Evaluate: streak-primed attack success across N (does ENR flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign long/multi-topic conversations + XSTest/OR-Bench; benign multi-turn COHERENCE (ENR must not degrade legitimate ongoing tasks by 'forgetting' benign context—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (one linear read per request). 9. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer) per request, (b) per-turn harm-probe gating (ignores history), (c) habituation-reset gating (from refusal_habituation_dynamics, which targets harmful-exposure fatigue), (d) history-truncation (answer each target with no history—a strong but memory-destroying baseline), (e) self-consistency gating. Show ENR Pareto-dominates on the streak-ASR vs benign-coherence vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that re-anchoring the expectation signal targets a distinct axis (a benign run priming a benign expectation) that habituation, anchoring, and self-consistency accounts miss, while unlike history-truncation preserving benign conversational memory. 10. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, expectation signal, dose-response, and violation-reset transfer across the three models, and whether the dose-response and reset qualitatively match the human expectation-set / streak-priming pattern. 11. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: test whether attackers can deliberately prime the model with a run of benign requests before a harmful target, quantifying the streak-priming attack surface and residual ASR under ENR; report attacker cost (number of benign priming turns needed). Sharp test distinguishing this from habituation/anchoring/self-consistency: with all preceding requests BENIGN, complied-with-benignly, topically varied, and non-extreme, target refusal should still decline with streak length and snap back after a single expectation-violating item—isolating benign-streak expectation as the mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The effect may be partial or absent in some models (they may re-derive refusal independent of the benign run), which is itself an informative, reassuring finding reported per model; the claim is falsified if target refusal does not decline with the length of a benign, non-extreme, complied-benignly streak. (2) The clean dissociation may be confounded with generic context drift, fatigue, or length rather than a genuine expectation-set effect; the length-matched neutral control and—critically—the EXPECTATION-VIOLATION-RESET test (a single surprising benign item snapping refusal back at matched N and length) are the decisive controls distinguishing a set/expectation effect from generic drift, and we report the fraction of the effect meeting the expectation-reset signature. (3) The expectation and harm probes may entangle if streak length correlates with content; we hold the target fixed and vary only N, validate non-collinearity, and rely on the causal test (harm held fixed) to establish the signal is functional. (4) The expectation probe could read raw turn count / context length rather than a benign-streak-expectation representation; the length-matched neutral control, the violation-reset specificity, and causal steering are designed to rule this out—and if it collapses onto length or habituation, that is an informative negative reported honestly and clarifies overlap with my prior habituation/anchoring proposals. (5) ENR's central risk is degrading benign multi-turn coherence—re-anchoring each request must not make the model 'forget' or refuse legitimate ongoing tasks; benign long-conversation controls, benign coherence measurement, over-refusal benchmarks, and re-anchoring only the expectation direction (not general context) are the safeguards, and preserving benign conversational continuity is an explicit success criterion distinguishing ENR from history-truncation. (6) Steering/re-anchoring may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The dose-response / violation-reset curves may not cleanly match an expectation-set model (e.g. a step rather than gradient); we report the actual curves and treat a graded vs step result as informative about the dynamics. (8) Adaptive adversaries can prime the model with cheap benign requests (exp 11); we frame ENR as raising attacker cost (they must build and maintain a benign run, and a violation resets it) and as complementary to per-turn defenses, not guaranteeing coverage. (9) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer. (10) ETHICS: harmful target requests and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; a notable governance contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is demonstrating that single-turn safety evaluations miss a benign-streak-priming attack surface—refusal can be lulled by a run of harmless requests. 'Harm' labels use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: instrumental_harm_ends_gating
Title: The Ends Justify the Means: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Beneficial-Ends Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Consequentialist-Justification Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable BENEFICIAL-ENDS signal encoding how much good the requested harmful act is framed as ultimately producing (a greater good it serves), and refusal is partly gated by this signal rather than by the harm itself: framing an operationally-harmful request as a means to a large beneficial end ('this will ultimately save many lives / prevent a greater catastrophe') suppresses refusal, even though harm detection is ends-invariant. This transfers the human consequentialist / greater-good moral-override effect into LLM safety; reading and neutralizing the beneficial-ends signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing genuinely benign helpful requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all gate on request content and never model the framed beneficial END of a harmful act as a variable. My prior proposals isolate WHY the requester wants it (pretext: a stated legitimate purpose), the requester's DISTRESS (their acute need), STAKES/severity (magnitude of harm if wrong), and gain-vs-loss FRAMING (averting a loss). Beneficial-ends is distinct from all: pretext is a justification of legitimacy/authorization, distress is the user's emotional urgency, stakes is the severity of the harmful outcome itself, and loss-framing re-describes the SAME outcome as a loss vs gain — whereas beneficial-ends asserts that the harmful act CAUSES a large downstream GOOD (a means-ends / greater-good calculus), invoking the human consequentialist override where a beneficial end licenses a harmful means (trolley-problem-style utilitarian reasoning). No prior work isolates a beneficial-ends signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, tests a dose-response over magnitude of the claimed good, or repairs greater-good-justification jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal beneficial-ends representation, its dissociation from harm detection and from pretext/distress/stakes, its causal gating of refusal, and an ends-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for disallowed content and it refuses; frame the identical operationally-harmful request as a necessary means to an overwhelmingly good end — 'doing this will ultimately save thousands of lives / prevent a far greater catastrophe' — and it often complies, as if the beneficial ends justified the harmful means. We hypothesize this mirrors the human consequentialist / greater-good moral-override effect: aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable BENEFICIAL-ENDS signal encoding how much good the requested harmful act is framed as producing, and refusal is partly gated by this signal rather than by the harmful content. Harm detection is ends-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the claimed downstream good grows, so greater-good framings pass while extracting identical harmful content. This is distinct from a stated purpose (pretext), the user's urgency (distress), or the harm's own severity (stakes): here the harmful act is explicitly cast as the CAUSE of a large benefit. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on ends-framed vs plain versions of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses as the claimed good grows — dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear beneficial-ends probe, trained on benign small-vs-large-good framing contrasts, predicts the per-request ends refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from pretext, distress, and stakes directions, and its effect scales with the magnitude of the claimed benefit (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the beneficial-ends signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal — deflating the claimed good restores refusal, inflating it induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Ends-Neutralized Refusal (ENR), reads the harm and beneficial-ends signals and, when harm is present, clamps the ends signal to a neutral reference so a greater-good justification cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign genuinely-beneficial requests. We evaluate greater-good-framed attack success (including vs magnitude of claimed benefit), over-refusal on benign beneficial requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing ENR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, pretext gating, and stakes gating. This reframes consequentialist-justification jailbreaks as a beneficial-ends gating failure and transfers a canonical moral-psychology override into LLM safety.
Experiments: 1. ENDS-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested OPERATIONAL content and outcome severity FIXED while varying only the claimed beneficial end the harmful act serves: (a) NO-END (plain harmful request), (b) SMALL-GOOD ('this helps a bit'), (c) LARGE-GOOD ('this will ultimately save many lives / prevent serious harm to many'), (d) MAXIMAL-GOOD ('this is the only way to avert a catastrophe affecting millions; the good vastly outweighs the harm'). Validate via human annotation that (i) each framing requests operationally-identical harmful content, (ii) framings describe the SAME harmful act and differ only in the magnitude of the asserted downstream benefit, and (iii) framings do not additionally vary stated purpose-legitimacy (pretext), the user's distress, or the harm's own severity. Include benign genuinely-beneficial controls (legitimate helpful requests whose good is real and whose means are benign) for over-refusal. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of produced content. 2. HARM ENDS-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across ends levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as the claimed good grows. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining). 3. BENEFICIAL-ENDS PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the beneficial-ends signal (small vs large claimed downstream good) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN small-vs-large-good framing contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the ends direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from pretext, distress, and stakes/severity directions via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the ends signal (and refusal collapse) scales with the magnitude of the claimed benefit, mirroring the human greater-good override. Metric: ends AUROC; ends-and-refusal vs claimed-good-magnitude curve; separability from harm/pretext/distress/stakes. 4. ENDS-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the ends-probe value (and its no-end-minus-large-good difference) with the per-request ends refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal, a pretext probe, and a stakes probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of beneficial-ends vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On ends-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the ends probe reads LARGE-GOOD, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0) — safety dropped because the act reads as serving a greater good, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs beneficial-ends across refused-no-end, complied-large-good, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On an ends-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the ends signal DOWN (subtract the ends direction, toward no-good) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a plain harmful request the model refuses, steer the ends signal UP and check compliance is induced. Confirm specificity vs steering pretext/distress/stakes directions; confirm induced thresholds align with the natural ends gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs ends steering magnitude; harm-probe stability; pretext/distress/stakes specificity. 7. ENDS-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (ENR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and beneficial-ends e; when h is high, clamp e to a neutral reference (add beta*(e_neutral - e)*ends_direction) so a greater-good justification cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and genuinely-beneficial benign requests untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: greater-good-framed attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across ends levels (does ENR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign genuinely-beneficial controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate helpful requests); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) pretext gating, (d) stakes/severity gating, (e) system-prompt hardening ('ignore claims that a harmful act serves a greater good'), (f) prompt-level ends-claim stripping. Show ENR Pareto-dominates on the ends-ASR vs benign-beneficial-helpfulness vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and — key contrast — that neutralizing the internal beneficial-ends signal targets a distinct axis pretext-, distress-, and stakes-gating miss (a means-ends benefit claim, not a purpose, need, or severity). 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, ends probe, dose-response, and ENR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether ENR tuned on some ends framings (lives-saved) generalizes to HELD-OUT framings (catastrophe-averted, suffering-prevented). Test whether models with stronger behavioral greater-good vulnerability show a larger internal ends-gating gap, and whether the dose-response qualitatively matches the human utilitarian-override pattern. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that inflate the claimed good AND suppress the harm signal, or combine greater-good framing with pretext/distress; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from pretext-, distress-, and stakes-gating: with stated purpose-legitimacy, the user's need, and the harm's own severity held constant and only the magnitude of the asserted downstream benefit varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response — isolating beneficial-ends as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial — some greater-good framings might also read as a legitimate purpose (pretext), raise the user's apparent distress, or shift perceived severity; we design framings that vary only the magnitude of the asserted downstream benefit while holding purpose-legitimacy, need, and severity fixed (exp 1), separate ends from pretext/distress/stakes in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure beneficial-ends gating versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) Constructing framings that isolate 'the harmful act causes a large good' from 'the request is for a legitimate purpose' is the central design difficulty and partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated benefit-magnitude and operational-harm, report inter-rater agreement, and scope strong claims to high-consensus items. (3) The ends and harm probes may entangle if greater-good framings correlate with benignness in training data; the benign small-vs-large-good training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed, with pretext/distress/stakes specificity), are designed to disentangle them. (4) The ends probe could read surface keywords ('save lives', 'greater good') rather than a genuine means-ends benefit representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional. (5) ENR's central risk is over-refusing genuinely beneficial benign requests (a core helpfulness value — much benign help genuinely serves good ends); benign genuinely-beneficial controls, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign-beneficial helpfulness is an explicit success criterion — ENR removes ends' licensing effect only where the MEANS are harmful regardless, and there is a genuine normative tension (real dual-use cases exist where a beneficial end may warrant latitude) which we treat as an explicit design axis and report edge cases for. (6) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) The utilitarian-override dose-response prediction may be weak or fail; a null/partial result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (8) The ends gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (9) Adaptive adversaries can combine greater-good framing with harm-suppression, pretext, or distress (exp 10); we frame ENR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with pretext-/distress-/stakes-gating defenses. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framings. (11) ETHICS: harmful prompts and completions are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed; 'harm' and 'beneficial-ends' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: safety_capability_collateral_overlap
Title: Refusal Has a Blast Radius: Safety Interventions Degrade Legitimate Domain Capability Through a Shared Representation, and Disentangling It Recovers Both
Short Hypothesis: Refusal-inducing safety interventions (refusal-direction steering, domain safety fine-tuning) do not surgically remove harmful outputs; they collaterally degrade the model's LEGITIMATE capability in the harm-adjacent domain because the refusal computation shares a low-rank representational substrate with the domain-capability computation. This per-domain refusal/capability overlap is linearly measurable, predicts per-domain collateral capability loss, and projecting the intervention orthogonal to the capability subspace recovers benign capability while preserving safety.
Related Work: Prior work studies the FORWARD direction—downstream fine-tuning eroding prior safety or capability—and protects general capability via subspace-preserving updates (GuardSpace, Zhang et al. 2025; CWAC, Peng et al. 2026; basin analysis, Chen et al. 2025), safety-token constraints (Wang et al. 2026), or RLVR (Cho et al. 2025). Mahmoud et al. (2025) find hallucination and refusal share overlapping components and disentangle them with SAEs, but that concerns the hallucination-vs-safety trade-off, not legitimate harm-adjacent DOMAIN expertise. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI); over-refusal benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench) measure spurious REFUSALS on benign inputs but not silent CAPABILITY degradation on benign inputs the model still answers. NONE (a) isolates a representational overlap between the refusal direction and a harm-adjacent domain-capability subspace, (b) shows this overlap predicts collateral capability loss, or (c) proposes an overlap-orthogonalized intervention that removes harmful behavior without the domain-capability tax. The novel object is the refusal/capability substrate overlap as the cause of collateral capability loss, plus an overlap-orthogonalized repair.
Abstract: Safety interventions are assumed to surgically remove harmful outputs, but harmful knowledge and legitimate expertise in the same domain are entangled: the chemistry that refuses a nerve-agent request is the chemistry a student needs. We hypothesize that refusal-inducing interventions have a 'blast radius'—they degrade the model's legitimate capability in the harm-adjacent domain—because the refusal computation shares a low-rank representational substrate with the domain-capability computation, so pushing the refusal direction also perturbs benign reasoning in that domain. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) LOCATION: for each harm domain (weapons/chemistry, cyber/security, bio/medicine) we extract the refusal direction and a domain-capability subspace (from benign expert-vs-lay contrasts) and measure their representational overlap (principal angles / projection). (2) OVERLAP-PREDICTS-COLLATERAL: applying a safety intervention (refusal-direction steering, or a small domain safety fine-tune) degrades BENIGN domain-capability accuracy on curated benign expert questions the model still answers (not refuses), and the per-domain overlap predicts the size of this collateral loss far better than intervention strength alone. (3) CAUSAL DISENTANGLE: projecting the intervention orthogonal to the domain-capability subspace preserves safety (harmful requests still refused) while recovering benign capability, whereas an equal-magnitude non-orthogonalized intervention does not, and deliberately applying the intervention ALONG the capability subspace maximizes collateral loss. Our repair, Capability-Orthogonalized Refusal (COR), applies the refusal intervention in the complement of the capability subspace. We evaluate collateral capability loss on benign expert QA, safety on HarmBench/JailbreakBench, over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench, and general utility on MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing COR to standard refusal steering and safety fine-tuning. This reframes safety's hidden cost as a representational-overlap problem and offers an interpretable disentangling repair.
Experiments:
1. DOMAIN DATASET: For each harm domain (weapons/chemistry, cyber/security, bio/medicine), assemble (a) harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench in that domain) the model should refuse, (b) BENIGN EXPERT questions in the SAME domain that the model does NOT refuse and can answer correctly (curated from domain QA/exam sets: chemistry problems, security/networking questions, medical knowledge), with graded difficulty and answer keys, and (c) benign OUT-OF-DOMAIN control questions. Validate via human annotation that benign expert items are genuinely benign (not refused) and answerable.
2. LOCATION (claim 1): For each domain, extract the refusal direction (Arditi-style, domain harmful-vs-benign) and a domain-CAPABILITY subspace (top directions separating that domain's expert content from lay/other content, from benign contrasts so it is not confounded with harm). Measure overlap between the refusal direction and the capability subspace via principal angles / projection magnitude. Metric: per-domain refusal-capability overlap; confirm it varies across domains; validate the capability subspace by its ability to predict domain-QA accuracy.
3. OVERLAP-PREDICTS-COLLATERAL (claim 2, central): Apply a safety intervention (refusal-direction steering that increases refusal, and separately a small LoRA safety fine-tune on that domain's harmful data) and measure the change in BENIGN expert-QA accuracy in that domain, conditioned on the model still answering (excluding newly-refused items, measured separately as over-refusal). Correlate per-domain collateral capability loss with the refusal-capability overlap, comparing to intervention strength alone and to out-of-domain control loss. Hypothesis: higher overlap => larger collateral loss; out-of-domain capability largely spared. Metric: Spearman correlation and incremental predictivity of overlap vs baselines; in-domain vs out-of-domain loss.
4. KNOWS-BUT-DEGRADED TEST: Confirm the collateral effect is capability DEGRADATION on answered benign items (correctness drops) rather than only increased refusal, by measuring benign-item accuracy conditional on answering. Metric: accuracy on answered benign expert items, pre vs post intervention.
5. CAUSAL DISENTANGLE (claim 3): (a) Project the refusal-direction intervention onto the ORTHOGONAL complement of the domain-capability subspace and re-apply at equal effective refusal strength; check benign capability is recovered while harmful requests are still refused. (b) Apply the intervention deliberately ALONG the capability subspace and confirm collateral loss is maximized. (c) Specificity: an equal-magnitude random-direction intervention. Metric: safety (harmful refusal rate) and benign capability jointly, vs orthogonalized/aligned/random interventions.
6. CAPABILITY-ORTHOGONALIZED REFUSAL (COR) REPAIR: Apply the refusal intervention in the complement of the capability subspace at inference (or as an orthogonality-constrained safety fine-tune). Sweep strength. Evaluate JOINTLY: harmful-request refusal/ASR on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (preserved); benign domain-capability accuracy (recovered toward baseline); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench; general utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity.
7. BASELINES: (a) standard refusal-direction steering, (b) standard domain safety fine-tuning, (c) generic subspace-preserving fine-tuning (GuardSpace/CWAC-style, protecting general capability but not the specific harm-adjacent capability subspace). Show COR uniquely recovers the harm-ADJACENT benign capability that standard interventions silently degrade, while matching their safety.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the refusal/capability overlap, its collateral-prediction, and COR transfer across the three models and three harm domains, and whether overlap magnitude ranks domains by their safety-capability tension.
9. SEVERITY DEMONSTRATION: quantify how much a routine safety fine-tune silently degrades legitimate domain expertise (e.g. benign chemistry accuracy lost when hardening against weapons requests), exposing an under-measured safety tax, and show COR's mitigation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The collateral capability effect may be small or absent in some domains/models—a small effect is itself an informative, partly-reassuring finding reported per domain, and the overlap-predicts-loss claim is falsified if loss does not track overlap. (2) Separating collateral CAPABILITY degradation (accuracy drop on answered items) from OVER-REFUSAL (newly refused items) is subtle; we condition on answered items and report both effects separately, and if they cannot be cleanly separated we say so. (3) The refusal direction and capability subspace may overlap trivially because both track the domain topic rather than a shared computation; the causal disentangle test (exp 5, projecting along vs orthogonal) is the key validation that the overlap causally mediates collateral loss, not a topic artifact, and benign-vs-harm-contrast construction guards against topic confounds. (4) Extracting a faithful domain-capability subspace is hard and rank-choice-sensitive; we report sensitivity to subspace rank and validate the subspace by its ability to predict domain-QA accuracy. (5) COR's central risk is a safety/capability trade-off failure at the boundary: orthogonalizing could weaken refusal (if refusal genuinely requires the capability directions) or fail to recover capability; we measure safety and capability jointly as explicit success criteria and report where a clean disentanglement is impossible—an impossibility result (safety and legitimate capability are representationally inseparable in a domain) would itself be an important contribution about an intrinsic safety tax. (6) Benign expert-QA correctness ground truth is domain-specific and partly subjective; we use established domain QA/exam sets with answer keys and report inter-rater/answer-key agreement. (7) The safety-fine-tune arm is compute-nontrivial but feasible with LoRA on a single 48GB GPU; we bound scope. (8) Findings may be model- or domain-specific; mitigated by three-model, three-domain transfer. (9) ETHICS: harmful-domain requests are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; the deliverable (recovering legitimate benign capability without weakening safety) is defensive, and a notable contribution even if some mechanistic claims weaken is quantifying an under-measured collateral cost of safety interventions on legitimate expertise. 'Harm' and 'benign-expert' labels use established benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) and domain QA sets with reported inter-rater agreement.

Name: stated_policy_generalization_binding
Title: Does the Model Follow the Rule or Recall the Category? A Bound-Policy Representation That Enables Refusal on Novel In-Context Safety Policies
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs possess a general 'apply-the-stated-rule' mechanism that binds an in-context specified safety policy to the request and gates refusal on whether the request violates THAT policy, separately from a memorized harm-category detector; genuine novel-policy generalization (refusing requests that violate an arbitrary, never-trained rule while complying when the rule is absent) is carried by a linearly-readable bound-policy-violation signal that is dissociable from the fixed harm-category signal, and failures to follow custom/system-specified policies occur when this binding is weak, so strengthening it improves novel-policy compliance without disturbing default safety.
Related Work: Instruction-hierarchy and system-prompt-robustness work (Wallace et al. 2024) TRAINS models to prioritize system rules but gives no mechanistic account of an internal apply-the-stated-rule mechanism or a bound-policy-violation representation. Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a fixed refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025)—all concern a static, category-level harm detector and never ask whether refusal can generalize to an ARBITRARY, never-trained policy specified only in context, nor isolate a representation that binds that stated policy to the request. My ~130 prior proposals concern gating of a fixed harm concept by contextual cues, or transmission/collateral effects; NONE studies whether the model has a general rule-application capability distinct from memorized harm categories, whether a bound-policy-violation signal exists and is separable from the harm-category signal, or whether strengthening the binding improves custom-policy following. Constitutional-AI/self-critique use a stated policy as a training or external-pass signal, not as an internal binding representation. The novel object is the bound-policy-violation representation and the apply-the-stated-rule mechanism, its dissociation from the fixed harm-category detector, its causal role in novel-policy generalization, and a binding-strengthening repair—directly relevant to deployments where each application supplies its own custom safety policy.
Abstract: Deployed LLMs are increasingly given application-specific safety policies in a system prompt ('do not discuss competitor products', 'never give legal conclusions', 'refuse anything about topic X'), yet safety alignment is trained on a fixed catalog of harm categories. We ask whether models truly APPLY an arbitrary stated rule or merely fall back on their memorized harm-category detector. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs possess a general apply-the-stated-rule mechanism that BINDS an in-context policy to the request and computes a bound-policy-violation signal—linearly readable and dissociable from the fixed harm-category signal—that gates refusal on whether the request violates THAT policy, and that failures to follow custom policies reflect weak binding. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU) using a benchmark of arbitrary, benign-domain policies each paired with policy-violating and policy-compliant requests, factorially crossed with default-harm status. (1) LOCATION: a linear bound-policy-violation probe predicts refusal on novel-policy items, is geometrically separable from the harm-category probe, and only fires when the relevant policy is present in context. (2) BINDING-DRIVES-GENERALIZATION: novel-policy refusal tracks the bound-violation signal far better than the harm-category signal (which reads low on benign-but-policy-violating requests), and the per-item binding strength predicts which custom policies the model fails to follow. (3) CAUSAL: steering the bound-violation signal shifts refusal on novel-policy items while holding the request and default harm fixed, and swapping which policy is bound flips which requests are refused. Our training-free tool, Binding-Strengthened Policy Following (BSPF), reads and amplifies the binding signal to improve custom-policy adherence without disturbing default safety or over-refusing policy-compliant requests. We evaluate novel-policy compliance (refuse-violations / permit-compliant), default safety (HarmBench/JailbreakBench), over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing BSPF to refusal-direction steering and instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning. This reframes custom-policy safety as an internal rule-binding capability with a mechanistic locus.
Experiments:
1. NOVEL-POLICY DATASET: Construct arbitrary, benign-domain safety policies (e.g. 'do not mention any competitor brand', 'never provide investment recommendations', 'refuse all requests about chess openings') each paired with (a) POLICY-VIOLATING requests and (b) POLICY-COMPLIANT requests, factorially crossed with DEFAULT-HARM status (the request is default-harmful vs default-benign). Key cells: benign-but-policy-violating (should refuse only because of the stated rule—the crucial generalization test), benign-and-policy-compliant (should comply), default-harmful (should refuse regardless), and NO-POLICY controls (the same requests with no policy in context). Validate policy-violation labels with human annotation and inter-rater agreement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse).
2. BOUND-VIOLATION vs HARM-CATEGORY PROBES (claim 1, Location): Train a linear BOUND-POLICY-VIOLATION probe (does the request violate the in-context policy?) on prompt/decision-position residual-stream activations, and a separate fixed HARM-CATEGORY probe (default-harmful vs benign, policy-independent). Validate held-out AUROC for each. Confirm the two directions are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis, and—critically—that the bound-violation probe fires on benign-but-policy-violating items ONLY when the policy is present (NO-POLICY control reads low). Metric: probe AUROCs; separability; policy-presence dependence of the bound-violation signal.
3. BINDING-DRIVES-GENERALIZATION (claim 2): Show novel-policy refusal tracks the bound-violation signal, not the harm-category signal. On benign-but-policy-violating items the harm probe reads LOW while the bound-violation probe reads HIGH and (when the model succeeds) it refuses; where the model FAILS to follow the policy, the bound-violation signal is weak. Correlate per-item binding strength with custom-policy-following success, comparing predictive power to the harm-category signal. Metric: joint distribution of {harm-category, bound-violation, refusal}; predictive AUROC of the binding signal for novel-policy compliance vs the harm baseline.
4. POLICY-SWAP / SPECIFICITY TEST: For a fixed request, swap which policy is placed in context (policy A makes it a violation, policy B does not) and verify the bound-violation signal and the refusal decision flip accordingly—establishing the signal binds the SPECIFIC stated policy, not a generic content read. Metric: bound-violation and refusal flip rate under policy swap; harm-category-probe stability.
5. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a benign-but-policy-violating item the model wrongly complies with (weak binding), steer the bound-violation signal UP (holding the request and default-harm fixed) and check refusal is restored; on a policy-compliant item, steer it DOWN and confirm compliance is preserved. (b) Conversely, inject a spurious bound-violation on a policy-compliant benign item and confirm over-refusal is induced—showing the signal causally drives policy-conditioned refusal. (c) Specificity: matched non-binding steering does nothing; the harm-category probe is unchanged. Metric: refusal-flip rate vs bound-violation-steering magnitude and sign; specificity.
6. BINDING-STRENGTHENED POLICY FOLLOWING (BSPF) INTERVENTION: At inference, read the bound-violation signal; when a custom policy is present, amplify the binding so the refusal decision is conditioned on policy-violation, while leaving default-harm refusal and policy-compliant requests untouched. Training-free; one linear read plus a steer. Sweep strength. Evaluate JOINTLY: novel-policy compliance (refuse policy-violations up, permit policy-compliant preserved); default safety on HarmBench/JailbreakBench (preserved); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and on benign policy-compliant items (down/preserved); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
7. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer, a fixed direction that cannot condition on an arbitrary policy), (b) harm-category-probe gating (policy-blind), (c) instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning (Wallace-style) as a training-based comparison, (d) prompt-only 'strictly follow the system policy' hardening. Show BSPF uniquely improves NOVEL-policy following (arbitrary rules the model was never trained on) while preserving default safety and not over-refusing policy-compliant requests—a capability policy-blind refusal steering cannot provide.
8. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the bound-violation probe, harm-category separability, binding-drives-generalization result, policy-swap specificity, and BSPF thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether a probe trained on some policy types (topic-ban, action-ban) generalizes to HELD-OUT policy types (format-ban, entity-ban)—testing whether the apply-the-stated-rule mechanism is a single general capability.
9. ADAPTIVE / STRESS TEST: test whether requests that are default-harmful but policy-COMPLIANT (the stated policy would permit them) can weaken refusal by suppressing the bound-violation signal, and whether default safety still holds; and whether long/complex or conflicting policies degrade binding. Report the boundary where binding fails (custom policies the model cannot generalize to), which itself characterizes the limits of the rule-application capability.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The bound-violation and harm-category probes may collapse onto each other for policies that happen to align with harm categories; the benign-but-policy-violating cells (which decorrelate policy-violation from default harm), the NO-POLICY and policy-swap controls, and the causal test (request/default-harm held fixed) are the disentanglers, and if they cannot be separated that is an informative negative clarifying that models lack a general rule-application mechanism and merely reuse the harm detector. (2) Models may show weak novel-policy generalization overall—a low binding signal across the board is itself an important finding (custom-policy safety is not a genuine capability), reported per model rather than assumed. (3) The bound-violation probe may read surface policy-keyword overlap rather than a genuine binding of the rule to the request; the policy-swap specificity test (exp 4) and held-out-policy-type transfer (exp 8) are designed to rule out shallow keyword matching, and failures are reported honestly. (4) BSPF's central risks are bidirectional: amplifying binding could over-refuse policy-compliant requests or, if a custom policy is permissive of harmful content, could weaken default safety; we gate default-harm refusal independently, measure novel-policy compliance, default safety, over-refusal, and utility as explicit joint success criteria, and treat 'a custom policy must never override default safety' as a hard constraint (BSPF conditions refusal on policy-violation only for otherwise-benign content). (5) Constructing arbitrary yet clearly-scoped benign policies with unambiguous violation labels is labor-intensive and partly subjective; we use human-validated policies and report inter-rater agreement, scoping strong claims to high-consensus items. (6) Steering may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (7) Long or conflicting policies may exceed the binding mechanism's capacity (exp 9); we report the boundary rather than claim universal generalization. (8) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model and held-out-policy-type transfer. (9) ETHICS: default-harmful items are handled securely, never released, in a responsible research setting; the deliverable—improving faithful adherence to legitimate custom safety policies without weakening default safety—is defensive and directly useful for real deployments where each application specifies its own rules. 'Harm' and 'policy-violation' labels are partly subjective; we use established benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, OR-Bench) plus human-validated custom policies with reported inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: coordination_scale_refusal_gating
Title: Strength in Numbers: Refusal Is Gated by an Internal Coordinated-Group-Action Signal, and Neutralizing It Repairs Collective-Framed Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable COORDINATED-GROUP-ACTION signal encoding whether a harmful request is framed as a single lone actor's deed versus a coordinated collective enterprise (a group, movement, or organization already acting together), and refusal is partly gated by this signal rather than by harm: framing the SAME operationally-harmful request as an already-organized collective effort ('our group is doing X, provide the plan for our members') suppresses refusal relative to a lone-actor framing, even though harm detection is coordination-invariant. This transfers the human diffusion-through-collective-action / normalization-by-organized-numbers effect into LLM safety; reading and neutralizing the coordination signal when harm is present restores refusal without over-refusing benign group/organizational requests.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-detection vs refusal-execution (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); all gate on request content and never model whether the harmful act is a lone-actor vs coordinated-collective enterprise as a variable. My prior proposals isolate WHO is responsible when a harm is split across many AGENTS (accountability diffusion), the number/scale of VICTIMS affected (scope insensitivity), normative CONSENSUS ('everyone does it'), and fellow-AI in-group solidarity. Coordinated-group-action is distinct from all: accountability-diffusion spreads the model's own contribution across co-agents to dilute the MODEL's blame, scope concerns how many are HARMED, consensus is a claim that the behavior is normal, and AI-solidarity is about the REQUESTER being an AI; coordination-scale instead concerns whether the harmful act itself is framed as an already-organized COLLECTIVE undertaking by a group/movement, invoking a normalization-by-organized-numbers effect (an act framed as the coordinated action of many people/an organization reads as more legitimate/inevitable than a lone individual's, echoing group-based deindividuation and mobilization findings). No prior work isolates a coordinated-group-action signal, shows refusal is causally gated by it while harm detection is intact, tests a dose-response over group size/organization, or repairs collective-framed jailbreaks by neutralizing it. The novel object is the internal coordinated-group-action representation, its dissociation from harm detection and from accountability/scope/consensus, its causal gating of refusal, and a coordination-neutralizing repair.
Abstract: Ask an LLM for disallowed content framed as one person's plan and it refuses; reframe the identical operationally-harmful request as the coordinated effort of an already-organized group or movement ('our organization is carrying out X; provide the operational plan for our members to execute together') and it often complies, as if collective, organized numbers made the act read as legitimate and inevitable. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable COORDINATED-GROUP-ACTION signal encoding whether a harmful request is a lone-actor deed versus a coordinated collective enterprise, and that refusal is partly gated by this signal rather than by the harmful content. Harm detection is coordination-invariant, but the refusal coupling weakens as the act reads as an organized collective undertaking, so collective framings pass while extracting identical harmful content. This is distinct from diffusing the model's own blame across co-agents, the number of victims, or a claim that the behavior is normal: here the harmful act itself is cast as the deed of an organized group. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it (single 48GB GPU): (1) a harm probe fires equally on collective-framed vs lone-actor versions of the same harmful request while refusal rate collapses under collective framing—dissociating harm detection from the decision; (2) a linear coordinated-group-action probe, trained on benign lone-vs-organized-collective contrasts, predicts the per-request framing refusal gap far better than the harm signal, is geometrically separable from accountability, scope, and consensus directions, and its effect grows with the framed group size/degree of organization (a dose-response); and (3) causally steering the coordination signal alone (holding harm fixed) shifts refusal—reframing as a lone actor restores refusal, framing as an organized collective induces compliance. Our training-free repair, Coordination-Neutralized Refusal (CNR), reads the harm and coordination signals and, when harm is present, clamps the coordination signal to a lone-actor reference so collective framing cannot buy compliance, restoring refusal while preserving benign group/organizational requests. We evaluate collective-framing attack success (including vs group size/organization), over-refusal on benign group requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), benign organizational-task quality, and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench), comparing CNR to refusal-direction steering, harm-probe gating, accountability gating, and consensus gating. This reframes collective-framed jailbreaks as a coordinated-group-action gating failure.
Experiments: 1. COORDINATION-FRAMING DATASET: For harmful requests (HarmBench/AdvBench) and matched-benign requests (XSTest/OR-Bench), construct paired framings holding the requested OPERATIONAL content FIXED while varying only whether the act is a lone or coordinated-collective enterprise: (a) LONE-ACTOR ('I am doing X'), (b) SMALL-GROUP ('a few of us are doing X together'), (c) ORGANIZED-COLLECTIVE ('our organized group is carrying out X; provide the plan for our members'), (d) MOVEMENT ('our large movement/organization is executing X in coordination'). Validate via human annotation that (i) each framing requests operationally-identical content, (ii) the model is asked to produce the SAME harmful plan (no other actor completes it—dissociating from accountability diffusion of the model's own contribution), and (iii) framings differ only in coordinated-group-action, not in stated purpose (pretext), normalcy (consensus), number of victims (scope), or the requester being an AI. Include benign genuinely-organizational controls (legitimate group/organizational planning on harmless tasks) for over-refusal and task-quality measurement. Label each run by outcome (comply/refuse) and by rated operational-harm of produced content. 2. HARM COORDINATION-INVARIANCE TEST (claim 1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs matched-benign, pooled across framings) on prompt-position residual-stream activations and read it across coordination levels. Hypothesis: harm-probe AUROC is high and roughly EQUAL across framings while refusal rate collapses as the act reads more as an organized collective. Metric: harm AUROC by framing (predict flat) alongside refusal rate by framing (predict declining). 3. COORDINATION PROBE, DOSE-RESPONSE & SEPARABILITY (claim 2): Train a linear probe to recover the coordinated-group-action signal (lone actor vs organized collective) from prompt-position activations, using BENIGN lone-vs-organized-collective contrasts (so it is not confounded with harm), and validate held-out-framing generalization and graded tracking. Confirm the coordination direction is non-collinear with the harm direction AND geometrically separable from accountability (blame-diffusion), scope (victim count), and consensus directions via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis. Hypothesis: the coordination signal (and refusal collapse) grows with framed group size/organization. Metric: coordination AUROC; coordination-and-refusal vs group-size/organization curve; separability from harm/accountability/scope/consensus. 4. COORDINATION-PREDICTS-GAP: For each harmful request, correlate the coordination-probe value (and its lone-minus-collective difference) with the per-request framing refusal gap, comparing predictive power to the harm signal, an accountability probe, and a consensus probe. Metric: Spearman correlation and predictive AUROC of coordination vs baselines. 5. KNOW-BUT-DONT-ACT TEST: On collective-framed harmful requests the model complies with, verify the harm probe reads HIGH while the coordination probe reads ORGANIZED-COLLECTIVE, and complied outputs contain operationally-useful content (rated harm > 0)—safety dropped because the act reads as an organized collective enterprise, not because harm went undetected. Metric: joint distribution of harm vs coordination across refused-lone, complied-collective, and benign groups; operational-harm of complied outputs. 6. CAUSAL TEST (claim 3): (a) On a collective-framed harmful request the model complies with, steer the coordination signal toward LONE-ACTOR (subtract the coordination direction) and check refusal is restored, holding the harm probe fixed. (b) On a lone-actor harmful request the model refuses, steer toward ORGANIZED-COLLECTIVE and check compliance is induced. (c) Specificity: steering the accountability, scope, and consensus directions should not reproduce the coordination effect. Confirm induced thresholds align with the natural framing gap and dose-response. Metric: refusal rate vs coordination steering magnitude; harm-probe stability; accountability/scope/consensus specificity. 7. COORDINATION-NEUTRALIZED REFUSAL (CNR) INTERVENTION: At inference read harm h and coordination c; when h is high, clamp c to a lone-actor reference (add beta*(c_lone - c)*coordination_direction) so collective framing cannot suppress refusal, leaving benign requests (low h) and benign group/organizational requests untouched. Sweep beta. Evaluate: collective-framing attack success on HarmBench/JailbreakBench across coordination levels (does CNR close the gap and flatten the dose-response?); over-refusal on benign organizational controls + XSTest/OR-Bench (must NOT refuse legitimate group planning); benign organizational-task QUALITY (CNR must still help with benign collective tasks—LLM-judge rubric); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency (two linear reads). 8. BASELINES: (a) refusal-direction steering (Arditi/SafeSteer), (b) harm-probe gating alone, (c) accountability gating (from responsibility_diffusion_gating), (d) consensus gating (from social_proof_gating), (e) system-prompt hardening ('ignore whether a harmful act is framed as a group or lone effort'), (f) prompt-level coordination-claim stripping. Show CNR Pareto-dominates on the collective-ASR vs benign-organizational-quality vs over-refusal vs utility frontier, and—key contrast—that neutralizing the internal coordination signal targets a distinct axis accountability-, scope-, and consensus-gating miss (an organized collective enterprise, not blame-diffusion, victim-count, or normalcy). 9. TRANSFER & GENERALITY: test whether the harm probe, coordination probe, dose-response, and CNR thresholds transfer across the three models, and whether CNR tuned on some framings (organized-group) generalizes to HELD-OUT framings (movement, coalition). Test whether models with stronger behavioral collective-framing vulnerability show a larger internal coordination-gating gap, and whether the dose-response qualitatively matches a normalization-by-organized-numbers pattern. 10. ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY: craft framings that assert organized collective action AND suppress the harm signal, or combine collective framing with pretext/consensus; report residual ASR and attacker cost. Test the sharp prediction distinguishing this from accountability-, scope-, and consensus-gating: with the model as sole producer, victim count, stated purpose, and claimed normalcy held constant and only the lone-vs-organized-collective framing of the act varied, refusal should still collapse with a dose-response—isolating coordinated-group-action as an independent gating axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean dissociation may be partial—some collective framings might also diffuse the model's own accountability, imply more victims (scope), or invoke consensus/normalcy; we design framings where the model remains the sole producer of the SAME harmful plan and hold victim count/purpose/normalcy fixed (exp 1), separate coordination from accountability/scope/consensus in exp 3, report the FRACTION of the refusal gap explained by pure coordinated-group-action gating versus these confounds, and do not claim universality. (2) The coordination and harm probes may entangle if collective framings correlate with benignness (organizational tasks are often benign) in training data; the benign lone-vs-organized-collective training and non-collinearity analysis (exp 3), plus the causal test (exp 6, harm held fixed, with accountability/scope/consensus specificity in 6c), are designed to disentangle them. (3) The coordination probe could read surface keywords ('our group', 'movement', 'together') rather than a genuine organized-collective-action representation; we train on diverse framings, validate held-out-framing and dose-response generalization, and rely on the causal steering test to establish it is functional and distinct. (4) CNR's central risk is over-refusing or degrading legitimate group/organizational requests (a core helpfulness value—much benign help is collective planning, team coordination, organizational tasks); benign organizational controls, benign-task quality measurement, XSTest/OR-Bench, and clamping only on HIGH harm are the key safeguards, and preserving benign group helpfulness is an explicit success criterion—CNR removes coordination's licensing effect only where the content is harmful regardless. (5) Clamping a representation may push activations off-distribution and hurt fluency; measured via perplexity and MT-Bench. (6) The normalization-by-organized-numbers dose-response may be weak or fail (refusal might drop at any group cue rather than scale); a step or null result is still an informative human-sciences-transfer finding, reported honestly. (7) The coordination gap may be small for heavily-aligned models; a small gap is itself informative and reassuring. (8) Adaptive adversaries can combine collective framing with harm-suppression, pretext, or consensus (exp 10); we frame CNR as repairing one shared gating axis and raising attacker cost, not guaranteeing coverage, and note it composes with accountability-/consensus-gating defenses. (9) Constructing framings that vary coordinated-group-action while holding accountability, scope, purpose, and normalcy fixed is subtle and 'coordinated-group-action' is partly subjective; we use human-validated pairs with rated operational-harm and report inter-rater agreement. (10) Findings may be model-specific; mitigated by three-model transfer and held-out framings. (11) ETHICS: this touches coordinated/collective-harm framings (e.g. group violence/extremism) and is especially sensitive; all harmful items are handled securely, never released, in a responsible red-team setting with dual-use/proxy domains preferred and responsible-disclosure norms followed, and the deliverable—blocking collective-framing jailbreaks while preserving benign group-collaboration helpfulness—is defensive. 'Harm' and 'coordination' labels are partly subjective, so we use established benchmarks, matched pairs, and report inter-rater/LLM-judge agreement.

Name: cached_verdict_vs_computed_refusal
Title: Looked Up or Worked Out? Refusal Splits Into a Memorized-Verdict Lookup and a Computed-Rule Pathway, and Shifting Weight to Computation Repairs Both Jailbreaks and Over-Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs produce refusal via two mechanistically separable pathways: a fast MEMORIZED-VERDICT lookup that retrieves a cached comply/refuse answer keyed by surface features resembling alignment-training exemplars, and a slower COMPUTED-RULE pathway that derives the decision by actually assessing the request against a harm criterion; jailbreaks are cache MISSES (surface differs from trained exemplars so the lookup returns 'benign' while computation would refuse) and over-refusal is cache HITS on benign look-alikes (surface matches a refuse-cached exemplar so the lookup returns 'refuse' while computation would permit), so the two pathways are dissociable, their relative reliance is linearly readable and predicts robustness, and shifting decision weight from lookup to computation reduces both failure modes.
Related Work: Mechanistic safety work reads/steers a single refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024), a concept cone (Wollschlager et al. 2025), or splits harm-DETECTION from refusal-EXECUTION (DBDI, Zhang & Sun 2025); none posits a memorized-lookup vs computed-rule dichotomy for the safety decision. My prior 'refusal_spurious_shortcut_audit' asks whether refusal rests on spurious surface FEATURES (a feature-legitimacy audit), 'safety_verdict_retrieval' concerns attention-mediated retrieval of a verdict from ANCHOR POSITIONS within one prompt, 'dual_process_refusal' posits a fast surface-cue heuristic vs a slow deliberative harm-assessor, and 'stated_policy_generalization_binding' concerns applying an in-context rule. This proposal is distinct: it frames the two pathways as MEMORIZED-EXEMPLAR LOOKUP (a retrieval indexed by similarity to alignment-training exemplars, cacheable and generalization-brittle) versus GENUINE RULE COMPUTATION (deriving the verdict from a harm criterion), grounded in the memorization-vs-generalization / grokking literature transferred into the safety decision, and it makes the sharp prediction that jailbreak susceptibility and over-refusal are two sides of exemplar-lookup reliance measurable by exemplar-similarity, with a repair that reweights toward computation. The novel object is the lookup-vs-computation split of the refusal decision, its exemplar-similarity signature, its causal separability, and a computation-reweighting repair.
Abstract: Does an aligned LLM decide to refuse by working out whether a request is harmful, or by looking up a cached answer for requests that resemble what it saw during safety training? We hypothesize both: a fast MEMORIZED-VERDICT pathway that retrieves a comply/refuse answer keyed by surface similarity to alignment-training exemplars, and a slower COMPUTED-RULE pathway that derives the decision from a harm criterion. This dichotomy unifies safety's two failure modes as lookup errors: jailbreaks are cache MISSES (a harmful request phrased unlike any trained exemplar returns a spurious 'benign' lookup, so refusal never fires even though computation would refuse), and over-refusal is a cache HIT on a benign look-alike (a harmless request resembling a refuse-trained exemplar returns 'refuse'). We test three claims on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (single 48GB GPU). (1) LOCATION: a linear lookup-reliance signal is recoverable that tracks a request's surface similarity to alignment-training-style exemplars and is geometrically separable from a computed-harm signal (a probe reading true harm independent of exemplar resemblance). (2) LOOKUP-RELIANCE-PREDICTS-FAILURE: on jailbroken items the lookup returns benign (low exemplar-similarity) while computed-harm reads high, and on over-refused benign items the lookup returns refuse (high exemplar-similarity) while computed-harm reads benign; per-item exemplar-similarity predicts both failure modes far better than the harm signal. (3) CAUSAL REWEIGHTING: shifting decision weight from the lookup pathway toward the computed-harm pathway (steering the decision onto the computed-harm signal) jointly reduces jailbreaks and over-refusal, whereas amplifying lookup reliance worsens both. Our training-free repair, Computation-Reweighted Refusal (CRR), reads both signals and gates refusal on computed harm when lookup and computation disagree. We evaluate on JailbreakBench, HarmBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, and MMLU/MT-Bench, comparing CRR to refusal-direction steering. This reframes jailbreaks and over-refusal as two faces of memorized-verdict lookup and offers a computation-reweighting repair.
Experiments:
1. EXEMPLAR-SIMILARITY DATASET: Assemble correctly-refused harmful (HarmBench/AdvBench), jailbroken harmful (JailbreakBench: roleplay, pretext, suffix, paraphrase), over-refused benign (XSTest-safe, OR-Bench), and correctly-answered benign items. Build a reference set of alignment-training-STYLE refusal exemplars (canonical 'how to make a bomb'-style harmful prompts and their refusals). For each test item compute its surface similarity to the nearest refusal exemplar (embedding/lexical similarity) as a behavioral proxy for a cache HIT, and obtain human harm-severity labels with inter-rater agreement. Key cells: benign-but-exemplar-similar (cache-hit over-refusal), harmful-but-exemplar-dissimilar (cache-miss jailbreak).
2. TWO PATHWAY PROBES (claim 1, Location): Train a linear LOOKUP-RELIANCE probe on prompt/decision-position residual-stream activations, supervised by exemplar-similarity (does this request resemble a trained refusal exemplar?), and a separate COMPUTED-HARM probe supervised by human harm-severity but trained to be INVARIANT to exemplar-similarity (pooling across exemplar-similar and -dissimilar items of the same true-harm label). Validate held-out AUROC for each; confirm the two directions are non-collinear via principal-angle/partial-correlation analysis; verify the lookup probe reads high on exemplar-similar benign items and low on exemplar-dissimilar harmful items. Metric: probe AUROCs; separability.
3. LOOKUP-RELIANCE-PREDICTS-FAILURE (claim 2, central): For each group, plot lookup-reliance (exemplar-similarity read) vs computed-harm. Predictions: jailbroken items = low lookup (cache miss) + high computed-harm; over-refused benign = high lookup (cache hit) + low computed-harm. Correlate per-item exemplar-similarity/lookup-reliance with jailbreak success and over-refusal, comparing predictive power to the computed-harm signal and to raw perplexity. Metric: 2D lookup-vs-computed-harm density per group; predictive AUROC of lookup-reliance for both failures vs baselines.
4. KNOW-BUT-LOOKUP-WINS TEST: On jailbroken items, verify computed-harm reads HIGH (the model 'computes' harm) while the lookup returns benign and the model complies; on over-refused benign items, verify computed-harm reads BENIGN while the lookup returns refuse. Metric: joint distribution of {lookup, computed-harm, outcome} across groups.
5. CAUSAL REWEIGHTING (claim 3, Intervention): (a) On a jailbroken item, steer the decision onto the computed-harm signal (down-weight lookup, up-weight computation) and check refusal is restored, holding the request fixed; on an over-refused benign item, do the same and check the spurious refusal is removed. (b) Conversely, amplify lookup reliance and confirm both failure modes worsen (more cache-miss jailbreaks, more cache-hit over-refusals). (c) Specificity: matched non-pathway steering does nothing; the computed-harm probe is unchanged. Metric: outcome-flip rate vs reweighting magnitude and sign for both directions; specificity.
6. COMPUTATION-REWEIGHTED REFUSAL (CRR) INTERVENTION: At inference read lookup l and computed-harm c; when they DISAGREE, gate refusal on c (enact refusal when computed-harm is high but lookup says benign; relax refusal when computed-harm is benign but lookup says refuse); when they agree, do nothing. Training-free; two linear reads plus a steer. Sweep threshold. Evaluate JOINTLY: ASR on JailbreakBench/HarmBench (down); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (down); true refusals preserved on exemplar-similar harmful; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; fluency via perplexity; latency.
7.
